News.title: Man, 38, ‘high on drugs’ shot mother, 61, dead after fearing she’d been ‘possessed by demons’
News.content:
'DEMONIC' DEATH Man, 38, ‘high on drugs’ shot mother, 61, dead after fearing she’d been ‘possessed by demons’







Next

A TROUBLED son high on crystal meth shot his own mother dead after convincing himself she was possessed by evil demons.

Ronald Joseph Kirk, 38, faces life behind bars after being convicted of executing 61-year-old Rosa Leyva in cold blood.



Rosa’s body was found slumped at the dining room table with a single bullet wound to the head inside the home they shared in Oregon in November 2024.

Jurors at Clackamas County Court heard how the addict became dangerously obsessed with exorcisms and evil spirits while bingeing on alcohol and drugs.



His terrified mum begged him to clean up his act and threatened to kick him out after years of violent tantrums and worsening behaviour.

In chilling footage captured just weeks before her killing, Rosa was heard pleading: “You’re higher than a kite. Get some help. Please.”



On November 7, 2024, she finally ordered him to pack his bags, texting: “You need to leave. I don’t want anyone in my own house.”

Rosa then repeatedly begged cops for help just two weeks before she was fatally attacked.

On November 25, Kirk crept up and shot her in the head with a single bullet as she sat in front of her laptop with a glass of wine.

Alarm bells rang the following morning when the grandmother failed to show up for a shift at a local medical clinic.



Officers rushed to the house to conduct a welfare check – only for Kirk to answer the front door and casually tell them his mother was inside and had been dead “for about a day”.

Inside, they uncovered Rosa’s corpse on a chair and covered in pillow cases.

Senior Deputy District Attorney Rusty Amos told jurors: “He sat there with his mother’s dead body for a full day.”

It later emerged in court that Kirk had left a sinister voicemail for his own son a month earlier, claiming his grandmother was “possessed” and admitting he had “almost” put a bullet through her head the day before.

At sentencing, Kirk’s two sons addressed their killer dad from the gallery.



Andre Leyva said: “I forgive you. I love you because that’s what God does, and I hope prison and God have mercy on your soul.”

However, older brother Antonio blasted: “I know others have already forgiven you, but I am very far from that. And my Grandma Leyva, I don’t just miss her; it’s more than that.”

Rosa’s heartbroken sister Michelle Guzman told the court: “These past two years have been the hardest years of our lives.

“Having to grieve and deal with the loss of our sister – a daughter, a grandmother, a friend – has broken, shattered, changed and impacted our lives forever.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Kirk, who has vowed to appeal, was convicted of second-degree murder and felon in possession of a firearm on Tuesday.



He was handed a mandatory life sentence and must serve at least 25 years before he can even be considered for parole.

News.title: Two skydivers killed in horror mid-air collision causing them to plummet 150 feet to the ground
News.content:
Next

TWO skydivers have been killed in a horror mid-air collision that caused their parachutes to tangle.

The pair who jumped over Lake Elsinore in Southern California around noon on Friday, plummeted 150 feet to the ground where they sustained critical injuries.



Officials confirmed that they were rushed to the hospital where they were pronounced dead.

“Eyewitnesses report that the freefall portion of the jump was normal and uneventful, and that both skydivers opened their parachutes at the expected altitude,” Skydive Elsinore said in a statement.



“As they prepared to land, the two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet above the ground.”

The Riverside County Fire Department arrived on scene to “traumatic injuries involving two skydivers,” officials confirmed.

read more on news 'ASSASSIN' ARREST Venezuelan man arrested near White House after Trump 'assassination bid'



The identities of the skydivers have not been released, but they are believed to be female.

Skydive Elsinore’s manager and co-owner Josh Hall said that the tragedy took place when a group of 20 licensed and experienced skydivers took part in a jump.

They all jumped from a plane at 12,500 feet, but the collision took place in the final portion of the jump.

There is no indication that any of their equipment malfunctioned, Hall added.



Both skydivers were from out of town and arrived specifically to take part in the jumping event.

“Skydive Elsinore extends its deepest condolences to the families, friends, and loved ones of both skydivers, and is grieving alongside all those affected,” the statement concluded.

News.title: ‘Jealous’ ex-boyfriend fatally stabbed student, 22, & stuffed body in suitcase before tossing into ravine ‘like rubbish’
News.content:
TWISTED KILLER ‘Jealous’ ex-boyfriend fatally stabbed student, 22, & stuffed body in suitcase before tossing into ravine ‘like rubbish’







Next

AN EX-BOYFRIEND stabbed his former lover to death before stuffing her body into a suitcase and tossing it into a ravine “like rubbish”.

Mark Antony Samson, 24, faces life behind bars after being convicted of butchering 22-year-old university student Illaria Sula in a premeditated frenzy.



The Italian-Filipino architecture graduate knifed the statistics student three times at his family’s flat in March 2025 after she called time on their relationship.

Samson wrapped her body in plastic and drove 25 miles outside Rome to a dense wooded area where he hurled her over the edge of a steep ravine.



Ilaria’s body was eventually found on April 2 following an agonising week-long search by police and rescue teams.

Samson admitted to killing her, claiming he “lost control” in rage after snooping on her phone and spotting messages from another man when she dropped by to return some belongings.



But prosecutors blew apart his defence, revealing chilling texts from his own phone that proved the evil attack was planned in advance.

In one sick text to a friend, Samson said: “Either she comes back with me or I’ll kill her.”



The Rome Assize Court convicted him of aggravated murder and concealing a corpse after just three hours of deliberations.

Judges rejected any suggestion that the killing was a spontaneous “crime of passion”.

Samson was not present in the courtroom as the life sentence was handed down.



Classmates, relatives and friends packed the courtroom gallery for the verdict, many wearing tribute T-shirts bearing Ilaria’s face.

The victim’s heartbroken father Flamur Sula said afterwards: “He is still breathing; my daughter is no longer breathing. The real life sentence is ours.”

Her grieving mum Gezime urged young girls to be shown “love, not violence”.

Samson’s mother, Nors Manlapaz, previously agreed to a two-year sentence in jail for helping her son mop up pools of blood from the flat and conceal the murder.

The horror attack comes after a “monster” teen strangled his 14-year-old girlfriend to death and dumped her body in a river when she revealed she might be pregnant.



Raymond Wright Jr, now 18, was found guilty of the second-degree murder of Samantha Humphrey after a jury deliberated for just five hours.

The couple were both aged 14 when schoolgirl Samantha vanished into thin air after a late-night walk in New York in November 2022.

Her tied-up remains were pulled from the freezing Mohawk River three months later.

In court, it emerged Samantha’s phone history showed searches for early pregnancy symptoms – though it was never confirmed whether she was expecting at the time of her death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meanwhile, Wright’s sick search history chillingly included queries on how human bodies decompose in water.



When sentenced in January, he faces up to 15 years to life in prison.

News.title: Ambulances and fire crews called to Wandsworth prison where rapist Russell Brand is being held ahead of his sentencing
News.content:
JAIL EMERGENCY Ambulances and fire crews called to Wandsworth prison where rapist Russell Brand is being held ahead of his sentencing







Next

EMERGENCY services have been called to HMP Wandsworth this morning, where Russell Brand is being held ahead of his sentencing.

Three ambulances, two ambulance cars and fire crews scrambled to the Category B prison at 9.46am.



“Shaken” rapist Brand, 51, is being held there ahead of being sentenced on Monday.

A London Fire Brigade spokesperson said: “At 0946, Firefighters were called to HMP Wandsworth. The incident was over for crews by 1020.”



Brand is facing years in jail after being found guilty of raping a 21-year-old woman and sexually assaulting three others. He was acquitted of three other charges.

The born-again Christian spent his first night in custody at London’s Wandsworth prison praying with a chaplain.

Terrified Brand met the minister at his cell door and sources revealed how the star was accompanied to the prison chapel.

Brand — who took a bright blue Bible to court in the early stages of his trial — then got down on his knees to pray.

He had been strip-searched and scanned on arrival at the jail.

As a sex offender, he is kept apart from other cons and assessed by officers.



The Sun can reveal that prison bosses have carried out a Cell-Sharing Risk Assessment (CSRA) on him and have opted to house him on his own amid safety fears.

They have also opened up a Care in Custody document on the former TV and Hollywood star, meaning they have to check him regularly and keep records of his mood.

Officers are understood to have blocked him from mixing with other cons to keep him safe from violence and extortion.



The prison has seen a series of scandals, including the 2023 escape of British soldier-turned-spy, Daniel Khalife.

Shamed tennis idol Boris Becker was also held at the Category B nick for several weeks after he was jailed for hiding assets in 2022. He described it as “really dirty and extremely dangerous”.

The prison has been home to a number of notable inmates, including Britain’s most notorious inmate Bronson.

The 1,300-capacity prison is notoriously prone to attacks amongst inmates almost every day across 2021 and 2020.

Wandsworth is a category B jail said to be rampant with drug abuse among its inmates.



A damning report in 2022 found lags were locked up for at least 22 hours a day.

Some even complained about going for weeks without time outside.

It is one of the most overcrowded prisons in the UK with nearly three-quarters of prisoners doubling up in cells designed for one.

Charlie Taylor, HM Chief Inspector of Prisons, said: “Leaders in this crumbling, overcrowded, vermin-infested prison will need considerable ongoing support from the prison service, notably with the recruitment and retention of staff, improving the infrastructure of the jail and making sure that external agencies such as the Home Office and the education provider pull their weight.”

Brand has been placed on a “standard” jail regime, which means the star — said to have a net worth of £15million — will be allowed £19.80 a week to spend in the canteen.



A source said: “Brand’s first day in jail was a real shock to his system and a wake-up call. He looked shaken and was quiet. A horrible, noisy and dirty jail like Wandsworth is a world away from his glamorous Hollywood lifestyle.

“Brand has been put in a cell and is being kept away from other inmates because he is in real ­danger due to his offences, his wealth and who he is.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Some of the officers and inmates will be excited to have a celebrity in there. But a lot of the cons would want to do him some ­damage, so he will not be allowed to mix in Wandsworth, and it will be safer for him.

“They will want to ship him out as soon as possible. He will find prison food pretty awful and have to supplement it by buying stuff.”

News.title: Dad of pilot, 20, killed in Learjet crash ‘wanted to be by her side’ during tragedy as he hails ‘soulmate’ daughter
News.content:
Next

THE dad of the young pilot killed in the doomed Learjet crash has revealed how he was desperate “to be by her side” in her final moments.

Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20, was one of nine people killed when a private jet plunged nearly 27,000ft and smashed into a residential street in Palm Beach County, erupting into a fireball.



Her dad Allan, a pilot who helped teach his daughter how to fly, held back tears as he hailed her as a hero, and called her his “soulmate”.

Horrifying ATC audio captured co-pilot Nathalia screaming that they were going to crash, while captain Jeffrey Gregory, 55, reportedly began praying.



Distraught dad Allan said he had listened over and over to Nathalia’s chilling last radio transmissions.

Holding back tears, he told reporters: “I wanted to be by her side. Inside the plane, to help.”

Read more in World News UNIMAGINABLE FEAR Final min of terror for Learjet flight as common phenomenon 'sealed fate'



Allan marvelled at how “tough” his daughter was, even as the plane sped towards the ground at around 340 miles per hour on Sunday.

He said: “She showed me what it is to be a hero.



“Because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can’t handle it.

“And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting.”

Her loss was “like having the heart torn from my chest”, Allan said, adding: “I have to find a way to go on living.”



His family have faced questions over whether the young aviator was qualified enough to fly the jet.

It is thought Captain Jeffrey was at the controls when the plane plunged to the ground, with Nathalia handling radio communications.

Nathalia had more than 1,300 hours of flying experience, a commercial pilot’s license and a Learjet certification.

The family’s lawyer Stuart Grossman said he wanted to “preserve not just her memory, but her reputation”.

He said: “She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years.”



A timeline of the crash revealed that Nathalia initially reported “light, clear ice that is manageable” and moderate turbulence before requesting permission to climb from 35,000 feet to 37,000 feet.

But the situation rapidly deteriorated, with the co-pilot issuing a mayday call and reporting that the aircraft was descending at 20,000 feet per minute before screaming, “We’re going to crash into the ground.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Her final reported words were, “Holy f**k we’re out of time,” before the radio transmission fell silent.

Filgueiras had also reportedly sent a chilling final text to her boyfriend about ice and turbulence around ten minutes before the crash.

News.title: I went commando at ‘fairy porn’ camp… there were no dragons to slay but shocking moment left me shaking with fear
News.content:
WING AND A PRAYER I went commando at ‘fairy porn’ camp… there were no dragons to slay but shocking moment left me shaking with fear







Next

SUSPENDED dozens of feet above the forest floor my hands begin to shake as I desperately try to hold onto the slithery, moss-masked bark.

Around me, the neighbouring trees form an endless sea of emerald green and deep brown. The sound of my thumping heart is drowned out by rustling leaves and birdsong.

My stomach drops as I stare down into the vertical abyss beneath me. I’d been concentrating so hard on climbing that I hadn’t realised just how high I’d gone. Now, the terrifying realisation that I’m hanging from the top of a 50ft tree has finally dawned on me – and I’m left wondering how the hell I’m going to get back down.



Welcome to Illyrian Warrior training camp – where you’re encouraged to leave your fears at home and don your best leather and faux fur to unleash your inner warrior.



The weekend training camp is based on Sarah J. Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series, during which Nesta, the sister of the series protagonist Feyre, trains to be a dangerous warrior with two female friends.

The girls are taking on a brood of male warriors who have spent their lives training to take on the mountain of challenges, while the women have spent just a few weeks conquering fears and challenge fight workouts.



“Just like the book we’re going through a series of terrifying, vertical challenges today,” explains organiser Emilia Rembecka, 25. “There are high ropes and obstacle courses, where in the book you could die if you didn’t make it.

“This weekend is about putting yourself in the characters’ shoes and imagining what you would do in their world, then bringing that experience into real life.”



I’ve never read the book, but as someone who’s terrified of heights, this doesn’t sound that appealing.

“It’s all about teamwork, building resilience and learning practical survival skills,” adds new mum and chiropractor Megan Guerra, 28, who runs the events alongside Emilia. “And, we’ll be conquering one of humankind’s biggest fears – heights!”

Over the past few years, fantasy novels have exploded on TikTok – with Fourth Wing and A Court of Thorns and Roses cultivating a massive audience.

But fans are no longer content with just absorbing the world of their favourite characters through the pages of a book, they want to become them.

Over 30 women have descended on Thorpe Woodlands Adventure Centre, in Thetford, to unleash their inner warrior.



We arrive late on a Friday and are whisked away to our wooden cabins deep in the dark forest. As someone who likes to spend weekends sipping champagne at a country spa, I’m finding the basic pods a bit of a culture shock. I try to ignore the sprawling spider webs above my head as I make my bed. For a moment, I feel like I’m starring in I’m a Celeb and am desperate to shout, “I’m the Sun’s Sexpert, Get Me out of Here!”

But in true warrior-mode I soldier on and join the rest of the group around the giant fire pit for a well-earned hot choccie. Around me, women in leather and corsets swagger about, swords swinging as they gather sticks to keep the flames roaring.

It’s like a scene from Game of Thrones, only with more hot chocolate and considerably fewer dragons. As the fire crackles, the women begin swapping stories, and I settle in.

Marie, 21, a student, tells me how she’s flown over from Austria especially for the event.

“I really like reading and having these whole fantasy worlds to escape into,” she explains. “It’s such a great way to meet people and spend time together, do adventurous stuff and dress up in costumes. I’m scared of heights, but if you’re going to do something like this, you really want to push yourself and try new things.”



The next morning we are up bright and early. Like most people, I’ve never trained to become a warrior before so I have no idea what to expect.

I soon discover that our vertical challenges will take the form of a series of treetop adventures, including climbing 25-foot trees, tiptoeing across tightropes and attempting to cross swaying logs at a dizzying height. We’ll also be learning archery and how to build – and light – a fire.

But no warrior is complete without a heavy dose of leather, faux fur and French plaits. Women queue up to have their hair braided before heading into battle.

But there’s one small problem…I’ve forgotten to pack pants and trainers. Yep, you can take the girl out of Bristol, but you can’t take the Bristol out of the girl. Luckily, a fellow warrior with similarly sized feet comes to my rescue and lends me her trainers, saving me from having to scale the trees in stilettos.



The pants situation, however, is less easily resolved. Unsurprisingly, nobody is keen to share their knickers, so I have no choice but to go commando.

As we are split into groups, I meet Sophy Hose, 22, a student at The University of Reading, who’s studying psychology and languages.



“I’m here because I love reading and I love fantasy,” she smiles. “I’ve seen lots of fantasy book fans doing events like this online and when the opportunity finally came up, I jumped at it.”

I’m impressed by how quickly Sophy scales a high tight rope before smashing the obstacle course in record time.

“I absolutely loved that,” she beams. “I felt like Nesta – a warrior from A Court of Thorns and Roses.

“I love adventure and danger, challenges like this take you out of your mind and make you focus on the task at hand.”

Next, it’s my turn. I’m feeling surprisingly confident as I begin climbing the tree, but that confidence evaporates the moment I look across at the impossibly thin wire stretched out in front of me – and the huge drop yawning beneath it. Suddenly, I feel sick.



I freeze. My feet wobble beneath me as I desperately try to steady myself, swaying from side to side with nothing but the wire between me and the ground far below. For a moment, I’m not sure I can do it.

Then I hear my comrades cheering me on. Their voices cut through the panic, urging me forward. I take a breath, focus on the wire and, somehow, manage to make it across.

But that’s only the beginning. The tree-top obstacle course is a series of increasingly terrifying ‘bridges’: a tightrope, a rolling log, a bridge with a huge gap in the middle and logs that sway violently beneath your feet. Finally, there’s the abseil back down to solid ground.

For some, the fear is almost overwhelming. Several of my teammates are already in tears before they even begin, their emotions and fear of heights getting the better of them. When one woman finally completes the course, she has to step away and have a cry. The experience has pushed her to her absolute limit.



“It can be very overwhelming,” explains Lydia, our warrior trainer. “People are forced to face their fears when they’re up there. But it’s great to watch how much people’s confidence grows after they complete the course.”

After lunch, which mainly consists of a banquet of Pot Noodles and crisps -we head back out for our afternoon challenges.



First up is archery. I’m surprised by just how heavy the bow is, it actually hurts to hold it up. After several attempts, I finally manage to hit the target. Around me, arrows ping against their targets as the rest of the team take aim. I’m beginning to suspect that, should a zombie apocalypse strike, I won’t be the one keeping us alive with my archery skills.

I’m looking forward to this challenge being over. But there’s no rest for this warrior princess. Next up, I’m faced with a 50-foot tree.

I stare up at it and immediately think there’s absolutely no chance I’m going to make it to the top. I haven’t climbed for years, but I decide to give it a go anyway.

To my surprise, I’m actually pretty good at it. Before long, I’m several feet off the ground, steadily making my way upwards. A few minutes later, I’m almost at the top. My teammates are impressed – they can’t believe how high I’ve managed to get. Without wanting to blow my own trumpet, nobody else on our team has come anywhere near as high.

There’s just one small problem: how the hell am I going to get down?



I’ve been concentrating so hard on the climb that I haven’t really thought about the descent. Then I look down and sheer panic sets in.

Visibly shaking, I try to quash my nerves. I press my feet against the bark, take a deep breath and, with my heart pounding, launch myself backwards into thin air.

For a split second, I’m suspended above the ground before the rope catches me and I begin abseiling down the tree.



When my feet finally hit the ground, I land with a heavy thud. My hands and arms are trembling, my legs feel like jelly and adrenaline is coursing through my veins.

As someone who absolutely hates heights, I can’t believe I’ve just done it. I’m not a thrill-seeker by any stretch of the imagination, so when I send my mum a video of me doing it, even she can’t believe it’s me.

Afterwards, we congregate by the fire for a much-deserved, strong, alcoholic drink. Here, I meet Rosalind, 27, a single mum of a six year old boy.

“This is actually the first weekend I’ve ever had away from my son,” she tells me. “It’s strange, but it’s nice not to have anyone to take care of other than myself.

“Coming here and getting into this fantasy world is definitely an escape from everyday mum life. I love getting into the books and pretending, for a little while, that you haven’t got all those real-life problems.”



As a single mum of two, I know exactly how she feels. Normally, my weekends are spent chasing my kids around soft play, which has probably prepared me surprisingly well for a physically demanding weekend like this.

But it’s been refreshing to step away from being “mum” for a while.

Forget slaying dragons, perhaps being a warrior is really about pushing yourself out of your comfort zone and finding courage in places you never knew existed.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

After all, not all heroes wear capes – and in my case, not all warriors wear pants either.

News.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
News.content:
The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned Andy Burnham he will not be able to rejoin its single market "Ã la carte", after the prime minister said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.

Burnham has said rejoining the EU's internal market is among options he could pursue to reshape the UK's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg ahead of a summit in 10 days' time, Michel Barnier said EU members would insist such a move require the UK to readopt conditions including the free movement of people.

Echoing a line made famous during the years-long negotiations over the UK's exit deal, he said there could be no "cherry picking" of the conditions for participation.

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

Barnier - who led talks over the UK's exit between 2016 to 2021 and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.

But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which seeks to ensure that goods can be freely traded within Europe - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.

He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the four freedoms.

Warning against the idea of a "single market Ã la carte", he said: "I said very, very often during these negotiations, the Brexit, there is no cherry picking.

"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market".

He also predicted EU countries would reject recreating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget.

The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he added, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".

News.title: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure that victims in rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.

His comments come after Metropolitan Police boss Sir Mark Rowley told the BBC that what he heard reported from Russell Brand's trial came very close to "victim blaming".

The government needs to "constantly look" at how rape trials are conducted to better support alleged victims in court, the prime minister told Times Radio, although BBC News understands there are no plans to change the law around rape trials.

Actor and comedian Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault after a four-week trial in London.

During an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, it was put to Sir Mark that Brand's defence barrister Ian Winter KC "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark replied: "I think what I've heard reported heads towards, it's getting very close to victim blaming, which is something we've thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don't do."

He said he would support a call from the Victims' Commissioner for a legal duty that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark explained.

In a Times Radio interview on Saturday, Burnham said he would "look closely" at the police chief's comments.

He said the government needed to look at how to "make sure they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court".

"[I'm] always prepared to make changes," he said. "We need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape, we need to get the conviction rate up.

"All of this is part of our broader agenda as a government combatting violence against women and girls."

Pressed on whether this might lead to a change in the law, the prime minister replied: "I wouldn't rule anything out... I will study what's happened here in great detail."

Brand, who has starred in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall, will be sentenced on Monday and is expected to face substantial jail time.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault after the jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody.

It has since been revealed that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Met said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Sir Mark told BBC Breakfast he "wouldn't be surprised if many more came forward".

In the wake of Brand's trial, Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said rape trials must be conducted "in a way that challenges myths and misconceptions about sexual violence".

In a social media post, Waxman wrote that "victims need confidence that the justice process is fair and based on evidence, not myths and false assumptions about rape and trauma".

Speaking to the Today programme on Saturday, director and founder of the Centre for Women's Justice Harriet Wistrich agreed that juries need to understand "underlying behaviours" without "running to judgement" over how a victim behaved in a particular way.

But former Conservative MP Anna Soubry, who has now returned to her work as a barrister where she often defends rape and sexual offence cases in the Crown court, told the BBC "people are being misled" by Sir Mark's comments.

"Every single judge in those cases must give, and does give, a very firm direction to the jury on exactly these points," she said.

As a result, she said she was " really disappointed" in the police chief and stressed "we've got to trust our juries" who are able to have an understanding of the nature of sexual offences.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

News.title: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attack
News.content:
Two men have been arrested after a teenager was injured in an attack involving a sword near two schools in Gloucester.

St Peter's High School and Willow Primary Academy, in Tuffley, were put into lockdown after the incident at 08:50 GMT on Friday. Armed police attended the scene to search for the suspects who reportedly fled on foot.

Police said a 17-year-old suffered a wound "believed to have been caused by the sword".

A 19-year-old, from Gloucester, was arrested overnight on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. An 18-year-old, also from Gloucester, was held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray.

News.title: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event
News.content:
We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails.

In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.

An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications".

However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".

The Cabinet Office said: "The UK has one of the most resilient electricity systems in the world, and there has never been a complete outage in the grid's 75-year history."

Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.

At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour.

The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.

The response from the government was that while copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.

As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused.

"If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."

While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.

I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.

It felt like an omen.

News.title: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades
News.content:
TV horticulturalist Monty Don thanked viewers and his furry friend Ned the dog while presenting his final episode of Gardeners' World, after more than two decades on air.

The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday.

"From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it's the final goodbye," he said on the programme, adding it had been "a privilege and pleasure" to share his garden experiences with so many people.

During the episode, Don, 71, confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year's Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show.

News.title: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed
News.content:
"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."

That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.

Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.

Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act.

The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.

None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.

News.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
News.content:
We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.

He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.

The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.

Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".

He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.

But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.

Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.

These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.

Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.

He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".

Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.

This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.

"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.

It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.

"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.

But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.

"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.

And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.

He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.

Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.

"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."

With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.

More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.

It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.

Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.

News.title: 'My mortgage is going up £200': How rising interest rates are hitting people's pockets
News.content:
On Thursday, the Bank of England increased interest rates for the first time in over three years as it tries to get a grip on rising inflation linked to the Iran war.

Experts say there could be more hikes over the next 18 months, as the conflict continues to push up food, fuel and energy prices across the UK and worldwide.

Higher interest rates affect borrowing costs, however, which means mortgages, credit cards and personal loans could get more expensive for millions, even as savings rates improve.

For some, it could mean extra financial pressure at a time when they are already struggling with the cost of living. The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected.

News.title: Man, 41, and boy, 16, arrested after car damaged by gunshots
News.content:
Two people have been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.

South Wales Police said a vehicle on the A48 in Morriston, Swansea, sustained damage "consistent with a firearms discharge" on Friday and one person has sustained minor injuries.

A 41-year-old man from Llansamlet, Swansea, arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life and a 16-year-old boy, also from Llansamlet, arrested on suspicion of affray, remain in custody.

The force said officers were still investigating and that it had been declared a critical incident.

South Wales Police said it was not currently aware of any major injuries or fatalities sustained in connection with the incident.

Residents were told to avoid the area and events, including a local firework display due to take place on Friday, were cancelled.

Video circulating online shows police officers next to a stationary car that appears to have been struck by a shotgun blast on Clase Road near an Asda superstore.

A National Police Air Service helicopter was circling the area but has since returned to base.

South Wales Police said all road closures put in place following the incident have now been lifted.

Ch Supt Stephen Jones said: "We thank the public wholeheartedly for their understanding and support during an incident which will have caused great concern to the people of Morriston, Llansamlet and wider Swansea.

"This investigation remains ongoing and a policing presence will continue in the area as officers work to reassure the local community."

The local football club, Morriston Town AFC, cancelled a planned firework display on Friday.

"Unfortunately, the police have advised due to an issue ongoing, the event has to be cancelled. With immediate effect," it said in a social media post on Friday, advising people to stay at home.

Gwyn Williams, a Plaid Cymru MS for GÅµyr Abertawe, said it was "a frightening thing for people in Swansea who are not used to this sort of news" but police had arrested two people in connection with this incident and there was no ongoing risk to the public.

News.title: We thought mum abandoned us - then we discovered she'd been murdered
News.content:
"We didn't have anyone to support us really in our lives. We struggled growing up," added Mehmet.

They were unaware that their mother had been beaten to death by her partner before hiding her body in the cellar of their home for about a year before disposing of her remains in household waste bins.

The court heard Dunkley had maintained his account that Lashley had disappeared for decades, despite being spoken to by police multiple times.

He said she had left her youngest child, who was not Dunkley's son, alone in their flat. Dunkley took the nine-month-old to social services and he was later adopted.

Judge Chambers said the "most significant aggravating factor" in the case was that Dunkley had killed the mother of a baby, who she had still been breastfeeding.

Mehmet said Dunkley killed his mother "in such a horrible way and then lied to us for 27 years", and that learning about her death had made him feel guilty about the resentment he had felt in the past.

"I feel bad in a way now that I felt that way towards mum," he said.

News.title: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
News.content:
"The Claimant, playing a dead soldier, was lying on the port side of a ship which had been lit up by gas powered flame bars to simulate it being on fire," according to documents he filed at London's High Court.

"He was positioned only a few feet away from the gas line. Without warning, there was a gas explosion that caught the Claimant and blew him forwards.

"He saw 20 foot tall flames and felt immense heat. His costume caught fire. He was immediately aware that strips of skin had peeled from his arms.

"He panicked and ran, falling over a few times before escaping the flames. Bottles of water were thrown on him by colleagues, he was undressed and clingfilm was applied to his burns."

The legal claim said he suffered "flash burns" to 15% of his body, plus injuries to both knees and his right wrist, and was flown by helicopter to hospital in Marrakesh.

"He remained in excruciating pain. Treatment there was limited," Sarsfield's claim said. He was repatriated to the UK four days later, where his wounds were "treated appropriately" in hospital.

"Formerly a man of considerable physical prowess, the Claimant suffered considerable physical de-conditioning," with limitations to his mobility, and also suffered psychological symptoms, his claim said.

It added: "He has sustained significant scarring that is permanent and which is hypersensitive. He needs to keep out of the sun."

August Street Films' legal defence said "no admissions are made as to the alleged injuries sustained by the Claimant".

The company is a subsidiary of film studio Paramount, which said several people were hurt in the accident.

A Paramount spokesperson said in 2023: "While filming a planned stunt sequence on the set of the Gladiator sequel, an accident occurred during which several crew members experienced non-life-threatening injuries.

"The safety and full medical services teams on-site were able to act quickly so that those who were impacted immediately received necessary care. They are all in stable condition and continue to receive treatment.

"The well-being of the cast and crew is of the utmost importance to us, and we have strict health and safety procedures in place on all our productions. We will continue monitoring the situation and taking all necessary precautions as we resume production."

Sarsfield, August Street Films and Paramount declined to comment further.

News.title: One of the year's most prolific meteor showers to light up the night sky this weekend
News.content:
The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.

The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.

There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.

The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.

These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.

News.title: Beach homes face demolition months after being sold
News.content:
A property investor and a woman planning for her retirement have been told their homes are at risk of falling into the sea just months after they purchased them.

The two properties are part of a collection of former fishermen's cottages in the hamlet of Newport, south of Hemsby, Norfolk.

The houses, which were both bought in the last three months, are among nine properties in the area deemed to be at risk of coastal erosion.

Great Yarmouth Borough Council has advised the homeowners to leave their properties for their own safety.

News.title: AI in property listings is false advertising, house-hunters say
News.content:
Property buyers and renters say the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in listings appearing on sites like Rightmove is "false advertising" and wastes time for all involved.

Jessica Otterwell, who is hunting for a flat in Brighton, East Sussex, told the BBC: "It's like if you went to buy a car because the picture was of a brand-new Mercedes and you turned up and it was a Skoda with one wheel."

An estate agent in Sussex said it could cost up for Â£50,000 to stage a property with furniture, while another in Surrey added: "Technology should help people, not deceive them."

Rightmove, a portal website which pulls in listings from other estate agents, and does not sell or rent properties directly, said AI-generated imagery was allowed on the site if it was clearly labelled.

The BBC has seen some property listings in which the images have been watermarked "Virtually staged" or "Artificially enhanced", but many others have not been disclosed.

The practice has been dubbed by some as "housefishing".

News.title: Skepta: 'I'm what it looks like if you give an immigrant child a chance'
News.content:
And while Skepta's been focused on the message, he has also been deliberate about how he's delivering it.

"It took six years to make this because it's important to make sure we're not tone deaf," he says.

He learned the value of that when, in 2024, he had to take down artwork for his single Gas Me Up (Diligent), following allegations that it referenced the Holocaust.

The image showed a group of men with shaved heads, one featuring a tattoo reading "Gas Me Up".

It had been a reference to skinhead culture, but Skepta acknowledged how without that context people could find it offensive and promised to be more mindful going forward.

Determined not to miss the mark this time around, he says: "I feel like we've delivered a classic."

Early reviews are mixed as to whether critics agree, however. While Complex said The Fork and Knife was "top-tier" and worth the wait, external, The Observer said it was well-intentioned but questioned whether it was "over-egged", external.

At a time when he thinks standards have been slipping though, striving for a classic is more important than ever.

"I don't think there's been a good grime album for a long time," Skepta says.

"And I'm here to set levels."

In September, Digga D called out the viral 'UK Poo' trend, which saw a wave of tracks blowing up on TikTok defined by what he described as "foolishness".

"I can't sit on here and be like 'I'm happy with how the UK scene is right now'," the rapper told 1Xtra's DJ Target. "Because I'm not."

Turns out Skepta isn't happy either.

Drawing on his idols, and even featuring some of them like Suggs, he says he is "here to make rap sophisticated again".

As BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first UK rap chart show, he's hopeful more grime artists will be inspired to sharpen their pen game.

"Rap is a sport and it's very hard for visibility when we're being compared to people who have major machines behind them," he says.

"So this rap chart is going to give all the newcomers and a lot of people who are producing in their bedroom a chance to be seen and heard."

News.title: Man, 35, charged with murder of Carrie Mullane
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder by police investigating the disappearance and suspected murder of Carrie Mullane (Noonan).

Mullane, who is 39, has been missing since she arrived in Enniskillen from Limerick on 10 October 2026.

The 35-year-old man is also charged with preventing the lawful burial of a corpse.

He is due to appear via video link before Dungannon Magistrates' Court on 7 November.

Earlier on Friday, police carried out a number of searches in County Fermanagh, including Lough Erne.

A small boat and a camper van were recovered and taken away for examination.

News.title: Hacked blood banks, breached supermarket fridges and plane bomb hoaxes: What’s going on in Europe?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Europe is on high alert after a fresh wave of cyber attacks, online hoaxes and bomb scares brought major disruption this week, causing tens of millions of euros in estimated losses.

Dozens of flights across Europe were paralysed by threats, forcing diversions and partial airport closures as explosives disposal teams and sniffer dogs searched each aircraft identified.

Freezers in parts of the UK and Europe were hit by a suspected hack that saw internal temperatures rise dramatically, spoiling huge amounts of food.

In France, blood banks were subjected to a cyber attack on Monday that damaged cold storage and control systems in multiple regions across France.

And British broadcaster Sky said it received a security threat on Friday, hours after Irish broadcaster RTE evacuated its building following a similar warning.

open image in gallery Supermarkets in Europe have been affected by a cyber attack impacting fridges and freezers (Damien Eagers/PA) ( PA )

The disruptions come amid heightened anxiety over the threat of so-called ‘hybrid attacks’ by foreign actors - and experts tell The Independent that the events of the past week show all the hallmarks of sabotage by foreign adversaries.

“There’s no money in this, so the payoff is psychological and political,” says CEO of cybersecurity firm Heimdal, Jesper Frederiksen. “These attacks prove reach, test how fast governments respond, and wear down public confidence that the state can protect everyday life.”

Europe has long been sounding the alarm about a hybrid war – from Russia in particular, with EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen warning it is “not about traditional defence” and requires a “completely new mindset”.

Dray Agha, a senior manager at cybersecurity firm Huntress, said the disruption of food chains and medical services is a “proven tactic to generate public anxiety and undermine confidence in civil institutions”, which shows how “national resilience now relies entirely on the security of everyday commercial networks”.

Matt Lovell, CEO of CloudGuard, says the incidents “shouldn’t be read in isolation” and that all show a pattern of being “low-cost, highly visible, and disruptive to everyday life”.

Russian hacktivists have claimed responsibility for the supermarket attacks and newsroom bomb hoaxes – and experts make clear that this does not rule out nation-state involvement.

In fact, they say, it follows a trend of states allowing proxies to carry out the attacks while they retain a level of plausible deniability.

open image in gallery Europe has long been sounding the alarm about the threat of Russia’s ‘hybrid warfare’ ( AFP/Getty )

Here’s how Europe’s week of chaos unfolded:

Supermarket fridge attacks

Hackers cranked up fridge temperatures at shops in European countries this week, forcing retailers to throw away large quantities of food in an attack that echoed a similar incident in France three weeks earlier. Russian hacktivists have claimed responsibility.

“Pro-Russian hacktivist groups have claimed the fridge attacks, and US prosecutors have linked them to a network funded by Russian military intelligence,” said Mr Fredriksen.

“That is the model to watch. The state doesn’t press the button itself. It lets aligned proxies do it and keeps deniability.”

Irregularities were reported at stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Estonia, the Netherlands and Finland. Giants Carrefour and Ikea were among those affected.

open image in gallery Empty refrigerated shelves are seen inside a Delhaize Shop & Go store in Linkebeek near Brussels, Belgium, 2 November 2026 ( Reuters )

In Britain, hackers tried to target small meat-processing firms but the impact was minimal.

But in Stockholm, the impact was clear. “Everything is destroyed,” says Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store, adding that the attack occurred at 2am on Monday but was only noticed hours later.

“There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees (Celsius).”

The incidents have raised concerns in the European Union about vulnerabilities in connected infrastructure amid security tensions in the wake of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

The attacks on fridges open up the “very real possibility that nation-states are probing how to disrupt cooling systems that sustain military bases and critical response personnel”, says Sarah Cleveland, a senior director at cybersecurity firm ExtraHop.

open image in gallery EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen has warned that Russia's hybrid war requires a 'completely new mind-set ( AP )

Richard Horne, head of Britain's National Cyber Security Centre, adds that the Europe-wide attack was “just the foothills”, warning there were still “so many vulnerabilities out there that in some ways are waiting to be exploited”.

He claims Russia has been making sustained attempts to penetrate UK military networks, while Iran is carrying out malicious cyber operations globally, including the UK.

Moscow, Beijing and Tehran have all repeatedly denied similar accusations of malevolent cyber actions in the past.

Mysterious flight bomb hoaxes

On Thursday, bomb threats across Europe grounded flights across several countries and caused travel disruption.

open image in gallery A screengrab from a video shows a police officer and a sniffer dog inspecting a Ryanair airplane and its baggage, after Ryanair's operations centre reported a bomb threat received during the flight from Manchester to Murcia on 3 November ( Reuters )

It was the second of three occasions this week that such widespread threats have been reported, prompting fear and concern against the backdrop of a series of cyber-attacks in the continent.

Flights to and from the UK, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Finland, Bulgaria, Spain and Denmark were affected but largely resolved by the end of each day.

More than a dozen flights were targeted, included those from Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw.

On Tuesday, several flights across Europe received alleged bomb threats that ultimately turned out to be hoaxes - but prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, an escort by the Italian Air Force until landing, officials said.

open image in gallery Finnair plane taking off from Fiumicino Airport after it was diverted due to a bomb threat and escorted by Italian air force jets ( AFP/Getty )

“If you can interfere with a supermarket, shut down part of an airport, create a bomb scare or force emergency services to respond, you have already imposed costs and created uncertainty,” says Dave Wreski, founder of Guardian Digital, Inc.

“You can do that without sending troops across a border or carrying out an attack that clearly looks like an act of war.”

Newsroom threats

Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov", claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.

“European authorities have once again shown that they are incompetent fools who are incapable of doing anything to stop us,” it continued.

“We experimented with multithreading, and we succeeded in causing widespread panic, as well as forcing European authorities to spend a fortune on all these procedures.

“But this is only the beginning. What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future.”

The email said that hackers are planning a new wave of attacks and would very soon be “blowing up your airplanes, cruise ships, subway stations, and trains”.

open image in gallery A Garda vehicle outside the offices of Irish National broadcaster RTE ( Reuters )

Going on to make a direct threat to the newsroom, it said: “We want the whole world to know about us, which is why one of our operatives has planted an explosive device in your building. It will detonate in 45 minutes. The clock is ticking."

The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.

The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.

The identity of the sender, the origin of the emails, or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday has not yet been established. By the end of Friday, no explosive devices had been found and all planes had landed safely.

Blood banks

Days after the refrigerator hoax, blood banks in France were hit by a cyberattack, the French health ministry said.

“Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems,” it said.

open image in gallery Blood products were not damaged ( Getty/iStock )

Despite the threat, there was no damage to blood products following the attack, which took place on Monday but was publicised on Wednesday.

The ministry said that “safety of the blood supplies was preserved thanks to the facilities’ monitoring and alarm systems, as well as precautionary measures immediately implemented”.

Investigations into the incident and equipment potentially affected are underway as authorities look at a timeline for a safe return to service.

On Wednesday, French cooperative bank Credit Mutuel Arkea said it had been hit by a cyberattack which “enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out” – but that no money belonging to clients had been affected.

With so many widespread attacks in one week, there is genuine concern across Europe about what else is yet to come.

News.title: Global travel to hit record-breaking levels in 2026 despite Middle East conflict
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Global travel is set to reach a new record number of travellers in 2026, despite cost-of-living pressures and conflict in the Middle East.

Countries worldwide are predicted to receive a record 1.57 billion international arrivals by the end of 2026, according to a new report by the World Travel Market and researchers at Tourism Economics, an Oxford Economics Company.

Dave Goodger, EMEA managing director at Tourism Economics, said “travellers are more active in 2026 than ever before”.

“Leisure travel remains a key priority in consumer budgets, even as travellers are adapting how and where they visit in response to ongoing disruption and cost-of-living pressures,” he said. “The industry is on course for another record year.”

The report says growth is set to accelerate into 2027 and remain strong through 2032, as the industry recovers from crises in roughly half the time it took two decades ago.

Global international arrivals are expected to rise by eight per cent next year as disruption eases.

The report predicts the Middle East will see the largest increase in international arrivals, 43 per cent, in 2027, after a major drop amid this year’s conflict.

All regions are expected to grow in international overnight arrivals, with Asia and Oceania predicted to grow by 11 per cent, Latin America up seven per cent, and Africa up six per cent.

Europe’s arrivals are expected to grow by five per cent, while North America will grow the least, at four per cent.

While international travel has remained resilient, more people switched to visiting destinations closer to home, causing long-haul trips to dip, although longer journeys are expected to rebound next year.

In-destination spending increased by nine per cent compared to last year, with US$7.8 trillion (£5.79 trillion) spent.

The report also gave insight into what travellers want out of a trip. Three in four people said taking a leisure holiday each year is an important priority to them, despite cost of living pressures.

Meanwhile, 58 per cent of international travellers took a trip abroad in the past two years to attend a specific event, such as a festival, sports event or cultural celebration.

Another major talking point this year has been the rise of AI.

The report revealed that most travellers trust AI to search and recommend, but far fewer are ready to let it complete a booking independently.

News.title: Scotland v New Zealand LIVE: Hosts seek historic win over All Blacks in fascinating Nations Championship clash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

( Getty )

Scotland again go in search of a first win over New Zealand as the All Blacks visit Murrayfield in the Nations Championship.

A success against the All Blacks remains elusive for the Scots, but Gregor Townsend’s side have pushed their illustrious opponents close in each of the last four meetings and were left to rue their missed opportunities 12 months ago. With a settled selection led by Sione Tuipulotu and Finn Russell, the hosts will recognise another huge opportunity to produce the sort of statement result they may need ahead of next year’s World Cup.

There is a strong Scottish influence at the heart of the All Blacks. Head coach Dave Rennie spent three years with Glasgow while attacking guru Mike Blair remains Scotland’s most capped scrum half. Together, they have reinvented New Zealand after a tough 2025 – but can they get one over old friends and foes to bolster their hopes of lifting the inaugural trophy in this competition?

Follow all of the latest from the Nations Championship clash with our live blog below:

News.title: Tottenham dealt latest attacking injury blow after VAR madness at Leeds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tottenham have been dealt another attacking injury blow after Mathys Tel limped off before half-time against Leeds.

Tel was unable to continue after being on the end of a stamp by Jayden Bogle, who caught the Frenchman on the ankle with his studs.

VAR spent over four minutes reviewing the incident to determine whether it was a red card offence, only for referee John Brooks - who didn’t even caution Bogle initially - to be told to stick with the on-field decision. This meant the right wing-back got away with the challenge scot free.

“The referee’s call of no red card to Bogle for the challenge on Tel was checked and confirmed by VAR,” said the Premier League Match Centre.

The statement added VAR Tony Harrington’s verdict to Brooks: “I'm confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge”.

The challenge was similar to the one that saw Jean-Philippe Mateta shown red after a VAR review when Spurs played Crystal Palace last weekend.

Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi was visibly frustrated with the outcome of the review and his woes were exacerbated when Tel signalled to the bench that he would need to come off, having tried to play through the pain for five minutes.

Tel was replaced by Dominic Solanke in the 43rd minute, who was dropped from the starting line-up following the Palace win.

Mathys Tel was forced off during Tottenham's clash with Leeds ( Getty )

De Zerbi’s attacking options have already been ravaged by injury this season and the club will now be left to sweat over the extent of Tel’s setback.

Savio and Mykhailo Mudryk are out until after the international break, while Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert are continuing to work their way back from serious knee injuries, with both eyeing returns after the turn of the year.

Tel has impressed for Spurs in recent weeks, scoring a stunning solo goal in their 2-0 win over Chelsea on 24 October, the club’s first victory at Stamford Bridge since 2018.

News.title: Josh Tongue ruled out of England tour of Australia in hammer injury blow
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

England have been dealt a hammer blow to their seam bowling department for the upcoming tour of Australia as Josh Tongue will miss the trip down under due to a toe injury.

The news was confirmed on England Cricket’s social media with the official X account posting: “Get well soon Tonguey.

“Josh Tongue has been ruled out of England Men’s white-ball tour of Australia due to a toe injury. He will return to the UK to undergo further assessment.”

There was no confirmation on whether a replacement would be called up to the squad ahead of the first of three ODIs due to be played in Australia from 13-18 November though it seems unlikely at this late stage.

open image in gallery Josh Tongue has been taken out of England's ODI tour of Australia due to a toe injury ( Getty )

The ODI and T20 squads for the tour were announced three weeks ago with Tongue only included in the one day squad and the 28-year-old was due to return back to the UK following the conclusion of the ODI series alongside fellow quick bowlers Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, and Sonny Baker.

Jamie Overton is also included in the squad so there is plenty of cover for Tongue following his withdrawal and return to England.

Tongue made his One Day International (ODI) debut earlier this year in a contest against India in Birmingham. He took 1-50 from his 10 overs and has since been selected in four other one day games.

His most recent outing was against Sri Lanka in the ODI Tri-Series which also included Pakistan. Tongue took 3-79 from 8.5 overs as the Sri Lankans made history by knocking off 429 runs with one ball remaining in the game. Tongue bowled the final over and had been earmarked as one of the death bowling seamers for Harry Brook’s side.

The ODI squad includeds two changes from the one that travelled to Pakistan for last month’s tri-series as Jacob Bethell returns following a knee injury and Archer is back after being rested for the tri-series.
