News.title: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The overwhelming victory by the Democrats in the midterm elections shook up Wall Street this week.

The biggest tremors were felt in shares of companies tied to the boom in artificial intelligence on concerns that a Democratic Congress will put the brakes on further development of data centers.

Defense and oil companies fell on expectations Democrats would push for an end to the U.S.-Iran war, which would likely lower energy prices.

Meanwhile, hospital shares rose on the possibility that funding for several government programs could be restored or boosted, while liquor companies and others buffeted by tariffs rose on hopes for relief.

Here’s a look at how certain stocks and industries reacted to the result of the midterms.

AI stocks

The frantic construction of data centers to power the AI boom has meant big profits for a wide array of companies — chip makers, power providers, cooling system producers, cloud computing companies and more. Investors hungry for a piece of those profits dove in, pushing some stocks up by double or more. But concerns grew that AI stocks got too pricey. And then the Democrats swept the midterms to take control of Congress.

Nvidia, Lam Research and others tied to the AI boom swung wildly this week on worries that Democratic victories in statehouses across the country could mean a slowdown in further construction, particularly in Texas. Hyperscalers, or those funding the buildout, like Amazon, fared better.

Defense

Defense companies have been volatile throughout the year, rising and falling with the shifts in the U.S. war with Iran. Hopes for an end to the war increased following the Democrats’ sweep in the midterms. An end to the war could mean slimmer business for several big defense companies, though the war has also depleted stockpiles of weapons, which could result in demand for resupplies by the U.S. government.

Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, RTX and General Dynamics fell between 4% and 12% after Tuesday.

Oil and gas

Oil exploration and refining companies have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the U.S. war with Iran, which has stifled global supplies since February and raised the price of crude oil and gasoline. Several big energy companies lost ground following the midterms because an end to the war would lower oil prices and reduce the companies’ profits.

Companies such as Exxon Mobil and Phillips 66 are still showing solid year-to-date gains.

Elon Musk’s companies

Elon Musk spent more than $445 million in an attempt to help Republicans maintain control of Congress. Not only was his return on investment not very good, but shares of his two publicly traded companies took a drubbing on concerns a Democratic Congress will investigate Musk’s work as Trump’s cost-cutting chief in 2025. SpaceX, which houses Musk’s xAI business, and Tesla, with plans for a fleet of mostly autonomous vehicles, fell 5% and 10.1%, respectively, after the midterms.

Trump Media

The president’s social media company, Trump Media & Technology, lost 33% of its market value in the three days after the election. Trump’s stake in the company was worth nearly $5 billion in March 2025. Now, it’s worth less than $600 million. The company is hoping to improve its fortunes by merging with the nuclear fusion company TAE Technologies. Completion of the deal is pending.

Power companies

Companies focusing on wind, solar and other forms of renewable energy could see sunnier days ahead with a more industry-friendly Congress. Democrats will have overwhelming influence on funding when they take control of Congress in January, raising hopes for a wide range of green energy companies.

Those companies involved in powering the data centers at the hub of the AI buildout didn't fare as well, however, after a number of data center skeptics got elected to Congress or governorships.

Ho spitals

Hospitals gained ground over hopes that funding for several government programs could be restored or boosted, including Medicaid and subsidies for the Affordable Care Act. Medicaid spending was reduced under Trump. Enhanced tax credits for the ACA were allowed to expire without being renewed, resulting in a decline in enrollment for insurance coverage nationally. More funding for those programs would result in an eventual boost to healthcare providers, including hospitals.

HCA Healthcare rose 6.9%, Tenet Healthcare gained 6.2% and Universal Health Services added 10.4% after Tuesday.

Homebuilders and home improvement

The housing sector, including builders, continues to face pressure from historically high home prices and mortgage rates. The shift in power in Congress could mean a greater focus on policies that address affordability, which was a key theme for Democrats. Cutting tariffs and lowering energy costs could lower supply chain costs. That could also help home improvement retailers by relieving pressure on consumers.

Mortgage rates, though, are a trickier issue for the industry. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate again in an effort to cool inflation. That likely means that interest rates on many types of loans, including mortgages, will remain high.

D.R. Horton gained 4.9%, PulteGroup rose 4.4% and Home Depot added 2.9%.

Alcohol

Beer, wine and liquor companies could see relief from tariffs that have hurt sales both in the U.S. and globally with Democrats taking control of Congress. The hope is that they will take action to end the global tariff conflict that has raised prices. S&P 500 members Constellation Brands, which has U.S. import rights for Corona and Modelo beers, and Brown-Forman, which makes Jack Daniel’s and other liquors, both had gains.

Household goods

Makers and sellers of everyday consumer staples gained ground as investors moved out of riskier sectors. They were also helped by hopes that a shift in control of Congress could mean policies that help cool inflation. Eliminating or reducing tariffs could help lower costs for businesses. Ending the U.S. war with Iran could boost global oil supplies, which would lower oil prices and costs for shipping on everything from food to clothing.

After the election, Costco Wholesale added 3.4%, Procter & Gamble rose 2.1% and Dollar General rose 2.5%.

News.title: The reinvention of Skye Nicolson: ‘I was a bit of a shell of myself’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Skye Nicolson laughs as she recalls the pain. That, in itself, is usually a sign of growth and peace.

“It was a really difficult time for me,” the Australian admits to The Independent over Zoom, reflecting on her sole professional loss: a split decision in March 2025. “I felt like a lot of the issues I needed to deal with were actually internal – mindset, mental stuff, more than physical. I had a great camp, we’d done everything right, I was boxing out of my skin in sparring...

“I think the occasion and other contributing factors, things I guess I hadn’t prepared for that happened in fight week, I let them weigh me down. I was a bit of a shell of myself going into that fight.

open image in gallery World champion Skye Nicolson in 2024 ( Getty )

“There was a lot of stuff I had to deal with away from the gym, nothing to do with my coaching team. For me, the most disappointing part was knowing how much better I am, and not being able to show that when it mattered.”

Women’s boxing moves quickly, on both a micro and macro level. The traditional ruleset of 10 two-minute rounds means fights fly, but the bigger picture is that fighters often become world champions while they are still being touted as the next big thing.

So it was for Nicolson. Now 31, the southpaw had emerged in 2022 as one of the faces of Matchroom’s next generation, with her spot on the undercard of Katie Taylor vs Amanda Serrano 1 allowing crucial exposure to the wider boxing world. She was an interim world champion by her eighth fight, and a full champion by her 10th.

But after winning the vacant WBC featherweight title and retaining it twice, Nicolson met her first major hurdle. Back home, Down Under, Nicolson went the distance with the unbeaten Tiara Brown. The distance brought defeat, Nicolson’s first.

Yet Nicolson subscribes to a certain, useful sentiment. “They say it’s not always a loss, it’s a lesson. I feel like there were many lessons in that. I guess that’s what those experiences are for.”

Defeats often signal a change of division for boxers, and it was no different for Nicolson, but while many fighters opt to move up in weight, Nicolson dropped down.

Enjoy 185+ fights a year on DAZN, the Global Home of Boxing Never miss a fight from top promoters. Watch on your devices anywhere, anytime. Buy Now . If you sign up to this service we will earn commission. This revenue helps to fund journalism across The Independent.

Enjoy 185+ fights a year on DAZN, the Global Home of Boxing Never miss a fight from top promoters. Watch on your devices anywhere, anytime. Buy Now . If you sign up to this service we will earn commission. This revenue helps to fund journalism across The Independent.

open image in gallery Nicolson handed Raven Chapman her first loss to retain the WBC featherweight belt in 2024 ( Getty )

“After that defeat, I was just looking at everything I was doing and working out where can I be better,” she says. “I wasn’t working with a nutritionist, so I wanted to get my body composition done, make sure I was actually boxing in the right division for me. There, I was told that super-bantam was probably ideal, and bantam was even possible.” That said, her own mention of bantamweight draws a nervous laugh out of Nicolson.

“So, to be boxing at featherweight, it just felt like: why not see how I feel going down? I’m really, really glad I did, because physically it’s the best I’ve ever felt – and probably where I should have always been. I definitely feel like I have the height and reach to box at 126lb and probably even 130, but based off my physique right now and a year ago... It was 122, so I feel very, very good at this weight.”

In Nicolson’s case, reinvention equalled reinvigoration.

On her debut at super-bantamweight, she won in two rounds, and her sophomore outing yielded the same result. Nicolson even managed one more win in 2025, before beating Mariah Turner this spring to win the interim WBC title – which was soon upgraded, when Britain’s Ellie Scotney vacated the main belt.

And then came an unusual career update.

open image in gallery Nicolson with MVP’s Nakisa Bidarian in July ( Getty )

With many of the sport’s top female talents flocking to Jake Paul’s Most Valuable Promotions (MVP), but with Matchroom keen to keep Nicolson, the two companies struck a “strategic alliance”. It means Nicolson will make her MVP debut on Sunday, taking on Miyo Yoshida, though she can still fight for Matchroom.

“Matchroom came to me with a conversation around what it would look like,” Nicolson explains. “For me, it did feel like a no-brainer to merge. I never would have wanted to leave Matchroom, so I kind of get the best of both worlds in the sense that we can make the biggest and best fights out there.

“Obviously MVP have such a big stable, Matchroom obviously have the experience, so I just feel like it made perfect sense for me. I want to be unifying the division, I want to be an undisputed world champion, so hopefully we can see those big fights in 2027.

“We could see me fighting the winner of Ramla Ali and Mikiah Kreps; they’re fighting for two of the belts [on Sunday]. Melissa Mortensen has the other belt, so I feel like within two or three fights, we could see me becoming undisputed. That has kind of become my main focus.”

open image in gallery Nicolson outpointed Mariah Turner to win the WBC super-bantamweight strap in April, and she has since been elevated to full champion ( Getty )

As much as she wants to unify the belts at her new weight, Nicolson knows that some of her biggest tests and business opportunities remain up at featherweight.

“I’ve said right from the get-go when I went to 122lb, it wasn’t goodbye to 126. I’m more than ready to take fights at 126 as well. Right now the 122lb division has opened back up, with Ellie moving up, so I guess that ever-elusive chance at finally fighting for undisputed feels a lot closer.

“But obviously, boxing is a business at the end of the day. I want to be in the biggest fights, I also want to be in legacy fights. I think the rematch with Tiara Brown will be inevitable. I’m excited for her vs Ellie, and obviously the winner of that fight is also a fight that I would definitely be chasing.”

Yet there were similar hopes for Nicolson during her first world-title reign, before the tumult of her first loss, meaning she cannot look past Yoshida in Dallas.

open image in gallery Nicolson celebrating her win over Turner on home soil in Australia ( Getty )

Of her preparation, Nicolson says: “I’m a very reactive fighter, so I feel like a lot of my style is very much on what’s in front of me. I think people have different performances against all different types of opponents – different heights, different stances.

“So I will always watch some tape of my opponents to get an idea for their style, but I never take that as gospel. I leave a lot of that kind of gameplan-type stuff, to my team. I’m more focused on what’s happening right in front of me. I focus on the work I do in the gym to make sure that I’m ready for anything.”

Reinvented, reinvigorated, and ready.

News.title: Ireland send out ominous warning with second-gear walloping of Argentina
News.content:
Is it time to fire up the emerald green bandwagon? Not quite yet. But this was not a bad start to Ireland’s autumn; a 42-12 walloping of Los Pumas with Andy Farrell’s team still nowhere near their best. That should be highly encouraging for those of an Irish persuasion.

A year out from the World Cups of 2015, 2019 and 2023, Ireland had enjoyed banner seasons, eyeing up global glory. They never made it past the quarter-finals.

The build-up this time has been tougher going – the Aviva, unusually for this time of year – was not even full for this Nations Championship encounter. But perhaps Ireland will be better for it. They had far too much on a crisp Friday night in Dublin for an Argentina team who were missing a few of their stars, notably Bath’s Santiago Carreras and Lyon prop Thomas Gallo, but still packing 750 caps’ worth of Test experience in their starting XV.

Farrell was missing a few big names himself. Caelan Doris and Jack Conan were out injured, with the Englishman opting to hand Sean Jansen and Nick Timoney starts in the back row. Farrell also chose to start Craig Casey rather than Jamison Gibson-Park – arguably their best player of the last 18 months – at scrum-half, with Sam Prendergast starting again at 10 given Jack Crowley’s absence.

All in all there was a slightly experimental feel to proceedings, making Argentina potentially dangerous visitors. But Ireland had far too much in reserve. Hugo Keenan grabbed a hat-trick and took the player of the match award. Robert Baloucoune was consistently excellent. Mack Hansen’s return on the wing was hugely welcome. Tominey stood out in the back row.

Farrell said he was delighted with the result, if not the entire performance, making special mention of the likes of Keenan, Hansen, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, all of whom were returning from long injury lay-offs.

“The game’s never going to be perfect. But if you look at the bigger picture, to win 42-12 against a really good side in Argentina, I don’t think too many teams have done that,” Farrell said. “You have to be pleased.”

Asked whether he was happier with the 42 points scored or the meagre 12 conceded, Farrell added that it was probably the latter: “We want to be known for our defence. It shows our mentality.”

Los Pumas scored the first try of the game, Mateo Carreras getting the jump on Casey in the corner to field a Tomás Albornoz crossfield kick.

News.title: ‘Air Caluori’ puts on show as England A offer exciting glimpse into future

England A 59 Argentina XV 24

On a night when England’s back line showcased plenty of attacking flair and free-flowing rugby, the hosts ran in nine tries to shrug off a dogged Argentina outfit.

News.title: Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place
News.content:
Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

Donald Trump’s administration was scheduled to convene a session on Friday with an industry panel known as the “President’s Council ​of ⁠Advisers on Science and Technology”, which advises Mr Trump on tech matters.

However, the meeting was cancelled by the White House and is yet to be rescheduled. Thursday’s tech rout, which saw the Nasdaq 100 fall the most in six years, wiped more than $1 trillion off the Magnificent 7.

The tech ​panel also includes top Silicon Valley bosses such as AMD’s ‌Lisa Su and Marc ​Andreessen, co-foudner of Andreessen ​Horowitz.

News.title: Cheap version of game-changing HIV preventive drug granted approval by US authorities
News.content:
Millions of people in low and middle income countries are set to get access to a game-changing HIV prevention drug within weeks, after US health authorities green lit a cheap form of the product.

Earlier this week the US Food and Drug Administration granted tentative approval to a generic form of the drug lenacapavir, made by Indian manufacturer Dr Reddy’s Laboratories.

Under an agreement hammered out between drug manufacturers and philanthropic donors in 2025 120 low and middle income countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East and the Caribbean, will get access to the generic drug, at just $40 per patient per year – compared to the US list price of $28,000.

Lenacapavir, a long-acting injection administered twice a year, was hailed as the scientific breakthrough of 2024 and a potential turning point in the fight against HIV. Clinical trials have shown it provides almost 100 per cent protection against catching the HIV virus for six months and it is more effective and convenient than taking daily pre-exposure prophylactic (PrEP) pills.

Last year, Gilead Sciences, which developed lenacapavir, signed royalty-free, non-exclusive voluntary licencing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable the production and supply of a generic. Dr. Reddy’s is the first to get FDA approval and it is hoped the first batches will be ready by the end of the year.

Jessica Burry, HIV technical officer at Unitaid, which in conjunction with the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI supported Dr Reddy’s in its bid to manufacture the generic, said it normally takes 10 years for a generic form of a drug to be launched.

“So we’re celebrating this milestone,” she said. “There’s a lot of demand in the countries where we’re working and we think having an affordable generic could make a real difference.”

Standard PrEP involves daily pills which some people find difficult to stick to.

“You can overcome the stigma, you can overcome the potential adherence difficulties so it’s really a game changer in terms of things to have in the toolbox,” she said.

News.title: The perilous road to parenthood: Mongolia’s fight to make childbirth safer
News.content:
As the 4x4 raced south, bouncing across Mongolia’s rocky valley roads and dusty forest steppes, an obstetrician was doing her best to ease Otgonbayar Odbayar’s pain and panic.

Hours earlier, the reindeer herder’s waters had broken. But Otgonbayar was six weeks early – and almost 250 miles away from the doctors who could provide the caesarean she knew she needed.

She contacted the nearest clinic, kicking off a relay of calls that spanned the length of Khuvsgul, a region bordering Russia. Soon, a plan came back through the chain: one health team would collect the 26-year-old and sprint south, while doctors from the provincial hospital in Murun would hurtle north. They’d meet in the middle.

Otgonbayar Odbayar with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But Otgonbayar’s three-hour journey was touch and go. “Halfway through, her contractions got very intense and very close together,” said Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh, the obstetrician who collected her. “She was in a lot of pain. We put her on an IV and were driving so fast.”

They made it to the small clinic in Tugul a little after 11pm, but then faced an excruciating 90 minute wait for the team from Murun, who had further to travel on Mongolia’s rutted roads. Dr Tsogbadrakh didn’t have a Plan B: the baby was in breech position, and the scar from Otgonbayar’s previous c-section still hadn’t fully healed.

Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“When [the doctors] arrived, I felt relief,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh. “If we had waited only 30 more minutes to start surgery, no one could tell what would have happened.”

Yet Otgonbayar’s ordeal is now the exception in Mongolia, underscoring just how far the vast country has come in its three-decade drive to tackle the childbirth risks posed by geography.

In 1990, 200 women died for every 100,000 births, but that ratio plunged to 47 by 2015 – making Mongolia one of only nine countries to hit global targets to reduce maternal mortality by 75 per cent over the 25-year period, according to analysis in the Lancet.

Strides have slowed but continued, and the rate now hovers at around 37. By contrast, other countries with a similar maternal mortality ratio in 1990, including Algeria, Brazil, the Philippines and Kiribati, still see more than 70 deaths per 100,000 births, according to Our World in Data.

In a country as vast and sparse as Mongolia – which is more than six times the size of the UK, but home to just 3.5 million people – health gains have been reliant “on overcoming the distance between women and the care they need”, said the health minister Batshugar Enkhbayar.

That has meant introducing telemedicine initiatives to bring specialist advice to remote clinics, waiting homes where pregnant women can stay in the final weeks before delivery, and better trained staff to spot risks before they become acute. In the last year, the country has also started to trial portable ultrasounds.

Northern Mongolia near the Russian border Credit : Simon Townsley

“We cannot always eliminate that distance,” said Mr Enkhbayar, “so we have to plan around it.”

The Telegraph spent a week in Mongolia to find out what this looks like in practice, driving hundreds of miles to meet pregnant women and new mothers in provincial hospitals, village clinics and remote herder communities.

“It is a lifestyle, not only a job,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, carefully sipping strong coffee from a flask as the 4x4 bounced the dusty steppe. “For example, in the last 14 days I’ve been all the time on the road – I was in the city for training, then I collected [Otgonbayar] for the emergency c-section, then I was on the road to treat people. My kids complain I’m sometimes very absent at home.

“Sometimes it is hard,” added Dr Tsogbadrakh, who’s been Renchinlkhumbe clinic’s obstetrician for eight years. “But the thing I love about my work is that moment when you safely deliver the baby, and you get to see the mother and the baby meet for the first time.

“It’s the beginning of a new human life.”

Sports.title: Can Clarke KO Billam-Smith? 'Incredibly arrogant to count me out'
Sports.content:
Chris Billam-Smith has never been dropped or stopped before, but Cheavon Clarke is still a clear and present danger to the former world champion.

The cruiserweights fight at the Copper Box Arena in London in the main event of Zuffa Boxing 12, live on Sky Sports from 7pm.

Clarke is nicknamed "C4" for a simple reason - he is an explosive puncher.

Billam-Smith is renowned for his toughness, that has seen him come through multiple brutal bouts and win a world championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ahead of Chris Billam-Smith's Zuffa Boxing 12 main event against Chev Clarke, here's a look back at The Gentleman's best moments

But Clarke thinks he could be the first person to knock out Billam-Smith. "What I can say is I have it in me. I think through my career where I've done things to fighters that's never been done before," he told Sky Sports.

"I'm not going to say I'm going to do this, I'm not going to say I'm going to do that.

"But I'm going to say in Chris' last fight [against Ryan Rozicki] he had a guy that was standing in front of him and he hit him as hard as he could hit him and the guy was still sitting there till the end of the fight. We shall see.

"I've been pushed in ways that I've never been pushed before, and I've applied things that I've never applied before. So the compound effect of that I'm looking forward to seeing."

Clarke objects to the underdog tag that's been attached to him for this fight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chev Clarke refuses to shake Chris Billam-Smith's hand ahead of their Zuffa Boxing 12 main event this Saturday

"You can't ever count somebody out. It's incredibly arrogant, or incredibly ignorant. Or both," he said.

"I'm already world class. But this will put more eyes on Chev Clarke.

"I don't need to prove nothing to nobody."

Billam-Smith, who has sparred with Clarke as well as boxing him as an amateur, knows the threats he poses.

"I know how good Chev is and I know how good he can be. I'm very switched on," Billam-Smith told Sky Sports.

"I'd argue that every time he's been down, he's come back and he's either won or performed really well in the fight. He carries a lot of danger."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chris Billam-Smith and Chev Clarke share a first fight week face-off ahead of their Zuffa Boxing 12 clash on Saturday

Billam-Smith is using his amateur losses to Clarke as motivation. "I can finally get one over Chev… I'm doing it for that version of me that was heartbroken," he said. "It's nice that I get the opportunity to do and go back to that.

"And also prove that it's not about where you start, it's about where you finish and how you improve and how you make progress."

The stakes are high for Billam-Smith though. He is on a mission to reclaim a world belt. But a defeat at this point could snuff out those hopes once and for all.

"Every fight's a must win, especially at this stage in my career and especially against Chev. There's a huge amount of pressure on it," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chris Billam-Smith believes Oleksandr Usyk's potential return to cruiserweight brings light to the division

Winning, though, would be the gateway to fights with the biggest names in the division.

"You have to see the lay of the land. It seems to change day by day in the cruiserweights at the moment with new information, new news coming out all the time," he said.

"But huge fights out there."

Watch Billam-Smith vs Clarke live on Sky Sports from 7pm.

Sports.title: Leeds United v Tottenham Hotspur: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
now 08.17 EST 45 min: There will be six minutes of additional first-half time, most of which a result of the on-field referee and VAR spending ages failing to make a decision. Share

1m ago 08.15 EST 44 min: Kudus fizzes a tempting low cross through the Leeds six-yard box from the right. What a ball. But neither Gray nor Solanke respond. Any touch and it was the opening goal. Share

3m ago 08.14 EST 43 min: Tel limps off. A heavy trudge, he’s in some difficulty. He’s replaced by Solanke. Share

4m ago 08.13 EST 42 min: Marmoush clips Muharemovic from behind. That should be a booking as well, but the referee has lost control of this with his unwillingness to make any sort of decision whatsoever. Meanwhile Tel goes down, he looks really unhappy. Share

5m ago 08.11 EST 40 min: Tel is getting dog’s abuse now. He’s also moving very gingerly, having recently had someone stand on his ankle. Share

6m ago 08.11 EST 39 min: Roberto De Zerbi isn’t happy about that. You can’t blame him. Meanwhile the game restarts, with Bogle, who shouldn’t be on the pitch, crossing for Nmencha, who plants a header straight at Kinsky. Had that gone in, there would have been some wild scenes all right. Share

7m ago 08.09 EST 38 min: No red card, no serious foul play. That is preposterous enough in itself; that there’s not even a yellow is beyond a joke. The on-field referee should have seen that, at the very least. Share

9m ago 08.07 EST 37 min: VAR is flapping taking a long time over this. You can overthink these things, you know. Share

10m ago 08.06 EST 36 min: It’s a really poor challenge, studs landing on Tel’s achilles, the Spurs player’s leg bending. It should be a red card. Share

11m ago 08.06 EST 35 min: VAR is in fact checking for a red card. The on-field referee, it should be noted, has completely abdicated responsibility. Share

12m ago 08.05 EST 34 min: Bogle leaves one on Tel, who was in the process of spinning him. It’s a really poor challenge, studs on ankle. A red card wouldn’t be out of the question here; there’s not even a yellow shown. View image in fullscreen Mathys Tel recieves treatment after the challenge from Jayden Bogle. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Share Updated at 08.17 EST

13m ago 08.04 EST 33 min: A long pass down the left confuses Elvedi into conceding a corner with a misjudged backwards header. One corner leads to another, then Marmoush heads harmlessly wide. To be fair, Trafford has had next to nothing to do as well, if you ignore a couple of long-range shots scuffed straight at him. Share

14m ago 08.02 EST 31 min: Some pinball just outside the Spurs box. Fernandes tries to walk the ball away from danger but loses it, and Nmecha nearly releases Calvert-Lewin down the inside-left channel. Kinsky comes out to block, then the flag goes up for offside anyway. Kinsky still officially unworked. Share

17m ago 07.59 EST 29 min: Gudmundsson floats a poor cross in from the left. Easy for Kinsky, who has had absolutely nothing to do so far. Share

18m ago 07.58 EST 28 min: Spurs have enjoyed 77 percent of possession in the last five minutes. Share

19m ago 07.57 EST 27 min: Kudus gets the chance to shoot now, though. He drifts infield from the right and shoots. Another one straight at Trafford. Spurs are beginning to create things. Share

20m ago 07.57 EST 26 min: That was a great run by Tel, who appears to have finally blossomed after that wonder goal against Chelsea. Share

21m ago 07.56 EST 25 min: Tel advances down the left at speed, one-twoing with Gray before laying off to Marmoush, who scuffs a shot straight at Trafford. A disappointing end to a slick move, especially as Kudus was free to Marmoush’s right, waiting for the killer pass. Share

22m ago 07.55 EST 24 min: Kudus diddles his way down the right in style, cuts back, then swings a dangerous ball into the mixer, forcing Trafford to punch clear under purple pressure. He does so with authority. Share

24m ago 07.53 EST 22 min: Longstaff steps across Fernandes and earns the second yellow card of the afternoon. Share

25m ago 07.52 EST 21 min: The pace drops, as does the volume in Elland Road. Spurs will be more than happy with all of that. Share

25m ago 07.51 EST 19 min: A long ball down the middle is contested by Marmoush, who looks to have been dragged down by Elvedi, but gets nothing from the referee. Justin was nearby, so Elvedi wasn’t the last man, but it should have been a free kick in a dangerous position. If nothing else, the officials are equal-opportunity inept. Share

29m ago 07.48 EST 17 min: Tonali plays a cute ball round the corner, hoping to release Porro down the right. Not quite. Goal kick. Porro is looking lively, though, and soon after he comes again, his long cross miscontrolled by Tel, just inside the Leeds box on the left. Had Tel killed that, it would have been a big one-on-one chance. Share

31m ago 07.46 EST 15 min: Bogle spins Van de Ven, who was too tight to his man. The Spurs captain grabs at Bogle, and goes into the book as a result. Share

32m ago 07.44 EST 14 min: Porro makes ground down the right and he’s got options in the Leeds box. He floats a poor cross straight into the hands of Trafford. Uncharacteristically meh from the world champion. Share

34m ago 07.43 EST 12 min: Roberto De Zerbi is already at the edge of his technical area, frowning quite a lot. Spurs haven’t put anything together yet. Share

35m ago 07.41 EST 10 min: The xG is currently 0.01 to 0. Something quite pleasing about that. Not sure what. View image in fullscreen Sean Longstaff extends a leg to clear from Tonali and Fernandes. Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 07.49 EST

36m ago 07.40 EST 9 min: Gudmundsson knocks the ball past Porro on the left, wins the footrace with ease, then cuts back for Ampadu, who skies a shot from long distance. This is an impressive start by Leeds. Share Updated at 07.43 EST

38m ago 07.39 EST 8 min: Tanaka drags a shot wide right. Then Gudmundsson wins a corner down the left. Longstaff takes; Kinsky claims. Leeds only turned up after the three-minute mark, but they’re here now, and they’re pushing Spurs back. View image in fullscreen Ao Tanaka with an early effort. Photograph: Ryan Browne/Shutterstock Share Updated at 07.42 EST

40m ago 07.37 EST 6 min: VAR waves away the penalty appeal. They’re making it up as they go along, kids, as anyone who watched last night’s Everton-Coventry fiasco will attest. Fernandes was leaning into that, unnecessarily so, and the ball hit his arm. The VAR has done Spurs a solid there. Everton 3-1 Coventry City: Premier League – as it happened Read more Share

41m ago 07.35 EST 4 min: A cross into the Spurs box from the left. The ball pings off Fernandes’s outstretched right arm. VAR will want a look at this. Why did Fernandes hang his arm out like that?! Share

44m ago 07.33 EST 2 min: Spurs keep hold of the ball for the first minute and 45 seconds. Eventually Trafford claims it. A calm, confident start by the visitors. Share

46m ago 07.30 EST A different fanfare for the common man – the Last Post – sounds poignantly. Silent, solemn remembrance of the fallen. After which Tottenham Hotspur get the ball rolling. View image in fullscreen Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters Share Updated at 07.33 EST

50m ago 07.27 EST The teams emerge from the tunnel, so … Leeds are in their Revie-approved white, so Spurs are forced into third-choice purple. It won’t be long now. Share

55m ago 07.21 EST Pre-match postbag. “Hands up who had Tottenham challenging for Europe and Manchester United challenging for the, er, Championship on their 25%-of-the-season-gone bingo card? No, me neither” – Dave Estherby “Let’s just nip this talk of Tottenham rounding into form in the bud, shall we? Three wins on the bounce is nice until you take a closer look at them. Coventry: ‘nuff said. Chelsea: missing Joao Pedro, and with a dreadful tactical setup in response. Crystal Palace: down a man before the match before the match was a quarter-hour old. You need a fair glob of polish to put a proper gloss on that run” – Eric Peterson Share

1h ago 07.13 EST Roberto De Zerbi’s turn to chat with TNT. “We keep going … keep pushing … a tough game for us … a tough game for them because we are in a good moment … every game starts nil-nil … we have to work hard if we want to win … [Pedro Porro] can bring everything … he is a fantastic guy, a fantastic player … [Archie Gray, who moves from right-back to midfield] deserves to play because he’s playing very well … I am sorry for [substitute] Conor Gallagher because he deserves to play as well.” Share

1h ago 07.00 EST Daniel Farke speaks to TNT Sports. “Spurs are normally dominant in possession so you need to find some solutions in order to be competitive … Sean [Longstaff] is smart … a bit like a third midfield player to control their processes … today is a chance for [Lukas Nmecha] to shine … we want to be dangerous today and score.” Share

2h ago 06.40 EST Leeds can leap to eighth place with a win today. Technically they can make seventh, but they’d need to win this game by seven goals, so come off it and come on. Meanwhile should Spurs win a fourth consecutive Premier League game for the first time in over three years, they can make their way up to sixth, but they’d need a two-goal winning margin to ensure that. Share

2h ago 06.28 EST Leeds have made two changes in the wake of their 2-0 defeat at Bournemouth. Sean Longstaff, starting for the first time this calendar year, and Lukas Nmecha come in for Harry Wilson and Daniel James, who both drop to the bench. Evanilson profits from costly Trafford blunder as Bournemouth punish Leeds Read more Share Updated at 06.36 EST

2h ago 06.27 EST The teams Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Longstaff, Nmecha, Calvert-Lewin.

Subs: Zetterer, Rodon, James, Wilson, Aaronson, Bijol, Okafor, Bard, Gruev. Tottenham Hotspur: Kinsky, Porro, van Hecke, van de Ven, Robertson, Gray, Tonali, Kudus, Fernandes, Tel, Marmoush.
