Sports.content: FIN SMITH interview: I fell a bit out of love with rugby after the Lions tour... it's not a healthy mindset at my age. Now with Jonny Wilkinson's help and England's new style of play, we can get Twickenham shaking again

Sports.title: FIN SMITH interview: I fell a bit out of love with rugby after the Lions tour... it's not a healthy mindset at my age. Now with Jonny Wilkinson's help and England's new style of play, we can get Twickenham shaking again
Sports.content:
FIN SMITH interview: I fell a bit out of love with rugby after the Lions tour... it's not a healthy mindset at my age. Now with Jonny Wilkinson's help and England's new style of play, we can get Twickenham shaking again

A packed crowd fills the main assembly hall at Warwick School to hear from Fin Smith, the England fly-half who has returned to his alma mater on the eve of a crunch autumn campaign.

There is plenty to discuss – England’s fortunes less than a year out from the World Cup, Smith’s personal ambitions, PREM Rugby’s try avalanche, Henry Pollock’s elaborate haircuts... but first, a reality check. ‘I’ve got your GCSE PE fitness test here,’ Warwick headmaster James Barker says ominously to his former pupil.

‘Bleep test... OK, your number of sit-ups a minute... not bad, 3.58 seconds for a 30-metre sprint... this is a message of hope for all of us – you can be bang average and still play for the Lions!’

By Smith’s own admission, he is not ‘the most athletically gifted player’. But he got all A*s at A-Level (biology, chemistry and maths) and was head boy at Warwick. Now, he is top of English rugby’s fly-half class and, after brushing off a calf injury, ready to lead Steve Borthwick’s side into their Nations Championship opener with Australia on Sunday.

‘I’m not sure what’s happened to your facial hair,’ Smith retorts, now able to answer back to Barker, who is sporting a handlebar moustache. ‘It must be a mid-life crisis! I did like my studies here. I was a bit of a goody two-shoes.

'There’s a big asterisk beside my grades though because I did my A-Levels in Covid and I think they just gave you whatever you wanted! Not so long ago I was a pupil in this room, just enjoying my rugby and loving coming to school with my mates. To be back here now is surreal. I’m trying to get out of the habit of calling the teachers sir!’

A packed crowd filled the assembly hall at Warwick School to hear from Fin Smith, the England fly-half who returned to his alma mater for a talk chaired by the Mail's Alex Bywater

But first a reality check from his old headmaster James Barker - who reads out Smith's GCSE PE fitness report

Now, Smith is top of English rugby’s fly-half class and, after brushing off a calf injury, ready to lead Steve Borthwick’s side into their Nations Championship opener with Australia on Sunday

Smith’s Warwick return provided a rare chance for him to reflect on his journey to date. Still only 24, he is already a two-time PREM Rugby champion with Northampton and now one of England’s most important figures after winning a race against his rivals and his fitness to keep hold of the No10 jersey.

He is honest about where England are at ahead of November Tests with the Wallabies, Japan and New Zealand, following five defeats in their last seven and the worst Six Nations in the country's history.

‘Let’s call a spade a spade. We didn’t do very well in the Six Nations,’ says Smith. ‘We got a bit wrong. It’s hard to assess where we are. I think we had a decent summer. The loss in South Africa was tough. But they’re an unbelievable side and beating Fiji and then Argentina away were good results.

'More importantly, I think the style of play we’re looking to use with England suits me, the type of players we’ve got, and the style of play we’ve seen in the PREM. There have been a lot of tries. I think it’s fun and rugby is better for it.

‘There are times with England when we will obviously have to kick the ball, but we’re looking to make a shift to being a team that wants to attack. All fly-halves love the sound of their own voice and feeling like they’ve got control!

'I want us to play and attack. It’s been great to have the backing of the coaches. But I also know if I have a couple of stinkers, I’ll be out of the team. I need to make sure I don’t muck it up! We’ll find out where we’re really at after this autumn.’

With next year’s World Cup in Australia looming, a defining campaign awaits England. After the momentum of a 12-match winning run was brought to a shuddering halt in the Six Nations, there is significant work to do.

England have the players to bid for glory Down Under. But to make up ground on the elites of South Africa, France and New Zealand, consistency in selection and clarity of approach are fundamental. One thing is widely acknowledged – Smith is the right man to guide the ship.

‘Let’s call a spade a spade. We didn’t do very well in the Six Nations,’ says Smith. ‘We got a bit wrong'

Smith is the right man to guide the England ship from the No10 jersey this autumn

To describe him as unflashy would be to underplay his fine ability. But Smith’s greatest attribute is that he brings out the best of those around him. That’s what he does at club level with Northampton. With more time in the saddle, he can do so for England too.

‘When I first started, I thought the coaches were looking for all the flashy stuff – nice tries and chip and chases,’ says Smith, who came through the Worcester academy before making the switch across the Midlands when the Warriors went bust in 2022.

‘Now I realise they are looking for a 10 who is a really good communicator. Someone who is not afraid to boss anyone around and has a strong skillset. I’ve never been the biggest or the fastest, but I’d like to think my team-mates would say I’m one of the hardest workers.

'I started at Worcester and when they went bust, some of my best mates had their careers pulled away in a matter of weeks. I feel a responsibility to them to make every day count.'

So ahead of what could be the biggest year of his career, how does Smith make the next 365 days count?

'At the start of each season, I reflect and set new goals,' he says. 'This year for me there are three – win the PREM again with Northampton, have a crack at winning in Europe, and be the England fly-half at the World Cup.

'It’s quite weird saying that out loud. I grew up watching videos of Jonny Wilkinson in an England No 10 shirt kicking a World Cup final-winning drop-goal in Australia. The fact that’s potentially less than a year away for me makes me hungrier than ever to put everything into this season. That would be me achieving a lifelong dream.

‘I’m lucky enough to know Jonny really well now and have him as a mentor. His drop-goal is the most iconic moment in English rugby. It would be pretty cool to try and recreate that!

‘I’m lucky enough to know Jonny (Wilkinson, right) really well now and have him as a mentor,' says Smith

‘When I first started, I thought the coaches were looking for all the flashy stuff – nice tries and chip and chases'

‘I remember being a pupil at Warwick, looking out of a maths lesson, and seeing the first XV kickers. I looked up to them as superstars,’ he says

'He’s the sort of character that within the first couple of minutes of meeting him, he makes you feel like the superstar and he’s a nobody. It’s slightly strange. He’s an amazing coach and every so often, he puts you back in your place when he pings a 50-metre drop goal off his wrong foot. He’s still got it!

'I text him most days and we call every other week or so. He’s helped me so much, not just with my kicking but the mental side of things too. He’s also quite a cool name drop to have in your back pocket!’

At Warwick, pupils are constantly told of the importance of the school’s Latin motto altiora peto – ‘I seek higher things’. With Smith at the helm, that must be the aim for England this month.

‘I remember being a pupil at Warwick, looking out of a maths lesson, and seeing the first XV kickers. I looked up to them as superstars,’ he says. 'I used to think it would be so cool if that was me. That is why it was so important to me to come back here and present my England and Lions shirts to the school.

‘If a few people here put on their TV in the next month, watch me play for England and think to themselves, “That’s Fin, he went to the same school as me”, I think that’s pretty cool. Hopefully, I can inspire others. That would mean as much to me as any trophy.’

Quickfire Q&A: Fin Smith

Best advice for young players?

The older I’ve got, the more I’ve learned to play on instinct. I try to see space on the field and use it. I don’t try and overcomplicate things.

Best part about being famous?

I’m not famous! Every so often you get some free stuff. I’ve just moved house and got a free mattress. My Scottish heritage means I’m tight, so that was good!

Have you ever had doubts?

I lost a lot of confidence after the Lions tour. I didn’t play as well as I would have liked and maybe fell out of love with rugby a little bit. That wasn’t a healthy mindset for someone who is still very young. I try to see rugby for what it is. It’s my job, but it’s also just a sport and it should be something you enjoy, even if you’re playing at the highest level.

What do you make of Eddie Hearn’s involvement in rugby?

It’s great. Rugby is a little bit old school and maybe some people don’t like those who are outspoken. But in terms of getting more eyes on the game, you can see he’s good at that. He’s done it with lots of other sports.

'I lost a lot of confidence after the Lions tour. I didn’t play as well as I would have liked and maybe fell out of love with rugby a little bit'

On Northampton team-mate Henry Pollock's cornrows: 'He’s playing well and with a fancy haircut, people will always talk about you! He’s the most talented individual I’ve ever seen'

'Twickenham is the best rugby stadium in the world. My fondest memory there was when we beat France in the last play on my first England start. I genuinely felt the ground shaking'

What’s it like when you’re injured?

It’s really difficult. At Northampton, we make a big thing about involving injured players. It’s easy when you’re injured to feel like you’re cast away. It’s important to use any injury as a positive and not a negative. For example, if you’ve hurt your lower body, use extra time to work on your passing.

Toughest opponent?

Malcolm Marx, the South African hooker. I ran into him when we played them in the summer and he didn’t move. I hit the floor, looked up, and he just smiled. I thought to myself, 'I’m in the wrong sport!'. He’s a big angry man. I was sore for the next week!

Twickenham verdict?

It’s the best rugby stadium in the world. My fondest memory there was when we beat France in the last play on my first England start (in 2025). I genuinely felt the ground shaking. We want to bring that back and give the supporters something to cheer about. Singing the national anthem there will never get old. It gives me goosebumps just thinking about it.

And finally... what did you think of Henry Pollock’s cornrows?

I thought it was very clever. He’s playing well and with a fancy haircut, people will always talk about you! He’s the most talented individual I’ve ever come across. It’s infuriating. I’ve never seen a player who rises to the big occasion like he does. He relishes it.

Sports.title: Derided Thierno Barry is no longer a source of frustration as star fires Everton to victory over Coventry on another big night for David Moyes amid Jack Grealish drama
Sports.content:
Maybe Everton should request to play under the lights every week. It certainly seems to push David Moyes' team to new heights. Following hot on the heels of consecutive night victories over Newcastle United, Friday's 3-1 win against Coventry City was a reminder of why, under Moyes, there is renewed sense of optimism at Everton. Up to fifth, above Liverpool, and in a Carabao Cup quarter-final at Fleetwood, it could prove to be a special season. This always felt like a big task for Frank Lampard, back at Everton for the first time since his sacking in 2023. Popular as the ex-manager may be, there's no room for sentiment, certainly not from Moyes on a night he took charge of his 592nd game, drawing level with Harry Catterick for managing the most games in the club's history. He'll set it outright after the international break against Brentford and Keith Andrews, who was 21 when Moyes first took up the reins at Everton.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Thierno Barry (right) now has 10 goals this season after being widely derided in his first season on Merseyside Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall had been left out of the England squad in the morning, but refused to let it spoil his night His side started impressively, fashioning three shots in the opening 10 minutes, before losing all momentum and allowing Coventry into proceedings. It took going 1-0 down, to a soft Yann Gboho goal, for the hosts to come alive. Thierno Barry, so often the source of frustration last season, was magnificent and all but won the game with a five-minute brace in the second half. The striker didn't score his first goal until December last season. This campaign, he's reached 10 before the second international break. Moyes joked post-match that Erling Haaland should watch his back in the Golden Boot race is starting to feel less absurd. Barry now sits joint second in the charts. Both goals against Coventry came via back post-duels. The first he confidently headed past Carl Rushworth, before bundling in a second five minutes later. The disgruntled home fans booed the team off at half-time, yet were jubilantly cheering and signing after Barry's brace. The Frenchman danced on the pitch at full-time and was serenaded by the South Stand. 'I don't see loads of young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League,' said Moyes. 'He's come in and has settled in a bit more. His language and communication is better and obviously he's worked to get himself into the positions to score.' Barry wasn't the only Everton goalscorer, of course. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was not one of the three Everton players named in Thomas Tuchel's England squad on Friday - only Arsenal had more representatives. MATCH FACTS EVERTON (4-2-3-1): Pickford 5; Rohl 5 (O'Brien 73min, 6), Tarkowski 5, Branthwaite 6 (Keane 89), Mykolenko 6; Armstrong 6 (Hackney 73, 6), Garner 6; Dibling 5 (Johnson 73, 5), DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 5 (Alcaraz 90); Barry 8. Scorers: Barry 56, 61 Dewsbury-Hall 81. Booked: Branthwaite. Manager: David Moyes 6. COVENTRY CITY (4-2-3-1): Rushworth 4; van Ewijk 5, Mfuni 6, Pinnock 6, Dasilva 6; Yirenkyi 6, Torp 6 (Grimes 86); Sakamoto 5 (Tchaouna 86), Rudoni 5 (Hamer 86), Gboho 6 (Thomas-Asante 73, 5); Awoniyi 5 (Cherif 87). Scorer: Gboho 52. Booked: Yirenkyi. Manager: Frank Lampard 5. Referee: Stuart Attwell 6. Attendance: 52,395. But the midfielder sent a pointed message to the Three Lions' boss with a superb showing that was capped with a late powerful goal to end the contest. 'It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie,' Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports after the game. 'It's a massive dream to play for my country. I know I was close. 'Yeah, sad, but really proud of myself and how I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up. I've got the mentality. I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens.' 'He's desperate to play for England,' added Moyes. 'You never know if England get a couple of injuries, or anything changes.' What ended as a comfortable win could have been a different outcome had Jame Tarkowski been punished for a hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi, or if Vitalii Mykolenko's tussle with Taiwo Awoniyi in the box had been deemed a foul. Both were checked and cleared by VAR, as was a handball claim in the build-up to Barry's second goal. 'Tarky pulls on Caleb's hair, they [VAR] are saying it's not enough of a pull,' said an aggrieved Lampard afterwards. 'That's a hard area to be in. What is hair pull and what's not? 'I think Taiwo, on the edge of the box was a penalty. I feel there's a penalty by the time Myko's knee is in the back of Taiwo's knee on the line of the box. 'Then the Barry one is handball. He flicks it in [with the hand] with the final touch. Nothing went for us tonight.'

Sports.title: Why it's all gone wrong for Charlton: JAMES SHARPE reveals the summer failures, a player's mysterious disappearance and murmurs of yet another sale as Nathan Jones' side teeter on the brink
Sports.content:
Fear is creeping back in at the Valley. Charlton’s defeat by Bolton on Tuesday night, their fourth on the bounce, was greeted with the cacophony of boos it deserved.

Eleven games without a win and teetering above the Championship relegation zone. A fanbase that has been down this long and treacherous road before, and sure as hell doesn’t want to tread it again.

Certainly not when they thought those dark days were, at last, behind them. Only 10 weeks ago, Charlton sat top of the table after victory over Preston completed a hat-trick of early season wins, including a famous triumph in front of a record Championship attendance of 62,264 at West Ham.

It was a false dawn. For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards.

Charlton looked destined for relegation to League Two for the first time in their history when Jones took over in February 2024. They went 14 games unbeaten and survived. After spending eight of the previous nine seasons in the third tier, he took them up via the play-offs at the next time of asking and, last season, kept them in the Championship.

For a club that had endured so much instability, a period of normality and steady progression was on the cards. Jones is Charlton’s ninth managerial appointment since June 2016. Only now, the wonder is how much longer this can go on before nine becomes 10.

Fear is creeping back in at the Valley with Charlton 11 games without a win and teetering on the brink of the Championship relegation zone

For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards

‘If I hadn’t done what I’ve done at this football club, it would have been an easier decision for them (the owners),’ Jones told South London Sport this week. ‘I have to win football games. Win games or you don’t survive.’

His next chance is against ninth-placed Sheffield United this Saturday afternoon. Jones insists he maintains a strong relationship with the Charlton board. The new chief executive Ben Mansford – formerly of Leeds, Blackpool and Barnsley and who ended the club’s spell of 19 months without one – twice tried to hire Jones at his previous clubs. Jones is understood still to have the backing of his players.

Perhaps it’s not best to let him know that both Alan Pardew and Chris Powell lost their jobs after defeats by the Blades.

‘We've spent a lot of time in League One recently and I think there is a kind of head-in-hands worry at the moment: please let's not go back there again,’ Heather McKinlay, chair of the Charlton Athletic Supporters' Trust tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘At the moment, it feels more like duty than fun. I think we have become a little bit worn down because we've been through the mill so much with the changes of ownership and the shenanigans over the near 20 years since we were in the Premier League.’

They have been through the mill, much of the difficulties driven by those in charge. Former owner Roland Duchatelet, who still owns the Valley and the training ground, once accused fans of wanting the club to fail. Charlton’s fans responded to his comments and mismanagement by carrying a red coffin to the Valley followed by a crowd of mourners in a mock funeral protest against his ownership.

They lobbed hundreds of plastic pigs on the pitch for one game, beach balls to halt another, and sent a black cab to Belgium as a ’Taxi for Roland’.

Within weeks of Duchatelet selling Charlton to businessmen Tahnoon Nimer and Matt Southall for £1, the two new men were embroiled in a bitter public row. Nimer accused Southall of using club money to fund his own lifestyle, which he denied, including renting a £150,000-a-year flat in London and giving a fleet of Range Rovers to his associates. Charlton fans occupied the boardroom in protest. Thomas Sandgaard, the next owner, was arrested by the FBI this year and charged with fraud. He denies any wrongdoing.

The highly impressive win away to West Ham in August now appears to have been a false dawn

Jones is Charlton's ninth manager in the last 10 years - but how long can he keep this up?

‘Charlton fans are a proactive lot,’ adds McKinlay. ‘If they feel they can make a difference, they’ll do something. I don’t feel we can do anything right now other than cheer them on. I think the ownership want the club to succeed. The manager wants the club to succeed. The players want the club to succeed. There's not really a baddie in this.’

As one club insider put it this week, it’s nice, in a strange way, that football is the main issue for once and not what’s going on off the field.

There is still a sense of that, mind. The current ownership group known as Global Football Partners is made up of seven shareholders, each with more than five per cent, but it remains unclear who is the driving force. Sources suggest some are more willing than others to put their money in with murmurings that the club is once again up for sale. Charlton insist they are merely looking for more investment to help drive the club forward.

Poor recruitment has not helped matters either. All the talk in the summer was about ‘evolving’ from a team that could get out of League One, then stay in the Championship, to one that could compete.

The club, however, spent a net total of just £1.5million this summer. They failed to find the right winger they needed, as a deal for Crystal Palace winger Jesurun Rak-Sakyi collapsed late on. Instead they signed teenager Junior Nkeng, who hasn’t played a single minute. A lack of creative midfielder is glaring too.

As for those who did arrive, Millenic Alli infuriated supporters in the defeat by Bolton when he headed the ball blindly into no man’s land during stoppage time with the team desperately searching for an equaliser. Nathaniel Chalobah arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He showed his class at the start of the season, got injured, returned and is now injured again.

That’s not to mention the bizarre mystery surrounding midfielder Timothy Ouma. The Kenya international, on loan from Slavia Prague, went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since. Ouma, who has not featured in a single matchday squad since the break, has previous for this, having also failed to return after international duty while on loan at Lech Poznan.

When Jones was asked about it a few weeks ago, he responded by saying: ‘We will address those rumours when they become relevant. Anything we need to put out, we will put out.’

Kenyan midfielder Timothy Ouma went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since

Nathaniel Chalobah (right) arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He got injured, returned and is now injured again

Charlton remain tight-lipped on whether Ouma is still absent, though one insider admitted they still hadn’t seen him since the players returned from international duty. The Kenyan FA did not respond to requests for clarification.

It makes the decision to part ways with club captain Greg Docherty in the summer look even more misguided, with this a team lacking in leadership. Jones has been left to throw all the pieces up in the air and see where they land with constant changes to the team and the line-up. Selection and formation roulette, as some are calling it.

The Welshman is not everyone’s cup of tea, frequently mocked for his David Brent style, but there’s still a belief, not least from himself, that he can turn things around. ‘He’s a maverick, but he’s our maverick,’ laughs McKinlay.

Time is running out, though, because if Charlton cannot find their way again, the alternative is already too unnerving to think about.

Sports.title: 'I want to win the Ballon d'Or': JJ Gabriel sets out his lofty ambitions as Man United wonderkid, 16, closes in on move to Real Madrid after quitting Red Devils
Sports.content:
Manchester United wonderkid JJ Gabriel has revealed his ambition to win the Ballon d'Or as he dropped the clearest hint yet that he is heading to Real Madrid in an interview with Spanish media.

The 16-year-old sensation stunned Manchester United with a formal transfer request in September and is now on the verge of finalising his move to the Spanish capital.

Daily Mail Sport exclusively revealed Madrid's growing confidence in securing the free-scoring starlet last month, with Gabriel now having secured a European Union passport through his mother's Cypriot heritage.

The youngster, who is currently working with a personal trainer in Madrid, practically confirmed the transfer in an interview with Spanish newspaper Marca on Friday night, admitting he had a clear preference to Real over archrivals Barcelona.

'Obviously Madrid,' Gabriel told the outlet when asked which LaLiga giant he preferred.

According to the newspaper, who expects his move to be finalised in January, Gabriel's response prompted a laugh from his father and mentor Joe O'Cearuill.

Manchester United prodigy JJ Gabriel poses for his interview with Spanish newspaper Marca

Gabriel is set to complete a move to Real Madrid after formally requesting to leave Old Trafford

'My dream is to win the Ballon d'Or,' explained the talented youngster, who scored a hat-trick for Manchester United in the UEFA Youth League just days before submitting his transfer request.

Although Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe and Barcelona's Lamine Yamal narrowly missed out on winning the 2026 Ballon d'Or - which was held aloft by England captain and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane - the two LaLiga giants have long had a rich association with the award, regularly producing the world's best footballer.

While sources at United insist there has been no club-to-club contact, it appears only a matter of time before Gabriel is sporting Real Madrid's iconic all-white jersey.

It is understood Gabriel will play for Madrid's Castilla team, which plays in Spain's third division, as well as in the Youth League.

Gabriel broke a series of records playing for United youth teams, including becoming the youngest player to feature in the Under-18s.

The prodigy, who was 14 when he netted twice on his debut, has also played - and scored - for Manchester United's Under-21 side.

The Red Devils were rocked in September when Gabriel and his representatives made a bombshell request to have his academy contract torn up. That request was immediately refused by United and, while there was faint hope that a compromise could have been found to keep him at Old Trafford, he has stayed away ever since.

Gabriel's dream is to win the Ballon d'Or, which was awarded this year to England's Harry Kane

As Daily Mail Sport previously reported, United's decline since the days of Sir Alex Ferguson has been the driving force behind Gabriel's family seeking an exit. United have not won a Premier League title since 2013.

A source close to the family explained that United are 'far away' from the likes of Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, as well as domestic rivals Arsenal and Manchester City, and that they want him to 'learn from the best' to maximise his talents.

His father has been described as a fiercely ambitious, pushy parent and is credited with the decision to get JJ out of United in an attempt to fast-track his career.

Sports.title: 'Winning at the Emirates is very hard... but we were a team of warriors': Hull City hero GEOVANNI on his iconic goal against Arsenal, why it very nearly never happened and why the Tigers 'will always be in my heart'
Sports.content:
The greatest moment in Hull City's Premier League history began with Geovanni trying to go home.

'I was ill all night, I barely slept at all,' says Geovanni, who was gripped by a fever and thumping headache less than 24 hours before he was due to walk out at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium in September 2008. The Brazilian rang his wife from the team hotel to tell her he was coming home and planned to have someone pick him up.

Thankfully, his wife Roberta would not hear of it.

'God really used her that day,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'She said: "Geovanni, stay there, God will honour you. Hang on and tomorrow try to get a bit of sleep."'

When Hull staff came to his room the next morning, he asked to be left to sleep. He dosed up on medicine and went for lunch, but sat out the light pre-match training session with his temperature touching 38 degrees Celsius.

'And then I got to that game, which was so spectacular,' he says, 'and I was able to score and help Hull beat Arsenal.'

Geovanni unleashes a spectacular equaliser for Hull at the Emirates Stadium back in September 2008

The goal inspired a famous comeback win for the Tigers, who became only the second team to win away at Arsenal

It was Hull's first league meeting with Arsenal for 93 years, in the first top-flight season of the club's then 104-year history.

Arsene Wenger's side had started the day top of the table and Paul McShane's own goal put Arsenal ahead after 51 minutes. Most expected the floodgates to open.

But 11 minutes later up stepped Hull's brilliant Brazilian, a marquee signing from Manchester City in the summer of 2008 after the Tigers' unexpected promotion.

Geovanni cut inside Theo Walcott and sent a 25-yard rocket into Manuel Almunia's top corner. Daniel Cousin headed in a historic winner four minutes later and Hull became only the second side to beat Arsenal at the Emirates.

'Beating Arsenal at the Emirates is very hard, and we pulled it off,' says Geovanni, now 46, speaking from his home in Brazil. 'That was a team of warriors, great players, and we had a really good friendship. And that day we walked away with a great win.'

On Saturday, Hull return to the Emirates to face the champions and league leaders. The Tigers are 11th after nine games. It is a strong start that few predicted.

'Hull have to give 100 per cent, the maximum, be switched on the whole time,' says Geovanni. 'It's difficult, but it's not impossible, because Hull really did beat Arsenal.'

Eight days after the Emirates match, Geovanni did it again. A stunning 30-yard free-kick at White Hart Lane nestled into the top corner past his friend and compatriot Heurelho Gomes.

'We beat Tottenham with Gareth Bale, Luka Modric, all those players,' he says. 'For me, those two are top-drawer. They're two great players who left a mark on me.'

The win moved Hull into third and by the end of October they were level on points at the top. 'London 0 Hull 2' read the headline in the local paper, in reference to Hull band The Housemartins' 1986 album London 0 Hull 4, as the city revelled in its newfound fame.

Geovanni (centre) was part of another iconic Premier League moment, when Phil Brown gave his team a public dressing down at half-time of a loss at Manchester City

The Brazilian returned to Hull's MKM Stadium last year and received a hero's welcome

Geovanni took centre stage. Arriving on a free that summer after being released by Manchester City, he credits manager Phil Brown and assistant Brian Horton for giving him a second chance in the Premier League.

'They were very special people in allowing me to stay in England, which was my dream,' he says. 'And I learned a lot from both of them. Brian was a very experienced coach, he played for Hull, he managed there, so the affection and respect are huge. Whenever I can talk about them, I do.

'In the first year, Hull surprised a lot of people precisely because of the way we played. Sometimes we'd start in a 4-3-1-2, I played as the No10 behind two strikers. And if we were struggling to mark, I'd drop in to close down the left flank and we'd go back to a 4-4-2.'

The dressing room did the rest. Richard Garcia, an Australian winger with Uruguayan parents, helped translate team talks from English into Spanish and captain Ian Ashbee, Nicky Barmby and Bernard Mendy all made Geovanni feel welcome. 'I'm really happy about the friendships I made in that dressing room,' he says.

Geovanni was part of another of the Premier League's most iconic moments, when he and his team-mates received a public dressing down from his manager on the pitch at half-time of a 5-1 loss to Manchester City on Boxing Day 2008. Eleven months later, Jimmy Bullard scored a penalty before recreating the telling off in celebration.

'It was good for breaking the ice,' says Geovanni. 'From that day on the atmosphere got better too, because we can all make mistakes. The most important thing is to admit the mistake and move on.'

Geovanni's finest moment for Manchester City, with whom he spent one season after stints with Barcelona, Benfica and Cruzeiro, came in the Manchester derby, where he was called into the side by manager Sven-Goran Eriksson because Stephen Ireland was ill.

'He called me over and said, "Geovanni, this game... are you ready?". That was the best news I'd had all day, knowing I was going to start.' The day did, in fact, get better. Geovanni scored the only goal in a 1-0 victory.

Geovanni smashes home a winner for City in the Manchester derby, a year before his move to Hull

United were a familiar victim. In December 2005, his diving header for Benfica helped knock Sir Alex Ferguson's side out of the Champions League in the group stages

He struck again against United in November 2008, in a 4-3 defeat for Hull at Old Trafford

United were a familiar victim. In December 2005, his diving header for Benfica helped knock Sir Alex Ferguson's side out of the Champions League in the group stages, while he also scored in a 4-3 defeat for Hull at Old Trafford in 2008.

'A player has to turn up in the big games,' he says. 'United were a machine back then: Giggs, Paul Scholes, Gary Neville, Anderson, Ronaldo, Rooney.'

Geovanni's greatest regret, though, remains that he didn't heed the advice of Barca boss Louis van Gaal, who wanted to turn the wannabe striker into a wing-back.

He reflects: 'If I could go back in time, I'd listen to what Van Gaal said, because it would have been easier for me to fight for a place at wing-back than as a striker, where there were great players: Javier Saviola, Rivaldo, Patrick Kluivert, Marc Overmars.'

Luiz Felipe Scolari, his coach at Cruzeiro, gave him his only senior Brazil cap, against Mexico at the 2001 Copa America. 'It was a dream for me: to leave a town of 4,000 people (Acaiaca) and one day represent Brazil,' he says. 'He (Scolari) was a father to me.'

These days Geovanni is a volunteer pastor in Belo Horizonte and runs a players' agency with his father-in-law and an old youth-team friend.

But Hull will always be in his heart. He has a picture of himself in a Hull shirt in his house and received a hero's return after heading back to the city last year.

'I love them (the fans). I have a very special affection for the Hull supporters,' he says. 'It was two years in which I gave everything. I went back there last year and was really well received, it was great: friends from my time there, the fans too.

Battling Blackburn's Damien Duff in a pre-season friendly in his Barcelona days. He spent only two seasons with the Catalan club, having left Cruzeiro to move to Europe

'I'm very grateful for everything they did for me. Hull and the fans will always be in my heart'

'And I know I left my mark on the club's history. Whenever people talk about Hull City, about Brazilians, they'll remember Geovanni, the time I spent there, the feats we achieved together.

'And I believe I gave those fans a lot of joy, in games that seemed impossible. God blessed me and I was able to score goals and bring joy to that city. I'm very grateful for everything they did for me. Hull and the fans will always be in my heart.

'My two years at Hull were perhaps the two most special years for me. The sweetest spell of my career.'

Sports.title: 'People keep telling me it's great I'm managing against my son... it's not - it's horrible': Peterborough boss ROBBIE SAVAGE and Reading star CHARLIE on their 'awkward' FA Cup showdown, playing for Man United and dangers facing modern young players
Sports.content:
The FA Cup cast its spell upon the Savages while they were out shopping for groceries.

Reading midfielder Charlie was strolling the aisles of the Marks & Spencer foodhall with his girlfriend when his phone began to buzz. He remembered it was first-round draw day.

He fished out the phone, saw the cascade of messages and realised, as they like to say in M&S, this was not just any FA Cup draw. He called his dad.

Peterborough United boss Robbie was in the Co-op. He had stopped on his way back to the rented lodgings he describes as a 'little annexe in someone's garden' and was rummaging through the ready meals in search of a spaghetti bolognese for one when he answered.

'The reception in Peterborough isn't great, it kept cutting out,' Robbie tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Charlie said: "You won't believe the draw." I thought he was going to say Forest Green. Or Macclesfield. I didn't think about Reading. He said: "You've got us." I just went: "Oh no."'

They were on a collision course from the moment Robbie left Forest Green for the Posh job last month. The teams were scheduled to meet in League One next month at Reading but the FA Cup draw caught them off guard.

Peterborough boss Robbie Savage (right) with his son, Reading midfielder Charlie. The pair will meet in the FA Cup first round at London Road on Saturday

'This will be the first time I hope my son doesn't have an impact, which is a horrible feeling,' Robbie tells Daily Mail Sport

And while they were both at great pains to stress that Saturday's tie at London Road, screened live on TNT Sports, is about Peterborough and Reading not their little family gathering, they can appreciate the fuss.

'Football is a beautiful game, it brings people together and creates rivalries,' says Charlie. 'This week it's created a rivalry in our family. I'm not sure who my mum, brother, grandparents and cousins will support but there's no better time for them to have a half-and-half scarf.'

For Robbie, the beauty of the occasion is yet to unfurl itself. 'It's going to be horrible,' he says. 'Every time I watch my sons play, I'm anxious. I'm nervous. I want them to do well. If they give the ball away and the other team attack, I've got butterflies thinking, "Please don't score".

'This will be the first time I hope my son doesn't have an impact, which is a horrible feeling. People keep telling me it's great. I've got to say it's not great, it's horrible. Usually we speak every day and I've not been able to speak to him all week because I don't want to put him in a position where anything gets out and anyone can point a finger at him.

'I don't want it to be billed as Savage v Savage because it's not. Charlie might not play but if he plays and makes a mistake and we score the winner, so be it. If he plays and scores the winner, well, wow.'

Robbie puffs out his cheeks and widens his eyes as he considers this scenario. 'We've got to win for Peterborough United,' he adds.

Ironically, it was a passion relit by coaching his sons which tempted the former Leicester, Birmingham and Blackburn midfielder out of the comfort of his media work and into coaching. Savage helped out with his youngest son Freddie's Under 13s team in the Timperley and District Junior Sunday League.

'Standing out at training on a Tuesday and Thursday night,' says Robbie. 'Sunday morning, putting the nets up. I've been that dad. In the first season we were hammered 13-0, but we built a team and won a lot of things.'

Charlie Savage in action for Reading. The midfielder played 45 games for the club last season but has yet to start a league match during this campaign

Savage offers some advice to his team in his new role as manager of Peterborough

Two years ago, Charlie and Freddie implored their father to follow his heart and make the switch from sporting director to manager at Macclesfield in the Northern Premier League.

'Even back then, he said one day he'd manage against me,' Charlie tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I was in League One and he was in Step Three and I'm thinking, "Well, give it a few years", but he always gets where he wants to get to.

'He's a competitor. He wants to win, wants to succeed. Even with my little brother's team it hurt him to lose in Sunday morning grassroots football. That's something inside him and it won't change.

'He will want to beat us. Unfortunately for him, I'm the same. I want to win. There might be an awkward car journey home.'

Charlie's memories of his father playing football are from Derby, the last stop of a 15-year professional career which started at Manchester United and took in seven different clubs, as well as 39 Wales caps. 'I remember seeing his long hair, scurrying around the pitch,' says the 23-year-old. 'Throwing his arms up and shouting at the refs.'

Like his dad, Charlie also came through United's youth ranks and made one first-team appearance, as a substitute at the age of 18 against Young Boys in the Champions League. It was an unforgettable night for Robbie, who was on co-commentary duty with a lump in his throat.

'He'll always have that on me,' says Robbie. 'All I ever wanted to do from 14 to 19 was play for one minute in Manchester United's first team. It didn't happen and he's done it. His name is on the wall at Carrington and mine isn't.

'I'm so glad his name is there instead of mine. You want the best for your sons. I'm proud of both my sons.'

Charlie has three Wales caps and counting. His father won 39...

...but despite both Charlie and Robbie coming through the Manchester United academy, only Charlie played for the first team (above), against Young Boys at Old Trafford in 2021

Freddie is studying for an economics degree at the University of Manchester. Charlie left United for Reading four years ago and now has 175 senior appearances and three Wales caps under his belt and a reputation in his own right.

'He's got a great left foot, passing range and incredible running ability,' says Robbie. 'He's intelligent. Nine As in his GCSEs. He doesn't drink, he lives his life 24 hours a day, seven days a week to be a footballer. He's a down-to-earth, humble kid.

'He was so brave to go and play senior football when he had three years left at Manchester United, and it's paid off. He played 45 games last season. He hasn't started a league game this season but hasn't sulked.

'I was a sulker, as Martin O'Neill and Nigel Clough (who coached Savage at Leicester and Derby respectively) will tell you. If that was me, my body language would be negative, but he's got a great attitude. And I've tried to tell him now he has to train harder than ever and conduct himself in the right way.'

If Robbie is a guiding light and inspiration for Charlie, vital information flows both ways for an aspiring manager with a young team.

'The mindset of a Millennial is completely different to when I played,' says the 52-year-old Posh boss. 'If they're not in the team or the manager has shouted at them, they go home to an apartment where they live alone away from their families, isolated from 2pm to 7am with all that time to think about it.

'We have to understand their vulnerabilities on and off the pitch. Charlie has been through that so without knowing it, he's made me a better manager. I try to think about what's best for my players, what I'd want a manager to do for Charlie in that situation.'

'He gives it out and he can take it and, unfortunately, it has become part of his life to be on the receiving end,' Charlie says of his dad Robbie

'Great left foot, passing range and incredible running ability,' says Robbie of his son Charlie

Being the Son of Sav cannot be easy. Not only the added scrutiny and expectation, and accusations doors have been opened for him by a famous and influential father, but also in a world where footballers are too often considered fair game for abuse whether inside the stadium or online.

'It's there in all forms of life,' admits Charlie. 'Maybe people subconsciously want me to fail a little bit more because of who he is. I get it. Football is a game and my dad is a divisive figure inside that game.

'He gives it out and he can take it and, unfortunately, it has become part of his life to be on the receiving end. Sometimes the abuse goes too far. People forget he's a human not just a football personality.

'But I wouldn't change who he is. I wouldn't change having him as my dad, I'm very proud of him.'

Sports.title: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina SNUBS photo op with rivals Aryna Sabalenka and Mirra Andreeva amid Russia conflict - weeks after ending marriage due to distress from the war
Sports.content:
Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina SNUBS photo op with rivals Aryna Sabalenka and Mirra Andreeva amid Russia conflict - weeks after ending marriage due to distress from the war

The Women's Tennis Association was forced to scrap its traditional group photoshoot ahead of the 2026 Finals on Friday, after Elina Svitolina refused to take part alongside her rivals.

The eight tennis stars set to feature in the Indian Wells showdown posed for individual photos in a new feature the association has branded Courtside Couture - in what they say allows players to show off their individuality and fashion.

But reports suggest that the change from the traditional group photograph to individual portraits stems in part from Svitolina's refusal to be pictured with Mirra Andreeva and Aryna Sabalenka, with her rivals hailing from Russia and Belarus respectively.

Svitolina, who has also refused to shake hands with Russian and Belarusian athletes since Vladimir Putin invaded her homeland, is set to face Andreeva and Sabalenka in the competition's group phase.

The 32-year-old made headlines last month after announcing her split from tennis husband Gael Monfils, citing distress from the four-year conflict as a leading cause of her marriage breakdown.

'This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share. Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside,' the world No 6 wrote on social media.

Elina Svitolina (left) has refused to pose alongside Aryna Sabalenka (right) and Mirra Andreeva

The world's best players are facing off in a showdown at the WTA Finals in Indian Wells

Ukraine's Svitolina is set to face Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva in the WTA Finals

'Gael saw all of it. He never let go of my hand. We fought through this together for a long time, with everything we had. But some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you.

'Please know that there is no one to blame here. There are only two people who loved each other deeply and a story that is changing shape.'

Svitolina, who married Monfils in July 2021 and shares a four-year-old daughter with him, stressed that their child will remain their top priority as they navigate their separation.

'Skai will always come first,' she continued. 'Our marriage is ending, but our family is not. We will always be her parents, side by side, at every step of her life.'

As part of her Instagram post, Svitolina shared a black and white picture of her and Monfils embracing solemnly, showing unity and togetherness despite ultimately deciding to go their separate ways.

Svitolina cut short her 2025 season due to psychological fatigue and exhaustion, expressing in an Instagram statement last year that she was 'not in the right emotional space' to continue and needed to 'heal and recharge'.

Her statement led to backlash from tennis fans, with a heartbroken Monfils cutting short his playing career earlier than his intended retirement date.

The 40-year-old Frenchman launched a staunch defence of his soon-to-be ex-wife, hitting back at his critics on Instagram: 'Even though she did not owe anyone an explanation, Elina chose to speak vulnerably and truthfully about her reasons for this decision.

'She did so in the best way she knew how. Many decided that her explanation wasn't perfect enough and Elina has now faced a kind of criticism that I have found unkind at best and venomous at worst.

View this post on Instagram

Svitolina announced her split from tennis star husband Gael Monfils last month

'Elina and I may no longer be a couple, but we are still a family. Though my heart hurts, I am forever grateful to her for her support and love over the years.

'While I am deeply grateful that the public feels so invested in my happiness, I have found the lack of grace and kindness shown towards Elina upsetting.

'While some may not understand her reasons, or agree with them, please remember that there is so much more that happens in a relationship behind the curtain that cannot be explained in a post.

'Elina has her battles to fight, just as I have mine. I respect her choices and reasons, and we will continue to support and care deeply about each other, especially as two people who share a child.'

Sports.title: Frank Lampard outlines crucial role for Coventry City's 12th man this season
Sports.content:
Frank Lampard outlines crucial role for Coventry City's 12th man this season

Coventry City have made a decent start to life in the Premier League despite Friday night's loss at Everton

View Image Frank Lampard believes Coventry City's fans are key to their Premier League survival

Frank Lampard believes the connection between Coventry City's players and supporters can be a major strength as the Sky Blues navigate life back in the Premier League.

‌



‌



The Coventry boss has praised the club's fanbase for the role they have played in the team's recent successes and insisted their backing has acted like having a 12th man on the pitch.

‌



Having guided Coventry back to the top flight after a 25-year absence, Lampard has seen a special relationship forged between the players and supporters during his time at the club.

‌



"The connection between players and fans is a huge thing," he said. “It's a two-way thing, with the players performing with passion and energy. Once that engages the fans and we have their backing, it can really heighten [the team’s] performance and make [the Coventry Building Society Arena] a very difficult place for opposition teams to come.

"Also, in certain tough moments, when the fans are behind the players, they can lift them and help them find renewed confidence. We've got an incredible fanbase and it's one of the biggest strengths of the football club.

“I'm certainly very appreciative of the support they've given me, and I try to keep working as hard as I can to keep getting it and paying my bit back.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Coventry's return to the Premier League was confirmed following a 1-1 draw away at Blackburn Rovers in April, ending a journey that had lasted a quarter of a century and had seen the club drop to League Two in 2017, before winning three promotions in nine years.

‌



And for Lampard, what Coventry achieved in Lancashire seven months ago carried extra significance because of the struggles the club and its supporters had endured before his arrival.

"I saw the Coventry story from the outside, and it was obviously a difficult story in football,” he continued. “A top-tier club that was going through so many challenges.

‌



"They have a certain robustness and resilience because of what they've been through, which is relatively unique. It's added to the story. It's brought not just a football club, but a city together.

"We really felt that in the celebrations at the end of last season. It shows you the power of football.”

‌



Lampard also acknowledged the bond between players and fans has been strengthened by the genuine commitment to the club shown on the pitch.

"I must give credit to the players too,” he said. “When fans see players who give everything for the club and buy into the connection and what the club is, and show that they're not just passing through and they're actually loving being at Coventry, that starts the connection.”

‌



"It's something that's been very, very good for us over the last two years. It's going to be tested more this season in the Premier League. But that connection can be a real strength of ours that will help us try to succeed in whatever way we can."

Lampard was speaking during filming to promote Coventry Building Society’s Sky Blue Line – a telephone that functions as a direct contact between friends, family and fans to help motivate and support Lampard and his players.

Article continues below

“When you hear personal messages, you realise how far football can reach beyond the pitch,” he added. “It is people's lives. It hits even harder, in a good way. They're a good reminder of why you do the job."

Sports.title: Australia star says ALL players knew about sandpaper scandal in bombshell claim
Sports.content:
Australia star says ALL players knew about sandpaper scandal in bombshell claim

Former Australia batter Usman Khawaja has lifted the lid on the sandpaper scandal of 2018, claiming the whole team new about the cheating against South Africa

View 3 Images Usman Khawaja has lifted the lid on the sandpaper scandal (Image: Darrian Traynor/Getty Images)

The entire Australian team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball against South Africa in 2018, despite the scandal being pinned on three people.

‌



‌



That's according to ex-Aussie batter Usman Khawaja who has come clean in an explosive interview ahead of the release of a new book. The use of sandpaper in the Cape Town Test saw Cameron Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith take the rap for the blatant cheating.

‌



TV cameras caught Bancroft, a junior member of the team, using sandpaper to help generate reverse-swing in the third Test. Bancroft served a nine-month ban, while captain Smith and vice-captain Warner were banned for a year.

‌



The rest of the team denied any knowledge of the cheating and bowling quartet Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon released a statement in 2021, hitting out at those questioning their integrity. Their claims of innocence are now set for fresh scrutiny after Khawaja's comments.

Mary Earps announces birth of 'secret' baby with partner in adorable video post READ MORE :

Former champion boxer Josh Frederiksen dead at 36 after tragic skydiving accident READ MORE :

“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” he told the Sydney Morning Herald. “In an ideal world, I don’t want to do this. I don’t want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

“Maybe I thought Davey (Warner) would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn’t think it was going to come down to this.”

‌



A spokesperson for Cricket Australia told the Press Association: “There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month’s series in South Africa.

View 3 Images Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft facing the music in 2018 (Image: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images/Getty Images)

‌



“During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process.”

Khawaja also slammed Cricket Australia's decision not to interview him while investigating the scandal. "I was sitting next to Cam Bancroft that whole Test match, and I didn’t get interviewed," he said. "I thoroughly feel that I didn’t get interviewed because they knew that I wanted to take it as a team, because they knew I was ready to tell the truth if I was interviewed.

‌



"And I was waiting for my phone to ring. It just never rang, and then the penalties were given, and I couldn’t believe it."

View 3 Images Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon and Mitchell Starc claimed no knowledge of sand paper (Image: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

‌



Khawaja played 88 Tests for Australia and has decided to bare all in his new autobiography, Sabr, which is likely to cause fresh turmoil in the country. The former batter claims he wanted the entire team to front up and accept culpability at the time, rather than allowing Bancroft, Smith and Warner to shoulder the blame.

“Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game, I said, ‘Take this as a team. We did this as a team’," he added.

Article continues below

“I’m not doing this for any other reason than I think it’s the right thing to do. I’ve always felt like there’s more to life than just cricket, and these guys, in some respect, deserve that justice. And it just doesn’t feel like anyone’s going to give it to them.”

Sports.title: Former champion boxer Josh Frederiksen dead at 36 after tragic skydiving accident
Sports.content:
Former champion boxer Josh Frederiksen dead at 36 after tragic skydiving accident

Former Australian boxing champion Josh Frederiksen has died following a skydiving accident near Brisbane, with tributes flooding in for the 36-year-old light heavyweight

View 2 Images Josh Frederiksen has died in a skydiving accident (Image: josh_frederiksen_boxing/Instagram)

A former champion boxer has died aged 36 after a horrific skydiving accident. Josh Frederiksen died despite his parachute successfully opening.

‌



‌



Tributes have poured in for the experienced skydiver, who had successfully completed over 100 jumps before the accident. He was taking part in a routine jump at the Skydive Ramblers Toogoolawah, near Brisbane.

‌



Australian outlet news.com.au reports that while Frederiksen's parachute opened as usual, he was caught in turbulence, resulting in a hard landing. He suffered injuries to his chest, pelvis and abdomen.

‌



The Australian was rushed to Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital by air ambulance, but sadly died overnight. His passing was confirmed by the Australian Parachute Federation (APF).

"Skydiving carries inherent risks, and while we work continually to reduce those risks, they cannot be eliminated entirely."

‌



Throughout his boxing career, Frederiksen competed 20 times, recording 13 wins, five losses and two draws, while also claiming the Australian light heavyweight title.

View 2 Images Josh Frederiksen was Australian light heavyweight champion (Image: josh_frederiksen_boxing/Instagram)

‌

Fellow boxer and close friend Nick Midgley was amongst those paying tribute. "The world lost a special man through a tragic skydiving accident last night, he said on Instagram.

‌



"I've honestly never heard anyone say a bad word about Josh Frederiksen. He walked out his values and morals in everything he did, and I considered him a brother to me. So I'm absolutely crushed, I also know how his death will impact a lot of other people too. My condolences to his family and loved ones."

Another friend added: "The man who has completed his mission on Earth. With you, I finally know what it actually feels like to have found my missing rib.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury issues response to Oleksandr Usyk trilogy snub
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury issues response to Oleksandr Usyk trilogy snub

Tyson Fury is not giving up hope on fighting Oleksandr Usyk for a third time despite the Ukrainian brutally snubbing his longtime rival

View Image Oleksandr Usyk and Tyson Fury fought twice in 2024 (Image: Getty Images)

Oleksandr Usyk has plans to return to cruiserweight for his next fight - but longtime rival Tyson Fury is not buying it.

‌



‌



The Ukrainian had relinquished his titles earlier this year, but still had plans to stay at heavyweight. Usyk was eyeing up a farewell fight against Deontay Wilder in 2027, but talks fell through. He also also expressed interest in a third meeting with Fury - despite beating the Morecambe brawler twice in 2024.

‌



Fury has long called for a third clash with Usyk and has insisted he should have won the previous two encounters. The 'Gypsy King' will return to the ring next month when he takes on Anthony Joshua. Usyk's future remains up in the air but is expected to fight next year.

‌



And he is hoping for a potential showdown with undefeated sensation David Benavidez. Usyk recently told DAZN: “I cleaned out heavyweight and now I’ll go back to my weight. Now [I weigh] 96/97kg. Today there is change at heavyweight, if I have an opportunity at cruiserweight, I’m back. It’s a big fight because Benavidez is a big champion. When I have an opportunity, I take this opportunity. This is life.”

FOLLOW OUR FIGHTING FB PAGE! Latest boxing and MMA news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Mike Tyson makes official Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua prediction READ MORE :

Tyson Fury injury concern raised ahead of Anthony Joshua mega-fight READ MORE :

Fury, though, is not convinced and is adamant that the Ukrainian will only fight again if he is the one standing across the ring from him. Speaking to Michelle Joy Phelps, he said: "I do not think that is going to happen (Usyk moving down to cruiserweight). If it is not me then Oleksandr Usyk will not be fighting again. Definitely not.

"I just think he wants a big payday and I am the man to give him that. Whether he does or not… I do not know. I cannot see him dropping down to fight (David) Benavidez. And I cannot see him fighting random fighters for no money. Not at 40 years of age (fighting for the glory of the titles). You are fighting for the glory of the paycheque.

Article continues below

Tyson Fury's dad makes worrying admission ahead of Anthony Joshua fight READ MORE :

Jake Paul makes bold retirement promise ahead of next fight READ MORE :

Fury has been handed some hope that a trilogy could come to fruition after holding talks with Usyk recently. The Brit offered the Ukrainian the chance to fill in for Joshua should something happen, but Usyk declined.

The 39-year-old is currently enjoying time with his family, but is targeting a potential return in March. “I actually spoke with Oleksandr to say ‘if Joshua does not fight, we will do it.’ And he said he was busy," Fury said. "He has gone on holiday with his family, but he could do a fight in March. So, maybe we do that in March."

Sports.title: Micah Richards reveals secret torment of dad's shock death and how he's supporting young son
Sports.content:
When BBC pundit Micah Richards commentated live to 20 million viewers on England's World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina this summer, he did it for his dad. He had just received the devastating news of his father, Lincoln’s “unexpected and shocking” death, but says: “I had my dad’s voice in my head telling me, ‘you've got to make the most of this opportunity,’ and that's what I tried to do. I did it for him.

“Everyone grieves differently. If you watch the game back, I kept tapping my foot. All these emotions were going through my body. I was getting myself through it.” Micah, 38, says his dad had been ill for a few years, but does not disclose his cause of death, just saying: “I didn't think it would happen then.”

An electrician, Lincoln also ran a grassroots football team - raising Micah and his seven siblings with the pundit’s mum, Heather, who worked in a social services office. Sadly, the couple separated, but Micah, who is single, says they both encouraged him to play football.

View 6 Images “I had my dad’s voice in my head telling me, ‘you've got to make the most of this opportunity,’ and that's what I tried to do. I did it for him." (Image: BBC)

‌



Starting with kickabouts in Chapeltown, Leeds, where he grew-up, Micah became a star at Man City, winning two Premier Leagues and one FA Cup trophy with the Blues. At 18 he became the youngest defender ever to play for England, and represented Team GB at the London 2012 Olympics.

Now living in Harrogate, North Yorkshire, he says: “My dad took me absolutely everywhere. “He probably missed 10 or 20 games throughout my whole career. He was just amazing. He always said, from when I was young, ‘If you apply yourself properly, you'll make it.’ He said, ‘The minute you take your eye off the ball, then someone will take your place.’ But he always believed that I had the ability to do it. It was just keeping me on track.”

As a teenager, when his friends were all out at clubs and discos, Lincoln told him: “That'll all come. Don't worry about that, just stay focused.” Now, life without his dad, who had been dealing with a drink problem, is tough.

Micah says: “He was the one who always gave good advice. I've got four sisters and three brothers - and I’ve lost count of the number of cousins. If I ever needed advice, he would be the one who I would turn to. But now, essentially, everyone turns to me. I'm like, ‘I'm only 38, I've not got the answers. Just do your best.’ What am I to say?”

‌



View 6 Images A young Micah (left), with brother and dad Lincoln

Despite his success, Micah says he has “wild imposter syndrome all the time.” Advising people just to “show up” if they want success, he adds: “Everyone looks at my career and says, ‘you played for England, won the Premier League, now working for all the big broadcasters.’ But I'm just enjoying the ride.”

Again, he praises his dad for his wise words in keeping him grounded. He says: “My dad always used to say to me, ‘never forget where you come from.’ What he meant by that is, just know if you're earning more money, or if you've got a bigger house, make sure you stay humble. Make sure you're always working hard. Make sure you have compassion with other people.’”

While Chapeltown was a tough area to grow up, Micah adds: “ I never strayed because I was always focused on football.” And now Micah is an ambassador for the Specsavers campaign, Best Worst Team, to support grassroots football. A community-driven initiative, Specsavers searches the UK for rock-bottom, underfunded grassroots and Sunday League football teams that suffer heavy losses, bad luck, or comical on-pitch blunders and gives them a makeover.

‌



View 6 Images Micah as a little lad. He grew up in Chapeltown, Leeds

This year, they’ve picked Bollington United in Cheshire, who will be given professional professional coaching, high-profile assistant managers and football legends, upgraded kits, and media coverage - before being included in an 8-part YouTube documentary series.

Micah, an assistant manager, says: “My job is to get them off the bottom of the table. Grassroots football gave me stability and a focus. It taught me a lot of things in terms of being personable, in terms of sharing. It makes you resilient. All those things that you need in life. It humbles you, too. I was at Oldham Athletic and I was the best player by far. I went to Man City at 14, and I was the worst.”

But he says Oldham gave him the skills to deal with it, without “throwing your toys out of the pram when you’re not getting picked.” He adds: “Grassroots is so important because that is the foundation, that's where it starts.”

‌



Micah says the community element of grassroots football is also important. He adds: “Community's where you've come from, what you are. My community in Chapeltown was absolutely amazing. I still go back to Chapeltown to get that chicken and rice from Maureen's. And the love and affection I get is just amazing.”

View 6 Images Micah in kids' team (bottom row, centre)

Micah rose through the ranks from grassroots to Leeds City Boys, then Leeds United, Oldham Athletic and Man City. He officially retired from professional football on July 26, 2019, aged 31, due to chronic and persistent knee injuries.

He admits: “I was lost when I retired. I thought, ‘What am I going to do, man?’ But football has given me everything in life, so I feel like I have the responsibility now to sort of send the message that football's for everyone.Grassroots or Premier League, you should enjoy it the same way.” He also works with charities, including British Heart Foundation and Shelter. "Helping people makes me proud,” he says.

‌



Fiercely private, Micah has never revealed the name of his nine year old son, or identified the boy’s mum. But he says: “He plays football, and I am one of those dads who doesn’t say a word on the sideline, but inside, I'm raging. It makes my blood boil when he doesn't work hard.”

And other parents expect a BBC-level commentary. Micah says: “When I'm on the side there, people are always looking at me when their son's scored to say, ‘Ooh, that was good, wasn't it?’ I'm like, ‘yeah, it's good! It's fine!’ What, you want me to give some expert analysis on the goal?’ I'm not going to do that! Let the kids have fun.”

View 6 Images Coaching Sunday League side on Specsavers' Best Worst Team Season 5

BBC Sport, and CBS Sports - Micah says his proudest achievement is being a dad. He says: “Having my son makes me proud. That and making my debut at 17 for Man City.”

‌



His prolific career also means Micah has some enviable contacts. But he confesses that there’s one famous woman who he can’t get hold of. Earlier this year, he claimed on The Rest is Football podcast to co-hosts Alan Shearer and Gary Linekar that Spice Girl, Mel B, was once his babysitter. However, she has neither confirmed nor denied it.

He says: “My mum said she did it, my sister did. And I actually tagged her, which I never do, I never tag people in Instagram. It did happen, but I need the confirmation from Mel B.” It’s not like Scary Spice to be silent!

*Micah Richards returns for season five of Specsavers' Best Worst Team, helping grassroots side Bollington United Sunday Blues, in an eight-part YouTube series.

Sports.title: England rugby stars 'really upset' with bombshell Steve Borthwick bust-up claims
Sports.content:
England rugby stars 'really upset' with bombshell Steve Borthwick bust-up claims

England's players allegedly grew unhappy with Steve Borthwick and called for crisis talks with RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney when they were in Argentina over the summer

View 3 Images England players lost faith in Steve Borthwick during the summer, a report claims (Image: David Rogers/Nations Championship via Getty Images)

England star Jamie George has fired back at claims of a rift between head coach Steve Borthwick and his players. Saracens star George says the squad are 'really upset' after a bombshell report into their summer tour was published two days before England are due to face Australia at Twickenham on Sunday.

‌



‌



The Times allege that during England's trip to Argentina, players wanted crisis talks with RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney after objecting to Borthwick's style of management. It's also said that the England boss was involved in a training-ground bust-up with Ellis Genge and that there are disagreements among his coaching staff.

‌



Sweeney has already thrown his support behind Borthwick, as England prepare for a run of three home matches against Australia, Japan and New Zealand in the inaugural Nations Championship before taking part in finals weekend later this month. And George, who Borthwick replaced as captain in 2025, insists that the report will only 'galvanise' the team.

‌



"I can tell you that a lot of it's untrue," the hooker told BBC Sport. "We, as a squad, are incredibly disappointed by it.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



"You just have to look at the timing of the article - two days out from our first Test match. I think it's clearly there to try and be divisive.

"It is the first time I think in my England career that as a group we've had to address an article that's been written, but we spoke about it brilliantly. Maro [Itoje] called a leader's meeting and thought that that was the best way of us going about it.

‌



"Whoever's written this article, obviously their aim was for it to be divisive. Unfortunately for them, it's going to go the other way. This is going to galvanise us, it's going to make us tighter.

Is Steve Borthwick the right man for England? Have your say in the comments section.

‌



View 3 Images Jamie George has attempted to rubbish the report (Image: Nations Championship/Getty Images)

"We speak a lot about standing up for people, we speak a lot about helping each other, and we've got to make sure that we do that for Steve. He has had a bit of a personal attack here and an unwarranted one at that."

‌



Borthwick has previously received criticism regarding his man-management skills from England's most-capped player, Ben Youngs, who won the Premiership under the 47-year-old at Leicester. Youngs said last year that Borthwick failed to give him emotional support when his family were affected by serious illnesses.

The topic of England's coaching staff, which has frequently changed during Borthwick's four-year tenure, was also broached in the article. Defence coach Felix Jones, who helped South Africa to back-to-back World Cups, only lasted seven months in the England setup, and it's claimed that an 'unstable working environment' prompted him to quit.

‌



View 3 Images Steve Borthwick's style of management has been scrutinised (Image: Massimo Insabato/Archivio Massimo Insabato/Mondadori Portfolio via Getty Images)

England began their Nations Championship campaign with a 45-21 loss away to South Africa before thrashing Fiji 73-8. Borthwick's side then toiled in a nervy 31-24 victory over Argentina, benefiting from a late disallowed try.
