Sports.title: Canelo Fought Kovalev, So Why Rule Out Beterbiev?
Sports.content:
Sergio Mora argues that Canelo Alvarez is simply too small for Dmitry Bivol or Artur Beterbiev, but that claim collides with Canelo’s track record. Moving up to light heavyweight did not stop Canelo from taking on Sergey Kovalev, so physical scale alone should not close the book on either matchup.

When Chris Mannix asked what should happen if Bivol gets past Callum Smith, Mora chose a third meeting between Bivol and Beterbiev over a Canelo rematch. He dismissed Canelo’s prospects, pointing to edges that reach beyond the 175-pound limit.

“Bivol’s bigger, he has faster feet, and he has one of the best jabs in boxing that gives Canelo issues. And Beterbiev is just way too big, way too strong, and he has smart footwork as well. Not in and out like Bivol, but it’s smart fundamentally. No, both of those guys are too big for him,” Mora told DAZN Boxing.

The technical points Mora raises hold far more substance than simple scale. Canelo climbed to 175 in November 2019, stopping the 36-year-old Kovalev in the eleventh round to capture the WBO belt. That victory remains a cornerstone of his four-division resume, keeping any future venture at light heavyweight open to legitimate discussion.

If Canelo truly cleaned out 168 and sits on a throne where nobody at super middleweight is worthy, then stepping up to fight Artur Beterbiev is the exact test he should take.

The critics who instantly rule out a Beterbiev clash point to size, power, and danger. Yet those same excuses vanish whenever people praise Canelo for jumping straight to light heavyweight in 2019 to take out Sergey Kovalev. If handling the physical jump to 175 was good enough to claim a belt back then, using size as a shield today doesn’t work. Canelo already established that he will willingly step into the ring against a light heavyweight champion when an opportunity presents itself.

The timing makes the matchup entirely fair game. Beterbiev is past 40, carrying the heavy mileage, wear, and physical toll of a brutal, extended career. When Canelo moved up to dethrone Kovalev, he targeted a 36-year-old champion with clear vulnerabilities. Facing a 41-year-old Beterbiev fits the identical blueprint. If Canelo’s supporters argue that Beterbiev’s age is catching up to him, then Canelo has zero excuses to avoid testing those waters.

Ruling the fight out gives Canelo a convenient pass to linger in safe territory. Instead of entertaining another slow, uneventful outing against Terence Crawford or settling for predictable matchups at super middleweight, Canelo ought to prove his greatness where the stakes are genuine. If he were brave enough to hunt Kovalev at 175, ruling out an aging Beterbiev looks less like caution and more like dodging a fight that would truly test his limits.

Sports.title: Liam Paro Calls Haney’s Knockout Talk A Bluff
Sports.content:
Liam Paro expects Devin Haney to abandon his knockout talk once they fight, leaving the Australian needing to create punching opportunities against an opponent he believes will avoid sustained trading.

Paro would welcome Haney standing with him. His preparations, however, must account for the cautious approach he expects rather than the aggressive one Haney has promised.

“I believe Haney is one of the hardest tasks, just his style. He’s not going to be there to engage. But look, he said that he’s looking for a knockout. I guarantee I’ll beat him in a firefight, but I know he’s not going to do that. He’s a good boxer,” said Paro to the Punch Podcast.

The first problem is getting past Haney’s jab without spending rounds following him. As a southpaw, Paro can contest that punch with his lead right hand, tapping or occupying Haney’s left to disrupt his ability to judge distance. That could help Paro bring his rear left into range without having to rush through a clean jab.

There is a cost to reaching for that control. If Paro becomes preoccupied with Haney’s lead hand, he can leave an opening for the straight right. His hand fighting needs to accompany his footwork, giving him a route to attack rather than becoming an exercise Haney can read.

Paro also needs to distinguish pressure from pursuit. Following Haney around the perimeter would allow the American to choose when to stop, punch, and move again. Short diagonal steps across his route would make Haney change direction or surrender space toward the ropes.

The straight left to the body could help there. Paro does not have to reach Haney’s head with every attack to make his movement less comfortable. Targeting the torso gives him a chance to score beneath the jab and draw a defensive reaction that creates his next opening. Overreaching would leave him vulnerable to a counter or a clinch.

What happens after Haney punches could be just as valuable. Paro needs to position himself to answer before Haney has completed his retreat. A short right hook or a straight left may catch an exit, but only if Paro remains balanced enough to throw immediately. Loading up would let the opportunity disappear.

Paro estimates they have shared close to 100 rounds of sparring. That experience could help him recognize when Haney intends to move, hold, or counter. It also means Haney has substantial knowledge of Paro’s approach. Familiarity becomes an advantage only if Paro can disguise what he does next.

His first-round knockout of Brock Jarvis demonstrates the danger when he lands cleanly. It does less to explain how he will manufacture that opening against Haney.

Paro’s clearest route is to make brief encounters productive: interfere with the jab, close space without reaching, and score before Haney gets clear. If he can do that consistently, he can win rounds without needing Haney to accept the firefight he expects him to refuse.

Sports.title: Melikuziev Crushes Sharipov To Keep Munguia Fight On Track
Sports.content:
Bektemir Melikuziev cleared his final obstacle before an expected world-title shot, knocking out Karomatullo Sharipov in the second round Friday night at Nikki Beach Resort in Dubai. The WBA mandatory challenger finished his overmatched opponent quickly, keeping his pursuit of super middleweight champion Jaime Munguia on course.

Uzbekistan’s Melikuziev (18-1, 12 KOs) needed less than two rounds to finish Tajikistan’s Sharipov (4-4-1, 3 KOs) in the main event of MUKA Boxing’s “Fury by the Sea” card. The scheduled four-round bout marked Melikuziev’s return after more than eight months out of the ring.

The decisive moment came late in the second round. Melikuziev landed a heavy shot that sent Sharipov flat onto his back, bringing the fight to an end. There was no recovery from the knockdown, and the 30-year-old southpaw had completed the immediate task in front of him.

Melikuziev pressed forward in the available second-round footage, finding opportunities to land clean power punches despite brief clinches and return fire. Sharipov could not keep the more experienced contender from getting into punching range, and the difference in their power became decisive before the round ended.

It was the result Melikuziev needed from a fight with limited competitive upside. Sharipov entered with only four professional victories, making this a substantial drop from the opposition the Uzbek contender must beat to become a world champion. A quick knockout met expectations, although it offered little evidence about how Melikuziev will handle a sustained fight against Munguia.

The practical benefit was ending his inactivity. Melikuziev had not fought since stopping Sena Agbeko in seven rounds in February. With his championship opportunity still awaiting a date, Friday’s appearance gave him another training camp and a short spell under fight conditions without committing him to a lengthy contest.

His title claim was already established. The WBA ranks Melikuziev No. 1 at super middleweight and previously ordered Munguia to defend against him. The organization subsequently permitted Munguia to face Nikita Zon on October 31, with the requirement that the winner face Melikuziev next.

Munguia retained his belt by unanimous decision, but his difficult sixth round against Zon gives the mandatory challenger reason for encouragement. Zon hurt the champion badly before Munguia recovered and took control over the second half. Melikuziev’s power makes those defensive openings a concern for Munguia, even allowing for the considerable difference between Friday’s opponent and a reigning champion.

The Ring reported earlier this week that a deal is in place for Munguia to face Melikuziev, although a date and venue have yet to be determined. Friday’s knockout leaves the challenger available to move toward that fight.

For Melikuziev, the title opportunity would represent the biggest step in a rebuilding run that began after Gabriel Rosado knocked him out in 2021. The 2016 Olympic silver medalist later avenged that defeat on points and has now won 11 consecutive fights.

Sharipov was never likely to provide the examination Munguia will. Melikuziev nevertheless did what a leading contender should against this level of opponent: he ended the fight early. The next question is whether he can produce the same damaging offense against a champion capable of surviving trouble and fighting back.

Sports.title: Johnny Fisher’s Kristian Prenga Target Could Backfire Horribly
Sports.content:
Johnny Fisher is flirting with disaster by targeting Kristian Prenga for his planned late-February return. Two confidence-building wins against Ivan Balaz and Michael Pirotton may have steadied the ship after his May 2025 stoppage loss to Dave Allen, but stepping straight into the pocket with the man who put Anthony Joshua on the canvas twice is a massive leap in lethality.

Fisher openly favors Prenga over former IBF titleholder Charles Martin, drawn primarily to the marquee value of the Albanian’s recent high-profile outing.

“I think Prenga would be a good one because he’s fought recently against Joshua,” Fisher told EverythingBoxing.

While that Joshua link offers undeniable promotional appeal, it also provides every reason for his corner to slam the brakes on. Prenga proved in July that he possesses sudden, fight-altering power by flooring Joshua twice in the opening round before being halted in the second. If Joshua struggled to stay upright under that initial barrage, Fisher’s punch resistance will face immediate trial.

The issue stems directly from how Fisher operates inside the ropes. His trademark front-foot assault demands constant forward momentum, letting his hands go in high-volume bursts. That aggressive approach requires meticulous defensive exits. Every exchange demands a snapped-back high guard, a sharp change of angle, or a clean exit out of range. Fisher cannot afford to linger in the pocket to hunt for an extra punch. Lingering against Prenga is an invitation for disaster.

Prenga’s failure to finish Joshua in the second round exposed his own tactical flaws, notably an apparent reluctance to press his advantage when his opponent needed time to clear the fog. Some attributed that hesitation to early fatigue from emptying the tank, while others saw it as costly indecision. Fisher cannot build an entire game plan on the hope that Prenga lets another hurt man off the hook. Slipping shots, disrupting Prenga’s rhythm, and forcing misses remain far safer than trading bombs in the pocket.

Martin offers an entirely different, perhaps more educational test. Dealing with Martin’s southpaw stance, deceptive reach, and straight left hand would force Fisher to sharpen his footwork and spatial awareness. While Martin still carries punch power, his style tests tactical discipline rather than delivering the raw, explosive trauma Prenga brings to the opening bell.

Fisher deserves praise for targeting a live wire, but Zuffa must weigh whether his defensive adjustments are genuinely ready for this level of fire. Another devastating stoppage loss would undo his rebuilding progress, leaving the promotion with a badly damaged asset whose flaws were exposed by the very first puncher capable of exploiting them.

Sports.title: Mora Warns Joshua Buatsi: Stop Brawling with Hutchinson
Sports.content:
Sergio Mora argues Joshua Buatsi can simplify his rematch with Willy Hutchinson by sticking to a disciplined jab and compelling the counterpuncher to initiate the action. The difficulty lies in implementing that strategy without muting the devastating rib attack that defines Buatsi, or getting dragged into brawling the moment Hutchinson scores.

Two knockdowns secured the verdict for Buatsi in their first encounter, yet Mora insists the Londoner gave away unnecessary openings by working inside the telephone booth. The former world champion urges Buatsi to command distance, bag rounds on the scorecards, and make the Scotsman gamble.

“Buatsi can make it so easy for himself. I know he’s a great body puncher, and he makes fights entertaining. But he can make this fight so easy if he uses more boxing than fighting, and he fights a little bit longer. If he pops behind the jab. Let Hutchinson make the mistakes because Hutchinson, he’s a good fighter, he’s a good counter-puncher, but he’s a reactive fighter. He’s not a go-get-you fighter,” said Mora to DAZN Boxing.

Strategic compromises exist within that blueprint. Hooking to the body requires closing the gap through the danger zone where Hutchinson’s hand speed can intercept incoming fire. Boxing at range shields Buatsi from check hooks, yet it inevitably caps the number of flush shots he can sink downstairs.

Stabbing jabs into Hutchinson’s chest and solar plexus provides an answer. Buatsi can disrupt breathing without smothering his own reach, keeping the target moving while assessing whether heavier artillery should follow. The body work shifts from an all-out physical press into an earned sequence.

Sharper feints also disrupt a reactive opponent. Buatsi has no obligation to commit fully with every twitch. Subtle level changes and shoulder feints will pull Hutchinson out of his stance, leaving him off balance when he reaches for air.

None of this functions without banking early points. Hutchinson will gladly sit back if he is allowed to dictate the pace from the outside. Mora’s scenario of a stoppage depends on Hutchinson feeling desperate enough on the scorecards to march forward into incoming traffic.

“So if Buatsi can win some early rounds and get Hutchinson to come at him, I could see Buatsi running him into a right hand and hurting him, and dropping him and maybe stopping him,” said Mora.

Securing ring center anchors this entire setup. Forcing Hutchinson to circle eats away at the Scotsman’s legs while preserving Buatsi’s stamina for the late rounds. An active lead hand must continually penalize every reset.

Temperament presents the true obstacle. The moment Hutchinson lands an eye-catching flurry, Buatsi must fight his natural urge to fire back instantly in the pocket. Stepping back behind the jab after tasting leather will reveal whether Buatsi values tactical efficiency over raw violence.

Buatsi faces Hutchinson in a rematch for the vacant WBC light heavyweight title this Saturday, November 7, at Manchester’s AO Arena, live on DAZN.

Sports.title: Outbox or Get Cracked: Shane Mosley’s Bentley Gamble
Sports.content:
Shane Mosley Jr. needed two trips to the scale on Friday, sweating off a stubborn final pound to reach the 160-pound limit after coming in at 161. That extra hour in the sauna creates immediate questions about his legs, particularly against a puncher like London’s Denzel Bentley over 10 rounds at the Copper Box Arena. Bentley checked in right on the mark at 160 on his first try.

Mosley’s stated strategy depends on superior activity and sustained output. With a five-inch reach advantage, his cleanest route to a points win is operating behind a busy, disciplining jab to trap Bentley on the perimeter. But if Friday’s late weight cut robs Mosley of fluid lateral movement, Bentley will not have to work hard to close the distance.

Middleweight madness incoming 👀 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 @2Sharp_D – 160lbs

🇺🇸 @IamShaneMosley – 160lbs 📺 @SkySports + @ParamountPlus | #ZuffaBoxing12 https://t.co/E1Rvtw2vJI — Zuffa_Boxing (@Zuffa_Boxing) November 6, 2026

Mosley made his intentions clear this week, saying that a points victory in hostile territory holds more value for him than an early finish:

“The reason why I feel like it’s even better to beat you on points than to knock you out is because if I can show everybody in here, everybody in the arena that I’m better than you, that’s better to me than knocking you out,” Mosley said to Sky Sports Boxing sit down. “What’s better is if I went to your hometown and in front of your fans and beat you convincingly, where everybody said, ‘Yeah, he won.’ That to me shows greatness.”

Aiming to win a clear decision on British cards requires a dominant volume gap, especially against a hometown fighter. Scraping by on split margins fails the standard of mastery Mosley outlined.

Bentley was initially unfazed by the prediction before recognizing the tactical insult behind it.

“At first I thought, ‘All right.’ I went back and I thought, ‘Wait, I’d rather he say he’d knock me out,’” Bentley admitted. “He’s basically saying he can outpoint me.” His response was blunt: “That’s not happening.”

For Bentley, winning does not require round-by-round territorial dominance. He carries an 82% knockout rate and thrives when opponents throw in prolonged combinations, creating counter-punching lanes for his right hand. If Mosley’s punch output dips in the middle rounds from dehydration, Bentley’s heavy single shots will stand out sharply on the scorecards.

“I want to crack that chin. I want to see if it’s real. Watch,” Bentley said.

Bentley has acknowledged Mosley’s chin and ring experience, so a wild blitz out of the gate is unlikely. Even with the WBO belt absent after Bentley opted for this bout over a mandatory assignment, the terms of the fight are clear: Mosley must execute a disciplined, 10-round boxing clinic at range, while Bentley needs only one sustained opening to punish him on the inside.

Ghana News.title: MSK Zilina Africa, Soccer Engineers head to Spain for ARG Nerja Cup
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian lower-division sides MSK Zilina Africa and Soccer Engineers have departed the country to participate in the ARG Nerja Cup 2026 in Nerja, Málaga, Spain.

The teams left Ghana on Saturday, November 7, and are expected to spend a week in Spain before travelling to Italy for further football programmes.

MSK Zilina Africa, who compete in the Division Two League, will be joined by their junior side, Soccer Engineers, who play in the Division Three League.

The trip marks the clubs’ second major international outing, following their participation in football programmes in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in 2022.

Having built a reputation for developing young players and creating pathways for talents to move abroad, the clubs will be hoping to use the tournament to expose another crop of promising footballers to international scouts and clubs.

MSK Zilina Africa and Soccer Engineers have departed Ghana for the ARG Nerja Cup 2026 in Málaga, Spain. The two Ghanaian lower-division sides will spend a week in Spain before travelling to Italy for additional football programmes. The tournament, organised by ARG Football Agency, will expose their young talents to international scouts and youth teams from clubs including Atlético Madrid, Málaga CF, Granada CF and UD Almería. MSK Zilina Africa compete in Division Two, while their junior side, Soccer Engineers, feature in Division Three. — Joseph Ayinga-Walter (@AyingaWalter) November 7, 2026

The ARG Nerja Africa Elite Showcase 2026 is organised by ARG Football Agency, led by young FIFA agent Aitor Román. The agency is also an official partner of MSK Zilina Africa in Ghana.

The tournament will offer participating African talents the opportunity to test themselves against youth teams from established Spanish clubs, including UD Almería, Granada CF, Málaga CF and Atlético Madrid.

ARG Football Agency has played a role in helping several Ghanaian players secure opportunities in European football.

Among the players who have benefited from the agency's work are Kenneth Yeboah, who joined Rapid Vienna in Austria; Yussif Haruna and Issah Seidu, who moved to MSK Žilina in Slovakia; Henry Opoku, who joined Deportivo Alavés in Spain; and Solomon Gyan, who moved to MFK Bytča in Slovakia.

The agency continues to work with promising Ghanaian players, with Román regularly visiting the country to scout talent, engage local clubs and academies, and help young footballers pursue professional opportunities in Europe.

Ghana News.title: Drug bust: Beirut officials’ accounts raise questions about NACOC’s cocaine ‘controlled delivery’ claim – Bright Simons
Ghana News.content:
The Honorary Vice President of IMANI Africa, Bright Simons, has questioned the claim by the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) that the movement of a 46.7kg consignment of suspected cocaine from Accra to Beirut was part of a controlled delivery operation.

He says accounts given by Lebanese authorities in interviews with local media do not suggest that they had cooperated with Ghanaian security agencies in advance to facilitate the operation.

Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 7, Mr Simons said his team had analysed several interviews granted by Lebanese officials, most of them published on Arabic-language news websites, and found inconsistencies with NACOC’s explanation.

“The accounts that they give does not suggest that they were cooperating with Ghana. That's one of our problems. It may be that we are mistaken,” he said.

He clarified that his concern was not whether Lebanese authorities had engaged Ghana after the suspect was arrested, but whether there had been prior coordination between the two countries to allow the consignment to pass through before the arrest.

“And of course, and I don't mean cooperating with Ghana as in not engaging Ghana at all. I'm saying that whether they are cooperating with Ghana on controlled delivery. Because that would mean that in advance, all of this was arranged in advance,” he explained.

Mr Simons acknowledged that Lebanese authorities had admitted to engaging Ghanaian Customs and security officials after the apprehension.

However, he said such post-arrest engagement did not establish that a controlled delivery operation had been jointly authorised before the suspect was arrested.

He further questioned the apparent absence of Lebanon’s Central Narcotics Bureau, which he described as the equivalent of NACOC and part of the country’s Internal Security Forces (ISF), from the operation.

According to him, the bureau is legally required to supervise controlled delivery operations in Lebanon, making its apparent non-involvement a significant concern.

“One critical element is that the Central Narcotics Bureau, which is part of the ISF of Lebanon, is the NACOC equivalent there. If you are doing controlled delivery, they cannot be absent in such an arrangement because in their law, they are supposed to be the supervisory authority,” he said.

He added that Lebanese officials’ failure to indicate that the bureau participated in the operation raised questions about whether the interception was instead handled as a customs operation.

“The fact that in this instance, the Lebanese authorities do not say that they were involved in the operation itself, of course, these matters we handed over to them eventually, also raised strong issues because it appeared to be a customs operation in Lebanon,” he said.

Ghana News.title: When the Law of the Streets confronted the Men in Uniform!
Ghana News.content:
(L) Grace Obeng at the Police station & the victim with his bruises (R).

By Jimmy Aglah

Once upon a time in the Republic of Uncommon Sense, the rule of law went on a brief holiday, leaving behind two gentlemen to look after the Republic. One was a minister of state, armed with the authority of government and the confidence of an elected representative. The other was a military officer, armed with the authority of the Ghana Armed Forces and, presumably, the confidence that comes with commanding men who carry rifles.

Unfortunately, nobody appeared to have informed either gentleman where his authority ended and the other's began.

The resulting encounter was a magnificent demonstration of what happens when two institutions of the Republic meet at a roadside without first agreeing on which chapter of the Constitution they are operating under.

At the centre of this national drama was Samuel Nartey George, Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, who had temporarily exchanged the complicated business of digital transformation for the more immediate challenge of transforming military behaviour in his Ningo-Prampram constituency.

The minister was furious. And judging by the allegations he made, he had reasons to be.

Soldiers had allegedly seized tipper trucks, brutalised residents and conducted themselves in a manner that suggested the difference between a military operation and a highway robbery was becoming increasingly difficult to explain to the ordinary taxpayer.

There were even allegations that police officers had been threatened with weapons. If true, this would represent a remarkable development in our national security architecture. The police, whose constitutional responsibility includes maintaining law and order, would apparently require protection from soldiers who had arrived to maintain another variety of law and order.

In the Republic of Uncommon Sense, such arrangements are not entirely unusual. We have perfected the art of creating institutions to supervise institutions, only to discover that the supervisors occasionally need supervision themselves.

But Sam George was not prepared to supervise this particular situation from the comfort of an air-conditioned office.

He confronted the military officer, Lieutenant Albert Goh, and proceeded to deliver what might generously be described as an unscheduled lecture in military accountability, constitutional responsibility and the consequences of irritating an elected representative.

At one point, the minister reportedly described the soldiers' conduct in terms associated with armed robbery and demanded the officer's dismissal.

Then came the statement that elevated an otherwise local confrontation into a national philosophical debate.

The minister invoked the law of the streets.

Now, this was a fascinating constitutional innovation.

For decades, Ghanaian lawyers have wasted precious time studying the 1992 Constitution, Acts of Parliament, legislative instruments and judicial precedents. Law students have spent sleepless nights memorising provisions that ordinary citizens struggle to understand.

Yet here was a senior government official introducing an entirely new branch of jurisprudence in broad daylight.

The Law of the Streets!

Nobody knew when Parliament had passed it, whether the President had assented to it or whether copies were available at the Assembly Press. But from the confidence with which it was invoked, one suspected it had been in force for some time, awaiting a suitable military officer on whom to test its provisions.

The beauty of this new law was its simplicity. Unlike conventional legislation, it required no parliamentary debate, no committee hearings and no publication in the Gazette. Its enforcement mechanism appeared to depend entirely on how angry the person invoking it had become.

One could almost imagine the bewilderment of the military officer.

He had probably received instructions from his superiors before embarking on the operation. Whether those instructions authorised everything allegedly done was another matter requiring investigation. But nowhere in his military training, one suspects, had he encountered a minister threatening consequences under a legal framework administered by the streets.

And yet the minister's anger raised a serious question that the Republic could not conveniently dismiss.

What exactly were armed soldiers doing in an operation involving tipper trucks and sand-winning activities? Under whose authority were the vehicles allegedly seized? What offences had their owners committed? And if police officers were indeed threatened, had the Republic reached the extraordinary stage where one security institution could intimidate another while both claimed to be enforcing the law?

These were not small questions.

A soldier's uniform is not a certificate of exemption from the Constitution. Neither is a rifle an alternative to a court order. If the allegations against the soldiers are established, those responsible must face the appropriate consequences.

But there was another little difficulty.

A minister's appointment letter is equally not a licence to establish a parallel judicial system at the roadside.

The Republic cannot complain that soldiers have exceeded their authority and then applaud a minister for appearing to exceed his own. Otherwise, we shall eventually arrive at the absurd situation where every public official carries a personal interpretation of the law, to be activated whenever his blood pressure rises.

The police will enforce the criminal law. Soldiers will enforce military instructions. Ministers will enforce the law of the streets. And ordinary citizens, caught between these competing jurisdictions, will be left wondering which authority to obey before somebody decides they are obstructing justice.

Fortunately, the controversy eventually travelled from the roadside to the conference room.

Sam George met the Defence Minister and the military high command, where the temperature of the discussion appears to have dropped considerably. The minister clarified that his remarks were not intended as an attack on the Ghana Armed Forces as an institution, while the military leadership reportedly undertook to investigate the incident.

This was reassuring.

Apparently, the Republic still possessed functioning institutions capable of resolving disputes without consulting the law of the streets.

But the meeting also exposed one of our enduring national habits. We are very enthusiastic about institutional authority when exercising it and remarkably sensitive about institutional respect when somebody else challenges us.

The military deserves respect, certainly. Its officers and men perform difficult duties in the service of the Republic. But respect cannot become a protective umbrella under which alleged misconduct is sheltered from scrutiny.

Equally, ministers deserve respect for the offices they occupy. But public office demands restraint precisely when anger seems most justified. The higher one climbs the ladder of authority, the less freedom one should have to turn personal indignation into public threats.

A Ghanaian proverb reminds us that when two elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers.

In this particular contest, however, the grass had already allegedly lost its tipper trucks before the elephants began arguing about constitutional authority.

And that is the tragedy beneath the comedy.

Somewhere in Ningo-Prampram are ordinary citizens whose livelihoods may have been disrupted. They are not interested in whether a minister can outshout a lieutenant or whether a lieutenant can outstare a minister. They want to know whether their rights were violated, whether their property was lawfully handled and whether anybody will be held accountable.

Those questions deserve answers, not merely a reconciliation photograph and a promise to investigate.

The Republic must therefore resist the temptation to turn this episode into another contest of personalities. The central issue is not whether Sam George is brave or abrasive, or whether the military officer was sufficiently respectful to a minister.

It is whether the law applies equally to the man carrying the rifle, the man carrying the ministerial title and the ordinary citizen carrying the burden of their decisions.

For if the allegations against the soldiers are true, the Republic has a military accountability problem. And if ministers believe they can remedy such problems by invoking the law of the streets, we have acquired an additional constitutional problem.

One cannot extinguish a fire by pouring petrol on it and then demand applause for displaying concern about fire safety.

Perhaps the Attorney-General should now commission a comprehensive review of this newly discovered Law of the Streets, just to establish its relationship with the 1992 Constitution.

Until then, the citizens of the Republic of Uncommon Sense would be well advised to travel with three essential documents: their national identity card, their driver's licence and a certified copy of whichever law happens to be in force on the particular street they are using.

Because in a country where soldiers allegedly seize trucks, ministers threaten street justice and everybody claims to be defending the rule of law, the ordinary citizen faces one increasingly difficult question:

If those entrusted with enforcing the law cannot agree on what the law is, who exactly is supposed to obey it?

Ghana News.title: Traffitech rollout: What Ghana can learn from countries that warn motorists about speed cameras
Ghana News.content:
By Jimmy Aglah

The rollout of Ghana’s automated traffic enforcement system, Traffitech, has brought into sharp focus an important aspect of road safety management: the responsibility of authorities to provide motorists with adequate road signs before enforcing traffic regulations.

As concerns grow over inadequate speed-limit signs and the absence of advance warnings about enforcement cameras, experiences from developed jurisdictions suggest that Ghana could benefit from a more comprehensive approach that combines technology, clear road signage, public education and effective enforcement.

In countries such as the United Kingdom, France and Australia, warning signs are widely used to alert motorists to speed cameras, although the legal requirements and enforcement policies differ.

The underlying policy question is whether motorists should be encouraged to comply with speed limits before reaching enforcement points or whether authorities should rely principally on detecting and penalising violations after they occur.

Ghana’s road infrastructure comes under scrutiny

Traffitech, which commenced operation on November 1, 2026, uses cameras and other electronic devices to detect traffic violations, including speeding and running red lights.

The system is intended to improve compliance with road traffic regulations and reduce crashes, injuries and fatalities.

However, its introduction has exposed concerns about the adequacy of the country’s road infrastructure, particularly the visibility and availability of speed-limit signs.

On Wednesday, November 4, the Director-General of the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA), Abraham Amaliba, acknowledged these concerns during an interview on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show.

He announced that Traffitech cameras would initially operate only on roads where speed limits were clearly displayed.

Mr Amaliba argued that it would be unfair to penalise motorists for failures attributable to the authorities responsible for providing road infrastructure.

He cited Boundary Road towards Mahama Road in Accra, where a speed limit of 50 kilometres per hour is displayed, as an example of a road where automated enforcement could operate.

The NRSA Director-General also acknowledged concerns about the absence of advance camera warning signs and indicated that steps would be considered to give motorists adequate notice.

He explained that the Department of Urban Roads, Department of Feeder Roads and Ghana Highway Authority would have responsibility for providing the necessary signs.

His comments followed a meeting on November 3 involving government officials, the police and transport operators to address concerns surrounding the implementation of Traffitech.

Police guidance raises a separate question

The Ghana Police Service’s official Traffitech guidance provides important clarification on the legal position.

According to the police, some roads and intersections have warning signs announcing enforcement cameras, while others do not.

The guidance states that there is no general legal obligation to announce traffic enforcement operations and that the absence of a camera warning sign does not invalidate a traffic offence.

It further explains that licensed drivers are expected to know the statutory speed limits prescribed under the Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519), whether or not a speed-limit sign is displayed.

The police identify general speed limits including 30 kilometres per hour in specified areas of predominant human activity, 50 kilometres per hour in urban or built-up areas, 90 kilometres per hour on highways and 100 kilometres per hour on motorways.

This introduces an important distinction between the legal obligations of motorists and the operational policy announced by the NRSA.

While motorists remain legally responsible for complying with applicable speed limits, the NRSA has indicated that automated enforcement will initially be restricted to roads with adequate speed-limit signs.

There is also a distinction between speed-limit signs and camera warning signs. The former communicate the maximum permissible speed, while the latter alert motorists to the presence of automated enforcement equipment. Both can contribute to safer driving, but they perform different functions.

NRSA orders urgent improvements to road signs

The concerns have prompted official action.

In a letter dated November 3, 2026, the NRSA directed the Ghana Highway Authority and Department of Urban Roads to urgently address deficiencies in road infrastructure, including missing signs, faded road markings, faulty traffic lights and inadequate street lighting.

The Authority warned that these deficiencies could undermine the effectiveness of Traffitech and compromise road safety.

The agencies were also asked to provide timelines for completing the necessary improvements.

The directive underscores the importance of ensuring that physical road infrastructure keeps pace with the deployment of digital enforcement technology.

United Kingdom: Warning signs are common but not compulsory

In the United Kingdom, speed camera warning signs are a familiar feature of the road network.

The signs typically display a camera symbol to alert motorists to the possibility of automated speed enforcement.

However, British police guidance makes clear that there is no general legal requirement for fixed or mobile speed cameras to be accompanied by warning signs. Their use is instead governed by operational policies and best-practice guidance.

This means that motorists can be prosecuted for speeding even where no advance camera warning has been provided.

Nevertheless, the widespread use of camera warning signs demonstrates that authorities can combine enforcement with measures intended to encourage drivers to moderate their speed.

France: Fixed speed cameras are announced

France operates an extensive automated speed enforcement system in which fixed speed cameras are generally announced through roadside warning signs.

These signs alert drivers to the presence of enforcement equipment and encourage them to observe the applicable speed limits.

However, the French system distinguishes between fixed and mobile enforcement. Mobile speed cameras may operate without advance warning, while red-light enforcement cameras are not subject to the same general warning arrangements.

The French approach illustrates how advance warnings can form part of a broader traffic enforcement strategy without eliminating the use of less visible enforcement methods.

Australia: A policy lesson from New South Wales

One of the clearest examples of the role of advance camera warnings comes from New South Wales, Australia.

The state operates an extensive automated speed enforcement programme, with fixed cameras installed at locations selected on the basis of road safety considerations, including crash histories and vehicle speeds.

According to the New South Wales Government, every regular fixed speed camera is accompanied by highly visible advance warning signs.

Three signs are installed on the approach to a regular fixed camera, informing motorists that a camera operates ahead, reminding them of the applicable speed limit and warning of the consequences of speeding.

Importantly, the government acknowledges that these advisory signs are not legally mandatory. Their installation is a deliberate transport policy intended to alert motorists before they reach enforcement points.

The authorities also publish information about fixed camera locations, including the reasons for their installation.

The state’s experience with mobile speed cameras is particularly instructive.

In 2020, the New South Wales Government removed advance warning signs from mobile camera operations as part of efforts to strengthen enforcement.

The decision attracted public criticism amid a substantial increase in speeding infringements. The government subsequently reversed the policy and restored advance warning signs.

The controversy highlighted competing approaches to traffic enforcement: using cameras to detect speeding wherever it occurs, and using visible warnings to encourage motorists to slow down before reaching enforcement locations.

Today, New South Wales uses warning signs for mobile speed camera operations as well as fixed installations.

Australia does not, however, have a uniform national policy. In Victoria, mobile speed cameras may operate without advance warning signs.

The different approaches demonstrate that the use of warning signs is ultimately a policy choice, even in jurisdictions with sophisticated road safety systems.

Should Ghana publish camera locations?

Another lesson from international practice concerns transparency.

In New South Wales, authorities publish the locations of fixed speed cameras and explain the road safety considerations behind their installation.

Such disclosures help motorists understand where enforcement is taking place and why particular roads have been selected.

For Ghana, publishing an accessible list or map of fixed Traffitech camera locations, together with the applicable speed limits, could improve public awareness and confidence.

This would not necessarily require the disclosure of mobile enforcement locations, which may change according to operational needs.

The objective would be to make fixed enforcement more transparent while preserving the ability of authorities to address dangerous driving across the wider road network.

Measuring success beyond the number of fines

The ultimate test of Traffitech will be whether it contributes to safer roads.

The number of speeding violations detected and fines imposed may provide useful enforcement data, but these figures alone cannot establish whether the system is achieving its road safety objectives.

A more comprehensive assessment would examine changes in vehicle speeds, compliance levels, road crashes, injuries and fatalities.

It would also consider whether enforcement locations have adequate signs, road markings and other safety infrastructure.

International experience suggests that advance warnings and automated enforcement need not be competing approaches. Both can contribute to a system designed to discourage dangerous driving and encourage compliance.

The challenge for Ghana is to ensure that the technology is supported by clear regulations, adequate infrastructure and transparent implementation.

The NRSA’s decision to restrict initial enforcement to roads with displayed speed limits, together with its directive for urgent improvements to road infrastructure, represents an acknowledgement of these concerns.

Its indication that advance camera warnings will be considered also opens the door to a broader discussion about the role of signage in automated traffic enforcement.

Ultimately, the success of Traffitech should not be judged solely by the number of motorists caught violating traffic regulations. It should be measured by the extent to which motorists change their behaviour, observe speed limits and contribute to a reduction in road crashes.

For Ghana, the most important question is not simply how many speeding motorists Traffitech can catch, but how many it can persuade to slow down before an accident occurs.

Ghana News.title: Controlled delivery allows drug suspects to remain unaware of investigations – NACOC
Ghana News.content:
NACOC Deputy Director-General Alexander Twum-Barimah

The Deputy Director of the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC), Alexander Barimah Twum, has explained that suspected drug couriers are deliberately kept unaware during controlled-delivery operations to enable investigators to identify other members of trafficking networks and uncover weaknesses in the country's enforcement systems.

He said the strategy allows law enforcement agencies to monitor suspected drug shipments without alerting the individuals transporting them, thereby creating an opportunity to trace those behind the trafficking activities.

Speaking on JoyNews' Newsfile on Saturday, Mr Twum said one of the key objectives of controlled delivery was to identify the people orchestrating drug trafficking operations rather than focus solely on the individuals physically carrying the substances.

He explained that suspects were not informed when intelligence about their activities had been shared with law enforcement agencies, as maintaining secrecy was essential to the success of the operation.

“When we are doing controlled delivery on you, you, the individual, are kept in the dark and you don't know what is happening,” he said.

Mr Twum added that the operation also enabled NACOC to examine loopholes and lapses within its own systems that criminal networks could exploit to facilitate drug trafficking.

He said investigators were therefore pursuing two objectives: identifying the individuals behind the drug trade and analysing weaknesses within the country's enforcement mechanisms to prevent similar incidents.

His explanation follows the seizure of 46.7 kilogrammes of cocaine at the Rafic Hariri International Airport in Beirut, Lebanon, in a consignment that originated from Accra.

The seizure renewed concerns about Ghana's involvement in international drug trafficking networks, particularly after questions emerged over NACOC's decision to allow a suspected courier to travel to Lebanon with the consignment.

The Commission has defended the decision, explaining that it formed part of a controlled-delivery operation intended to identify and apprehend other members of the international trafficking network.

Three foreign nationals have subsequently been arrested in Ghana in connection with the shipment.

Ghana News.title: AMA to make room for Christmas traders along Cocoa Board–Kantamanto stretch
Ghana News.content:
The Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) will close selected roads within the Central Business District (CBD) in December to create additional trading spaces for traders ahead of the Christmas festivities.

Accra Mayor Michael Kpakpo Allotey announced the arrangement while addressing traders during the November edition of the National Sanitation Day exercise.

He said the initiative was intended to provide temporary trading spaces for traders without permanent shops, enabling them to take advantage of the festive season to increase their sales.

According to the Mayor, the stretch from the Cocoa Board area to Kantamanto will be closed to facilitate the arrangement, following a directive from the Minister of Local Government, Mahama Ayariga.

Mr Allotey encouraged traders to make good use of the opportunity to maximise their earnings during the Christmas period.

“We want you to make more sales this December than you have ever done. The Local Government Minister has asked us to block some of the roads to create space for traders who do not have shops to sell their goods. The stretch from Cocoa Board to Kantamanto will be closed,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Mayor has directed traders operating at bus stops to vacate the spaces before Monday to ensure the smooth movement of vehicles and pedestrians.

The directive is part of efforts to improve movement and maintain order within the busy commercial district.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Pro-Russian hackers leak Italian foreign minister’s data on dark web
World.content:
The prime minister blames pro-Russian hackers for the leak, as her top diplomat says the cyberthreat was ongoing.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blaming pro-Russian hackers for the leak.

Tajani announced in a social media post on Saturday that “for days now, cybercriminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation”.

The threats against Tajani, who is also vice prime minister of Italy, come amid a spate of hoax bomb threats across Europe that have forced flight diversions, security alerts at broadcasters, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems.

“They are also targeting my family; they are willing to pay for more details about me and my loved ones,” Tajani added in his X post. “My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way.”

‘Matter of grave concern’

Meloni expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data”.

She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination”.

Tajani added in his statement that Italy’s “position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted: defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation’s democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities”.

He also suggested that the cyberthreats may also be a reaction to the Italian government’s efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry’s digital defences.



Tajani did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.

He added that the ministry was taking the threats seriously and was coordinating its response with allied countries.

World.title: Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: La Liga – predictions, team news, lineups
World.content:
Barcelona and Atletico clash on Sunday in a blockbuster encounter which could upend the La Liga title race this season.

Who: Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona

What: La Liga, match day 12

Where: Riyadh Air Metropolitano, Madrid, Spain

When: Sunday, November 8, at 9pm (20:00 GMT).

How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream

A top-of-the-table clash headlines Sunday’s La Liga action, with Barcelona looking to retain their top spot before the international break as they face challengers Atletico Madrid.

With only two points separating the teams, the blockbuster clash could well be the turning point in the 2026-27 title race should Atletico upset Barcelona.

Diego Simeone’s side have been in terrific form all season and take on Barcelona, bolstered by a seven-game winning streak in the Spanish top flight.

Atletico’s striker Julian Alvarez struggled to find his feet early in the campaign, with a dramatic transfer saga involving Barcelona adding to the uncertainty. But the Argentinian has since rediscovered his form, scoring in each of his last two league outings.

If Atletico have been impressive, Barcelona have been irresistible.

Hansi Flick’s team have netted an incredible 46 goals in just 11 league games; the only team to score more in their first 11 matches of a campaign were Athletic Club in 1930-31 (49).

Raphinha and Lamine Yamal have been the architects of Barca’s lethal attack, with the Brazilian winger leading the goal-scoring charts this season with 15 league goals in 10 games. He is just the second player to reach this tally within 10 games at the start of a campaign after Real Madrid icon Cristiano Ronaldo, who did so in 2014-15 (18 goals in 10 matches).



Ahead of Atletico vs Barcelona, here’s everything to know:

How have Atletico played this season?

Atletico are second in the La Liga standings, with 28 points from 11 games. They have won nine matches, lost once and drawn as many.

How have Barcelona played this season?

Barcelona lead the La Liga points table with 30 points from 11 games. They have won 10 games and lost only once, suffering a 2-1 Clasico defeat to bitter rivals Real Madrid last month.

Raphinha thriving where Barca envisaged Atletico’s Alvarez

Raphinha is back to his devastating best as Barcelona’s centre-forward, suggesting the Catalan giants have little reason to regret missing out on Atletico’s Alvarez this summer.

The Argentina international tried to force his way out of Atletico to join Spanish champions Barca, whose attempts to engineer a deal angered the Rojiblancos. Barcelona were fined about 600 euros ($675) for their approach for striker Alvarez by the Spanish football federation in October.

Alvarez stayed and later apologised to Atletico fans to try and rebuild bridges, while Barcelona moved on fast, with winger Raphinha developing into an unstoppable force in a previously unfamiliar number nine role.

Raphinha’s form has made the chances of Barca returning for Alvarez next summer remote, and, after penning a new contract until 2030 on Thursday, he will look to underline that against Atletico.

With the Brazilian firing on all cylinders, Flick’s side won 11 games straight across all competitions at the start of the season.

Currently, he has 19 goals in 13 games across all competitions, including a brace each in the last two games.

After joining Barcelona from Leeds United in 2022, the winger grew frustrated under coach Xavi Hernandez, who did not seem to trust him completely.

However, Flick’s arrival and his high-pressing game suited Raphinha to the ground, and the winger has gone from strength to strength, becoming one of the team’s most influential players and one of the captains.

What happened the last time Atletico played Barcelona?

The last time the teams met was in a 2025-26 Champions League knockout game on April 14.

Although Barcelona defeated Atletico 2-1 in Madrid that day, Atletico edged their Catalan opponents 3-2 on aggregate and reached the semifinals.

Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Predictions

Opta’s supercomputer gives Barcelona a 49.3 percent chance of winning, while Atletico’s probability of a win stands at 27.5 percent. There is a 23.3 percent chance of a draw.

Atletico Madrid vs Barcelona: Head-to-head

Atletico have won two of their last five games against Barcelona in all competitions (L3), all of which have taken place in 2026.



The teams faced off twice in the Copa del Rey semifinals in March, with Atleti grabbing a solid first-leg 4-0 win at home before holding on for a 4-3 aggregate triumph, while they also won 2-0 at Camp Nou in the Champions League quarterfinals in April, going through 3-2 on aggregate on that occasion.

In La Liga, though, Barcelona have won in each of their last four trips to the Metropolitano. They are bidding to become just the third team in La Liga history to clinch five straight away wins over Atletico, after Athletic Club in 1955 and Real Madrid in 2013 (both runs of six).

Form guide

(Last five games in all competitions; latest match first)

Atletico: L-W-W-D-W

Barcelona: W-W-L-L-W

Team news

Atletico Madrid

Cristian Romero is out with a muscle injury.

Predicted starting XI:

Jan Oblak; Marcos Llorente, Marc Pubill, David Hancko, Alejandro Grimaldo; Giuliano Simeone, Obed Vargas, Morten Hjulmand, Alex Baena; Kang-in Lee, Julian Alvarez

Barcelona

Barcelona midfielder Rodri has been ruled out of Sunday’s clash because of a hamstring injury. He was substituted at half-time of Barcelona’s 3-0 Champions League win over Aston Villa on Tuesday.

Spanish media have reported Rodri could miss up to a month.

Jules Kounde (sprained ankle), Xavi Espart (ankle), Dani Olmo (thigh) and Roony Bardghji (knee) are also sidelined with injuries.

Predicted starting XI:

Joan Garcia; Brian Farinas, Pau Cubarsi, Frenkie de Jong, Joao Cancelo; Gavi, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Fermin Lopez, Karim Adeyemi; Raphinha

World.title: Why are oil traders refusing to buy Russian diesel after Trump-Putin deal?
World.content:
Zero Russian diesel has reached the US under the deal as buyers fear legal action, with Congress’s ban on Russian energy imports still in place.

Share Why are oil traders refusing to buy Russian diesel after Trump-Putin deal? on social media

At least three tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States have changed course, casting doubt over US President Donald Trump’s October deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.

Nearly a month after Trump agreed to let Russia release diesel stocks to the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions, zero diesel has reached the US, where prices have nearly doubled since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran.

Russia has sent out a total of four tankers loaded with diesel since the deal was agreed.

Here’s what we know.

What’s happened to tankers carrying Russian diesel to the US?

The Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo left the Baltic port of Primorsk last month, with the US East Coast as their declared destination.

As of Thursday, however, one was heading towards Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine analytics firm Kpler and the vessel-tracking site MarineTraffic.

A third tanker, still in the North Atlantic, has changed its destination from New York to “for orders”, leaving its unloading point open.

The Financial Times also reported that Beast, a sanctioned Seychelles-owned tanker that was loaded at the Russian port of Primorsk in late October, has set sail towards the US and is currently signalling “Atlantic”.

What did Trump and Putin agree?

A deal big on numbers, but scant on details.

Trump first announced the agreement following a call with Putin on October 9. He said Russia would make more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel available immediately to US and global markets.



Long-range product tankers, which carry diesel supplies, can carry up to about 100,000 tonnes of diesel at a time.

Another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, then 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

The agreement Trump brokered with Putin allows Russian diesel to be sold, delivered, unloaded and imported until April 7. It came after Trump blamed Ukraine for causing diesel shortages by targeting Russian energy facilities amid the Russia-Ukraine war.

It also reversed years of US policy after Washington banned imports of Russian energy following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the US Department of the Treasury has since issued a temporary sanctions exemption, much to the ire of a cross-party group of lawmakers in the US Congress who passed a new sanctions package in the name of the late, pro-Ukraine Senator Lindsey Graham in September.

In a statement to the AP news agency, the Treasury said the exemption was “in compliance with all applicable laws”.

Russia announced its first shipment of diesel during a visit to St Petersburg in October by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.

Yet much about the deal remains unclear.

Neither the White House nor the Kremlin has said whether the agreement was put in writing, and neither has revealed the price to be paid for the diesel, the payment terms or which companies are involved.

How much Russian diesel is now waiting to be sold?

It’s not clear exactly, but it’s less than was promised.

The volumes involved have not been made public, but analysts say the first shipment is unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to US consumers.

US retail diesel prices topped $6 a gallon ($1.59 per litre) in September – nearly twice their pre-war levels – and have remained elevated.

“The reported shipment is equivalent to roughly two hours of US distillate consumption,” Aarathi Krishnan, CEO of Raksha Intelligence, told Al Jazeera, referring to the first tanker to be dispatched by Russia.

“Even if it arrives as planned, it will make very little difference to national supply,” he said.

Why don’t traders want to buy Russian diesel?

Because of the legal risk.

Despite the US Treasury temporarily authorising Russian diesel sales that would normally fall under sanctions, Congress’s ban on Russian energy imports remains in place, leaving a high level of uncertainty for traders.



New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill wrote to port and terminal operators in her state on Monday, telling them to turn away ships carrying the fuel.

She warned that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”

Sherrill argued the Trump administration had no authority to override the ban.
