Other locations included Okpuno, Uwani Village, Ebenebe, Inyaba Umudim, Nnewi, Umuchu, Iyiagu floodplain in Awka, St Patrick’s Catholic Church, Awka, New Tarzan Junction, Agulu Avenue, Okpuno-Umuota, Obosi, and New Era Girls’ Secondary School, Onitsha.

He also listed drainage and waterway interventions, including the dredging of the Nwangene River in Onitsha, desilting of the Okpoko/Obodouwku road channels and Okpoko Creek, as well as desilting of the Sacamori channels in Fegge and Housing Estate, Onitsha.

According to him, other erosion-control projects were undertaken at several communities, churches, schools and public institutions across the state, including Obosi, Oraifite, Ebenator, Okpuno, Nimo and Agulu.

Obienyem argued that the projects demonstrated that erosion control was a major component of Obi’s administration’s development agenda and not an afterthought.

He said the former governor’s interventions went beyond saving roads and buildings to protecting livelihoods, communities and the economic future of residents.

The writer urged that governance should be assessed based on problems identified, initiatives undertaken and results achieved rather than political propaganda.

World.title: Explainer: Who won 2023 presidential 2023 in Kaduna, Katsina – the 161,829 votes difference
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi – ABUJA

Atiku Abubakar of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, won Katsina State in the February 25, 2023 presidential election by only 6,762 votes over Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress, APC, according to results declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC.

Read Also:

*How Buhari promised me APC presidential ticket in 2022; I regret listening to him – Amaechi

He also won neighbouring Kaduna State, where his lead was far wider.

Katsina: a margin of 6,762 votes

Atiku polled 489,045 votes in Katsina, against Tinubu’s 482,283. Out of 1,058,673 valid votes, that is a gap of about 0.64 of a percentage point.

Rabiu Kwankwaso of the New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP, came third with 69,386 votes. Peter Obi, who ran on the Labour Party, LP, ticket, had just 6,376 votes.

Katsina had 3,516,719 registered voters. The 1,058,673 valid votes represent about 30 per cent of that figure.

Kaduna: a lead of 155,067 votes

Kaduna was not close. Atiku scored 554,360 votes to Tinubu’s 399,293, a lead of 155,067.

Obi came third in Kaduna with 294,494 votes, and Kwankwaso was fourth with 92,969.

The state had 4,335,208 registered voters, of whom 1,418,046 were accredited. INEC recorded 1,360,153 valid votes and 41,223 rejected votes, making 1,401,376 votes cast in total.

Where the two states differ

Obi’s vote shows the sharpest contrast. He polled 294,494 votes in Kaduna. But he got only 6,376 in Katsina, where he finished fourth behind Kwankwaso.

Across both states, Atiku polled 1,043,405 votes and Tinubu 881,576, giving Atiku a combined lead of 161,829. Obi had 300,870 votes and Kwankwaso 162,355.

Nearly all of Atiku’s combined lead came from Kaduna. Katsina added only 6,762 votes to it.

World.title: Kalu urges Igbo leaders to unite, engage in Nigerian politics
World.content:
Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, has urged Igbo elders, leaders and stakeholders to unite and take a more active role in Nigeria’s politics, warning that disunity and political apathy have weakened the South-East’s influence in national affairs.

The call was contained in a statement issued on Saturday by his Chief Press Secretary, Levinus Nwabughiogu.

Kalu also called for a change of mindset among Igbo people, particularly those who have traditionally focused on developing their communities while keeping away from national politics.

He made the call on Friday at the South-East Stakeholders’ Convergence, also known as the South-East Elders and Stakeholders Meeting, held at the Imo State Government House, Owerri.

The meeting, convened to discuss unity, peace and development in Igbo land, was chaired by a former Military Governor of Imo State and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Senator Ike Nwachukwu.

Kalu, who represents Bende Federal Constituency of Abia State, said unity was essential to the political relevance and development of the South-East, stressing that the region could achieve more if its leaders and people worked towards common goals.

“Unity is strength. We will achieve more when we are united. The need for unity cannot be overemphasised. Peace leads to the development of communities,” he said.

Commending the elders and stakeholders for attending the meeting despite their individual engagements, the Deputy Speaker described their gathering as an expression of patriotism and commitment to the progress of Igbo land.

He said their example would encourage younger generations to sustain the quest for unity and development, likening leadership to a relay race in which older generations hand over the baton to their successors.

Kalu, however, warned that the Igbo people risked losing their heritage and political direction if they continued to operate in isolation.

On the region’s political influence, he said the numerical strength of the Igbo was not adequately reflected in the political fortunes of the five South-East states, partly because many people from the region lived in other parts of the country.

He argued that a common political agenda would enable the Igbo to consolidate their strength and make their voices more influential in national decision-making.

“The number of votes of Ndi Igbo is not what we are getting across the five states because we are scattered around the country. If we take a position now and say, Igbo, this is our agenda, this is what we want to do, I can assure you, the whole of Nigeria will feel our impact,” he said.

The Deputy Speaker also urged the people to abandon what he described as the post-civil war mindset of avoiding national politics and concentrating solely on developing their communities.

According to him, the approach has not yielded the desired political results, making it necessary for the region to become more actively involved in Nigeria’s governance.

“After the war, we had believed we will work it out on our own and develop our place. We say we are not interested in politics. It is not our business. We have tried to develop on our own. It is about time we changed that mindset.

“The politics and governance of Nigeria should be our concern. We should get involved and play an active role because if we are not in the room, we can’t be part of the decision. We need to be part of the decision-making process,” he said.

Kalu called on Igbo leaders to agree on a common position and pursue it collectively, insisting that the region would command greater respect and achieve better results through political cooperation.

The meeting was attended by Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, traditional rulers, representatives of religious organisations, women and youth groups from the five South-East states, as well as prominent figures from politics, business and academia.

Among those present were former Senate President and Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Senator Anyim Pius Anyim; former Vice-Chancellor of the Federal University of Technology, Owerri, Prof. Nnenna Oti; former Chairman of the Police Service Commission, Chief Simeon Okeke; and former President-General of Ohanaeze Ndigbo, Nze Ozichukwu Chukwu.

Others included Chief Tony Chukwu, Ambassador Greg Mbadiwe, Prof. Osita Ogbu, Mazi Sam Ohuabunwa and Ambassador Okey Emuche.

World.title: Explainer: What INEC’s 2023 results in Lagos, Oyo, Osun actually reveal
World.content:
Collage of Tinubu, Atiku and Obi, others: Big promises ahead of the 2027 presidential election. Who can fix Nigeria?

By Omeiza Ajayi, ABUJA

Lagos, Oyo and Osun states each backed a different candidate in the February 25, 2023 presidential election, according to the results declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC.

Read Also: How Buhari promised me APC presidential ticket in 2022; I regret listening to him – Amaechi

Peter Obi of the Labour Party, LP, won Lagos; Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress, APC, won Oyo, and Atiku Abubakar of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, won Osun.

What happened in Lagos?

Lagos produced the closest of the three contests. Obi polled 582,454 votes (45.81 per cent), while Tinubu, the APC candidate, followed with 572,606 votes (45.04 per cent).

The gap was 9,848 votes, less than one percentage point. Atiku trailed far behind with 75,750 votes (5.96 per cent), and Rabiu Kwankwaso of the New Nigeria Peoples Party, NNPP, had 8,442 votes (0.66 per cent).

What happened in Oyo?

Oyo was not close. Tinubu polled 449,884 votes (55.58 per cent), well ahead of Atiku’s 182,977 votes (22.60 per cent).

His lead of 266,907 votes was the widest of the three states. Obi came third in Oyo with 99,110 votes (12.24 per cent), and Kwankwaso had 4,095 votes (0.51 per cent).

What happened in Osun?

Osun was nearly as tight as Lagos. Atiku won with 354,366 votes (46.88 per cent), while Tinubu had 343,945 votes (45.50 per cent), a difference of 10,421 votes.

Obi finished third with 23,283 votes, and Kwankwaso had 713 votes (0.09 per cent).

What the combined figures show

Added together, the results tell a story that the three winners alone do not. Tinubu won only one of the states, yet he finished first or second in all three and polled 1,366,435 votes across them.

Obi, who topped the Lagos poll, totalled 704,847 votes across the three states because he fell to third in both Oyo and Osun. Atiku polled 613,093 votes, and Kwankwaso finished fourth in each state, with 13,250 votes combined.

Put differently, Obi’s win came by the thinnest of margins in the most populous of the three states. But Tinubu’s lead in Oyo was large enough to leave him comfortably ahead of both rivals on the combined tally.

World.title: Pope Leo begins South America tour in ‘fairly good shape’
World.content:
This photo taken and handout on November 6, 2026 by The Vatican Media shows Pope Leo XIV addressing journalists during the flight to Montevideo for a 12 days visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. (Photo by Handout / VATICAN MEDIA / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE – MANDATORY CREDIT “AFP PHOTO / VATICAN MEDIA” – NO MARKETING – NO ADVERTISING CAMPAIGNS – DISTRIBUTED AS A SERVICE TO CLIENTS

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Uruguay, where he will celebrate a Mass on Saturday, as he began a 12-day tour of South America in “fairly good shape.”

Leo’s sixth international tour takes him to the continent that helped shape his priesthood, just three weeks after surgery for a tumor on his right lung.

The 71-year-old pontiff will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on one of the most intense papal trips in decades, meeting political leaders, prisoners and the poor, as well as old friends.

Thousands of people, some waving yellow-and-white Vatican flags, lined the seafront of Uruguay’s capital Montevideo to greet him as he waved from a custom-made popemobile.

But the crowds were relatively sparse in Latin America’s most secular country compared with Leo’s recent visits to France and Spain.

Speaking in a half-empty Plaza Independencia, after being welcomed by left-wing President Yamandu Orsi, the pope lamented Uruguay’s high suicide rates — among the highest in the world — and appealed for healthcare to be “accessible to everyone.”

He said the care he received after his lung cancer diagnosis made him think of the “many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis” or receive treatment.

Leo will celebrate Mass on Saturday in a park in Paysandu, a city in western Uruguay, where 30,000 pilgrims are expected.

He will then return to Montevideo to visit Casavalle, the neighborhood with the highest homicide rate in the capital, as well as the Catholic University and the Centenario Stadium, where he will preside over a prayer vigil for 60,000 people.

Leo’s visit to Uruguay is the first to the country by a pope in nearly four decades.

– In ‘fairly good shape’ –

He told reporters on the plane carrying him across the Atlantic he was “in fairly good shape” following his surgery, and his advice for others facing their own cancer diagnosis was “not to be afraid.”

The pontiff said he was bringing a message of “hope” to the world’s most Catholic continent.

Liberal Uruguay is at odds with the Catholic Church — as well as Latin America’s new crop of conservative leaders — on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia, which was legalized there last year.

Leo issued a call for the “protection of the unborn” but also spoke about issues specific to Uruguay, such as its high suicide rates, which he called “painful.”

A committed environmentalist, he had praise for the small country’s “remarkable” achievement in greening its economy, which runs mainly on renewables.

– ‘One of my many homes’ –

The highlight of his tour will be Peru, where he spent nearly two decades as a missionary and which he has referred to as “one of my many homes.”

The Church’s first US-born pope, who has repeatedly clashed with President Donald Trump over the Middle East war, spoke on his plane about voting in this week’s US midterm elections.

His mail-in ballot made history because he was the first pope known to have voted in a political election.

“I’m proud to be an American and to exercise the right” to vote, he said.

He will travel on Sunday to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis, who disappointed many Argentines by not returning to visit during his papacy.

His trip is seen as a double homecoming of sorts, US-based Vatican expert Christopher White told AFP.

“History’s first Latin American pope, Francis, never returned to his homeland. Leo, a Peruvian citizen, now carries forward that mantle and legacy,” said White, who wrote a book on Pope Leo.

Peru has been gripped by pope fever in the run-up to his arrival.

Vendors in Lima are selling T-shirts and rosaries with his image on them, while Leo bread is on sale in bakeries.

A towering, 14-meter (46-foot) statue of Leo has also been erected in the port city of Callao, which he is set to visit.

The trip will take him to the former Inca capital of Cusco and the Amazon rainforest, but the pope will also revisit his former life as Robert Francis Prevost, with a supper among priests from his old diocese of Chiclayo and a private visit to a chapel he helped rebuild.

World.title: You would need wheelbarrow load of Naira to buy tomatoes if we didn’t act – Tinubu
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu said that Naira would have been so worthless, it would be moved about by wheelbarrow if not for his economic policies that moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse.

Read Also: Tinubu to Nigerians: ‘I promise better future’

Tinubu, the presidential candidate of All Progressives Congress, APC, said this during his visit to Akwa Ibom State, where he urged voters to support his administration and Governor Umo Eno.

He described the January 16, 2027 election as consequential, saying it would determine the country’s direction.

Defending his economic policies, Tinubu said his administration had moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse.

According to him, “This coming election, on January 16th is a consequential election. It will define the direction of this country.

“When I took over, 27 governors out of 36 of this country were unable to pay salary, not to talk of pension, and gratuity. Today, I can say that we are out of that tunnel.

“And I can beat my chest to say we are out of the despair, the dark tunnel of uncertainty and the calamity of a possible bankruptcy.

“By now if we didn’t take over, if we didn’t do what we did, we will be using the wheelbarrows to move our naira about because it will have become valueless.

“We are talking of 1,300 now to a dollar because it still has pocketable value. If we had left it, it would have been a wheelbarrow when you go to the market to buy tomatoes. That is the truth.”

On young voters

The President urged the electorate, particularly young people, to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs. He described it as their most potent instrument for determining the country’s political future.

At a reception held in his honour at Ibom Palm Resort, Tinubu praised Eno. He described the resort as evidence of purposeful leadership and the possibility of reclaiming environmentally degraded land for productive use.

“We are standing on a resort to the glory of God. It is a product of 73 acres of land of gully erosion, reclaimed, surrounded with a good, romantic, artificial lake, demonstrating a serious vision that is achievable when honest people are working for their homes,” he said.
