World.title: Pursue Unity, Peace, Play Active Role in Nigerian Politics, Deputy Speaker Kalu Urges Igbo Elites, Leaders
World.content:
Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie Kalu has called on Igbo elders, leaders and stakeholders to close ranks and speak with one voice in politics, cautioning that disunity has continued to weaken the political strength and heritage of Ndi Igbo of the South East region.

He also urged them to pay more than passive attention to socio-economic issues and get deeply involved into the national politics of Nigeria.

Kalu made the call at the South East Stakeholders’ Convergence (SESC), also described as the South East Elders and Stakeholders Meeting, convened in Owerri, the Imo State capital on Friday to discuss unity, progress and peace in Igbo land.

Addressing the gathering chaired by the former Military Governor of Imo State and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Senator (Gen) Ike Nwachukwu (Rtd), the Deputy Speaker said unity remains the foundation for development, stressing that peace in Igbo communities would only come when leaders reason together in harmony.

He said: “Unity is strength. We will achieve more when we are united. The need for unity cannot be overemphasized. Peace leads to the development of communities”.

Kalu who represents Bende Federal Constituency of Abia State at the National Assembly commended the elders for setting aside their personal engagements to attend the meeting, describing their action as patriotism and genuine love for Igbo land.

“I salute you all, my elders and stakeholders for this thoughtfulness, this great idea to come together and discuss the unity, progress and peace of Igbo land. This is patriotism. You all have what you are doing but for you to leave it and come here to discuss the development of our place, it means you love Igbo land. It shall be well with you all,” he said.

The Deputy Speaker said the upcoming and the contemporary younger generation are encouraged by the elders’ example, likening leadership to a relay race in which one generation hands the baton to the next.

“Some of us who are coming up are encouraged by this unity and patriotism you display. We are glad to see our elders sit together to discuss the future of Igbo land. This is like a relay race, where you run and later hand over the baton to the next person and the next generation. We are coming behind you so that whenever you hand us the baton, we collect it from you and continue with the race of progress and development,” he said.

Kalu however said that without unity, Ndi Igbo risk losing their direction and heritage.

“But if we are not in unity, we will miss our bearing and lose our heritage. But when we reason together in unity and harmony, we achieve greatness,” he said.

Speaking about Nigeria’s political structure, the Deputy Speaker noted that Igbo as one of the major tribes in Nigeria is not standing strong in the national politics.

He further argued that the political numbers of Ndi Igbo are not fully reflected across the five South East states because the people are scattered across the country.

To encourage active political participation, the Deputy Speaker urged a change of mindset, saying the post-war decision by many Igbo people to focus only on personal development and stay away from national politics had not served the region well.

“And it will not be good we shake and be left out in the scheme of things. Please, let’s come together. Let’s unite. When we unite, we gain more respect as a people. But when we work in isolation and silos, we lose our heritage.

“The number of votes of Ndi Igbo is not what we are getting across the five states because we are scattered around the country. If we take a position now and say, Igbo this is our agenda, this is what we want to do, I can assure you, the whole of Nigeria will feel our impact.

“But if we work in silos, every man to himself, to your tent O Israel, it is not encouraging at all. It yields no positive result. It reduces our number.

“After the war, we had believed we will work it out on our own and develop our place. We say we are not interested in politics. It is not our business. We have tried to develop on our own. It is about time we changed that mindset. The politics and governance of Nigeria should be our concern. We should get involved and play an active role because if we are not in the room, we can’t be part of the decision. We need to be part of the decision making process,” he said.

Kalu therefore called for a common position to help Ndi Igbo to deliver with one mind.

“There is no wisdom in saying we are not interested in the politics of Nigeria. It should be our business. Let us say one thing and stick to it with one mind, then, we will see the result of our togetherness. God bless you,” he said.

The stakeholders meeting held in Imo State Government House attracted the presence of Governor Hope Uzodinma as the chief host, some traditional rulers, representatives of religous leaders, women and youth groups from the five eastern States, other prominent Igbo sons and daughters in politics and governance, business, academia amongst whom are former Senate President/Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator Anyim Pius Anyim; immediate past Vice Chancellor of Federal University of Technology, Owerri (FUTO); Prof. Nnenna Oti; former chairman, Police Service Commission, Chief Simeon Okeke; former President-General, Ohaneze Ndigbo, Nze Ozichukwu Chukwu; Chief Tony Chukwu; Amb. Greg Mbadiwe; Prof. Osita Ogbu; Mazi Sam Ohuabunwa and Amb. Okey Emuche.

World.title: Champion Breweries, Bature Brewery Partner to Take Nigerian Craft Beer Nationwide
World.content:
Champion Breweries Plc has entered into an agreement with Thistlerock Enterprises Limited, owner of Bature Brewery, to manufacture and distribute Bature’s craft beers across Nigeria.

The agreement also grants Champion Breweries an option to acquire three Bature brands, subject to agreed sales performance milestone.

Under the agreement, Champion will brew, package and distribute Bature’s core beers, Lagos Lager, Black Gold Stout and Harmattan Haze, at its brewery in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, leveraging its national distribution network to expand their availability across Nigeria.

Bature will license the brands to Champion Breweries for manufacturing and distribution in Nigeria, retaining ownership and control of product development, brand strategy and consumer engagement, while still serving its Lagos hospitality accounts directly.

The acquisition option, which covers the brands’ trademarks, recipes and goodwill, would be exercised once annual sales reach 40,000 hectolitres, at a pre-agreed, performance-linked valuation, subject to the necessary corporate and regulatory approvals.

Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Champion Breweries, Malolan Sampath, said: “Our ambition is to build a diversified beverage business that creates value through the brands we own, the capabilities we develop and the partnerships we establish. We see significant opportunities to leverage our manufacturing expertise and distribution network to help distinctive Nigerian brands reach more consumers.

“Bature is a strong example of that opportunity. It has built a reputation for quality, creativity and innovation, and we believe that combining its brand strengths with Champion’s operational capabilities will help bring its award-winning beers to consumers across Nigeria. This partnership reflects our confidence in the long-term potential of Nigeria’s beverage industry and our commitment to playing a meaningful role in its growth.”

Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Bature Brewery, Kevin Conroy, said: “When we started Bature, we believed Nigeria could produce world-class craft beers with a character and identity entirely their own. What has been most rewarding is seeing people embrace that vision and build a community around our beers. We are incredibly proud of what we have created in Lagos, but we have always believed Bature could go much further.

“This partnership marks an exciting new chapter for us. It means more Nigerians will have the opportunity to discover and enjoy our beers, while we stay true to the creativity, originality and passion that made Bature what it is today.”

The beers will be rolled out nationally in phases, beginning with Lagos Lager, which is targeted for launch at the Calabar Festival in December 2026, one of the largest consumer gatherings in the Nigerian calendar.

Harmattan Haze is expected to follow in the first quarter of 2027, with Black Gold Stout later in 2027.

World.title: Institutional Memory, Professional Knowledge and the CORFEPS Journal
World.content:
By Tunji Olaopa

The Council of Retired Federal Permanent Secretaries (CORFEPS) is an association of patriotic former public servants that embodies administrative experiences, institutional memories and professional knowledge that could pull a lot of political and administrative weight within the reform imperative to transform governance architecture, the civil service and its ecosystem. As a multidisciplinary body of retired public servants with vast knowledge of the workings of the system, CORFEPS possesses a huge significance in connecting the institutional and reform dots in terms of where the civil service system is coming from, where it is at the moment and where it intends to be, given the democratic imperatives and development necessities of the current Tinubu administration. It is one of the most critical stakeholders in the public administration communities of practice and service that articulates a continuing professional and institutional interest in furthering the relevance of the civil service as a significant player in the development process in Nigeria.

The necessity of such a body derives from the fact that patriotic and meritorious service does not need to end with retirement. Indeed, more can still be done in entrenching the institutional memories that retired permanent secretaries embody. CORFEPS, under the able chairmanship of Mahmud Yayale Ahmed, has been energetic in its consistent push to regain the vocational honor, professional ethos and administrative efficiency of the civil service. And in furtherance of this enthusiastic push for the significance of the civil service system as one critical cornerstone of democratic governance in Nigeria, CORFEPS has just launched an amazing initiative: the CORFEPS Journal on Pubic Policy and Governance.

This significant initiative must be situated within a larger context of the institutional reform of the civil service system, especially its status as a value-based institution founded on merit, public spiritedness and professionalism. That context facilitates a framework that allows the past and the present to initiate conversation, and for both retired and current public servants to incessantly brainstorm the future of the bureaucratic system and its capability readiness to shoulder the burden of public policy implementation. The journal, I must say, presses the advantage of escalating the fundamental significance of professional knowledge and its role in deepening institutional progress. In other words, through it, CORFEPS provides a rare forum—draw, I dare say, from the administrative history of that golden era when administrative theorists (the gown) and practitioners (the town) were in conversation—within which administrative ideas, practices and initiatives could be discussed, extended and applied.

The inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is indeed a full, rich and exciting package that is sufficiently exciting to signal to the communities of service and practice that something new and challenging has arrived in the administrative space. This is because the editorial board went all out to create a splash especially with the range of topics covered, and even more specially with the array of contributors and their unique specialties. As is to be expected, CORFEPS pulled strongly from within its own ranks for reflections that combine past administrative experiences with current observations from behind the scenes. The majority of the contributors are retired permanent secretaries who have served in one capacity or the other, and who have faced one crucial challenge or the other with wide ranging levels of successes.

In this regard, the CORFEPS journal, in its inaugural edition, is drawing on the immense institutional memories and professional knowledge of its members to ventilate both diagnostic, recuperative and reformative insights. And this is salutary in ways that serve to complement the mediatory role CORFEPS has been playing as a staunch and energetic stakeholder in the civil service reform project in Nigeria. We now have an opportunity to listen and take note, outside of the usual high-power meetings, of the single-minded understanding of the civil service system from those who have manned its various aspects, especially the ministries, departments and agencies. Their reflections and analyses are complemented by others, critical watchers of the civil service, whose many years of dealing with the system make them significant participants in the ongoing efforts to transform it into a value-based, public-spirited, meritocratic and high-performing world class institution.

In terms of the range of topics and themes discussed in the inaugural edition, the CORFEPS journal becomes an automatic administrative keepsake. The inaugural edition is divided into eight parts. Each of the segments, with the exception of the last two, speaks intentionally to the most dominant issues involved in assessing and transforming Nigeria’s democratic governance experiment. This is indeed a well-thought out scholarly first step by the editorial board. Part one, titled “The Nigerian Civil Service,” has four essays; part two with seven essays is concerned with governance tools; part three has just one essay dealing with Nigeria’s infrastructural development; part four has two essays surrounding leadership and management; the two essays in part five are wrapped around the theme of health and lifestyle; part six is dedicated to three book reviews; part seven signals recent appointments and tributes to distinguished former public servants; and part eight speaks to the activities of CORFEPS itself. In all, these thematic segments are all-encompassing. They are meant to lay on the table the diagnoses, prognoses and resolution frameworks for understanding the totality of Nigeria’s administrative and governance challenges and the ways forward to transcending them.

Without daring any in-depth review of each essay—which goes beyond the space of this piece—I will touch on some of the significant contributions. And of course, we start with the civil service system. This is key, even to the current advocacy responsibilities of CORFEPS itself. And the four essays in this segment did not disappoint. Their different focuses are without doubt current and contemporary—the status of the public administrator within the civil service and governance framework; the relationship between the civil service and the task of nation building; the significance of the MDAs in the achievement of state capacity; and the relationship between administrative leadership and performance management system. These are issues that are critical in reflecting on the challenges the civil service system is facing—how can we instigate the emergence of a public manager with twenty-first competences and literacies who can supervise a civil service system that is flexible, agile, technology-based and result-oriented through performance management that transforms Nigeria’s productivity?

In the second segment of the journal, containing the most essays, the contributors engaged with governance matters that richly scope the depth of the key issues. I am particularly thrilled by the essays that investigate (a) public financial management and development financing, (b) the intervention of the executive in the institutional autonomy of public institutions, (c) decentralization and local governance, (d) capacity development to achieve service delivery and (e) the significance of corporate governance in the public sector. These issues connect with the earlier one on the administrative system. Budgeting and the financial management discipline that must attend it are critical for servicing development planning. And this goes beyond merely increasing budget size to the fundamentals of ensuring transparency and accountability in financing and execution that speaks to sustainable outcomes.

I am also fascinated, as my many public interventions have demonstrated, with the place of local governance in Nigeria’s democratic governance. This also ties with the concern with the health of fiscal federalism in the Nigerian federation. Indeed, the author of the essay argues that constitutional autonomy to back the essence of local governance will be grossly less than optimal. Rather, what is needed is what he calls the “Nigeria Local Governance Reform Framework (2026-2035)” meant to reposition the local governments as key drivers of grassroots development. This is right on point. Similarly, the authors of the essay on training and capacity development attempt to recuperate training programmes “as genuine capacity-building instrument, anchored on competency-based needs assessment, transparent procurement, post-training accountability and the professionalization of Nigeria’s training institutions.”

The third and fourth segments of the journal are tied together by the relationship between leadership and sustainable development. Sound leadership is the difference between successful and failed infrastructure projects. This then directs critical reform attention to the issue of leadership training and selection, the focus of the first essay in part four. Part five would seem to be off the path of a direct focus on administrative and governance subject matters in its focus on health and lifestyle. But that is not the case. Most reform blueprints, unlike the practice during the golden era of the public service in the 1970s, fail to factor in work-life balance in human capital development. This is crucial in the sense that when the public servant is healthy, it goes a long way in affecting performance and productivity. Thus, the two chapters on breast cancer and prostate health are key factor in institutional reform.

To recapitulate: the inaugural edition of the CORFEPS journal is really a mouthful! It is like a reader on institutional and governance reform that all MDAs and key parastatals must have in their libraries. More than this, the edition already raises the bar that the editorial board cannot afford to undermine, going forward. I have a series of recommendations in this regard. One, the journal must not attempt to be academic. It must rather be styled and intended as a journal for public administration and public service professionals. This then demands that the editorial board must give deep reflection, again, to the objective of the journal and its intended audience. The fundamental question in this sense would be: What does the CORFEPS journal aim to become in the next five years within the Nigerian communities of service and practice? This question impacts the idea of style and content. For example, every edition could then be themed around some specific subject matter of administrative and institutional reform, governance challenge, democratic consolidation, leadership, financial management, civil service mentoring, etc. Contributions can then be sourced from seasoned experts, public servants, administrators, while online search can also be made for syndicated columnists with innovative ideas and initiatives that speaks to the concerns of the journals.

Indeed, special editions can be proposed on any theme for which the guest editor is renowned. Departments of public administration, as well as the MDAs, could serve as key studies for reflection on the overall health of the civil service system and public administration in Nigeria. Websites of other professional bodies will serve as veritable source of publishable materials to introduce new ideas, tools, techniques, etc. Young mentees, volunteers and analysts could also be enlisted and commissioned to write features on some current affairs that are relevant to public administration. Interviews and autobiographical notes are critical elements for understanding the progress and reform of the public service. The editorial board must therefore also think of segmenting the journals to give room for special features, from interviews to critical reform highlights in some of the MDAs.

I will end this piece with a note of deep appreciation of those who thought the idea of the journal into existence. This is no mean feat in the total scheme of things concerning institutional reform in Nigerian civil service system. Kudos, first, to Alhaji M. Yayale Ahmed, the National Chairman of CORFEPS and the distinguished publisher of the journal. And then to Ambassador Dr Godknows Igali as the chair of the editorial board. I recognize every member of the editorial board and commend the efforts that went into birthing this inaugural edition. We have commenced a journey into a legacy of reform activities.

World.title: Mutfwang Uniting Plateau For Renewed Hope, Continuity And Shared Prosperity
World.content:
By Gyang Bere

There is an African proverb that says, “The man who carries his people in his heart will always find a place in their hearts.” This timeless wisdom reflects the political philosophy of the Executive Governor of Plateau State, Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang, who has demonstrated a strong commitment to addressing the needs and aspirations of his people.

His quest for selfless service and purpose-driven governance speaks to the enduring relationship between his administration and the people, reminding us that the true measure of leadership lies not merely in the authority one exercises, but in the sincerity of purpose, compassion and commitment demonstrated in the service of the people.

Governor Mutfwang, who remains conscious of his social contract with the people of Plateau State, took a decisive political step on Monday, November 2, 2026, by inaugurating and setting in motion the Tinubu/Shettima and Mutfwang/Piyo Campaign Council, with the mandate of coordinating support for the re-election of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the Governor’s re-election and the emergence of all APC candidates in the January 16 and February 6, 2027 elections.

The significant political event brought together respected men and women of integrity, drawn from across the electoral wards of Plateau State, who have served the state and the nation in various capacities.

At the helm of the campaign as Chairman is Governor Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang, with the National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, serving as Adviser; Deputy Governor, Ngo Josephine Piyo, as Deputy Chairperson I; State APC Chairman, Hon. Rufus Bature, as Vice Chairman II; Hon. Dr. Bernard Doro, Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, as a member; and Sir Joseph Ari as Director-General, entrusted with the responsibility of coordinating the campaign’s activities.

The inclusive Campaign Council also has former Governors, Senator Joshua Dariye and Senator Simon Lalong, as members, alongside former Deputy Governor, Dame Pauline Tallen; Senator Simon Mwadkwon; retired Air Vice Marshal Napoleon Bali, Coordinator of the Southern Zone; serving members of the National and State Assemblies; all APC candidates for the National and State Assemblies; political stakeholders, community leaders and party faithful.

Beyond the political significance of the occasion, the inauguration places an important responsibility on members of the Campaign Council to engage citizens with humility, respect and a clear understanding of the issues that matter most to them.

Governor Mutfwang believes that the campaign should transcend the mere mobilisation of political structures. Rather, it should provide an opportunity for honest conversations about governance, security, economic opportunities, infrastructure, education, healthcare, agriculture and the collective aspirations of the people of Plateau State and Nigeria.

For Governor Mutfwang, the 2027 political journey will inevitably invite public reflection on the promises made, the decisions taken, the challenges encountered and the results recorded since he assumed office in May 2023. He has acknowledged the trust, support and confidence he has enjoyed from the people of Plateau State and has appealed to them to continue the journey with him in the forthcoming election, with the aspiration of positioning the state more prominently on Nigeria’s national development landscape.

From the outset, Governor Mutfwang’s approach to governance has reflected an understanding that meaningful development must begin with the people. He has woven their concerns, aspirations and everyday challenges into his development agenda, translating these realities into practical interventions and implementing them systematically to improve lives and advance the collective prosperity of Plateau State.

For the 2027 elections, Governor Mutfwang’s message is anchored on a unification movement, built around the aspiration of bringing the people of Plateau State together under a common political direction under the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC). He has emphasised a factual, issue-based and peaceful campaign that places the people at the centre of every conversation.

The Governor’s argument for a second tenure rests on the record of his first term: the task of rescuing Plateau State from the brink of institutional and economic collapse, restoring confidence in governance, and laying a solid and enduring foundation for sustainable development across all sectors. Having undertaken the difficult work of recovery, reconstruction and repositioning, his administration is beginning to see citizens reap the benefits of these deliberate interventions.

The security of lives and property remains a central responsibility of the Mutfwang administration and a defining priority of its governance agenda. Recognising that peace and security are indispensable to development, Governor Mutfwang has approached the challenge with a strong sense of responsibility, commitment and institutional coordination.

His administration has revitalised Operation Rainbow, strengthened community-based security through the training and deployment of personnel and Forest Guards, and embraced technology by integrating modern surveillance systems into the state’s security architecture to enhance intelligence gathering, monitoring and response capabilities.

Equally significant is the Governor’s sustained engagement and harmonious working relationship with the leadership of security agencies at the national and state levels. Through cooperation, regular consultations and coordinated security interventions, he continues to strengthen the collective capacity to address security threats, protect vulnerable communities and restore public confidence.

Governor Mutfwang has prioritised strategic investments across critical sectors of the state’s economy, recognising that sustainable development must be built on infrastructure, human capital development and improved access to essential services. His administration has committed resources to transportation, healthcare, agriculture, education, water supply, energy, tourism and road infrastructure, with interventions designed to improve the quality of life of citizens and expand economic opportunities.

In transportation, the introduction of subsidised Metro bus services has made public mobility more accessible and affordable, while investments in road infrastructure are opening up communities, facilitating the movement of people and agricultural produce, and strengthening commercial activities across the state.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s development footprint is increasingly visible in Plateau State, particularly through strategic federal infrastructure projects and humanitarian interventions aimed at improving connectivity, stimulating economic activities and enhancing the welfare of citizens.

The ongoing construction of the Akwanga–Jos Road, the rehabilitation of the Sharram–Garram–Babban Lamba Road, and the recent approval of the Mararaban Jama’a–Kanke–Langtang–Shendam–Ibi Road, extending towards Taraba State, represent significant federal infrastructure interventions.

Equally noteworthy are the humanitarian interventions of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, through the distribution of relief materials and support to vulnerable individuals and communities. These gestures have provided meaningful assistance to beneficiaries, brought relief to households facing difficult circumstances and reinforced the importance of compassion and social protection in governance.

The Director-General of the Campaign Council, Sir Joseph Ari, has extended an invitation to over 115 support groups and the people of Plateau State to come out and receive the President on Saturday Novermber 14, 2026, while highlighting the Federal Government’s engagements and interventions in the state as evidence of its commitment to Plateau’s development.

However, as the African proverb reminds us, “Little by little, the bird builds its nest.” Great nations are not built in a day; they emerge through deliberate decisions, consistent effort, patience and enduring commitment.

This principle underscores the development aspirations of President Tinubu and Governor Mutfwang for Nigeria and Plateau State respectively: a commitment to building on existing foundations, consolidating progress and creating a more prosperous future for generations to come.

World.title: Golden Morn At 40, Promoting Nigeria’s Tourism
World.content:
Charles Ajunwa

The Nestle Nigeria, Agbara Factory, nestled in a massive ambience in Ogun State, has become a tourism landscape which attracts educational, entrepreneurship and business excursions from institutions.

Golden Morn, one of the brands produced by the Nestle Nigeria Plc, on Tuesday attained 40 years.Its Agbara Factory where it all started played host to guests who witnessed the milestone.

Guests at the event, were welcomed by female dancers into a well-decorated open field, where some adult games had been arranged and winners were given tickets to buy any item of their choice from a makeshift store. Also, visitors and staff of the company were on hand, exchanged pleasantries and were served Golden Morn mixed with groundnuts, sliced apples and other fruits as music from Nigerian artistes played intermittently.

What makes Golden Morn truly Nigerian, is that all the ingredients – maize, soya and millets- are sourced and produced within Nigeria. The cereal is fortified with Vitamin A, Iron, Calcium, Protein and dietary fibre.

The Category Manager, Golden Morn, Omofasa Orhiunu, described the celebration of 40 years of Golden Morn as special.

“For 40 years, Golden Morn has been nourishing generations of Nigerian families and earning a special place at the breakfast table.

“Today, we are not only celebrating a brand, we are celebrating the people, the passion and the dedication that has kept Golden Morn going strong for four decades. And what better place to celebrate it than here at the Agbara Factory where so much of Golden Morn’s story comes to life every day. From the grains that go into every pack to the people who work tirelessly to ensure we continue to deliver the quality and nourishment families have come to

know and love, this 40-year milestone belongs to all of us. Because at Golden Morn, we believe in making everyday golden. It is the fuel for the day ahead. Whether you are heading to school, going to work, caring for your

family, or like many of us here, making the product that nourishes millions of homes. So today is about pausing to celebrate how far we’ve come, appreciating everyone who has contributed to this incredible journey and looking forward with excitement to what lies ahead.”

“To celebrate our consumers who’ve been loyal to Golden Morn for over 40 years, we’ll be rolling out a promotion this November where for every 900gram pack of Golden Morn our consumers buy, they get 50gram extra free. So that’s an extra bowl of Golden Morn to nourish our wonderful families in Nigeria.”

On what stands Golden Morn out, Orhiunu said “We are uniquely Nigerian and we are the only cereal that can proudly claim to have been developed in Nigeria, and to have been nourishing Nigerians for the last 40 years.

“We will continue to nourish Nigerians, we will come up with new variants which will excite Nigerians, new things that will make the breakfast table a lot more interesting and of course, we continue to fortify Nigerians because all our products are fortifying. Golden Morn is a fortifying product which is good for the health of everybody in Nigeria.

Factory Manager, Agbara, Nestle Nigeria Plc, Talla Fall, also described Golden Morn as unique Nigerian brand and only Nigeria.

Fall, a Senegalese who has lived in Nigeria for over 20 years, said Golden Morn doesn’t exist anywhere else. “Since 1986, Golden Morn has been cherished home-grown brand in Nigerian

households. It has grown into a trusted choice of families, offering wholesome nourishment that fits into everyday life, whether in the morning or at any time of the day. That is the most important thing for Golden Morn. You can eat it at every time in the day.

“It is at our Agbara factory that every pack of Golden Morn is made. Golden Morn is 100 per cent Nigeria. So it has been created here in Nigeria, developed here in Nigeria, produced in Nigeria, and all the raw materials are coming from Nigeria. It is made with the goodness of maize and soya, grown by Nigerian farmers and created in Nigeria by Nigerians. Behind every pack are the farmers who grow the grains and the men and women in the factory who turn them into the nourishment that families trust. Over four decades, we have grown alongside our consumers. We began with high protein recipes in 1986, moved to a soft pack for greater affordability, adopted whole grains, fortified with iron and Vitamin A, and introduced Grainsmart. This is really a great journey.

“More recently, we modernised our packaging and pioneered the Golden Morn 3-in-1, Nigeria’s first ready-to-eat complete cereals. Throughout every changes, one thing has stayed the same, our commitment to quality and nourishment.

But beyond the milestones, what truly stands out are our people, our greatest asset. Every pack that leaves Agbara carries the dedication of our colleagues across production, quality, engineering, logistics, and supply chain, and of those who came before us and led the foundations.

“Our commitments to safety, quality, and food safety is what makes this anniversary possible.

Because 40 years is not one day. It means that you are really consistent and sustainable. That is what makes today special.

“Today, we also look forward to an exciting moment as we unveil the limited edition of Golden Morn 40 years anniversary pack. Our way of saying thank you to the families who have made this journey possible, because if it was not you, the consumers, we will not be there. So it will be our ways of saying thank you to our families who made this journey possible. The pack looks different, but inside it is the same. So Golden Morn you know and love with the same quality, taste, and nourishment.

“To our farmers and partners, colleagues, and every consumers who has welcomed Golden Morn into their home, we say thank you for being part of this 40 years journey. As the home of Golden Morn, we remain committed to the highest standards of quality and safety so that for the next coming years and beyond, Golden Morn continues to nourish Nigerian families and feel promising futures.

Nurse Olusolape, said that Golden Morn apart from containing the right nutrients for a healthy living, “gives you a fresh start for your day and it’s very easy to prepare.”

“As we celebrate 40 years of Golden Morn, let’s make a commitment all of us present here today and everyone out there to nourishing ourselves, prioritise our well-being, and keep showing up as our best self. Swell your day, nourish your potential, and build your future,” she added.

World.title: Spain’s Puente And Africa’s Elusive ‘Political Dignity’
World.content:
By Mobolaji Sanusi

“The first requirement of a sound body politic is that there should be public integrity; and next, that there should be personal dignity.”

—-Theodore Roosevelt (1858-1919)

Oscar Puente, Spain’s Minister of Transport, was largely unknown outside his home country until a little over a week ago. He came into the international limelight after at least 69 people died and dozens more were injured in a high-speed train collision in his country. He was not the driver of the train, nor has it been officially established that he was negligent in the accident.

But six days after the collision, he took responsibility as the man in charge of the ministry and voluntarily resigned. At his appearance before his country’s Congress to give evidence about last week’s disaster near the town of Adamuz, south of the capital, Madrid, where a moving train smashed into the back of a stationary train, he announced his decision to resign.

That collision involved a train run by the state-owned operator Renfe, with 397 passengers on board, and a stationary train run by a private operator named Iryo that was carrying 147 passengers. The accident reportedly stemmed from an issue with the automatic signalling system, a computer failure that forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch. Another appointee seeking to evade responsibility would have blamed unforeseen technical glitches beyond human control.

He did not filibuster before Congress but simply resigned in a manner that exemplified a touch of patriotic courage when he declared: “A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year.” The first crash under his watch happened on the same line in January this year and left 46 people dead.

He did not just resign; he stated that he was also withdrawing his name from “the lists for the early legislative elections” scheduled for November 29. Sadly, Spain’s train crash last week was described as one of the worst rail disasters in modern European history, and the country’s worst since 2013. Rescue operations deployed heavy lifting equipment to access derailed carriages where passengers were trapped.

No wonder Puente’s position came under immediate scrutiny after the crash. The main conservative opposition People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox party called for his resignation. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez admitted that public trust in the credibility of the high-speed rail system had been “broken.” But Puente resigned because he wanted to, not because of any opposition pressure, which is particularly dignified considering the incident’s closeness to an imminent election.

Puente’s act, which he described as being done for the sake of “political dignity,” is worthy of emulation. Prime Minister Sánchez was proud of him when he said that he “faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside… out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims.”

When juxtaposed with the public service attitude across the Black man’s continent, political office is largely misconstrued as a personal reward rather than a public trust. When disaster strikes, when a grid collapses, or when a flood that was clearly made worse by years of neglected drainage occurs, the routine response from the appointees in charge is not resignation, but inexcusable explanations.

Such an appointee’s responsibility is diffused until it is effaced by time, since our people are believed to have a short institutional memory. Usually, on our continent, when disasters or accidents happen, condolences are issued, a committee is set up, and the minister or other such appointees remain in office to supervise the committee investigating their own ministry or agency.

The reports of such committees are submitted only to gather dust on shelves in offices, like in the instance of the latest report of the inquiry into the deaths of miners in Niger State while in the custody of the civil defence corps. No one will eventually be sanctioned for treating the lives of (illegal) miners so shabbily. Even the current Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, sometime ago reportedly confessed in the media that NECO examination papers leaked, with no heads rolling, voluntarily or otherwise, for the poor handling of such examination papers. This is why “political dignity” remains so elusive on our continent.

Even in clear instances of underperformance, appointees in our clime find it difficult to resign voluntarily from their appointments. This administration, and even the one before it, have had to send some ministers packing. Examples abound, including Prof. Tahir Mamman, former Minister of Education, who was dismissed by President Bola Tinubu on October 23, 2024, for underperformance.

Barrister Uju Kennedy-Ohanenye, then Minister of Women Affairs, was removed on October 23, 2024, because her tenure was marred by avoidable altercations that hampered the ministry’s operations. Also, Lola Ade-John, former Minister of Tourism, was relieved of her position due to poor performance. The same applied to Dr. Jamila Bio Ibrahim, former Minister of Youth Development. Both were relieved of their duties on October 23, 2024.

In addition, Betta Edu, the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Alleviation under this administration, was suspended in January 2024 following public outcry over a controversial transfer of ₦585 million into a private account. She failed to resign voluntarily before she was suspended, after which her position was filled.

Adebayo Adelabu, former Minister of Power, despite severe criticism for repeated collapses of the national electricity grid and chronic power outages, stayed put in office until the electoral timeline for political party primaries compelled his departure.

The head of the previous administration, former President Muhammadu Buhari, sacked Sabo Nanono, his Minister of Agriculture, and Saleh Mamman, Minister of Power, on the same day in September 2021 for failing to meet the operational expectations of his administration. Despite glaring signals that they were performing below par, the aforementioned appointees failed to throw in the towel voluntarily.

Under the same Buhari administration, Adamu Adamu, the Minister of Education, served out the tenure of that government despite his inept handling of protracted strikes by the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) that paralysed the tertiary education system. His subsequent confession at the end of his tenure that he knew nothing about education-sector management and had refused to resign confirmed the alien nature of voluntary resignation among political appointees in this part of the world.

However, Puente could voluntarily resign because, in Spain, the system allowed him to. His prime minister could accept his resignation without it looking like a confession of guilt for the entire government, while a credible press of that country treated the victims as more important than the minister’s political future. No cover-up. Resignation under such institutional circumstances should be understood for what it is: it should not be seen as a criminal admission but as an acceptance of political responsibility. On our continent, including in Nigeria, these conditions barely exist because loyalty is largely personal with no iota of consideration for institutional sanctity.

A minister on our continent owes their appointment to a political godfather or a president, not to the public. To resign voluntarily is therefore read as disloyalty or betrayal, and most of the time with serious communal consequences for toeing the path of honour.

So, clinging to office is perceived as a form of self-defence. For example, Hope Uzodimma, incumbent governor of Imo state, and others perceive the National Assembly as a retirement home because there are no institutional checks for overstaying in power even without commensurate achievements. The only consequence is that the public is temporarily outraged, while the opposition remains largely disunited and institutional pressure remains persistently weak due to corruption and affinity for impunity.

Men like Puente are in short supply on the African continent, and the few available ones are always afraid to act for the sake of institutional growth because our system punishes honour and rewards graft. The bar of public service overseas is high but not because the whites are from a different planet. The Europeans who colonised and committed the worst atrocities against Black people and mankind are not more moral than we are. It is just that their culture promotes political dignity and a political culture that largely embodies institutional dignity.

In their clime, public office is seen as stewardship, where the parliament actually checks power, the judiciary truly resolves conflicts impartially, and stepping aside out of respect for victims is understood as strength, not a weakness. Such resignations on our continent should be made normal by developing a political culture that makes loyalty to the public outweigh loyalty to the appointing authority.

As rightly pointed out by the 26th President of the United States, Theodore Roosevelt, attaining a sound body politic requires “public integrity… and personal dignity.” And despite the riotous political quagmire that Roosevelt’s country is currently experiencing under President Donald Trump, there are inbuilt institutional checks to correct such.

Until we separate political responsibility from criminal guilt on our continent as well, we will continue to watch from afar as others show us what “I take responsibility” truly means. I hereby rest my case for this week.

•Sanusi, former MD/CEO of the Lagos State Signage and  Agency, is currently Managing Partner at AMS RELIABLE SOLICITORS. (WhatsApp only: 07011117777)

World.title: M4STV To Beam Flamingos Vs Japan U-17 World Cup Final Live Today
World.content:
Nigerians will be able to watch the Flamingos’ historic FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup final against Japan live on M4STV on Saturday, following approval by FIFA for the station to broadcast the encounter within the country.

M4STV will bring viewers extensive coverage of the final, with seasoned broadcasters Toyin Ibitoye and Ralph Chidozie George leading the live transmission. The studio programme will begin at 6pm, ahead of the 7:30pm kick-off.

The final offers Nigeria an opportunity to win their first U-17 Women’s World Cup title and become the first African nation to claim both the boys’ and girls’ U-17 world crowns.

Coach Akeem Busari’s Flamingos reached their maiden final after an impressive recovery from a 2-1 opening defeat to Poland. They subsequently defeated Puerto Rico and two-time champions Korea DPR in the group stage before eliminating Mexico 2-1 in the Round of 16 and overcoming Venezuela in the quarter-finals.

Nigeria then produced an outstanding performance to defeat Brazil 3-1 in the semi-finals, registering 30 attempts on goal to book their historic place in the final.

Oluebube Umejiaku leads the Nigerian scorers with three goals, while Awawu Bashiru and Oluwakemi Adegbuyi have two each. Kanyinsola Yusuf, Queen Joseph, Mary Dunstan, Precious Oscar and captain Azeezat Oduntan have also scored.

Japan, however, will provide a formidable challenge. The Little Nadeshiko are appearing in their fourth final and have scored 150 goals in the competition’s history, the highest tally by any country.

They booked their place in Saturday’s showdown after drawing 1-1 with defending champions Korea DPR before winning the semi-final penalty shootout. Japan previously won the title in 2014 and finished runners-up in 2010 and 2016.

The final will take place at Pitch 3 of the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat, with kick-off scheduled for 7:30pm Nigerian time.

M4STV will provide live coverage through its streaming platform, reinforcing its position as a hub for news, entertainment, sports, hospitality and health. The station offers audiences news and analysis, diverse entertainment, live sporting action, hospitality insights and health content.

With Ibitoye and George leading the broadcast from 6pm, M4STV is inviting Nigerians to join the coverage and watch history unfold as the Super Flamingos pursue their maiden world crown.

World.title: Tinubu, Shettima Fire Salvos at Obi, Atiku, Take 2027 Re-election Battle to South-south
World.content:
President approves establishment of Ibom deep sea port

Yilwatda, Yari: APC won’t rig elections to retain power in 2027

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu and Vice-President Kashim Shettima yesterday launched blistering attacks on the presidential candidates of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi and that of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, taking the All Progressives Congress’ (APC) 2027 re-election campaign to the South-south and challenging the opposition figures over their leadership records and political accomplishments.



The President is expected to take his campaign to Rivers State today.

While Tinubu questioned Obi’s capacity to provide the leadership required to tackle Nigeria’s challenges, citing his record as Anambra State Governor, Shettima challenged Atiku to account for the political structures, successors and enduring institutions he had built during his decades in public life.



The President, who spoke during a state visit and APC presidential rally in Akwa Ibom State, also approved the establishment of the Ibom Deep Sea Port, describing it as a major catalyst for economic development and prosperity in the state and the South-South region.

Governor Umo Eno had, in his welcome address at the APC presidential rally at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium, Uyo, appealed to the President to approve the project, assuring him that the people of Akwa Ibom would remain grateful if the request was granted.

“Your request for the Ibom Deep Sea Port is hereby approved. The Ibom Deep Sea Port will bring associated economic value and economic development to the people, just as the governor has said,” the President stated.



Tinubu commended Eno for his strides in infrastructure development and human capital investment, noting that he had promptly approved the upgrade of Victor Attah International Airport following the governor’s request.

He acknowledged the benefits of visionary leadership and continuity in governance, saying no societal challenge was insurmountable with focused and determined leadership.



He also urged those seeking elective positions to serve their people with sincerity and commitment.

“There is no reason why Akwa Ibom cannot leverage the value of its palm trees and agricultural produce. There is no reason that we cannot create skills development — skills that are enduring and everlasting. When your governor requested international status for the airport, I did not hesitate; I approved it. Now, as you do for one, you do for the other,” Tinubu added.

The President urged youths at the rally to remain focused and assess the credibility, track record and determination of politicians seeking their votes in the January 2027 general election.



“You, the youth—do you have your PVCs? That is the weapon with which you can defeat tyranny and reject those deceiving you. The weapon you have is the PVC.

“I don’t have to enumerate what I’ve done for you. I’ve committed my remaining years to struggling for democracy, freedom, authenticity, development, and progress. But you have heard details from one of our best friends—you’ve heard from Senator Adams Oshiomhole.

“Have you seen development or not? You have seen progress. Your universities are no longer on strike. Economic value is being added to your lives. Governor Eno, thank you for working so hard for the love of your people,” he stated.

On the forthcoming election, Tinubu described the January 16, 2027 poll as consequential, saying it would determine the direction of the country.



“This coming election on January 16, 2027, is consequential. It will define the direction of this country. When I took office, 27 out of 36 governors in this country were unable to meet salary obligations, let alone pensions and gratuities. Today, I stand before you to say we are out of that dark tunnel.

“I can beat my chest and say we are out of the greatest despair—the dark journey of uncertainty and possible bankruptcy,” he said.

The President criticised Obi, accusing the former Anambra State governor of failing to demonstrate the leadership required to confront major environmental challenges during his tenure.



Drawing a comparison between erosion problems in Anambra and the threat posed by the Atlantic Ocean to Lagos, Tinubu said effective leadership required courage and the determination to tackle difficult problems.

“In Anambra State, he could not confront erosion. I, Bola Tinubu, confronted the Atlantic Ocean,” he said.

He faulted Obi’s record compared with Eno’s efforts to tackle erosion and other infrastructure challenges in Akwa Ibom, arguing that political leadership should be measured by the willingness to confront problems rather than avoid them.



Tinubu also questioned Obi’s movement across political parties, asking whether the inability to manage political differences and maintain relationships demonstrated the qualities required for national leadership.

“Is that a leadership trait? Is that a leadership character?” he asked.

The President subsequently commended Senate President Godswill Akpabio for his leadership of the National Assembly, describing him as “a round peg in a round hole”.



Speaking during the commissioning of the new Victor Attah International Airport terminal, Tinubu acknowledged Akpabio’s management of the legislature and the support the National Assembly had given his administration.

“I recognise our host governor, Pastor Umo Eno and other members of the National Assembly here present, but let me single out our very able and respected Senate President who has navigated the affairs of the parliament very effectively,” he said.

Tinubu also described his visit to Akwa Ibom as a homecoming, recalling his time as a Mobil auditor in the state.

“I worked here as a Mobil Auditor. We built Ibeno, developed Eket and I never knew I would be the President of Nigeria one day. We did what we needed to do,” he said.



He again commended Eno for his performance, describing him as a man of conscience, commitment and vision.

“Governor Eno is a great man of conscience, commitment and visionary. When your request for the upgrade of the airport got to my desk, I didn’t hesitate because of your track record of performance,” the President said.

Earlier, Shettima challenged Atiku to demonstrate the enduring political institutions and successors he had produced during his decades in public life.



He argued that political experience should be assessed by tangible accomplishments, the development of successors and the ability to sustain political structures, rather than the length of time spent occupying public offices.

“The presidency is not a retirement benefit for long years in politics. It is a responsibility that must be earned through ideas, competence, organisation, public confidence and demonstrable results,” Shettima declared.



He questioned Atiku’s political influence in Adamawa State, challenging him to identify governors and deputy governors he had nurtured who remained committed to his current political ambition.

Shettima maintained that a presidential candidate seeking to unite Nigeria should demonstrate the ability to reconcile competing interests within his immediate political constituency.

“Charity, they say, begins at home. It does not end there, certainly. But what does not take root at home can hardly be expected to flourish elsewhere,” he said.



The Vice President also raised questions about businesses associated with Atiku, including Gotel Communications, Adamawa Plastics and Adama Beverages, saying their performance deserved scrutiny because the former Vice President had repeatedly presented his entrepreneurial experience as a qualification for managing Nigeria’s economy.

He contrasted Atiku’s political record with Tinubu’s leadership of Lagos State, where former governors Babatunde Fashola and Akinwunmi Ambode, alongside incumbent Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, had continued to identify with the President’s political structure.

“The question is no longer how long you have been in politics; it is what your years in politics have built, whom you have raised and what has endured,” he said.



Shettima also criticised Obi, accusing him of squandering the political goodwill he previously enjoyed through what he described as falsehoods and misleading statistics.

“Peter Obi has clearly messed up and squandered away his goodwill. He no longer excites when he speaks these days. He only draws suspicions,” he said.



On his part, Akpabio commended the six South-South governors for their developmental strides and support for the APC, assuring them that the National Assembly had provided a strong foundation for Tinubu to complete the structures he had laid.

He also thanked the President for approving the establishment of a Federal University of Agriculture, a Federal University of Technology and a Police Academy in Akwa Ibom State, reiterating that the South-South states stood firmly with the APC.

Akpabio’s remarks came as he praised the President’s leadership and the cooperation between the executive and legislative arms of government.



Also speaking, APC National Chairman, Yilwatda, maintained that the ruling party would not need electoral manipulation to secure Tinubu’s re-election, citing the administration’s achievements and the party’s expanding political structures.

“We don’t need to rig. We don’t need to add one vote to Mr President. He can win squarely,” he declared.

Yilwatda said Tinubu received more than 10 million votes durig the party’s presidential primary, exceeding the votes he secured in the 2023 general election.



He also cited the APC’s numerical strength among governors, federal lawmakers, state legislators and local government chairmen as evidence of its organisational capacity.

The National Chairman defended Tinubu’s economic reforms, highlighting investments in infrastructure, education, consumer credit, student loans and support for small businesses.



He said the administration’s policies were positioning Nigeria towards the President’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy by 2030.

Yilwatda particularly commended the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and Calabar-Itu-Ikot Ekpene road projects, saying they would improve transportation, reduce logistics costs and strengthen trade across the region.

Similarly, Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, insisted that the ruling party would not manipulate the 2027 election, maintaining that Tinubu’s achievements were sufficient to earn him another mandate.

“We are not going to rig the election, but Nigerians are going to vote for Asiwaju Bola Tinubu because he has laid the foundation for a better Nigeria,” he said.



Yari set a target of at least 1.6 million votes for Tinubu in Akwa Ibom, challenging the party’s leadership to mobilise eligible voters.

He also challenged opposition politicians over complaints about hunger and unemployment, arguing that the government had introduced programmes to support farmers, small businesses, market women and job creation.

“What programme do you have in place that is better than what Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu has today?

“In terms of unemployment, what do you have in place that Asiwaju has not put in place that you are going to present to Nigerians?” he asked.



Speaking on behalf of the Nigeria Governors Forum and the South-South governors, Bayelsa State Governor, Douye Diri, applauded Tinubu for the ongoing construction of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and the establishment of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), among other legacy projects.

He also commended Eno for the massive turnout of supporters at the stadium.

“The Coastal Highway is a masterpiece. No President, living or dead, ever conceived it. All six governors of the South-South are solidly behind you. Carry go,” Diri assured the President.



At a reception in his honour at the 70-hectare Arise Palm Resort, Eno told Tinubu that he felt fulfilled by the approval of the Ibom Deep Sea Port project.

President-General of the Akwa Ibom Council of Traditional Rulers and Chancellor of Akwa Ibom State University, His Eminence Dr Ntenyin Solomon Etuk, expressed pride in identifying with the administration and prayed for the President’s success in his second-term bid.

Upon arrival in the state, Tinubu inaugurated the new Victor Attah International Airport terminal building, Ring Road 3, linking Idoro Road to Ikot Ekpene Road through Uyo and Ibiono Ibom, and the Arise Palm Resort.

World.title: SASSA pensioner reveals the one expense that swallows her entire grant
World.content:
Avril Lloyd has nothing left by the end of each month. The retired KwaZulu-Natal pensioner, aged over 65, has received the Older Persons Grant for more than five years. It is her only income, and she says it does not cover her basic needs.

Lloyd shared her experience in The South African’s SASSA grant survey.

Older Persons Grant swallowed by rent

The old age pension pays R2 400 per month for people aged 60 and older, applying from April 2026.



For Lloyd, almost all of that money goes to one expense. She uses her grant mainly for rent and housing costs, and by month-end, nothing remains.

“Would be really grate if the pension amounts were substantially increased as my Grant only covers my rent,” Lloyd said.

The pressure reaches the dinner table. Lloyd confirmed that someone in her household went without food in the past month. She says she regularly struggles to make ends meet.

Housing costs top her list of worries

Lloyd names housing costs as her biggest financial concern. As a private renter, she has no buffer when rent consumes her monthly payment.

She spent her working life in childcare and caregiving. Today, she can only travel under five kilometres for work, which limits any chance of earning extra income.

Lloyd has never applied for additional government support. She explained that she did not know what else was available to her.



When asked what one thing she would change about SASSA, her answer matched her comment. She wants the grant amount increased.

Smooth service, but the money falls short

Lloyd has no complaints about how SASSA runs her grant. Her payments go straight into her bank account, and she says the process has been straightforward from the start.

She rates SASSA’s communication with recipients as very good. When asked about her biggest challenge with SASSA grants, she said she has none.

That makes her story stand out. The system delivers her pension on time every month, yet she still cannot afford both a roof over her head and regular meals.

For now, her grant pays the landlord, and little else.

World.title: Severe thunderstorms threaten parts of North West and Free State
World.content:
SAWS has issued a yellow level 2 warning for severe thunderstorms in parts of North West and the Free State. Image: Unsplash

Residents in parts of North West and the Free State should prepare for severe thunderstorms as the South African Weather Service (SAWS) issued a yellow level 2 warning for Saturday and Sunday.

The warning, which took effect at 1pm on Saturday, will remain in place until 9.59pm on Sunday.

Yellow level 2 warning for severe thunderstorms

Area: Eastern parts of North West and Free State

Validity: 7-8 November 2026 #saws #weatheroutlook #Warning pic.twitter.com/uEBK7yJ03B  November 7, 2026

SAWS expects severe storms to develop over the eastern parts of both provinces during this period.

The storms could bring excessive lightning, heavy downpours, damaging winds and large amounts of small hail.

Heavy rain and strong winds could cause damage

The thunderstorms could bring enough rain to cause localised flooding, particularly along roads and bridges that are vulnerable to flooding.



Strong winds could also bring down trees and block smaller roads, while severe weather could temporarily disrupt electricity supplies and communication services.

The weather service cautioned that these conditions could cause localised damage to infrastructure, homes, vehicles and people’s livelihoods.

SAWS also warned that informal settlements could experience localised damage during the storms.



Severe thunderstorms: What residents should watch out for

Residents in the affected areas should remain alert as thunderstorms develop over the weekend.

Heavy downpours could make driving conditions dangerous, while hail and strong winds could damage vehicles and property.

Motorists should take extra care on roads, avoid crossing flooded roads and bridges.

World.title: Child Support Grant mom reveals what happens in her home when the R580 runs out
World.content:
Beunice Williams runs out of money before the month ends. The young Gauteng mother, aged 24, has received the Child Support Grant for three years. She says it does not cover her household’s basic needs.

Williams shared her experience in The South African’s SASSA grant survey. She lives in a shared family home, where one to two people depend on her income.

Child Support Grant runs dry before month-end

The Child Support Grant now pays R580 per child per month, up from R560 previously. For Williams, that increase has not closed the gap.



She spends her grant on a mix of essentials, including food, transport and household necessities. By the end of each month, nothing is left. Williams says she regularly struggles to make ends meet while she waits for the next payment.

The shortfall has hit her household hard. Williams confirmed that someone in her home went without food in the past month.

Unemployment remains her biggest worry

Williams is unemployed and actively looking for work. She has experience in retail and customer service and can travel between five and 20 kilometres for a job.



She names unemployment as her biggest financial concern. Without a salary, the grant carries most of the weight in her household.

Williams has not relied on the grant alone. She applied for additional government support beyond her Child Support Grant, and her application was successful.

Even so, when asked what one thing she would change about SASSA, her answer was simple. She wants the grant amount increased.



Grant recipient calls for clearer SASSA information

Williams says her grant itself has been straightforward. She has never had a problem with her payments and rates SASSA’s communication with recipients as adequate.

Her biggest frustration lies elsewhere. Williams says finding clear, accurate information online is her greatest challenge as a grant recipient.

She had a direct message for the agency.

“Please make information that’s required via your app or websites 100% clear,” Williams said.



Her story reflects a reality many caregivers share: payments arrive on time, but the money and the information still fall short.

World.title: WEATHER: Orange level 5 warning as heavy rain threatens KwaZulu-Natal
World.content:
SAWS has issued an orange level 5 warning for disruptive rain in KwaZulu-Natal. Image: Unsplash

KwaZulu-Natal residents face a risk of flooding on Sunday as the South African Weather Service (SAWS) issues an orange level 5 warning for disruptive rain.

The warning takes effect from midnight on Sunday, November 8, and remains in place until 22:59.

The weather service expects between 30mm and 80mm of accumulated rainfall in less than 48 hours across central and southern parts of the province.



Orange level 5 warning for disruptive rainfall

Area: KwaZulu Natal

Validity: 8 November 2026#saws #weatheroutlook #Warning pic.twitter.com/B08pCuxHyT — SA Weather Service (@SAWeatherServic) November 7, 2026

SAWS says persistent rainfall over the past few days, followed by more widespread showers and thundershowers today and tomorrow, could worsen conditions.

Why has KZN received an orange level 5 warning for disruptive rain?

A strong surface high-pressure system over the eastern parts of KwaZulu-Natal, supported by an upper-air trough over southern South Africa, will bring widespread showers and thundershowers to the province.



The system will maintain wet conditions today and tomorrow, with further rainfall adding to the amounts already recorded in recent days.

SAWS warns that the accumulated rainfall could result in significant impacts, particularly in central and southern parts of the province.

Flooding and damage among possible impacts

The weather service warns that heavy rainfall could flood roads and settlements and damage bridges.



Fast-flowing, deep water could also endanger lives and force some communities to leave their homes.

Motorists should prepare for major traffic disruptions as flooding could force authorities to close roads.

The rainfall could also disrupt essential services, including water supplies, electricity and communications.



Residents urged to take precautions

Residents in affected areas should remain alert as conditions deteriorate.

Avoid crossing flooded roads, rivers and streams, whether on foot or in a vehicle. Fast-flowing water can sweep away people and vehicles, even when it does not appear particularly deep.

Motorists should also allow extra travel time and avoid routes where water covers the road.



Residents should follow updates from the South African Weather Service and local disaster management authorities as the situation develops.

World.title: Cape Town man, 69, arrested after discovery of dead dogs
World.content:
One of the dead dogs was discovered floating inside a water tank. Image: Cape of Good Hope SPCA

A 69-year-old man has been arrested and charged with animal cruelty after two dogs were found dead at a property in Factreton, Cape Town.

The arrest took place on Thursday, 5 November 2026.

DOG IN DISTRESS

According to the Cape of Good Hope SPCA, a witness heard the sound of a dog crying. They saw it “alive and in distress” inside a water tank on the property.



Per the witness’s account, the man on the property allegedly claimed that the dog kept stealing their food, prompting him to put it inside the tank. The man then allegedly rebuffed the witness’s offer to take the dog and left it in the tank.

The witness subsequently alerted the Cape of Good Hope SPCA that Friday afternoon.

TRAGIC DISCOVERY

An SPCA inspector arrived at the property but was refused access. The inspector then called for assistance from the City of Cape Town Law Enforcement’s Animal Control Auxiliary Unit. Once officers arrived, entry was obtained with the property owner’s permission.

“The man told Inspector Siviwe Noko, who leads this investigation, that the dogs had been sick and that he had placed them inside the tank to bathe them,” the SPCA explained. “He said they had died and indicated where he had buried one of them.”

The second dog was found buried beneath a tree on the property. Image: Cape of Good Hope SPCA

The body of a black-and-brown dog was found wrapped in a towel and placed inside a black plastic bag beneath a tree. Officers then recovered the body of a tan-and-black mixed breed dog that was floating inside the water tank.

The SPCA took custody of both dogs’ bodies for post-mortem examination and further investigation.



SPCA: REPORT ANIMAL CRUELTY

The man was arrested and transported to Kensington SAPS. He was charged with animal cruelty and was scheduled to appear in the Cape Town Magistrates’ Court on Friday, 6 November 2026.

A dog accused of stealing food still deserves protection,” the SPCA said. “Illness demands care. Neither circumstance excuses cruelty. The allegations in this case demand a thorough investigation and accountability through the courts.”

Members of the public are urged to report animal cruelty to the Cape of Good Hope SPCA by contacting either 021 700 4158 or 021 700 4159 during office hours. For after-hours emergencies, you can call 083 326 1604.

In other news, a dog in Cape Town died after trying to flee from Guy Fawkes fireworks this week.

World.title: 3-bedroom Cape Town home goes to auction for R380 000
World.content:
Bank auctions are ramping up again as owners struggle to make payments in this economy.

In Cape Town, about half a dozen properties have gone to auction.

One has a R380 000 reserve, 59% less than the City of Cape Town’s R930 000 valuation in 2025.



Home goes for one-third of its R930 000 market valuation

This 312-square-metre semi-detached home has 3 bedrooms, 1 bathroom, a carport, and a garage.

Located on Bokmakierie Street in Kleinvlei, the City of Cape Town’s 2025 valuation puts the home’s market value at R930 000.

The area’s average sale price, according to the South African Deeds Office, is R485 000 as of October 2026.

Yet, Absa has the home up for auction with a R380 000 reserve. The auction will take place in Kuilsriver on 17 November 2026.

However, any bidder should know the current homeowner owes R40 647 in rates arrears.

And according to Barnard Incorporated Attorneys, the buyer should be prepared to settle the arrears after the sale.



Buying a property at auction

The reserve price, the amount the bank must sell the property for if a bid exceeds it, isn’t the full price the buyer pays.

At auction, a successful buyer pays what they bid.

They may also pay VAT, transfer duties, sheriff or auctioneer’s commission, and any arrears.

If the home is still occupied at the time of the auction, a buyer will have to pay for an eviction.

These costs can add up and, if the home is still occupied, prevent a buyer from accurately assessing the home’s condition.

Evictions also aren’t easy in South Africa, especially if the occupier opposes. The process can take over a year, even after a successful sale.

Then there are legal costs.

An unopposed eviction can cost up to R18 000, according to Simon Dippenaar and Associates.

Opposed evictions can surpass R45 000 in legal fees.

Before bidding, buyers should consider these costs.

More auctions in Cape Town

Other properties are also going to auction in Cape Town.

A flat in Kenilworth has hit the market with a R735 000 reserve, and so has one in Woodstock with a R600 000 reserve.

The Kenilworth flat, however, owes R44 172 in levy arrears.

In Landsdowne, there’s a 2-bedroom flat on auction with a R700 000 reserve and no levies or rates arrears.

In Kraaifontein East, there’s a 5-bedroom home which the city values at R1.2 million, with an R850 000 reserve.

World.title: ELECTIONS 2026 | Result: DA wins Nelson Mandela Bay metro
World.content:
The Democratic Alliance (DA) has emerged as a resounding winner in Nelson Mandela Bay in the 2026 Local Government Elections. Image: X @Our_DA

The Democratic Alliance (DA) has emerged as a resounding winner in Nelson Mandela Bay in the 2026 Local Government Elections, securing 44.17% of the vote and significantly extending its lead over the African National Congress (ANC).

With the vote count completed, the DA secured 53 seats in the 120-seat Eastern Cape metro council, compared with 32 seats for the ANC.

READ | Cyril Ramaphosa leads ANC to WORST-ever election result



The result represents a major setback for the governing party, which has lost 16 seats compared with the previous council.

The DA’s 44.17% support puts it 18.69 percentage points ahead of the ANC, which managed just 25.48%.

However, despite its commanding lead, the DA has fallen short of an outright majority and will need coalition partners to govern the metro.

A party needs 61 of the council’s 120 seats to secure a majority.

Nelson Mandela Bay election results

The Electoral Commission’s results show the following distribution among the leading parties:

Party Seats Vote share DA 53 44.17% ANC 32 25.48% EFF 7 5.55% SACP 4 3.19% Patriotic Alliance 4 3.04% Freedom Front Plus 3 2.48% UDM 3 2.42% Mayibuye Civic Movement 2 2.2% ActionSA 2 1.8% MK Party 2 1.2%

Several smaller parties also secured representation, including the ACDP, ATM, PAC, Mayibuye Afrika Movement, African Independent Congress, United Progressive People Alliance, Democratic Movement and National Alliance.



In total, 18 political parties will be represented in the new council.

DA strengthens its position as ANC loses ground

The result represents a significant improvement for the DA in Nelson Mandela Bay.

The party’s 53 seats put it in a considerably stronger position to negotiate a coalition government than in the previous council.

The ANC, meanwhile, has seen its representation fall from 48 to 32 seats, losing a third of its previous council representation.

The EFF secured seven seats, while the South African Communist Party (SACP) made its first independent electoral contest in the metro count, winning four seats.

The Patriotic Alliance also secured four seats, doubling its previous representation.

Coalition negotiations will determine who governs

Despite winning the election convincingly, the DA cannot govern Nelson Mandela Bay alone.

It needs at least eight additional councillors to reach the 61-seat majority threshold.

This puts smaller parties in an important position as coalition negotiations begin.

The PA, SACP, Freedom Front Plus, UDM, ActionSA and other smaller parties could all become relevant to discussions about the next municipal administration.

The DA’s mayoral candidate, Retief Odendaal, has previously indicated that restoring stability to the municipality would be a priority.

Nelson Mandela Bay has experienced repeated political instability and coalition disputes, which have affected municipal governance.

Odendaal has also highlighted the municipality’s financial challenges, including a reported R1.7 billion revenue shortfall in its electricity department.

The DA now faces the challenge of turning its electoral victory into a stable governing arrangement.

For the ANC, the result represents another major electoral blow in the Eastern Cape, a province where it has historically enjoyed strong support.
