They also report difficulties in treating medetomidine withdrawal, which can lead to complications like heart attacks or strokes from the blood pressure, said Dr. Monty Ghosh, a Calgary-based addictions physician and researcher.

"These are the things that we kind of have to match that we didn't have to match before," Ghosh said. "It's sort of skewed our management strategies for these individuals."

WATCH | Canada's toxic drug supply evolves: Overdose deaths remain 'unacceptably high' despite 2025 decrease, Canada's top doctor says | Duration closed caption 2:07 Canada's Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Joss Reimer says bringing overdose deaths down 'even further' will take co-ordinated action, particularly as emergency medical services are called on to deal with 'polysubstance overdoses' that require more complex interventions.

Drowsy patients coupled with heart attack risks

Taking opioids can make it difficult for a person to breathe. Add in medetomidine, said Ghosh, and they'll also become much drowsier, with low blood pressure and a low heart rate that can stay down for long periods of time.

"It can be very dangerous," he said, because that reduces blood flow to vital organs, which can lead to serious complications, as well as slow breathing.

At overdose prevention sites in B.C. and Montreal, nurses also say they're concerned about users having very low heart rates and becoming dizzy and unresponsive for hours, according to a CCSA presentation. Regularly monitoring a person's pulse, heart rate and oxygen levels now matters more, because these changes can be delayed compared with previous drugs and adulterants.

When reversing an overdose where medetomidine is involved, Substance Use Philly noted it is important to focus on the person's breathing rather than their responsiveness, given that medetomidine is a sedative and therefore does not respond to naloxone, which reverses opioid overdoses.

Medetomidine withdrawal, meanwhile, can come on quickly and brings its own set of problems, like the question of how much vomiting is too much.

Dr. Sahil Gupta, who works in Toronto, says patients experiencing medetomidine withdrawal require hospitalization or intensive care medications because breathing and consciousness need to be monitored for a longer period of time than with opioid withdrawal.

"In our emergency departments, [these] patients take a longer amount of time, both from a nursing, staff physician and time within the hospitals" perspective.

While the goal is to support breathing to prevent the brain from starving of oxygen, in extreme circumstances, patients will need to be put on a ventilator, he said.

A box of Narcan sits at a community outreach storefront in Philadelphia in 2023. Generically known as naloxone, the medication used revive people who have stopped breathing doesn’t reverse the effects if opioids are absent. (Matt Rourke/The Associated Press)

"[Resource] strains like this tend to actually create a lot of disruption and cause increased wait times, overcrowding," Gupta said. "Often the patients experiencing the medetomidine withdrawal are requiring hospitalization or intensive care meds, as well, which are much more high-resource areas."

Gupta said unless the whole continuum of homelessness and socioeconomic factors are addressed, "we're really not going to make inroads."

Proposed solutions

One doctor in Alberta helped create a program meant to try and address emergency room overcrowding.

The Edmonton program, called Bridge Healing, looks to address homelessness among those making repeat hospital visits, said Dr. Louis Hugo Francescutti, a professor in the School of Public Health at the University of Alberta who works as an emergency physician.

If someone comes to the emergency department with no fixed address, Francescutti said they're asked two questions: whether they are homeless, and whether they want a chance to get their life together again.

"If they say yes and there's beds available, we send them by cab to these purpose-built buildings, where we provide them free-of-charge accommodation ," he said, along with services including access to a medical clinic to start to address their needs.

"Emergency department staff are becoming morally distressed," he said. "They're burning out because they see a problem that is solvable if we had the right people intervening."

He said that includes better access to specialized clinics and practitioners like social workers.

WATCH | Hospitals & housing: Many homeless people return to the ER after being discharged. This program hopes to change that | Duration 2:53 A new pilot project at the Tupper YMCA in Westmount, Que., aims to fundamentally change what happens when patients experiencing homelessness are discharged from the hospital by offering them temporary housing.

However, some practitioners say there is another missing element: safe consumption sites, many of which were closed down in provinces like Ontario, with the provincial government saying the sites encouraged drug use.

At these sites, workers would be able to assess comatose overdose patients, potentially giving them oxygen or a small dose of naloxone so they can avoid being put into full opioid withdrawal, said Dr. Raghu Venugopal, an emergency physician at three downtown Toronto hospitals.

"This really matters because if you want safe subways, if you want safe parks, if you want a better-functioning ER, there is a place for people who need to use drugs," he said.

Indeed, without the supervised sites, people who previously would have been revived at the sites now need to go to emergency, a 2026 report by Gillian Kolla of Memorial University's medicine faculty and epidemiologist Tara Gomes of the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network suggests, delaying care for other life-threatening conditions such as heart attacks and traumatic injuries from vehicle collisions.

Asked to respond to the emergency physicians' calls, Ontario's Health Ministry pointed to its approach.

"Instead of giving people tools to use harmful, illegal drugs, our government is helping people break the tragic cycle of drug addiction by making record investments in more mental health and wraparound supports," Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario's health minister, said in an email.

"Across the province, we are investing a historic $560 million to build 29 Homeless and Addictions Recovery Treatment (HART) Hubs, including 4 in Toronto, replacing the failed approach of drug injection sites."

Barnes said Ontario's 29 HART hubs are open to set people on a path to recovery, with each hub receiving four times more funding than the drug sites.

World.title: Tax relief could be coming for Canadian artists — but how does it work?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If you're a Canadian artist who followed Thursday's federal budget release, you might believe you're getting a windfall.

"In Budget 2026, we’re backing the Canadian artists who tell our stories," Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X, shortly after Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne made a similar announcement in the House of Commons, revealing the Canada Creative Credit.

This tax credit is aimed specifically at those earning their income from "original and creative artistic works" in the country, according to the budget.

"That means if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to $45,000 of income derived from your creative work," Carney added in his post.

But how much can artists really expect in their pockets? Which kind of artists can even benefit from this? And when — if ever — is this actually taking effect?

WATCH | How the new federal budget could affect museums: What the latest federal budget means for national museums in Ottawa | Duration closed caption 1:44 Canada's national museums are getting a $783-million boost in the federal budget over the next five years. Here's what that might mean for the National Capital Region. The CBC’s David Fraser reports.

What is the Canada Creative Credit?

The budget says it will likely take the form of a non-refundable tax credit that would "provide tax recognition on up to $45,000 of annual qualifying net business income derived from original and creative artistic works."

A non-refundable tax credit is a set reduction in the amount of income tax someone owes at the end of the year, says Chris Raymond, a tax consultant and content creator.

In short, the government decides your total income tax based on your income. The credit is then subtracted from that amount to reduce your total taxes owed.

What makes credits like the Canada Creative Credit "non-refundable" is that they cannot reduce that amount below zero. If the credit is bigger than your taxes, you don't get to cash out the remainder as a refund.

"The taxable income is the number that we actually calculate how much tax you owe on," Raymond said. "Once that tax number is calculated, that's where the non-refundable credits come into play."

How much money could you get?

Canadians are already covered by a non-refundable tax credit called the Basic Personal Amount, which applies to roughly $16,000 for most incomes.

The Canada Creative Credit would likely cover the difference between the Basic Personal Amount and the government's goal of $45,000, says Robert Gillezeau, an assistant professor of economic analysis and policy at the University of Toronto.

"If you're an artist making whatever, $40,000, $50,000, all the way up to $100,000, this is going to be a meaningful shift in what your income looks like at the end of the day," he said, adding that it could amount to several thousand dollars annually for those eligible.

"It should be a large enough incentive that it will cause some people to work in this area who would otherwise work somewhere else."

However, that ignores a potentially large additional source of tax, said Toronto-based chartered professional accountant (CPA) and content creator Mohammed Al-khooly.

"If someone wants to truly be exempt on the first $45,000 income, then the provinces would also have to propose a similar credit for the provincial taxes," Al-khooly said.

"It's not necessarily tax-free. It's tax-free for just federal purposes."

Who would be eligible?

This is where things get tricky.

CPA Sam Cao pointed out that the budget says the government will support young Canadian artists and "Canadian painters, sculptors, ceramicists, writers, musicians, actors are our storytellers."

But there is "no exact definition" within the budget that specifies which types of artists would be eligible. So there's little to no way to know whether, for example, a violin teacher or a filmmaker is more likely to be approved.

"They're going to have some type of prescriptive list that demarcates a bunch of workers being in, and other workers being out. It's going to be arbitrary in some ways," Gillezeau said.

"They talk about supporting creativity and the arts broadly; like, any type of writing could fall within that. And if, you know … any type of original writing is going to be eligible, the cost of this credit will just absolutely balloon."

When asked whether there was any firm definition of which artists would qualify, a Department of Finance official referred CBC News to the budget release. It said further details will be announced in the spring economic update in 2027.

Printed copies of the 2026 federal budget. (David Thurton/ CBC)

How likely is it to happen?

Far less than a confirmed payday, Raymond said, the Canada Creative Credit is more the proposition of a plan.

"Obviously the budget hasn't been passed. But they haven't said that if the budget is passed, that this is coming into play," he said. "What they have said is that they have an idea and a concept of how this would work. They're going to consult with people in the industry about it."

There are other targeted tax credits in Canada, such as for teachers and volunteer firefighters. Still, Cao said, if the Canada Creative Credit took a form even somewhat similar to how it is currently described, it would be a unique step.

"This is probably the first tax credit of its kind that specifically targets self-employed individuals through a non-refundable personal income tax credit," he said.

LISTEN | The federal budget explained: The Current 20:14 Breaking down the federal budget The federal finance minister Francois-Philippe Champagne joins Matt Galloway the morning after the federal budget. Plus analysis from CBC's chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

Gillezeau noted tax policies targeted at specific professions are typically disliked by economists, comparing the Canada Creative Credit's possible end-status to the "boutique" tax credits of the Stephen Harper era that ballooned the tax code to absurd lengths .

There are also similarities to subsidies for the arts seen in the New Deal of the 1930s, in which the U.S. government subsidized works of art for the public good .

What is different here is the proposal of large, profession-targeted tax credits for income, Gillezeau said. Though what it looks like should it come to fruition is still almost entirely a mystery.

"It's enough to think about [whether] it is a valuable piece of public policy or not," he said. "But the actual implementation details certainly are nowhere close to being there."

World.title: Problematic or protected? The debate over filming police in real time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Peel police are warning the public not to post videos of officers during active incidents, following an armed standoff that locked down University of Toronto Mississauga's campus. While police caution that broadcasting tactical movements can jeopardize officer safety, experts say whether the practice is actually illegal remains a grey area.

Social media posts showing real-time positions of police officers in a standoff with an armed suspect at the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus on Monday night prompted a stern warning from police, but legal experts say the law isn't clear-cut on the issue.

"We saw many members of the public uploading images of the position of police officers during this active incident," Peel Regional Police Const. Tyler Bell said at a news conference on Tuesday. "This is a blatant safety concern. Doing so puts our officers in harm's way and any potential victims or hostages inside."

"Canadians have the right that is constitutionally protected to film on-duty police officers, but that right ends the second it interferes with the police operation or compromises the safety of people involved."

The comments followed a lengthy standoff between officers and a 19-year-old man who allegedly barricaded himself with a weapon inside a residential unit the university's McLuhan Court residence. The school issued a shelter-in-place order for students in the area that was later lifted after police said the man was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Bell said photos and videos of officers in their tactical positions, with weapons pointed toward the buildings were circulating on social media as the incident was evolving. While people are allowed to film police in public settings, he said doing so during an active incident can can jeopardize investigations.

"The act of filming isn't the issue. It's the putting it out so everybody can see it, including bad actors. Giving up the position of an officer can compromise their safety or the safety other others. It's a no-no," Bell said in an interview with CBC News.

"By all means, film it and post it afterwards when the situation safe."

What does the law say?

However, some legal experts say whether the practice is actually illegal is a grey area.

While it is generally legal to film the police in public settings, it can become a problem if it interferes with officers doing their job, said Howard Sapers, executive director of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA).

Examples include physically obstructing the police or filming evidence, which could result in a phone being seized.

"The police could advise and say 'We wish you wouldn't do that,' but that's very different from them ordering you not to do it," said Sapers.

"And if they do order you not to do it, the general advice is to comply because that could or could not be a lawful request or a lawful demand. That would be something that could be tested in court, but if you refuse to comply, the refusal becomes an offence."

Sapers says in those instances, people should seek clarity from police on why they're asking them not to record. In the case of Monday's incident, there was no explicit legal order to not film and share.

Police officers and the SIU outside of a student residence at the University of Toronto's Mississauga campus on Nov. 2, 2026. Officers were involved in a lengthy standoff after a 19-year-old man allegedly barricaded himself inside a residential unit with a weapon. (Jacob Estrin/CBC)

Posting in real-time can fall under the umbrella of obstructing a police officer, which is a criminal offence under Section 129 of the Criminal Code, said Howard Morton, a former Special Investigations Unit director and criminal defence lawyer.

But in order for someone to be found guilty, "wilful intention" must be proven, he said.

"You would have to intentionally, with a specific intent, interfere with an investigation — either by jeopardizing an officer or just letting the bad guys know what the police are doing," he said.

"You could interfere by streaming [incidents] live."

Students say social media kept them in the loop

Some students CBC News spoke to, said although they were receiving regular updates with safety instructions from police and UTM campus officials, Instagram and Reddit allowed them to share information and learn why there was a lockdown in the first place.

"I saw one [person] from a window who I think was videoing the police, some other posts were just rumours of what could have possibly happened because when it first happened, no one knew what was going on," said second-year student Efe Otomewo.

"Some people were saying fire, some people were saying shooting, some people saying fireworks were being set off. So that was mostly the way that we got our information."

There was a large police presence in the area of Mississauga Road and Outer Circle Road, at the University of Toronto Mississauga campus, on Monday night. (Zachary Proulx/CBC)

Many students said they didn't share the videos because residence leaders told them not to and they didn't want to add to online rumours.

"More details would've been more helpful but I understand that they can't really give the full rundown to not cause so much panic," said first-year student Beulah Karibo. "But it still creates a panic if people hear there's a lockdown and a shooting.

Meanwhile, Bell said he understands the curiosity but explained police were releasing information on a need-to-know basis, adding that resolving the incident safely was their top priority.

World.title: Canada's military is using Palantir software. What are the risks?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is growing scrutiny over Canadian defence contracts with American tech giant Palantir. For The National, CBC’s Ashley Fraser breaks down how its software is being used and why politicians and privacy experts are warning about national security and data sovereignty risks.

Canada has multimillion-dollar contracts with Palantir, a controversial U.S. software company. Experts warn the deals could expose Canadian military data to U.S. authorities and leave Canada reliant on critical technology supplied by a foreign company.

Documents obtained by the Investigative Journalism Foundation revealed that the Department of National Defence (DND) has had a contract for Palantir's Gotham software since 2020 that was internally flagged as "not for public disclosure." Initially valued at $14 million, it could be worth up to $63 million.

DND told CBC News that Gotham brings together information from military databases and operates on closed, classified networks inside secure facilities in Canada. The department declined to say exactly what information Gotham processes, citing national-security concerns.

DND says its security assessment determined that no government data, prompts, outputs or metadata handled under the contracts could be stored, accessed or processed outside Canada.

But experts argue U.S. law could still provide American authorities with a means to acquire information within an American company's possession, custody or control. Others warn Canada could become dependent on military technology that would be difficult to replace.

A view of the Palantir building is seen during the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2026 in Davos, Switzerland, in January. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

Why is Palantir controversial?

Palantir Technologies was co-founded in 2003 by five people, including CEO Alex Karp and board chair Peter Thiel. It has since become a major technology contractor for governments and militaries.

Its software integrates information from multiple datasets so users can identify connections and patterns across large amounts of information.

Michael Steinberger, a journalist and author of The Philosopher in the Valley: Alex Karp, Palantir, and the Rise of the Surveillance State, said the company has drawn criticism over its involvement in military operations and immigration enforcement in the United States.

Some of its most important work, he said, involves Project Maven, the U.S. military's artificial-intelligence program used to analyze military data and support targeting operations.

"This is being used extensively now in U.S. military actions," Steinberger said.

When asked about Project Maven, a Palantir spokesperson told CBC News: "We do not conduct surveillance. The Maven platform provides the U.S. warfighter a live, synchronized view of the battlespace to help them make better-informed decisions and reduce errors … all of this is conducted with strong safeguards and accountability logs."

Palantir's work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also drawn criticism.

"Its technology seems to be a critical node in the immigration crackdown that's happening here in the United States right now," Steinberger said.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp is shown at the 48th Annual Meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos in 2018. (Peter Klaunzer/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock)

The company has also increasingly identified itself with U.S. national interests.

U.S. President Donald Trump praised Palantir earlier this year for having "great war-fighting capabilities and equipment."

In June, Palantir posted on X a list of 22 principles drawn from The Technological Republic, a book co-written by Karp. They include the assertion that Silicon Valley has an "obligation to participate in the defense of the nation" and describe some cultures as "dysfunctional and regressive."

Karp has also appeared in company advertising saying "the West is superior, and we have to fight for these values."

Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, an independent public policy think tank, said the concern extends beyond Palantir's politics to Canada's reliance on an outside supplier for critical digital infrastructure.

"We're potentially growing a digital dependency, enriching what is fundamentally a U.S. company at the expense of our sovereignty," she said.

A protester opposed to data analytics firm Palantir Technologies' role in the National Health Service (NHS) holds a sign in a demonstration outside St Thomas' Hospital during a global day of action against the company's healthcare contracts, in London, in October. (Toby Shepheard/Reuters)

Other countries becoming less reliant

The debate over Palantir comes amid a broader push in Europe for "digital sovereignty" — greater domestic control over technology and data.

In July, France and Germany pledged to reduce reliance on foreign providers by examining domestic alternatives after ending Palantir's contracts with their intelligence services.

In the U.K., MPs have called on the government to end Palantir's 330-million-pound ($619 million Cdn) National Health Service contract, citing "serious mistrust" of the company after a Financial Times report that a small number of company employees had access to identifiable patient data in the Palantir-built platform. The National Data Guardian, an independent adviser on the use of health and social-care data in England, said the incident breached data-governance principles.

A Palantir spokesperson at the time told the Financial Times that "Palantir software can only be used to process data precisely in line with the instruction of the customer. Using the data for anything else would not only be illegal but technically impossible due to granular access controls overseen by the NHS."

Barry Appleton, an international lawyer who practises both Canadian and American law, says the U.S. CLOUD Act could compel U.S. companies to produce data stored outside the United States. (CBC)

Should Canada be concerned?

One potential concern is whether U.S. authorities could compel access to Canadian information.

Barry Appleton, an international lawyer who practises both Canadian and American law, pointed to the U.S. CLOUD Act, which allows authorities, with appropriate legal process, to compel covered U.S. companies to produce data within their possession, custody or control, regardless of whether it is stored inside or outside the United States.

"I'm talking to you today while we're having massive trade wars," Appleton said. "Do I want Canada's trade strategy to be able to be surveilled and read by the United States today? No, I don't."

DND says its Palantir systems have been assessed for this kind of exposure. It says government data, prompts, outputs or metadata could not be stored, accessed or processed outside Canada and that Gotham information is protected on closed, classified networks in secure Canadian facilities.

"The United States CLOUD Act does not have any authority over servers located in Canada," DND said.

Appleton disputes that interpretation.

"The CLOUD Act is not about where the server is located," he said.

"Any data at any time that Palantir has, if it was subject to an order under the CLOUD Act would have to be produced," Appleton said because "it's decided by American courts under American law, not under Canadian law."

Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a reception with business leaders, at the 56th annual World Economic Forum (WEF), in Davos, in January 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Jennifer Evans, a policy researcher and founder of PatternPulse AI, said DND's statement that data is stored on closed, classified networks in Canada doesn't make clear what level of security is being used.

She agreed with Appleton that the CLOUD Act "means that there is potential data visibility to some of the highest levels in the U.S. government."

Evans said DND should disclose more about its contract with Palantir, including whether it uses air-gapping, which isolates computers or networks from unsecured networks and the internet.

A Palantir spokesperson told CBC News in an email that it is "a software company" and rejected suggestions that the company takes ownership of or uses its customers' information.

"Our customers own and control their own data. Palantir never uses or retains customer data for its own purposes or shares data with other customers," the spokesperson told CBC News.

A second potential risk is Canada's dependence on a foreign supplier for military technology.

A Ukrainian artilleryman sets up a Starlink satellite internet system near the front line in the Donetsk region in October 2026. Ukrainian officials said Starlink speeds had been throttled earlier that month, disrupting military operations. (Stringer/File Photo/Reuters)

Bednar points to Space X's Starlink internet technology, owned by Elon Musk. Beginning Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink's speeds, disrupting military activity. The accusations came after Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply the world with millions of tonnes of Russian diesel.

While it's unclear who was responsible for the slowdown, Bednar says the episode shows how reliance on a company with ties to the U.S. government can leave militaries vulnerable.

"These are not neutral technologies. So let's stop treating them as if they're neutral," Bednar said.

Canadian alternatives?

Evans said few companies compete with the breadth of Palantir's software but pointed to Canadian alternatives, including Vancouver-based Caseway and Ottawa-based Anvil.

"They don't come anywhere close to the breadth and depth that Palantir offers," she said. She added that it will take time for them to develop comparable technology.

Bednar said Canada should nevertheless invest in developing that technology domestically.

"Building and owning this kind of necessary digital infrastructure for defence should be a primary goal for Canada," she said.

World.title: Northern, remote RCMP detachments chronically and critically understaffed: internal report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Northern and isolated RCMP detachments have become "chronically and at times critically" understaffed, according to an internal evaluation report — the latest document pointing to retention and recruitment issues within the storied organization.

The June 2026 evaluation, made public last month, found Mounties' interest in staffing northern and isolated posts is limited and the RMCP's recruitment practices are not aligned with the staffing needs in these detachments.

"Northern and isolated posts face a complex set of barriers that significantly hinder recruitment, retention and overall staffing stability. A central challenge is isolation, both physical and organizational," said the report.

Several divisions report critical shortages in their northern and isolated posts.

Hard vacancy rates, where positions are open due to things like retirements, resignations or permanent transfers, were over 20 per cent in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut during the third quarter of this fiscal year. Manitoba's vacancy rate hovered just below 20 per cent, while Saskatchewan reported nearly 15 per cent.

"A critical theme identified in participant feedback was the cumulative impact of operational pressures, isolation and the severity of violence in some posts on mental health," said the report.

Women, racialized members and those with adult dependents who took part in the RCMP's review rated a feeling of isolation as a barrier higher and more often than other groups.

The report also noted a generational shift "with younger members placing greater emphasis on proximity to family and work-life balance than on traditional notions of duty."

Testifying before a parliamentary committee earlier this fall , RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said that's changed in his decades with the organization.

"When I went through training, a lot of people were seeking a northern adventure — and it was an adventure. It's a good way to be embedded in community policing. It's completely different policing," he said.

"When people have to mobilize a family, or if they're divorced and have shared custody, it's a challenge sometimes to get people up to the North."

Limited success in past efforts

The RCMP has tried to bring in strategies to confront some of those issues with limited success, according to the report. One program gave members their preferred division in exchange for first accepting a posting to a less desirable location. However the report raised concerns about the RCMP approving more postings than they could accommodate.

Historically the RCMP would assign cadets to their first post after completing their training. In 2023, it brought in a plan that allowed new applicants to choose their division. While that successfully increased the number of applicants, it resulted "in divisions in need receiving less cadets, thus compounding existing staffing challenges."

The report said that recruiting for policing careers has become increasingly challenging across Canada, not just for the RCMP. But it noted that competitive environment can make it harder for the force to attract candidates who don't want to move.

"Despite these strategies and incentives, northern and remote detachments are chronically, and at times critically, understaffed," according to the evaluation.

RCMP staffing should be Arctic security issue: author

Kent Roach, author of the book Red Alert: The Future of the RCMP, said as the federal government looks to shore up Arctic security it needs to consider the long-term viability of the RCMP as the police of jurisdiction in the North.

"It seems to me that we're spending billions on Arctic security, national security, while there are some real problems with community security and community safety in the Far North," the University of Toronto professor said.

"You cannot have national security and national sovereignty in the North without doing the basics of community safety."

Retention and recruitment issues are RCMP-wide. An auditor general report earlier this year said the RCMP had not recruited enough new officers or effectively assigned its members to meet its operational needs "which could make it more challenging for the force to prevent and investigate crime, maintain peace and order and contribute to national security."

In his book, Roach argues it's not feasible for the RCMP to continue to split its mandate between the front-line policing it does in eight provinces and the three territories and its federal policing mandate leading investigations into terrorism, espionage and organized crime.

WATCH | New RCMP commissioner on recruitment: ‘I want us to grow in numbers:’ New RCMP commissioner discusses his top priority for the organization | Duration 1:43 Addressing the change of command ceremony, new RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme identifies recruitment as his first priority. Duheme says the RCMP ‘must be an organization of choice.’

Despite calls for transformation, Prime Minister Mark Carney's government has said it will keep the RCMP's dual mandate.

"I am not terribly optimistic about how we're going to pull out of this downward spiral," said Roach.

The report recommended developing a co-ordinated strategy to address northern staffing needs and calls on the RCMP brass to explore opportunities to increase targeted recruitment efforts to attract applicants who best meet the requirement in these posts.

It also calls on leadership to review and modernize incentives to help the organization attract and retain members in northern and isolated locations.

According to the report, the RCMP has reviewed and accepted the findings and recommendations.

World.title: MLB teams face tough calls on signings, trades as current labour deal runs out
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Major League Baseball teams have tough calls to make this month, as they scramble to get the players they want on their rosters during an off-season that may be truncated amid contentious labour negotiations.

MLB's collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, at which point a lockout is widely expected. That's because team owners are pushing to change the economic system of their game to limit how much teams can spend on their payrolls. This has received strong opposition from the players.

The two sides appear dug in. They've each amassed large war chests and MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has admitted concern that a long work stoppage could be coming.

For now, the league's 30 teams have the rest of November to get their organizations set up for next season, while the existing agreement winds down.

Bruce Meyer, the interim executive director of the Major League Baseball Players Association, has described the owners' push for a salary cap as a 'nuclear bomb' that will make labour negotiations much more difficult. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)

While organizations will have done their homework on what the next labour agreement could bring, no one knows what the final deal will be until it is reached.

Observers with front office experience say that teams navigating this moment will have to weigh their need to get better against the risk that contracts signed today could carry unforeseen consequences tomorrow.

Dan Duquette, a former baseball executive with three MLB franchises, expects teams may have to temper their spending plans to some extent, given the uncertainty.

"I think teams are going to tighten their belts and take a look at what their critical investments are for next season," he said in an interview with CBC News.

Tim Purpura, left, reacts to being doused with champagne by Houston Astros infielder Adam Everett on Oct. 2, 2005, the day the club clinched a wild card spot on the last day of the regular season. The Astros went to the World Series that year, with Purpura as team's general manager. (Richard Carson/Reuters)

Fellow former MLB executive Tim Purpura says teams will nonetheless be on the lookout for ways to improve their rosters, whether or not a new labour agreement is on the horizon.

"You've got to strike while the iron's hot and get in there," said Purpura, whose career in baseball included serving as the general manager of the Houston Astros for several seasons, including in 2005, when the team went to the World Series.

Preparing for the unknown

While there's no guarantee the team owners will get a salary cap enacted, the league's teams will still weigh the implications of a potential cap coming forward.

Purpura says it's the norm that teams have to prepare for a variety of scenarios when the off-season arrives, including labour shortages.

"When we were in those situations, we were constantly doing financial models to see, 'OK, if they change this rule, this is going to affect us in this way,'" said Purpura, who was working in baseball during the 1994 season in which a strike — also over a proposed salary cap — wiped out the World Series.

The owners threw MLB teams a change-up of sorts this week, when they suggested that a cap could be delayed until 2028, backing down from an earlier call to have a cap in 2027.

Milwaukee Brewers catcher William Contreras, the MVP of the recent World Series, is seen celebrating with fans during the victory parade held for the Brewers on Oct. 30. Milwaukee won this year's World Series, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)

Under this revised proposal, teams would be obligated to limit spending to a hard cap of $258.2 million US — a level that would require eight high-spending MLB teams, including the Toronto Blue Jays, to trim payroll to meet such requirements for 2028.

The owners also want teams to achieve a minimum spend of $180.2 million US — and management says 12 MLB teams, including the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers, would have to boost their payroll to reach this threshold.

'A prudent way to go'

Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro has been through labour negotiations in the sport before, and says the plan is the same this time around — cap or no cap.

WATCH | Jays' front office on a tough 2026 season: Blue Jays front office speaks after end of disappointing season | Duration closed caption 3:02 The Toronto Blue Jays' front office spoke to the media Wednesday after a disappointing season that saw the team unable to clinch a berth in the playoffs. It comes after a historic post-season run last year that saw them make it all the way to game 7 of the World Series. As CBC’s Greg Ross reports, the team president and the general manager tried to explain what went wrong.

"You prepare under the current system and then you adjust along the way," he told media at the end of the season.

"That's a prudent way to go," said Duquette, who served as the general manager of the Montreal Expos in the early '90s.

But Duquette said it's hard for organizations to make long-term investments — such as player contracts — if they lack certainty in what the rules are going to be in a new labour deal.

He points to a moment from the '90s, when he was in talks with the Boston Red Sox about joining their organization (which he did, leaving the Expos to become the general manager of the Red Sox, ahead of the 1994 season).

Dan Duquette is seen speaking to then-Baltimore Orioles manager Buck Showalter during spring training in February 2014. Duquette was the Orioles' executive vice-president for baseball operations. (Gene J. Puskar/The Associated Press)

Boston had plans to build up its capacity to recruit international players, but Duquette said the organization waited to make that investment until the next labour agreement was a done deal.

"When they have certainty, they can go ahead and invest," said Duquette, who also held an executive role with the Baltimore Orioles.

The flip-side of this situation is that any contractual obligations that teams have already inked with players don't go away just because a new labour agreement comes into effect.

"The obligations that the teams have made to date, those remain club obligations," said Duquette.

Free agency begins

The off-season is the time that teams can use to improve their rosters for the year to come — whether via signing free agents, trading player contracts, or through other transactions.

Starting pitcher Tarik Skubal is seen delivering a pitch for the Los Angeles Dodgers, during Game 1 of the National League Championship Series in October. Skubal is a free agent this off-season and one of the marquee pitchers available to sign. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)

Some observers believe the short window of time left on the current MLB labour agreement will spur the parties involved to get things done while there is certainty about the rules of engagement.

"There's a lot of pressure, in my opinion — on the GMs, on the agents, on the players — to get transactions done," Jim Bowden, a former general manager of the Cincinnati Reds and also the Washington Nationals, told the Foul Territory podcast.

MLB's free agency period got underway late on Monday. This is the time of year when teams can sign any players who lack contractual obligations to any clubs.

In the first few days of free agency, no major free agent signings had been announced. That's not unusual for the rhythm of baseball's free agent market, which tends to pick up later in the fall.

But any fears of a potential lockout did not appear to have ignited an immediate signing frenzy.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing
World.content:
Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:55 UTC Full article

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, will visit the Falklands and South Georgia from Monday, November 9, the day before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on Argentina’s case against the Sea Lion oil project, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment. The Princess, who will travel with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, will begin with a series of engagements in the Falklands: she will meet members of the community, visit Cape Pembroke Lighthouse, Tussac House and the newly completed Falkland Islands National Sports Complex, and attend a reception at Government House in Stanley.

In South Georgia, a territory with no permanent civilian population, she will see the Trust’s work, meet British Antarctic Survey staff and members of the territory’s government, and commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton (1874-1922), who sailed some 1,500 kilometres in a lifeboat to the island to seek help for his crew, trapped by ice in Antarctica.

The palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit. Its timing, however, coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands: the Hamburg tribunal will hear Argentina and the United Kingdom on November 10 and 11, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies plans to debate the sovereignty defence bill on November 12, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

World.title: “They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets
World.content:
“They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:50 UTC Full article

Many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums

Thousands of Paraguayans celebrated in Asunción on Friday as the Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office, but the joy turned almost immediately to anger among those who wanted a complete change of government. “Out with them all,” hundreds of protesters chanted outside Congress as Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as the new head of state.

Celebrations erupted at the news that Peña, 47, was leaving office without immunity and, hours later, was placed under house arrest accused of breach of trust over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which had more than 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people. But many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums. “If the same people stay, there is no change”, “We want jail” and “Where is the money?” read the signs.

“The people are staying here until they all go,” Celicia Lugo told the EFE news agency, adding that Peña and Alliana “are the same”. “The incoming government is more of the same, because only Peña will be gone, the rest will stay,” said Milda Cuevas, who celebrated the removal and demanded that the former president “be tried” and “go to prison”. For Andrea Gutiérrez, Ueno “was just one example” of what she sees as the ongoing plundering of citizens.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday, when the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank, which had received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, and froze its deposits. Those affected include some 32,000 pensioners of the Social Security Institute, according to EFE.

In an attempt to contain the anger, Alliana announced after being sworn in that those affected by the bank’s closure “will be fully compensated”, without saying how. The legal deposit guarantee covers up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes per depositor.

World.title: Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia
World.content:
Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:30 UTC Full article

Photo: AFP

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Montevideo on Friday, the first stop on his South American tour, and in a speech to Uruguayan authorities praised Mercosur, peaceful coexistence and care for the environment, but also defended life “even that which is still growing in the mother’s womb” and questioned euthanasia, in a country where both are legal and which is considered the most secular in the region.

The pontiff’s plane landed at 4.19 p.m. at Carrasco airport, where he was met by President Yamandú Orsi and the Cardinal Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla. Leo XIV travelled in the popemobile along the waterfront promenade to Plaza Independencia, accompanied by some 3,000 volunteers, received the key to the city and visited the Cabildo and the Cathedral. Orsi welcomed him to a region “where there are no wars between countries”, called him “dear friend” and noted that in Uruguay former presidents sit together “in peace and joy”. Former presidents Julio María Sanguinetti, Luis Alberto Lacalle Herrera and Luis Lacalle Pou attended the ceremony, along with Lucía Topolansky, widow of former president José Mujica.

In his speech, the Pope took up Francis’s ideas on the common good and care for natural resources, and praised the transformation of Uruguay’s energy mix. He stressed the importance of peace and dialogue in resolving differences and praised the role of Mercosur, the bloc Uruguay forms with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. “Coexistence between people of different origins and traditions is also part of Uruguay’s history,” he said.

Leo XIV also addressed the most sensitive issues for the country. He defended life from conception, a reference to abortion, legal in Uruguay since 2012, and to euthanasia, approved in 2025. “Everyone deserves to receive [care] until the natural end of life,” he said. He also referred to the high suicide rate: “No one should feel like a stranger among their own or think that their absence matters more than their presence.” And he said secularism does not mean religion must be confined to private life.

Uruguay separated Church and State in its 1919 Constitution. Only 36% of Uruguayans describe themselves as Catholic, according to Latinobarómetro, and one in ten of those consider themselves practising. A survey by Usina de Percepción Ciudadana found that 37% of Uruguayans attach importance to the visit and 63% little or none.

On Saturday the Pope will celebrate Mass in Paysandú, visit the Montevideo neighbourhood of Casavalle and the Catholic University of Uruguay, and lead a vigil at the Centenario Stadium. On Sunday he will celebrate Mass in Florida, before the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country’s patron saint, and travel to Buenos Aires. After Argentina and Peru, he will return to Rome on November 16.

World.title: Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office
World.content:
Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:17 UTC Full article

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours

Paraguay’s Senate on Friday removed President Santiago Peña from office in an impeachment trial for “poor performance of his duties” over the collapse of Ueno Bank, and hours later prosecutors ordered him placed under house arrest over alleged economic crimes. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in before Congress that night as the new head of state and will serve out the term until August 15, 2028.

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours. With it, Peña loses the lifetime Senate seat and parliamentary immunity he would have obtained had Congress accepted the resignation he tendered on Thursday, which was never considered. Thousands of savers gathered outside Congress celebrated the decision.

Prosecutor Christian Benítez said Peña will remain detained at home until he is placed at the disposal of the Specialised Unit for Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption. According to La Nación, prosecutors are investigating him for alleged breach of trust, influence peddling and self-serving administration. The order also covers former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to the Associated Press. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The Senate rejected the 72-hour extension the president had requested to prepare his defence. Peña, who had said on Thursday that he would appear, ultimately did not attend and sent his lawyers, Adolfo Ferreiro — who in 2012 defended President Fernando Lugo, also removed through impeachment — and Ricardo Preda. Both argued they had not had enough time to prepare a defence and that the trial was moot after the resignation, arguments the Senate rejected.

“I submitted my resignation to avoid further harm to the country and help restore calm to Paraguay. I do not want my presence to be a cause of further division or instability,” Peña wrote in a farewell message. “I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today.”

Alliana, 52, born in Pilar, a former governor of Ñeembucú department and former president of the Colorado Party, was sworn in minutes after the removal. Antonio Barrios took over as vice president, according to ABC Color. The opposition accepted the succession, albeit with reservations. “We accept this situation to ensure institutional continuity for the country,” said opposition senator Rafael Filizzola, who called Alliana “complicit” in what happened. Alliana had publicly distanced himself from Peña on the eve of the bank takeover and is expected to make changes to the government and the Central Bank.

The fall of Peña, a 47-year-old economist who took office in August 2023 with a modernising message, unfolded in just four days. On Tuesday, the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank over insolvency and irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, freezing the deposits of nearly three million customers, about 60% of the adult population, as well as hundreds of millions of dollars in public and pension funds. Carvallo had been the bank’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, and Peña himself was a shareholder in the bank’s holding company until April 2025. On Thursday, the Colorado Party withdrew its support, led by its president, former President Horacio Cartes, who backed the impeachment.

World.title: Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country
World.content:
Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:56 UTC Full article

“We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced on Thursday night that he will appear before the Senate to defend himself in the impeachment trial against him, after Congress failed for lack of a quorum to consider the resignation he had tendered hours earlier, leaving him formally in office. Argentina’s government, meanwhile, denied any record of Peña entering Argentina, following reports that he might have left Paraguay.

“Given the continuation of the impeachment trial, I will appear and exercise my right to a defence,” Peña said in a message released after the joint session of Congress called to accept or reject his resignation was suspended. The session lost its quorum when deputies of the ruling Colorado Party walked out. The Senate called an extraordinary session on Thursday night to set the impeachment trial in motion, on grounds of “poor performance of his duties”, and another on Friday morning to begin proceedings in the president’s presence, according to the Paraguayan press. The Chamber of Deputies had approved the charges by 78 votes to none. A two-thirds Senate majority is needed to remove him.

Uncertainty over Peña’s whereabouts persisted through the afternoon. Presidential spokesman Guillermo Grance acknowledged he did not know where the president was, according to ABC Color, and the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Colorado Party member Raúl Latorre, also admitted not knowing. “While we debate, the media are saying that President Santiago Peña has already set foot on Argentine soil,” opposition deputy Johana Ortega said during the session. In Buenos Aires, official sources quoted by La Nación ruled it out: “We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

The reports recalled the departure of former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who on October 27 crossed into the Argentine city of Puerto Iguazú and flew from there to Miami after refusing to accept his defeat by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The dispute between resignation and impeachment has legal consequences. If Congress accepts the resignation, Peña would take a lifetime Senate seat with parliamentary immunity; if the Senate removes him, he would lose that protection. The opposition and much of the ruling party, including Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, back the impeachment. According to the press, prosecutors have announced they are opening proceedings against Peña, although no formal charges have yet been brought.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday with the takeover of Ueno Bank, which froze the deposits of nearly three million customers and hundreds of millions of dollars of public funds. If Peña leaves office, Vice President Pedro Alliana will take over the presidency until August 15, 2028.

World.title: Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump
World.content:
Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:42 UTC Full article

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva described his October 25 re-election as “a lesson for the world” and linked it to the electoral setbacks suffered in recent days by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump. “In the same week, Netanyahu lost in Israel and I think my friend Trump is losing in the United States,” he said on Thursday in a live broadcast on YouTube.

Lula, 81, spent an hour and a half on a livestream with congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback, watched by some 600,000 viewers. “I am more afraid than in my first term,” he admitted. “My obsession is back: I cannot fail, I cannot betray them. I have to do better.” The president defended some of his priorities, such as ending online betting, the sovereign exploitation of critical minerals and the importance of the university entrance exam, and promised to find ways for people to take part in government decisions.

Lula said he would speak more often through social media. “I will speak more directly to the people through social media. I will no longer allow the press to interpret what I think,” he said. He also invited Janones to accompany him next week on his first official trip since re-election: the UN climate summit, COP31, in Turkey, and a summit with Southeast Asian countries in Manila.

In Israel’s October 27 election, Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority, winning 53 of the 120 seats, although his Likud party came first; Netanyahu has alleged fraud. In the United States, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 5.

World.title: Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit
World.content:
Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:38 UTC Full article

US-based organisation Bishop Accountability on Thursday presented in Lima a list of 77 members of Peru’s Catholic clergy publicly accused of sexually abusing minors, days before Pope Leo XIV, who lived in the country for more than two decades, begins his tour of South America. Victims and the organisation called on the pontiff to take concrete steps, including setting up a truth commission.

The list, published on the website of the organisation, which documents sexual abuse cases in the Catholic Church, includes priests, brothers, seminarians and consecrated laypeople who have worked in Peruvian parishes and schools, as well as Church officials accused of allegedly covering up complaints. It is based mainly on the book Den of abusers or safe Church?, published this year by Reinaldo Nann, a former bishop of Caravelí in southern Peru who has left the priesthood. Those on the list have been publicly accused; not all have been tried or convicted.

“The Peruvian Church is stubbornly putting children at risk by covering up for abusers,” said Bishop Accountability co-director Anne Barrett Doyle. José Enrique Escardó, president of the Peruvian Survivors’ Network and one of the first to denounce the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Catholic movement Pope Francis suppressed in early 2025 after abuse allegations, said “victims need comprehensive reparation” and that “the most important thing is prevention”.

The organisations made three requests to the Pope: that bishops and religious superiors in Peru publish the names of clergy accused of abusing minors; that a Truth Commission be set up to investigate the cases; and that a universal zero-tolerance rule be enshrined in canon law.

Leo XIV, who holds Peruvian nationality, was bishop of Chiclayo and chaired the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference Commission for the Protection of Minors, where he worked alongside Nann. According to the former bishop, the current Pope was then “more open to listening to victims than the rest of the bishops”, although he considers him “too cautious a man” who is not driving change fast enough. According to El País, the Vatican has announced that the Pope will meet victims during his visit, although the meeting is not yet on the official schedule. There has been no response from the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference to the list.

The Pope will visit Uruguay and Argentina before arriving in Peru, where he will stay from November 11 to 17.

World.title: What Game Providers Tell You About an Online Casino
World.content:
What Game Providers Tell You About an Online Casino

6th Friday, November 2026 - 00:56 UTC Full article

Most players look at the welcome bonus first and the game catalogue second, yet the list of companies that actually build the games often says more about a site than any welcome offer. Game providers are the studios that design slots, develop live dealer tables and run the random number generators behind every round.
