World.title: Skaters get three hours on natural ice as first frost arrives
World.content:
The first frost has appeared after temperatures dropped below freezing overnight in parts of the Netherlands, in Brabant, Limburg and parts of Zeeland, according to the national weather service KNMI.

It also allowed the season’s first natural ice skating in Gelderland for a couple of hours in early morning.

The lowest temperature was recorded in Woensdrecht in Brabant, at minus 1.2°. Ell in Limburg reached minus 1.1° and Westdorpe in Zeeland minus 0.4°.

It does not yet count as an official frost day though. For that, the temperature at the KNMI’s base in De Bilt, near Utrecht, has to fall below zero. Overnight it stayed at 0.8° there.

In Winterswijk, in Gelderland, the local skating club opened the country’s first natural ice rink of the season, even though there was only ground frost there. The club uses special techniques to make ice quickly.

“When you tell people that, they say ‘it can’t be done’. But it can,” chairman Auke Spijkstra told broadcaster NOS. “It’s wonderful to see all those enthusiastic people.” About 20 skaters took to the ice. The sun soon melted it, and the rink closed again at around 10am.

World.title: Verwey-Jonker Institute facing bankruptcy amid AI rise
World.content:
The Verwey-Jonker Institute, an independent research institute in Utrecht, appears to be on the brink of bankruptcy, citing budget cuts and the rise of AI as the culprits. The Institute has applied to court for a suspension of payments.

Moving to a less expensive location and downsizing its board hasn’t been enough to save the beleaguered Institute. Broadcaster NOS also reported there’s been unrest within the agency’s leadership.

The Verwey-Jonker Institute, founded in 1993, addresses societal issues, providing research to governments, municipalities and others with “social value and impact”, according to its website. They work on issues such as poverty, youth, education, discrimination and domestic violence, among others.

The Institute says technological developments mean many of their clients are now using AI instead of engaging researchers.

While they say they want to continue their work, it will now be up to an administrator to see just how they can do that.

World.title: Graffiti group posts video of attack on Amsterdam metro
World.content:
A group of some 20 masked and hooded graffiti writers stopped a metro in Amsterdam Nieuw-West and sprayed the entire train with paint within minutes, leaving passengers inside stranded.

The action took place at the Henk Sneevlietweg stop last Saturday on Halloween. A video uploaded Tuesday on YouTube by the anonymous graffiti writers’ group Locos Worldwide, titled “Amsterdam Nightmare”, shows the sprayers entering the station and speed-spraying the train in orange, purple and black before running away cheering.

They also threw a bicycle onto the tracks and spray painted the driver’s window, leaving the train unable to move.

Shaken and shocked

“Our driver is quite shocked by the incident,” a spokesman for Amsterdam transport company GVB said. “We can also imagine that this was a frightening situation for travellers.”

The GVB, which called the incident a “serious form of vandalism”, has filed a police report. It’s still not known who is responsible for the action, but the GVB says it plans to seek compensation from the “perpetrators” when they are identified.

They tagged the train with apparent acronyms ‘NSPSKU’ and ‘LCSNTC’. NSPS has been tagged on transit vehicles in the past.

Police say they are taking the incident “seriously” and have appealed to the public to come forward with any video images they may have.

The GVB says that while graffiti does happen, the scale of the Halloween night action is extraordinary. Not only was the driver severely shaken, but the ordeal was a “potentially terrifying situation for passengers as well”.

And, according to the GVB, it put them at risk. “There was not only a subway smeared, but also a bicycle thrown on the track. That entails major security risks,” a spokesman said.

Five years ago, Locos Worldwide uploaded another video showing a masked group spray painting an in-service Amsterdam metro. The group also posts similar actions that have taken place across Europe, including in Paris, Madrid and Copenhagen.

Credit rating agency S&P has revised Poland’s outlook to negative, saying that the country has seen “one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally” and that “political polarisation hinders fiscal consolidation”. It also lowered the country’s long- and short-term local currency ratings. S&P’s decision follows similar ones by the other members of the big three rating agencies. Fitch has had Poland on negative outlook since last year, while Moody’s cut the country’s credit rating in September this year to its lowest level since 2002. In a statement issued on Friday evening, S&P said that its “negative outlook reflects the risk that elevated budgetary deficits and rising government debt could constrain policy flexibility in the face of future shocks”. “This could expose Poland to shifts in investor sentiment or necessitate a sharp fiscal adjustment that would weigh on economic growth,” they added. 🚨Bardzo źle to wygląda! S&P o finansach Polski: „Takie pogorszenie sytuacji budżetowej należy do najpoważniejszych na świecie”. Dług netto ma wzrosnąć o ponad 20 pkt proc. PKB w 5 lat i przekroczyć 70% PKB w 2029 r. S&P obniżyła rating długu w PLN i perspektywę do negatywnej. — Piotr Nowak (@PiotrNowak_PL) November 7, 2026 Poland has struggled with ballooning budget deficits in recent years, driven by a rapidly expanding defence budget in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and longer-term increases in social spending. Last year’s deficit, at 7.3% of GDP, was the second-highest in the European Union. This year it is forecast to drop slightly, to 6.7%, according to recent finance ministry projections. But next year’s budget foresees a deficit of 7.1%. Those figures are much higher than those the government pledged to reach when, in 2024, Poland was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. For example, the deficit was supposed to fall to 3.7% of GDP in 2027. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has cut Poland’s rating from A2 to A3. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level was 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland since 2016 https://t.co/qUAEouqhlx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 19, 2026 S&P says that it projects Poland’s net debt exceeding 70% of GDP by 2029. That rise of “more than 20 percentage points over five years marks one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally”. The agency notes that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in 2027, making any “meaningful consolidation unlikely” before then. Moreover, the veto power of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki means the government “faces constraints in advancing its legislative and fiscal consolidation agenda”. Pointing to the ongoing crisis around the constitutional court, S&P also warns that “renewed institutional tensions could weigh on policy predictability”. However, the agency notes that Poland’s economy remains “resilient”, with real GDP growth projected to average around 3% between 2027 and 2029. It also points to the fact that the country has seen a peak in EU-funded investment this year, while exports have picked up. As well as shifting Poland’s overall outlook to negative, S&P downgraded its local currency ratings – meaning its assessment of the country’s willingness and ability to service debt denominated in domestic currency – from A/A-1 to A-/A-2, the same level as its foreign currency ratings. “Our fiscal projections are now weaker than previously envisaged, and we note a track record of recent fiscal slippages amid a challenging policy environment, which underpin our assessment of Poland’s reduced fiscal flexibility,” wrote the agency. Finance minister Andrzej Domański acknowledged S&P’s decision to lower Poland’s outlook to negative in a social media post. However, he pointed to the section of the agency’s report in which it said that the government is constrained by presidential vetoes. Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year, including several fiscal measures. “Despite the presidential vetoes, we will continue taking steps to strengthen the country’s finances,” wrote Domański. 🇵🇱 Agencja S&P utrzymała rating Polski na poziomie A-, obniżając jednak jego perspektywę do negatywnej. W uzasadnieniu decyzji czytamy wprost: „Rząd premiera Donalda Tuska napotyka ograniczenia w realizacji swoich planów legislacyjnych i konsolidacji finansów publicznych ze… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) November 6, 2026 However, Nawrocki notes that the ballooning budget deficits preceded his coming to power, and has blamed the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk for overseeing budgetary “chaos” and causing “a deep crisis of credibility”. In response to S&P’s announcement, Marcin Ociepa, deputy head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of “trying to shift responsibility for Poland’s credit rating downgrade [sic] onto the president”. “Any family that managed its finances the way Donald Tusk manages our country’s finances would drown in debt and go bankrupt,” wrote Ociepa. “That is exactly what awaits Poland if this government remains in power.” ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: 2,000-year-old Vandal artefacts anonymously handed to Polish museum
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland. The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery. The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary. The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground. They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position. The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken. Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered. The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice. “We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.” The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts. The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów. The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC. They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period. Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish deputy PM proposes “constitutional reset” to resolve crisis around top court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has put forward plans for a “constitutional reset” that he hopes can resolve the crisis around the country’s top court. The proposal, presented on Thursday by deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, head of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), would remove all current judges on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and allow new judges to be chosen only with the approval of 60% of members of parliament and the president. To take effect, the measure would require amending Poland’s constitution, something that has happened only twice since the document was adopted in 1997 and which also requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament. Deeskalacja sytuacji wokół Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jest konieczna aby przywrócić obywatelom niezależny sąd konstytucyjny. Apelują o to przedstawiciele organizacji społecznych, Rada Przedsiębiorców, Naczelna Rada Adwokacka, Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka i Episkopat Polski.… pic.twitter.com/3RCsKRlSiM — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 5, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz’s announcement comes amid the fallout from events last Friday, when eight new judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s majority in parliament seized control of the court. They announced that its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties, including by refusing to allow most of those judges to take up their seats on the court. Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023. As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges. The government points to the fact that PiS unlawfully appointed three judges to the TK in 2015. As a result, both Polish and European courts have found the tribunal in its current form to be illegitimate. Meanwhile, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of the eight judges appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026 The standoff has led some NGOs and experts to call for a “constitutional reset”, whereby the TK would be reformed to make the process of selecting judges more consensual and less politicised. Indeed, the current government even proposed legislation in 2024 that would have required new TK judges to be approved by a three-fifths parliamentary majority. The plans would also have removed unlawfully appointed judges from the PiS era and annulled rulings they were involved in. That prompted the president at the time, Andrzej Duda, who was also aligned with PiS, to send the bills to the TK, which was still packed with PiS-era judges, for assessment. The tribunal rejected them as unconstitutional the following year. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Now, Kosiniak-Kamysz has proposed new legislation intended to resolve the issue. His solution would create a mechanism under which parliament, at the request of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), could declare the TK “permanently incapable of performing its duties”. Such a status could only be declared with the support of a three-fifths majority of both houses of parliament – the Sejm and the Senate – combined. It would have to come at the request of the KRS because, says Kosiniak-Kamysz, the terms of judges cannot be shortened without the participation of other judges. The process of appointing new TK judges would involve the speaker of the Sejm proposing candidates after obtaining the opinions of the heads of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court – which are separate from the TK – as well as professional bodies representing legal professions. The candidates proposed by the speaker would also have to receive the prior consent of the president. For a new TK judge to be approved, they would have to receive the support of three fifths of members of the Sejm and Senate combined. 💬 336 głosów posłów i senatorów. To wykracza poza większość jakąkolwiek koalicyjną dzisiaj sformułowaną – @KosiniakKamysz w Warszawie pic.twitter.com/iLUuM5TSxQ — 🍀 PSL (@nowePSL) November 5, 2026 Whereas TK judges currently all serve nine-year terms, under Kosiniak-Kamysz’s proposal, five of the judges would serve three-year terms, five of them six-year terms, and the final five would serve for nine years. Unlike now, the new judges would not have to swear their oath before the president, but before parliament. Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised, however, that the measure was intended as a “one-time” emergency tool. “Later, we will return to the method of selecting judges described today in the constitution, or a better one, if there is a majority for it.” The current method of choosing new TK judges requires only the support of a majority in the Sejm. However, judges must then swear an oath “before the president”, an issue that has become a bone of contention this year. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz’s plans would require changes to Poland’s constitution, which specifies the manner in which TK judges are chosen. A constitutional amendment requires the support of a three-fifths majority in the Sejm and a simple majority in the Senate. It does not need presidential approval. PSL itself has only 28 members of the 460-seat Sejm and four senators. Kosiniak-Kamysz acknowledged that “it won’t be an easy road” to win the necessary support for his idea. He appealed not only to his fellow ruling parties, but also to opposition groups that have expressed their backing for a constitutional reset, such as the centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). On Thursday evening, one of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a photo of himself meeting Kosiniak-Kamysz, with the caption: “It’s going in the right direction”. However, some voices within the ruling coalition expressed scepticism towards the idea. Borys Budka, a former leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which is the largest governing party – said it was “hard to imagine changing the constitution alongside someone like PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński”. Tomasz Trela of The Left (Lewica) likewise said that, “if anyone thinks The Left will change the constitution arm in arm with PiS, they’re mistaken”, reports Polsat News. World.title: Chinese fashion platform Shein to invest €500 million in Polish logistics hub
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year. The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area. SHEIN investește 500 mil. euro în Polonia. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM — Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026 The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022. The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items. Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours. “This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs. “Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.” The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%. The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition. In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs. China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, ending a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot https://t.co/U6rQwfEJ7I — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 Shein has also faced accusations of labour-law violations at its facilities in China, including concerns that it may use cotton produced through forced labour. The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers. China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods. Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office. 🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. PRZEMYT CZĘŚCI DO PRODUKCJI UZBROJENIA. 6 ZATRZYMANYCH.@ABW_GOV_PL rozbiła grupę podejrzaną o działalność na rzecz rosyjskich służb specjalnych. 🔴6⃣ osób zatrzymanych, 🔴2⃣1⃣przeszukanych lokalizacji, 🔴 4⃣osoby z zarzutami szpiegostwa – wszystkie trafiły… pic.twitter.com/L90n3rf5rY — ABW (@ABW_GOV_PL) November 5, 2026 Prosecutors report that all six suspects have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group that sought to export weapon components from Poland to Russia in violation of a ban on such trade. Four of the suspects have also been charged under Poland’s espionage law, accused of acting on behalf of Russian intelligence in return for financial benefits. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place. The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”. “This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency. Prosecutors say that the group operated at least between June 2023 and December 2025 in Poland, Lithuania and Russia. Members were responsible for procuring goods and transporting them to Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania. “Vehicles equipped with hidden compartments were used to transport the goods,” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The suspects repeatedly crossed the Polish-Russian border, and some of the transports were intercepted by Polish border guards.” Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, revealed that the six suspects include five Polish citizens, aged 25 to 52, and one Russian woman, aged 37. Onet, a leading news website, reports, based on unnamed sources, that the Russian citizen acted as a liaison between the group and the foreign intelligence agency behind the operation. Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 6 osób podejrzanych o udział w zorganizowanej grupie przestępczej działającej przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej. Wśród zatrzymanych jest pięciu Polaków w wieku od 25 do 52 lat i 37-letnia Rosjanka. 🛑 Sąd – pod zarzutem szpiegostwa -… — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 5, 2026 Poland has seen a huge rise in espionage cases in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun to face second trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun will again stand trial, after prosecutors filed an indictment against him for a series of anti-Ukrainian, anti-Jewish, anti-LGBT and anti-EU acts committed during his presidential election campaign last year. Braun is already separately on trial for a number of other alleged crimes, including an attack on a Jewish religious ceremony in parliament. He is also facing further charges for a range of other alleged offences. Grzegorz Braun stanie przed sądem. Prokuratura Okręgowa w Warszawie skierowała dziś akt oskarżenia za zuchwałą kradzież flag Ukrainy w Białej Podlaskiej i Unii Europejskiej w Katowicach, zniszczenie wystawy LGBT w Sejmie oraz zniesławienie organizatorów akcji Żonkile i Muzeum… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 4, 2026 On Wednesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw announced that it had indicted Braun for four alleged crimes. It was able to do so after the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, stripped him of immunity earlier this year. One of the charges, for criminal defamation, stems from Braun’s claim, during a televised presidential debate in April last year, that the yellow paper daffodils distributed each year in Warsaw to mark the anniversary of the 1943 Jewish Ghetto Uprising against German Nazi rule are “symbols of shame”. Prosecutors say that Braun’s words were “extremely xenophobic, manipulative and aggressive”, and that they defamed the organisers of the daffodil campaign, in particular the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews in Warsaw. During the same debate, Braun also warned about the “Judaisation” of Poland, saying that “Jews have far too much say in Polish affairs”. That prompted protests by some of his opponents, one of whom filed a notification to prosecutors. Two other charges relate to thefts of flags. In one incident, Braun and his supporters removed a Ukrainian flag hanging outside city hall in the town of Biała Podlaska during a campaign event. In another, he removed a European Union flag from the industry ministry in the city of Katowice and set it on fire. Braun regularly rails against what he calls the “Ukrainisation” of Poland, warning of the supposed dangers of having so many Ukrainian refugees and migrants in the country. He is also a vocal critic of the EU. On those and other issues, Braun’s rhetoric often echoes Russian propaganda. The final charge, of destruction of property, relates to an incident in June 2025, when Braun vandalised an exhibition about the LGBT+ community in the Polish parliament. He regularly condemns what he calls the “perversions” of LGBT+ people, and has called for homosexuality to be criminalised. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes. The decision marks the sixth time it has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial https://t.co/O9FN1YbchE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 The charges Braun faces carry prison sentences of up to five years in the case of destruction of property, and up to one year in the case of criminal defamation and theft. Additionally, the deputy leader of Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, Roman Fritz, was indicted for assisting in the theft of the EU flag, while four other men (who have not waived their right to anonymity under Polish law) were indicted for their alleged roles in stealing both the EU and Ukrainian flags. All four incidents for which Braun has been indicted took place when he was campaigning for the May 2025 presidential elections, in which he finished a surprise fourth, with 6.3% of the vote. Since then, KKP has continued to perform strongly in polls, with its support currently standing at around 9%. If it obtained that kind of result at next year’s parliamentary elections, it would be likely to play a major role in deciding what kind of government could be formed. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Much of Braun’s political brand has been built around provocative statements and actions. The politician is already on trial for his attack on a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony taking place in parliament, at which he put out the candles with a fire extinguisher. In their statement on Wednesday, the Warsaw prosecutor’s office noted that the latest hearings in that trial had been cancelled after Braun presented a medical certificate justifying his absence. However, the prosecutors pointed out that, last Friday, the day that the hearings had been due to begin, Braun attended a protest by opposition supporters outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, which that evening had been taken over by government-backed judges. Braun was pictured “jostling with police riot police, addressing the crowd and giving interviews”, showing “no signs of health problems that would prevent him from attending the hearing”, wrote the prosecutors. They have therefore asked the court to investigate the doctor who issued the medical certificate. World.title: “Democracy won in America”: Polish leaders react to US midterm election results

Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans. The outcome was welcomed by Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally. 🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen? Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing. Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT — NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026 Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.” “As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.” Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration. It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland. Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”. “We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński. “If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added. .@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l — Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026 The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump. Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it. “Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority. Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”. Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2 — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026 Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki. Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results. However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the president’s International Policy Bureau, did address the issue in a social media post. “As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.” Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections. Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026 Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans ahead of the midterms. Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: International Commission of Jurists criticises takeover of Polish constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”. However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis surrounding the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament. 🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings. 🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx — ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026 On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties. Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds. Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence. Nawrocki has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”. The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton. In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate. “At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.” In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”. Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański. The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO. On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal. It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made it clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”. That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska. Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”. Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored. However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”. World.title: No Price Cap, No Limits: Tourist Charged CZK 8,000 for a 3 km Taxi Ride
World.content:
Prague received 70 complaints from taxi passengers during a three-week period when the city’s maximum taxi fares were temporarily not in force, according to information published by the Chamber of Taxi Service Operators.

The complaints included several cases involving foreign visitors who were charged thousands of crowns for relatively short journeys. In one of the most extreme cases, a passenger paid CZK 8,096 for a 3.2-kilometre trip from Duplex Club to Na Františku Hospital.

Another passenger was charged CZK 9,955 for a journey through Prague but was reportedly unable to provide the exact route when filing a complaint. The published list of cases shows that, with one exception, the complaints involved foreign tourists.



Among the other reported fares were more than CZK 7,500 for journeys of around 15 kilometres between central Prague and Václav Havel Airport.

According to the list, a passenger travelling from the city centre to the airport paid CZK 7,560 for a 15-kilometre journey. A similar trip from Smetana Embankment cost CZK 7,554.

The issue was highlighted by the Chamber of Taxi Service Operators, which asked Prague City Hall how many complaints had been submitted during the period when fare limits were not being applied.

“There were 70 in total. Some of them really did not hold back,” Štěpán Hradečný, speaking on behalf of the chamber, wrote on Facebook.

Prague City Hall confirmed that the complaints related to the period when taxi price regulation was temporarily absent.

“These complaints relate to a period when taxi price regulations were not in effect. When prices are not regulated by the city, the only regulator is the market itself,” City Hall spokesperson Vít Hofman told *Blesk*.

The situation followed the removal of Prague’s maximum taxi fare limits on September 30. According to Prague Deputy Mayor for Transport Jaromír Beránek of the Pirate Party, the move was not intended as a political decision by the city’s leadership.

Beránek said he had asked the relevant department to prepare materials for a discussion on taxi fare regulation. Instead, the preparatory process resulted in the limits being removed altogether.

The price caps remained absent until October 20, leaving a 21-day period during which taxi fares were not subject to the city’s maximum limits.

World.title: Two-Michelin-Starred Austrian Chef Comes to Prague for Exclusive Dinner
World.content:
Prague’s Zlatá Praha restaurant will host an exclusive four-hands dinner bringing together two-Michelin-starred Austrian chef Andreas Döllerer and Maroš Jambor for one evening of contemporary fine dining.

The special collaboration will see the two chefs create on November 22 a bespoke menu combining their individual culinary styles, seasonal ingredients and modern interpretations of gastronomy.



Based in Golling, Austria, Andreas Döllerer is one of the country’s most acclaimed chefs.

His restaurant, awarded two Michelin stars, is known for its distinctive approach to Alpine cuisine, which reinterprets traditional regional ingredients and culinary influences through contemporary techniques.

For the occasion in Prague, Döllerer will join forces with Maroš Jambor, creating a menu that brings together their respective approaches to fine dining.

The four-hands concept offers guests the opportunity to discover the work of both chefs through a single, specially designed dining experience.

The exclusive menu is priced at CZK 6,000 per person and includes a welcome drink and water. Guests can also opt for a wine pairing at an additional CZK 2,500 per person.

The event requires full prepayment. Reservations are available online.

World.title: American Man Suspected of Racist Assault at Prague’s Želivského Stop
World.content:
Police are investigating an alleged racist assault at the Želivského tram and metro stop in Prague’s Vinohrady district after an English-speaking man reportedly attacked a passerby and damaged his phone.

The suspect has since been identified, although police have not confirmed reports linking him to an American previously detained in Russia.

The incident took place on the morning of November 4 on Vinohradská Street, close to the Želivského stop.



According to the victim, an Arab man who has lived in the Czech Republic for several years, the confrontation began when a stranger started shouting racist remarks in public.

The man allegedly called for the deaths of Black people, Jews and Arabs.

The victim challenged the statements, telling the stranger that racist abuse and threats against people because of their background were unacceptable.

He then began recording the encounter on his mobile phone, fearing that the situation could turn violent.

“I started recording in case I was attacked—and, unfortunately, that is exactly what happened,” he later wrote in the Facebook group Vinohradská parta.

Footage of the confrontation shows the alleged attacker directing insults at the victim. At one point, he raises his phone and says, “Hello, Trump?” He also appears to threaten the other man with death before the confrontation turns physical.

The suspect then allegedly grabbed the victim’s mobile phone and threw it into the road. According to the victim, the device was struck by a passing truck. Although he managed to recover it, the phone was damaged.

The victim said he had reported the incident to the police and called on local residents to help identify the alleged attacker.

“I am dealing with this through the police, but the perpetrator has vanished. Let’s find him and show that violence and racism have no place in Vinohrady,” he wrote.

The original Facebook post containing the video was subsequently removed. The victim suggested that its disappearance might have been connected to the ongoing police investigation.

Police later confirmed that they were dealing with the case as a suspected criminal offence.

“We are handling the matter as a suspected criminal offense, and we have identified the suspect,” police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová told Czech tabloid Blesk.

Suspect reportedly linked to Russia

The investigation has also raised questions about the man’s identity.

The suspect could be an American citizen who previously faced criminal proceedings in Russia and was ordered by a Russian court to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment.

The man was reportedly accused of assaulting a female police officer in Russia. Media reports have also suggested that he holds Czech citizenship and travelled from Russia to Prague, where he is currently staying.

However, Czech police have not confirmed whether the individual identified in connection with the Želivského incident is the same American mentioned in the Russian case.

World.title: Fake Apartments and Rental Scams Target Students in Prague, Police Warns
World.content:
Prague Police are warning about a growing number of rental fraud cases, with international students among the groups most vulnerable to fake apartment listings.

Leaving everything you know behind is the beginning of a new chapter. A new city. A new home. A new life.

After weeks of searching, you finally have the keys to your apartment in Prague. You climb the stairs of an old building, find the right door and put the key in the lock.

But it will not turn.

You try again. You check the address, look at the contract and reread your messages with the supposed landlord. Everything appears to be in order, except for one crucial detail: the apartment was never yours.

The address exists. The building is real. But the home you thought you had rented does not belong to you.



A Key That Opens No Doors

Rental scams are an increasingly common problem in Prague’s housing market, with international students among the most vulnerable targets.

Many arrive in the Czech capital without knowing the local rental system or having the opportunity to view an apartment in person. The pressure to secure accommodation before the start of the academic year can also make students more vulnerable to convincing-looking fraudulent listings.

In 2024, Czechia ranked ninth among Erasmus+ programme countries for incoming higher education mobility, with approximately 17,000 arrivals, according to Dům zahraniční spolupráce.

The growing number of international students in Prague has also increased the demand for accommodation.

Charles University, one of the city’s largest universities, has repeatedly warned prospective international students about rental fraud. According to its 2024 annual report, the university had 11,455 international students from 139 countries, out of a total student population of more than 54,000.

The university advises students to watch out for several warning signs, including requests for deposits or other payments before a contract has been signed, pressure to finalise an agreement unusually quickly, and landlords who claim to be living abroad.

Offers that appear too good to be true should also raise suspicion.

Three Cases, Nearly CZK 150,000 in Losses

Prague Police have also warned about an increasing number of rental fraud cases involving apartments.

In mid-January, three cases were reported within a single week, resulting in combined losses of nearly CZK 150,000, or approximately €6,000.

One increasingly common method involves collecting deposits from prospective tenants for apartments that are never actually rented out. In some cases, fraudsters advertise properties they do not own or have no right to rent.

Police have not ruled out the possibility that the suspect involved in the January cases may be connected to other similar incidents, meaning the number of victims could be higher.

For international students, the consequences can be particularly severe.

Police and universities therefore advise prospective tenants to verify listings carefully, avoid sending money before signing a contract and viewing the property, and remain cautious of unusually cheap offers or landlords who create pressure to pay quickly.

World.title: Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show Brings Las Vegas Classics to Prague
World.content:
Fans of Frank Sinatra and the golden age of Las Vegas entertainment will have a chance to relive the era this Christmas.

The Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show will arrive in Prague on December 29, bringing its tribute to the legendary Rat Pack to O2 Universum.



Originally created to mark the 100th anniversary of Frank Sinatra’s birth, the international production features Stephen Triffitt, George Daniel Long and Mark Adams, three performers known for their portrayals of Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr.

All three previously starred in the acclaimed The Rat Pack Live from Las Vegas, performing for nearly a decade in London’s West End. Their careers have also taken them to stages alongside prestigious orchestras, including the BBC Concert Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Amsterdam Metropole Orchestra.

The trio has since taken the show around the world, recreating the music, humour and spontaneous stage chemistry that made the original Rat Pack one of the most celebrated entertainment acts of its time.

The Prague performance will feature more than just the three leading artists. They will be joined by the Golddiggers, a trio of singers and dancers whose costumes and choreography add a classic Las Vegas revue atmosphere to the production. The show will also feature a special appearance by Nancy Sinatra.

The programme includes classics such as Fly Me to the Moon, My Way, New York, New York, Strangers in the Night and more.

Combining live music, comedy and theatrical performances, the production aims to recreate the atmosphere of the Las Vegas stages that defined an era of popular entertainment.

World.title: Beyond the Usual Order: 7 Prague Restaurants to Try on Bolt Food
World.content:
We all have one. The order you place without thinking. Same app, same five restaurants, same Thursday night. It is comfortable, it is reliable, and if we are honest, it is getting a little boring.

Prague’s food scene runs far deeper than the places that sit at the top of your feed. Tucked into Nusle side streets, Dejvice corners and the quieter end of Libeň are small kitchens with loyal regulars, big personalities and dishes worth crossing the river for.

The good news? You don’t have to cross the river. They deliver.

So as the evenings get darker and the sofa gets more convincing, we asked Bolt Food to point us towards the city’s hidden gems. Here are seven places worth adding to your rotation, from an Aussie pub in Vinohrady to a half-metre pizza you will want to share (or not).

For when you miss home (or just miss a proper pie).

On Vinohradská street sits what bills itself as Prague’s only Australian restaurant. The menu reads like a trip home: a whole section of beef, chicken and vegetarian pies, a chicken parmy, a proper schnitty, fish and chips and, for the curious, a bag of “Skippy’s” kangaroo jerky. Wash it down with something from the Aussie bottled beer list.

Can’t make it in? The pub classics travel well. A pie with a side of gravy and the match on your own TV is a very respectable Sunday.

What to order: the Melbourne Pie, the most popular pie on the menu, with gravy on the side. Or the chicken parmy if you’re properly hungry.

For when you want a pizza with a story

During lockdown, half of Prague learned to bake sourdough bread. Pavel Petřík went for sourdough pizza instead. A few years, many pop-ups and one very customised electric cargo bike later (yes, it carries a pizza oven that runs hotter than 500°C), Pizza Bici has a permanent home on Na Hutích in Dejvice.

The shop is decorated with vintage bike parts, and the sourdough dough is the star. The menu is short and built for takeaway, with picks like the Marinara Sprint, a Mortadella & Pistachio and the spicy Diavola Express.

What to order: the Mortadella & Pistachio for something different, the Diavola Express if you like heat.

For flatmate nights and office Fridays

Yes, a second pizza place. But this one comes with a measuring tape. Near the Žluté lázně riverside, Pizza Napoletana bakes proper Neapolitan pies with San Marzano tomatoes and Sabelli mozzarella, plus its party trick: pizza by the half metre.

The mezzo metro pizzas are built for sharing (in theory). The Margherita D.O.P. comes with buffalo mozzarella, the Parma version with cured ham and rocket, and the Carciofara is a little wild, with artichoke cream, salsiccia, pistachios and crispy potato. Prefer your own pizza? The classic 32 cm range covers everything from marinara to quattro formaggi.

What to order: one half-metre pizza for the table, and a slice of torta caprese for whoever wins the last piece.

For when Tex-Mex just won’t cut it

If you have ever lived somewhere with a serious taco scene, you know the difference between Mexican food and “Mexican-style” food. Alambre, on náměstí Bratří Synků in Nusle, is firmly in the first camp: modern, casual and easy to love.

The menu leans into the dishes taco lovers actually crave: tacos al pastor, loaded nachos, quesadillas and the house namesake, Alambre Camarón. The real headliner, though, is the birria de res quesadilla.

What to order: birria quesadilla, no debate. Add tacos al pastor if you are feeding two.

For the hummus purists

Supermarket hummus is fine. Then you try the real thing and there is no going back. Tahini on Nuselská street calls itself the home of legendary hummus, with Israeli roots and, lately, an Indian twist on the menu too.

Start with the classic hummus plates, topped with anything from falafel and chicken shawarma to sabich or a full shakshuka. Feeling adventurous? Check the daily specials, which have included mezze spreads and hummus with lamb kebab.

What to order: Hummus & Sabich, or Hummus & Shakshuka on a slow weekend morning.

For proper American-style burgers

Out on Sokolovská, far from the burger joints of the centre, Hadog has quietly built a loyal following. Expect 200 g beef patties, melted cheese and sauces with a kick, like the Chipotle burger with smoked cheese, bacon, BBQ sauce and chipotle mayo.

Smash fans should head straight for the Smash Juicy Lucy, one of the most popular picks on the menu. Any burger can come in a gluten-free bun or with a Beyond Meat patty, so nobody gets left out of burger night.

What to order: the Smash Juicy Lucy, or the Chipotle burger if you like it smoky.

For when you can’t decide which Asian cuisine you’re craving

Small room, fresh flowers on the tables, big portions. Bento Café & Bistro in Holešovice is the kind of neighbourhood spot locals tend to keep to themselves.

The menu hops across Asia, from Vietnamese bun nem to udon noodles and a red curry ramen that regulars rave about.

It is exactly what you want on a grey November evening: something warm, something fresh and a little bit of everything. Don’t skip the homemade passion fruit lemonade.

What to order: red curry ramen on a cold night, bun nem when you want something lighter.

Your new rotation, sorted

An Aussie pie in Vinohrady, sourdough from a cargo-bike pizzaiolo, birria in Nusle and ramen in Holešovice. Prague tastes a lot more interesting once you look past the usual suspects.

All seven are available on Bolt Food, so the only thing you need to explore is the app. Open Bolt Food, search for any of the names above and try something new this week. Your Thursday-night order will forgive you.

Ordering more than once a week? Then Bolt Plus is worth a look. Members get free delivery from Bolt Food partner restaurants marked with a “+” in the app, on orders over 170 CZK (delivery discount up to 45 CZK), with no promo codes to type in.

The membership covers your rides too, with cashback on every trip and up to three free cancellations a month. And the first month is free, so you can test it on your new hidden gems before deciding.

World.title: Your Next Weekend Away: A Renovated Neoclassical Spa Hotel in Františkovy Lázně
World.content:
The hotel, housed in a 1918 Neoclassical building, has renovated its rooms, restaurant and wellness facilities.

Františkovy Lázně, one of the Czech Republic’s best-known spa towns, is offering visitors a renovated accommodation option following an extensive refurbishment of the five-star Harvey Spa Hotel.



Located in the town’s park zone in western Bohemia, the hotel occupies a Neoclassical building dating back to 1918. The recent renovation covered all 105 rooms, as well as the lobby, corridors and restaurant, updating the interiors while retaining the building’s historic character.

The hotel is situated next to the town’s central park, within walking distance of its main colonnades and mineral springs. Glauber I Spring, one of the town’s traditional drinking cure springs, is located in the nearby park by Swan Lake.

Spa treatments and wellness facilities

The hotel offers a range of spa treatments, massages and wellness services, alongside a relaxation pool, sauna and fitness centre. Guests can combine traditional spa procedures with recreational facilities during both short stays and longer wellness programmes.

The property also features a restaurant and BAR 222, which has been renovated as part of the wider refurbishment.

Františkovy Lázně has a long history as a European spa destination, attracting visitors with its mineral springs and therapeutic treatments for more than 200 years. In 2021, the town became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing Great Spa Towns of Europe, together with ten other historic spa towns across seven countries.

Its compact centre, historic colonnades and landscaped parks make it suitable for visitors looking to explore the town on foot. The surrounding region also offers opportunities for walking and excursions beyond the spa centre.

Staying at Harvey Spa Hotel

The hotel has 105 air-conditioned rooms, all refurbished as part of the renovation. You can book your room directly here.

Its location directly beside the central park also means guests can reach the town’s main spa attractions on foot, while the hotel’s five-star facilities make it possible to combine accommodation with spa treatments and wellness services during the same stay.

World.title: Christmas Charity Market Brings Gifts and Flavours from 50 Countries to Prague
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known international Christmas events will return this November, bringing gifts, food and traditions from nearly 50 countries under one roof.

The DSA International Christmas Charity Market 2026 will take place on Saturday, November 21, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Hilton Prague Atrium.



Organised by the Diplomatic Spouses Association (DSA) together with Prague’s international diplomatic community, the annual event allows visitors to shop for Christmas gifts while supporting Czech charities.

Stalls representing almost 50 countries will offer a wide range of products, including traditional sweets and spices, gourmet food, handicrafts, toys, glassware, porcelain, cosmetics, fashion accessories and Christmas gifts.

The market is held under the patronage of First Lady Eva Pavlová and regularly attracts thousands of visitors.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by DSA Prague (@dsa_prague)

Shopping for a Good Cause

The event also serves as one of the DSA’s main fundraising initiatives. Money raised through the market, together with donations and sponsorship, is distributed to Czech charitable organisations.

Earlier this year, the association awarded a total of CZK 1.32 million to 16 Czech charities during its Grant Award Ceremony in June.

According to Jana Muranska, President of the Diplomatic Spouses Association, the event is intended to bring together Prague’s international community while supporting organisations working across the Czech Republic.

“The Christmas Charity Market is about much more than Christmas shopping,” Muranska said. “It brings together people from across the world in a spirit of friendship, generosity and solidarity.”

World.title: India’s Minister Jitin Prasada visits Hungary to strengthen trade and technology ties
World.content:
Indian Minister Jitin Prasada visited Hungary from 4 to 6 November 2026, holding high-level political and business meetings aimed at expanding cooperation in trade, investment, pharmaceuticals, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing. His programme included visits to Hungarian pharmaceutical giant Gedeon Richter and Foxconn’s manufacturing operations, as well as talks with government officials and business representatives in Budapest.

According to an official statement issued by India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry on 6 November, the three-day visit was intended to strengthen economic and technological cooperation between India and Hungary while supporting broader relations between India and the European Union.

Minister Jitin Prasada holds high-level talks in Hungary

During his visit, Minister Jitin Prasada, India’s Minister of State for Commerce and Industry and Electronics and Information Technology, met senior Hungarian officials to discuss bilateral cooperation.

He held talks with the Deputy Speaker of the Hungarian National Assembly, focusing on strengthening diplomatic and economic relations, including opportunities arising from closer India–EU engagement.

Prasada also met Hungary’s minister responsible for science and technology. Their discussions explored cooperation in emerging technologies, research, innovation and partnerships between industrial companies and academic institutions.

The minister’s programme also included a visit to the Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences (MATE), where potential cooperation in agricultural research, agri-technology and sustainable farming practices was discussed.

If you missed it: India and Hungary strengthen ties in Budapest: Yoga, digital skills and a unique cultural fusion

Gedeon Richter and Foxconn among key industrial visits

One of the significant stops on the minister’s itinerary was Gedeon Richter Plc., one of Hungary’s leading pharmaceutical manufacturers.

The company already has an industrial presence in India through Richter Themis Medicare (India) Pvt. Ltd. According to the Indian government, the visit highlighted opportunities for further cooperation in pharmaceutical manufacturing, research and development, and healthcare technologies.

Prasada also visited Foxconn’s manufacturing operations in Hungary, which are involved in producing advanced data centre infrastructure, network communication equipment and artificial intelligence server technologies.

The discussions highlighted opportunities to strengthen cooperation in electronics manufacturing, digital infrastructure and emerging technologies, particularly in developing more resilient industrial supply chains.

These sectors are increasingly relevant to Hungary’s industrial economy, where electronics manufacturing, automotive production and pharmaceutical development play important roles.

More than 100 business representatives attend Budapest seminar

On 5 November, Minister Jitin Prasada addressed an India–Hungary Business Seminar in Budapest, attended by more than 100 business representatives.

The event, organised by the Embassy of India, focused on expanding commercial partnerships between Hungarian and Indian companies.

The seminar, entitled Deepening India-Hungary Commercial Relations: A Look Ahead, took place at the InterContinental Budapest hotel. Its principal focus areas included the automotive, pharmaceutical, chemical, information technology and artificial intelligence sectors.

Prasada encouraged businesses from both countries to explore investment opportunities, establish new partnerships and strengthen industrial cooperation.

The accompanying Indian business delegation also engaged with representatives of the Hungarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (HCCI), the Hungarian Export Promotion Agency (HEPA) and the Hungarian Investment Promotion Agency (HIPA).

Business-to-business meetings provided opportunities for Indian and Hungarian companies to establish direct commercial contacts and discuss potential projects.

What the visit means for India–Hungary relations

For Hungary, closer economic relations with India could offer additional opportunities for its export-oriented industries, particularly in pharmaceuticals, electronics, agricultural technology and research.

India, meanwhile, represents a major potential market for Hungarian businesses seeking to diversify their international partnerships beyond Europe.

The visit also reflected the importance of Hungary’s position within the European Union, which provides a broader framework for economic cooperation with India.

During his stay in Budapest, Prasada also met members of the Indian community at the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre, acknowledging their role in strengthening cultural and personal ties between the two countries.

Although the official statement did not announce specific new investment commitments or signed agreements, the discussions identified several areas for potential future cooperation.

The minister’s visit therefore marked another step in developing India–Hungary economic relations, with the practical results depending on subsequent business partnerships, research projects and investment decisions.

Indian community and Hungarian friends celebrate ties in Budapest

During his visit, Minister Jitin Prasada also attended a special gathering hosted by the Embassy of India in Budapest, bringing together members of the Indian community living in Hungary and Hungarian friends of India. Daily News Hungary was also represented at the event, where its representative had the opportunity to meet India’s Ambassador to Hungary, Anshuman Gaur. The gathering took place in the festive atmosphere of Diwali, the Hindu Festival of Lights, providing an opportunity for cultural exchange, informal conversations and the strengthening of personal connections between the two countries. The warm reception reflected the important role of people-to-people relations alongside the growing diplomatic and economic cooperation between India and Hungary.
