World.title: Yemeni ambassador: Peace remains possible, but temporary truces have failed
World.content:
Yemen’s ambassador to Hungary has warned that temporary ceasefires are no longer a viable solution to the country’s prolonged conflict, arguing that previous truces have allowed the Houthi movement to strengthen its military capabilities. In an exclusive interview with Hungary Insider, Ambassador Ahmed Abdulla Nagi discussed the prospects for peace, Iran’s influence and the growing risks to international shipping in the Red Sea.

Speaking to Alpár Kató in an exclusive interview published by Hungary Insider, the Yemeni ambassador presented his government’s position on the latest military escalation and explained why he believes a lasting political settlement must address the underlying causes of the conflict rather than merely suspend fighting.

His central message was that Yemen’s internationally recognised government remains committed to peace, despite its decision to pursue military operations against the Houthis.

Yemeni ambassador explains why temporary ceasefires are no longer enough

According to Ambassador Nagi, previous ceasefire arrangements have repeatedly failed to produce lasting stability. He accused the Houthis of exploiting periods of reduced fighting to recruit personnel, replenish weapons and prepare for further military operations.

The ambassador said the latest escalation followed attacks on Yemen’s western coastal areas, which he attributed to Houthi forces. He argued that these developments had left the government with little choice but to respond militarily.

However, he stressed that military action should not be interpreted as a rejection of diplomacy.

The government, he explained, continues to support a comprehensive political settlement that would restore state institutions and establish a political framework based on Yemen’s constitution and laws.

His remarks raise a fundamental question about the country’s future: can renewed military pressure create conditions for a sustainable peace, or will it deepen an already devastating conflict?

Yemen Ambassador to Hungary Ahmed Abdulla Nagi

Iran’s role and the strategic importance of the Red Sea

A significant part of the interview focused on Iran’s relationship with the Houthis and the wider geopolitical implications of the conflict.

Ambassador Nagi described the relationship as a strategic partnership extending beyond military assistance to political, ideological and security cooperation.

He also argued that Yemen’s geographical position has become increasingly important to Tehran’s regional strategy.

Of particular concern is the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow maritime passage connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. The waterway forms part of a major international shipping route linking European and Asian markets through the Suez Canal.

Disruption in this corridor can affect shipping costs, delivery times and global supply chains, making developments in Yemen relevant to European economies, including Hungary’s.

The ambassador warned that control over strategic maritime routes could give Iran additional leverage in its wider confrontation with Western powers.

These assessments represent the Yemeni government’s position, and the broader conflict involves competing political and military narratives.

Questions over international security and regional alliances

Beyond Iran, the interview addressed another potentially significant security concern: reported cooperation between the Houthis and Somalia’s al-Shabaab militant organisation, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda.

Ambassador Nagi discussed allegations involving weapons transfers, training and smuggling networks across the Gulf of Aden.

He also criticised the international community’s response to Yemen’s conflict, arguing that political statements and diplomatic support have not been accompanied by sufficiently effective practical measures.

The interview explores why the ambassador believes these developments are interconnected and what they could mean for regional security.

What does the future hold for Yemen?

Yemen has endured more than a decade of conflict since the Houthis seized control of the capital, Sana’a, in 2014. A Saudi-led military coalition intervened in 2015, and the ensuing war has contributed to one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises.

The ambassador also addressed contested interpretations of Saudi Arabia’s involvement, responsibility for the humanitarian emergency and restrictions affecting Yemeni ports.

His responses reveal how differently the parties involved understand the origins of the war and the conditions necessary to end it.

For European readers, the interview is a reminder that Yemen’s future is not solely a regional concern. The security of maritime trade, the stability of the Middle East and the prospects for a diplomatic settlement have consequences far beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

What evidence does the Yemeni government present regarding Iranian support for the Houthis? How does the ambassador respond to criticism of Saudi Arabia? And what would a lasting peace agreement actually require?

Read the full exclusive interview with Yemen’s ambassador Ahmed Abdulla Nagi on Hungary Insider for his detailed answers and assessment of Yemen’s future.

World.title: Battery plant leaking turned waterstream blue in Hungary, authorities immediately suspended production
World.content:
A battery manufacturing plant near Tatabánya, Hungary, has been ordered to suspend production in one of its facilities after blue contamination was detected in a nearby watercourse. Authorities have launched an environmental investigation into the incident at Volta ESH’s factory in Környe, following reports of pollution on 30 October.

Battery plant shut down due to environmental risks

According to Tatabánya’s municipality, a local resident reported blue discolouration in the Szentgyörgy stream and the battery plant’s rainwater drainage ditch. An official inspection subsequently identified visible contamination along a stretch of approximately 100 metres.

The company acknowledged that the pollution originated from its premises. On 4 November, the Komárom-Esztergom County Government Office, acting as the environmental authority, ordered the immediate suspension of all production in the plant’s Hall 101.

The facility will only be allowed to resume operations once the source of the contamination has been identified, the necessary repairs have been completed and experts have confirmed that the system is leak-free. A separate regulatory decision will also be required before production can restart.

Contaminated water removed as investigation continues

Volta ESH said it began environmental remediation on 31 October, alongside efforts to stop the leak. Temporary barriers were installed to prevent the pollution from spreading, and approximately 30 cubic metres of contaminated water were pumped out of the stream.

The company stated that no technological liquids or other pollutants had escaped from its site since the morning of 31 October. However, authorities said the elimination of the contamination source and the prevention of further leakage had not yet been independently verified. The precise cause of the incident remains unclear. Nikolett Árvay, a Tisza Party MP representing the area, said the leaking solution was suspected of containing copper sulphate.

The manufacturing plant started operations in late 2020

The environmental authority launched a comprehensive review on 3 November, with a 60-day deadline for its completion. Tatabánya’s municipality has stressed that, although the pollution occurred in neighbouring Környe, the battery factory’s proximity and the protection of local water resources make the incident a matter of concern.

Volta ESH is a subsidiary of South Korean company Solus Advanced Materials. In early 2022, the European Commission approved EUR 24 million in Hungarian state aid for the company, equivalent to approximately HUF 8.7 billion. The investigation is expected to establish the full circumstances of the leak and assess its potential environmental consequences.

World.title: Hungary to receive EUR 400 million in financing push from EIB
World.content:
Hungary is set to benefit from a EUR 400 million financing push backed by the European Investment Bank (EIB), aimed at strengthening businesses, accelerating green investment and improving access to education. The initiatives involve financing agreements with CIB Bank, EXIM Hungary and the state-owned Student Loan Centre, alongside a guarantee scheme expected to expand lending to medium-sized companies.

European Investment Bank approved huge financial boost for Hungary

The EIB has signed a EUR 100 million risk-sharing agreement with CIB Bank, part of the Intesa Sanpaolo Group. This is the first deployment in Hungary of the EIB’s Growth for MidCaps (G4M) programme. The guarantee is expected to enable CIB to provide up to EUR 200 million in new loans and mobilise approximately EUR 280 million in investment by Hungarian businesses.

The scheme is designed to help medium-sized enterprises finance projects, expand operations and improve competitiveness. Such companies can be large enough to drive innovation and create skilled jobs, yet may struggle to access financing available to larger corporations or state-backed guarantee programmes. The renewed partnership, following a 15-year interval, is expected to offer borrowers larger loans, longer repayment periods and lower collateral requirements. More than 60 per cent of the financing is expected to reach businesses in Hungary’s less developed regions.

EUR 100 million for green investment

A separate EUR 100 million EIB financing agreement with EXIM Hungary will support renewable energy, energy efficiency and other green projects across the country. Eligible investments may include solar power installations, upgrades to industrial and commercial buildings, electric vehicles and associated charging infrastructure.

The funding is intended to help companies reduce energy consumption and costs, cut carbon emissions and lessen reliance on fossil fuels. EIB Vice-President Marko Primorac described the green transition as both an environmental necessity and a business opportunity, pointing to its potential to strengthen competitiveness and energy security. EXIM Hungary said the agreement would widen access to sustainable financing by combining international resources with domestic market experience.

Student loans to support access to education

The EIB has also signed a EUR 100 million loan agreement with Hungary’s Student Loan Centre to finance affordable student lending. The programme is intended to help cover tuition fees, training expenses and living costs, supporting access to higher education, vocational training and adult education.

The funding is expected to benefit around 136,000 people by the end of 2028, with more than 63 per cent of recipients projected to come from less developed regions. The Student Loan Centre said the agreement would help ensure that financial barriers do not prevent students from pursuing education and professional development.

World.title: Budapest’s iconic City Park ice rink faces costly renovation delay – Will it open on time?
World.content:
Budapest’s famous City Park Ice Rink (Városligeti Műjégpálya) is facing uncertainty ahead of its centenary season, as holes in its ageing cooling pipes have pushed the planned renovation beyond the original deadline and more than doubled its estimated cost. However, a separate repair contract could still allow the rink to open as planned on 20 November.

The rink, located beside Vajdahunyad Castle, is due to celebrate its 100th anniversary this year. The Budapest Municipality has been preparing special events for the season opening, but concerns have emerged over the condition of the cooling system and the handling of its planned replacement.

According to reports by Index and Népszabadság, the renovation has become significantly more expensive than initially expected. The Budapest Sports Service Centre (BSK), which operates the facility, originally included HUF 400 million in its budget for a complete replacement of the cooling system. By June, however, a preliminary estimate had risen to HUF 776 million. The contract eventually signed with the winning contractor was worth HUF 798 million net – more than HUF 1 billion (approx. EUR 2.8 million) including VAT.

The deadline has also slipped considerably. Although the project was initially expected to be completed before the current skating season, the latest schedule puts the end of construction in August 2027. The work is now planned to begin after the current season, once the necessary materials have been purchased.

Photo: Facebook/Városligeti Műjégpálya és Csónakázótó

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Why has the renovation become so expensive?

BSK technical director László Happ said the first HUF 400 million estimate was based on the original plans and had been prepared without a detailed assessment of the cooling system’s current condition. More detailed calculations and preliminary offers later revealed that some specialised components would cost considerably more and take longer to obtain than expected.

The Budapest Municipality was reportedly not informed in advance that the project would be split into two stages, with material procurement scheduled to run until January 2027 and construction starting only after the skating season.

The capital’s property committee rejected a proposal concerning the revised deadline in a vote of six against and two in favour. Its chairman, Árpád Orbán, announced plans for an extraordinary internal audit and called an on-site committee meeting for 11 November.

Check out our article from last year: Budapest’s magical City Park Ice Rink returns — Here’s when you can skate by a castle again!

Will the rink open this November?

There is still hope for the 2026–27 season. A separate contractor has been selected to carry out urgent repairs to holes in the main steel pipeline running through the utility tunnel beneath the rink. The work has a budget of HUF 15 million and is intended to keep the facility operational for the coming months.

The cooling system has suffered problems for years. The rink underwent a major renovation between 2008 and 2011, costing HUF 4.9 billion net, including HUF 3.3 billion in EU funding. Further repairs costing HUF 580 million were carried out in 2014, but corrosion has increasingly affected the pipe network in recent years.

World.title: EPP Vice-President calls for end to EU rule-of-law procedure against Hungary in Budapest
World.content:
The European People’s Party (EPP) believes it is time to end the Article 7 procedure launched against Hungary in 2018, arguing that reforms introduced by Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government have addressed the serious rule-of-law concerns that originally prompted the process.

Speaking at a press conference in Budapest on Friday, EPP Vice-President Tomas Tobé said the Hungarian people had sent a clear message in the 12 April election that they wanted a new chapter in the country’s history.

According to Tobé, the election represented a victory for democracy, the rule of law and Hungary’s return to the heart of Europe. He praised the new government’s early reforms, including measures targeting corruption and discrimination, and noted that Hungarian participation in the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes had been fully restored.

“It is time to end the Article 7 procedure,” he said on behalf of the EPP group in the European Parliament. He acknowledged that Hungary still had a long way to go and needed further reforms, but argued that the process should nevertheless be brought to a close.

If you missed it: EU Parliament set to drop Article 7 against Hungary as Magyar government wins Brussels backing

EPP hopes for a decision before the end of the year

The Article 7 procedure was initiated by the European Parliament in 2018 over concerns about the deterioration of democracy and the rule of law in Hungary. It has made little progress since then.

The mechanism can ultimately lead to the suspension of certain EU membership rights, including a member state’s voting rights in the Council, if the required findings are made by national governments.

Tobé said the EPP would seek a broad majority with pro-European political groups in the European Parliament to support ending the procedure. These include the Socialists and Democrats, Renew Europe and the Greens. He also welcomed support from other groups.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Asked by Index whether the procedure could be closed before the end of 2026, Tobé said he was hopeful. He argued that the reforms introduced by the new Hungarian government were genuine and reflected a clear political commitment to rebuilding the rule of law.

EPP MEP Eszter Lakos, who leads the Tisza Party’s delegation in the European Parliament and is also an EPP vice-president, said the group no longer considered the risk of a serious breach of EU values to exist in Hungary.

She thanked the EPP for supporting the closure of the procedure, while acknowledging that rebuilding the rule of law after 16 years would take time.

The European Parliament’s November agenda already includes a debate on the situation in Hungary, with a resolution expected to be put to a vote in December. The exact legal route for formally ending the Article 7 procedure remains unclear.

Tobé responds to Fidesz criticism of term limits

During the press conference, Tobé was also asked about criticism from Fidesz politicians of the new government’s plans to introduce term limits for MPs and the prime minister.

He welcomed the fact that Fidesz politicians were now discussing the rule of law, adding that the proposed limits were not directly connected to the Article 7 procedure.

Personally, he understood why the Tisza government had introduced the idea after 16 years of the previous political system. He argued that term limits could help prevent the emergence of a closed political elite that uses public resources for its own benefit.

Lakos added that the restrictions were unusual but, in her view, necessary to prevent another entrenched political elite from developing.

World.title: Europe could face Arctic cold snap as low gas reserves raise energy concerns
World.content:
Europe could face a significant Arctic cold spell in early December, potentially putting further pressure on the continent’s already low natural gas reserves. Signs of an unusually early disruption of the polar vortex have appeared in weather models, raising concerns that Arctic air could reach parts of north-western Europe in the coming weeks.

The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) has indicated a possible disruption of the polar vortex, a large circulation of cold air high above the Arctic. Such changes can influence weather patterns further south, potentially allowing colder air to move towards North America and parts of Europe. OilPrice reports that the development could bring Arctic conditions to north-western Europe within weeks.

However, the potential impact on gas supplies is particularly concerning because Europe is entering the colder season with relatively low storage levels.

One week of extreme cold could use up Europe’s gas buffer

An analysis by BloombergNEF suggests that even a single week of unusually cold weather could significantly increase Europe’s heating demand.

The researchers examined a scenario in which average temperatures between 2 and 8 December were 5°C below the average for the same period over the previous ten years. Under these conditions, heating-related natural gas demand across north-western Europe, Italy, Spain and Austria would increase by approximately 1.1 billion cubic metres.

If all of this additional demand had to be met from underground storage, European gas reserves could fall to around 15.5% of capacity by the end of March, compared with approximately 17% under average weather conditions.

That would leave inventories only about half a percentage point above BloombergNEF’s estimated minimum level before Europe would need to start using gas held as strategic reserves rather than normal commercial stocks.

Europe enters winter with its lowest reserves since 2022

The situation is made more difficult by the fact that European gas storage facilities are currently around 74% full, their lowest seasonal level since the 2022 energy crisis.

October’s relatively mild weather did provide some relief. Lower heating demand allowed countries to continue filling their storage facilities later than usual, leaving inventories approximately 1 billion cubic metres above the October average for the 2021–2025 period. However, a serious cold spell could quickly erase that additional buffer.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) also warned this week that European gas storage levels could fall below 10% by the end of March. It said the market would become particularly vulnerable to further cold spells, technical failures or other supply disruptions.

One important factor is that gas withdrawal rates tend to decline when storage facilities fall below 30% of their working capacity. This means that extracting gas could become more difficult precisely when demand is high and reserves are running low.

European gas prices remain far above US levels

The continent also faces a significant price disadvantage compared with the United States. European natural gas futures are currently trading at roughly 11 times the US price, according to the figures cited by OilPrice.

Another major cold spell could therefore put further upward pressure on European wholesale gas prices, potentially keeping energy costs elevated well into spring.

For households and businesses, the eventual impact will depend on the severity and duration of the winter weather, as well as the availability of alternative supplies. While an Arctic cold spell in early December is not yet certain, Europe’s limited storage buffer leaves the continent more exposed to any unexpected increase in demand or disruption to supply.

World.title: Hungary’s 2027 motorway vignette prices announced: annual passes to cost more
World.content:
Hungary’s motorway vignette prices will rise again from 1 January 2027, with most fees adjusted in line with the country’s 1.3 per cent inflation rate recorded in August. However, the M1 regional vignette, introduced in connection with the motorway’s renovation, will remain unchanged.

Using Hungary’s motorways won’t get cheaper

For passenger cars in the D1 category, the annual nationwide motorway vignette will cost HUF 62,560 (currently EUR 172), while an annual county pass will be priced at HUF 7,280 (EUR 20). The official 2027 rates for shorter-term D1 vignettes will also increase. A daily pass will cost HUF 5,630 (EUR 15.50), a ten-day vignette HUF 6,990 (EUR 19.22), and a monthly pass HUF 11,320 (EUR 31.10).

Drivers of vehicles in the D2 category will face higher charges. The daily vignette will be priced at HUF 7,990 (around EUR 22), the ten-day pass at HUF 10,170 (almost EUR 28), and the monthly option at HUF 16,030 (EUR 44.07). The annual nationwide entitlement will cost HUF 88,790 (EUR 244.10), while the annual county vignette will be HUF 14,560 (EUR 40).

M1 regional vignette remains unchanged

The M1 regional vignette will continue to cost HUF 15,000 (EUR 41.24) for D1-category vehicles, U-category vehicles and motorcycles. For D2 vehicles, the price will remain HUF 30,000 (EUR 82.50). The regional entitlement covers toll motorways in four counties: Pest, Fejér, Komárom-Esztergom and Győr-Moson-Sopron. The pass was introduced in connection with the renovation of the M1 motorway.

Meanwhile, motorists purchasing a vignette for Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County will lose the discounted rate available in 2026. From next year, the standard county vignette price will apply. Penalties for using toll roads without a valid vignette will also increase. Drivers paying within 60 days will face a surcharge of HUF 28,150 (EUR 77.40), while those settling the penalty after the deadline will have to pay HUF 96,970 (EUR 266.60).

Motorists are advised to consider their regular routes and travel frequency when selecting a vignette for 2027, as the most suitable option may depend on how often and where they use Hungary’s toll road network.

World.title: Week in Review: Between Hope and Apathy
World.content:
Bulgaria has a newly elected president – government-backed candidate Iliana Iotova. In the November 1 run-off for the presidency, she won 57.6 per cent of the votes cast to her challenger Andrey Gyurov’s 39.5 per cent.

Yet unlike their neighbours in Serbia, who voted in record numbers in recent elections, Bulgarians voted in record low numbers. Only 29.1 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots in the run-off, slightly more than in the first round. Our analysis looks at why many Bulgarians are tuning out of politics altogether.

World.title: With Change of Power, Serbia Can Reinvigorate EU Accession Bid
World.content:
“Catastrophic” - that’s how Dragana Djurica describes the current state of Serbia’s European Union accession process.

On Wednesday, the bloc’s executive arm, the European Commission, delivered its annual assessment of the progress made - or not - by countries bidding for membership. One of the main takeaways was the substantial progress made by Montenegro; another was the dramatic backsliding by Serbia.

“This is not a progress report, as it is officially called, but a report on backsliding,” said Djurica, head of the European Movement in Serbia, an NGO that advocates for Serbia’s EU integration.

“It is one of the most critical, and I would even say the worst, reports Serbia has received from the European Commission since the start of accession negotiations.”

World.title: Turkey Arrests Former Minister Over Stock Market Fraud Scandal
World.content:
A court in Istanbul on Friday ordered the arrest of Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a former minister and deputy chair of Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, over her alleged role in a major stock market financial fraud.

The Istanbul Prosecutor’s Office accused Kaya of “being a member of an organised crime group and violating stock market law”.

Her husband, Ilyas Kaya, and a former chair of the Capital Markets Board, Ibrahim Omer Gonul, were given a travel ban but not arrested.

Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, who was family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned in September as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling AKP after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

She is accused of illegally profiting through share-price manipulation after she received 2.17 billion Turkish lira (about 38.4 million euros) after reportedly investing 163 million lira (about 2.7 million euros) in an investment fund.

The couple deny wrongdoing. They have transferred some of the profits to an account designated by the banking regulators.

The AKP and the government welcomed the arrest order as proof of their good governance.

“We move forward by renewing ourselves! We are constantly reborn. We part ways with those who do wrong and those who succumb to their own desires, and we continue on our path stronger than before,” Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek wrote on X after Sayan Kaya’s arrest on Friday.

The investigation has already resulted in more than 100 detentions while Turkey’s Capital Markets Board has ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds managed by seven portfolio management companies.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. A Turkish television channel put the total number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya comes from a family with experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Serbia’s Anti-Terrorism Unit Chief Detained Over Alleged Abuse of Protesters
World.content:
A court in Belgrade on Friday ordered up to 30 days of detention for nine current and former employees of Serbia’s Interior Ministry, including the commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Igor Zmiric, over allegations of abusing and torturing students and others inside the government building following protests in August 2025.

According to the court, the nine suspects were remanded in custody over concerns that they could influence witnesses and obstruct criminal proceedings. The court also cited the seriousness of the alleged offence and the public concern it had caused, which could jeopardise the fair conduct of the proceedings.

The suspects are accused of jointly committing the criminal offence of abuse and torture.

According to the prosecution, the suspects used force and threats to inflict pain and suffering on students and other people in the government building’s garage between 10.30 p.m. on August 14 and 1 a.m. the following morning, with the aim of obtaining information, intimidating and unlawfully punishing them.

At the time of the offence, they were working as officers of the JZO, a police unit used to protect high-ranking state officials and major government buildings.

The suspects were arrested earlier this week. Among them is Milan Vukovic, a retired JZO officer who is now acting director of the detention facility where former JZO chief Marko Kricak is being held.

Kricak, who headed the unit at the time of the alleged abuse, has also been arrested, but in connection with a separate investigation into a murder in Belgrade.

During the mass anti-government protests of the past two years, some protesters have accused Kricak of using excessive force. Student Nikolina Sindjelic alleged that Kricak had threatened her with rape while she was detained in the garage beneath the government building in August 2025.

At least 15 people were detained in the garage beneath the government building on the night of August 14, 2025, amid anti-government protests, BIRN reported.

BIRN obtained testimonies given to prosecutors by four detainees and interviewed five others, who described being beaten, threatened with sexual violence and death, and having their personal belongings destroyed. Rights groups Amnesty International and Civil Rights Defenders warned that the alleged treatment could amount to torture and violate international law.

At the time, the Interior Ministry rejected the allegations, insisting that the officers had acted in accordance with the law. Then President Aleksandar Vucic later announced that the ministry’s internal affairs unit would investigate the allegations made by Sindjelic.

At the time of BIRN’s investigation, it was not clear whether the promised internal probe had been carried out.

World.title: Albania’s ‘Coordinator’? The Rapid Rise and Sudden Fall of Ergys Agasi
World.content:
On the afternoon of August 26, as the sun was setting over Durres beach, police in several unmarked vehicles pulled over a black Audi on the southern outskirts of the Albanian port city. Inside the car was Ergys Agasi, a businessman and former official at the environment ministry who had been on the run for the past eight months.

In video released by the police, 39-year-old Agasi is seen in a white T-shirt and shorts, hands cuffed behind his back, head bowed.

Albania’s Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, accuses Agasi of leading an organised criminal group that manipulated public tenders linked to the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, sometimes through violence.

Less than a month after his arrest, investigators moved against the head of the State Intelligence Service, SHISH, Vlora Hyseni, accusing her of aiding Agasi to evade arrest and providing him with classified information. Hyseni was placed under house arrest and dismissed from SHISH.

World.title: Serbian President’s Controversial Last-Minute Pardons Face Legal Challenges
World.content:
This Friday, a court in Belgrade was supposed to hear the verdict in the case against a man who rammed a car into a 20-year-old female student, Sonja Ponjavic, who was blocking a traffic intersection during an anti-government protest in the Serbian capital in January 2025.

The blockade was one of many rallies organised by students in memory of victims of the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster – an incident that transformed Serbian politics and ultimately led to the ousting of the government led by Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party at last month’s elections.

However, now the driver might not be punished for hitting the student because Vucic pardoned him in one of his last actions as President before stepping down to run for the premiership in the elections.

World.title: Transnistria’s Separatist Leader Decorated by Moscow, Denounced by Moldova
World.content:
In a ceremony at the Kremlin on Wednesday, Russian President Vladmir Putin formally pinned the Order of Honour award on the lapel of Vadim Krasnoselsky, the leader of Transnistria - a separatist region of Moldova where Moscow has maintained a military presence since the Soviet bloc disintegrated.

Putin said the decoration was awarded to recognise Krasnoselsky’s efforts to "strengthen ties" with Russia and amidst "pressure" from the West. Moldova is seeking to join the EU, but separatist Transnistria remains a potentially disruptive Russian lever of influence that Moscow wants to preserve.

“Despite difficult conditions and attempts at external pressure, the republic [Transnistria], under his leadership, is developing consistently. Its inhabitants, who are of various nationalities, defend their rights and interests together, uphold the historical truth and preserve the Russian language,” Putin explained.

Located on Moldova’s border with Ukraine, and home to 1,600 Russian troops, Transnistria is strategically important for the Russian leader. Speaking in Moscow, Krasnoselsky seemed happy to fall into line.

World.title: Wanderlust Readers Crown Dubrovnik Second Most Desirable European City
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Wanderlust readers have once again crowned Dubrovnik as the second most desirable European city to visit.

The City of Dubrovnik has once again confirmed its position as one of the most desirable European tourist destinations by winning the Silver Award in the Most Desirable City in Europe category. Dubrovacki Dnevnik reports that the city took home the award at the prestigious Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards 2026, which was held on the 4th of November in London. This recognition continues a series of international successes for Dubrovnik, which in recent years has regularly ranked among the best European city destinations according to readers of the respected British travel magazine Wanderlust.

The awards ceremony was held in the impressive Painted Hall, located in the historic Old Royal Naval College complex in London’s Greenwich. The Silver Award was accepted on behalf of the Dubrovnik Tourist Board by its director Miro Drašković. In this year’s selection Dubrovnik competed against some of the best-known European city destinations, including Copenhagen, Madrid, Lisbon, Istanbul, Bordeaux, Genoa and Tbilisi. This success confirms Dubrovnik’s international recognisability, its rich cultural and historical heritage, unique architecture and exceptional tourist appeal.

Wanderlust is otherwise one of the oldest and most respected British travel magazines, which for more than three decades has been promoting authentic travel, the discovery of new destinations and responsible and sustainable tourism. Its annual Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards, which this year mark their 25th edition, rank among the significant recognition in the international tourism industry. Special value is given to the awards by the fact that the winners are decided by the readers and travel lovers themselves.

Croatian islands were declared the Most Desirable Region in Europe. This recognition for the Croatian National Tourist Board, together with the silver award for Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik Tourist Board, additionally confirms the strong position of Croatian destinations on the international tourism market.

Dubrovnik has in recent years been repeatedly awarded in Wanderlust’s selection, including winning the gold award in the Most Desirable European City category. At last year’s ceremony it also received a special recognition from Wanderlust editor-in-chief George Kipouros for outstanding achievements in sustainable tourism management. With that recognition Dubrovnik was highlighted as an example of responsible destination development, thanks to the City of Dubrovnik’s “Respect the City” project and measures for managing tourist flows, regulating cruise ship arrivals, and preserving cultural heritage and the quality of life of the local population.

The continuous recognitions from one of the most respected British travel magazines have special importance for Dubrovnik, especially given that the United Kingdom is one of its most important source tourism markets. They represent additional confirmation of Dubrovnik’s international recognisability as a destination that combines exceptional cultural and historical heritage, authentic experiences and a responsible approach to tourism development.

World.title: Croatia Records Strong Cruise Tourism Growth in 2026
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Croatia has recorded some particularly strong cruise tourism growth throughout 2026, with almost a million passengers arrived at Croatian ports on foreign cruise ships.

Over the first nine months of 2026, almost a million passengers arrived at Croatian ports on various foreign cruise ships. Dalmacija Danas reports that the aforementioned figure is as much as 11.7 percent more than in the same period last year. The latest data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics reveals that Dubrovnik and Split are among the most visited ports in the entire country, while the largest share of cruise voyages took place precisely in two Dalmatian counties.

According to data published by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) this week, in the period from January to September 2026, 80 foreign cruise ships entered Croatian seaports and completed a total of 677 cruise voyages. On those massive vessels, there were as many as 958,109 passengers, which is around 100 thousand more than in the same period of 2025, when 858,066 were recorded. The number of cruise voyages rose by 9.9 percent, and the number of passengers by 11.7 percent. At the same time the number of foreign ships decreased slightly, by 1.2 percent.

Foreign cruise ships spent a total of 1,557 days in Croatian territorial waters, which is an increase of 7.7 percent compared to last year.

dubrovnik and split lead the way

The most interesting data concern Dalmatian ports, which continue to play a key role in Croatian cruise tourism. Dubrovnik is by far the most visited Croatian port, with a total of 505 visits by foreign cruise ships in the first nine months of this year. In second place is Split with 284 visits, while third is Zadar with 191 visits. Among the seven most visited ports are also Korčula with 95 visits, Hvar with 89, Rovinj with 84 and Šibenik with 81 visits. This latest data shows exactly how important Dalmatia is for the arrivals of foreign cruise ships, with Dubrovnik and Split particularly standing out.

According to DZS data, of the total of 677 cruise voyages by foreign ships, the largest share was achieved in Dubrovnik-Neretva County – as much as 46.5 percent. Split-Dalmatia County follows with 25.1 percent. This means that in these two counties a total of 71.6 percent of all recorded cruise voyages by foreign ships in Croatia were realised. Further up north in Dalmatia, the expansive and particularly island-strewn Zadar County accounted for 12 percent, and then further up in Istria County the number stood at 7.5 percent, in Šibenik-Knin County 4.9 percent, and finally Primorje-Gorski Kotar County four percent.

the maltese flag reigns

In the first nine months of 2026, Croatian ports were visited by foreign cruise ships sailing under the flags of 15 countries. The most cruise voyages were made by ships under the Maltese flag – a total of 201, which accounts for 29.7 percent of all recorded voyages. They are followed by ships under the flags of the Bahamas with 174 voyages, Norway with 66 and Panama with 52 voyages. Interestingly, ships sailing under the Bahamian flag carried the largest number of passengers – 294,569 – while ships under the Maltese flag carried 265,838 passengers.

184,000 cruise passengers in september alone

In September this year alone, 132 cruise voyages by foreign ships were realised, carrying 184,523 passengers. Compared to September last year this is an increase in the number of voyages of 18.9 percent and in the number of passengers of 11 percent. The highest number of passengers recorded in one single month was recorded in July – 196,389 – while in August, 186,048 passengers were recorded. DZS data thus confirms the continued growth of cruise tourism in Croatia, with Dalmatian ports, led by Dubrovnik and Split, occupying the leading positions.

World.title: Tourism in Central Dalmatia Up in 2026 – Polish Visitors Top the Charts
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Tourism in Central Dalmatia has seen an increase in 2026, with Polish visitors in particular topping the charts as far as visitor numbers go.

“We’re now entering the final stretch of another tourist year, a period in which we’re summing up the results, but at the same time already directing our gaze towards what still awaits us. Although the tourist rhythm is gradually changing, Central Dalmatia continues to do well through all sorts of events and experiences that give people a reason to visit the area outside the main summer months.

The Advent period is on its way, which brings another new opportunity to present Dalmatian cities, places, islands, as well as the Dalmatian hinterland, their traditions, food scene and special festive atmosphere,” stated the director of the Tourist Board of Split-Dalmatia County Ivana Vladović.

18.6 million overnight stays in central dalmatia

Dalmatinski portal also reports that this year’s statistical data also confirms that the effort has well and truly paid off. In the first ten months of this year, Split-Dalmatia County, according to data from the eVisitor system, was visited by 3.9 million guests. They achieved 18.6 million overnight stays in commercial accommodation, which is 1% more arrivals and 0.5% more overnight stays than in the same period last year. The largest number of overnight stays was achieved by guests from all of Europe, including Poland, Germany, elsewhere across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Great Britain and the Czech Republic.

“We’re now intensively preparing for 2027, which will be particularly significant for the county because it will carry the title of European Region of Gastronomy. This is fantastic recognition, but also an opportunity to present even more strongly the richness of our gastronomic heritage, local producers, traditional dishes and the people who preserve and pass on the culinary heritage of Central Dalmatia. We’re already working on new promotional campaigns, projects and activities with which we will bring this title closer to domestic and international guests and additionally connect the local food scene with our cultural identity, way of life and year-round tourist offer,” Vladović added.

dalmatia is still aiming to attract visitors throughout november

This November, this region of Dalmatia is also offering an entire series of interesting events that enable visitors to get to know its food, cultural and traditional heritage. In Omiš, the international gastronomic festival Grand Gourmet is being held, in Dugopolje the International Honey Fair Dalmatina, and Kaštela through the manifestation Zinfest – Fešta o’ Crljenka present the rich wine tradition and connection with one of the most famous world varieties.

Lovers of active holidays can participate in or follow the State Championship in rafting on the Cetina and the Hileja Marina Trail, while in Gornji Dolac at the end of the month the popular Christmas Village opens. The Split offer is additionally enriched by Štorije o’ spize, a manifestation dedicated to Dalmatian gastronomy, local producers and traditional flavours, and the Dalmatia Film Festival, which gathers lovers of domestic and international film production.

dalmatia beyond the summer season

Precisely the connection of different experiences and values of the region is one of the directions in which the Tourist Board intends to continue developing and presenting Central Dalmatia. Gastronomy, culture, natural heritage, active holidays, nautical tourism, islands and the Dalmatian hinterland form a diverse offer that goes beyond seasonal frameworks.

“In the period now just behind us, we continued to present Central Dalmatia on important international markets and business events, talk with partners and tourism professionals and monitor the changes that shape global tourist demand. Such meetings are important for strengthening how recognised we are, but also for the timely recognition of new opportunities. I believe that with joint work we will turn the title of European Region of Gastronomy into a strong opportunity for the promotion of Central Dalmatia, its people, tradition and quality offer,” director Vladović said, wishing all stakeholders in tourism a successful end of the year and a lot of creativity and enthusiasm in the preparation for the next tourist year.

World.title: As the European Union Prepares for Crisis, How Prepared is Croatia?
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – The European Union is currently preparing itself and its member states for crisis by encouraging the stocking of food and other supplies, but just how prepared is Croatia?

Just how ready is Croatia for more serious crisis situations, such as major power outages, supply disruptions, natural disasters or security threats? Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this specific question is opening up once again after the European Commission published guidelines in which it recommends that people prepare stocks of food, water, medicines and other basic necessities for at least 72 hours of crisis.

The emphasis is placed on three-day self-sufficiency of the general public. The European Commission recommends that households have basic stocks of food, water, medicines and other necessities ready and prepared, as well as a pre-packed bag or backpack with the most necessary things in case of emergency evacuation. In addition, the guidelines cover three more areas: education of children on how to act in crisis situations already from kindergarten age, with an approach adapted to their age, special protection measures for persons with disabilities, and clearer and much more timely information about possible dangers.

All of this is a continuation of the broader Union Preparedness Strategy, which the European Commission presented back in March 2025. The strategy covers 30 measures by which it seeks to strengthen the ability of the EU and its member states to respond to various crisis situations.

the government hasn’t bothered to show much interest in the eu’s recommendations

The new European recommendations have been intensively discussed in the media in recent days, yet the Croatian Government has so far not publicly presented the new guidelines nor explained whether and in what way it plans to implement them whatsoever in Croatia. Although the guidelines are not legally binding for the member states, the absence of official communication is somewhat surprising. The European Commission, namely, expressly states that it wants with them to encourage national authorities to develop their own preparedness measures, adapted to the circumstances and needs of individual countries.

It should be said that Croatia already has its own recommendations for acting in crisis situations. The Directorate of Civil Protection has published on its pages instructions for preparing a survival kit, which includes food, water, medicines, a battery torch, a radio receiver, documents and other necessary necessities. The existing Croatian instructions recommend stocks of food and water for at least two days.

An inquiry was therefore sent to the government in which an answer was requested specifically to the question of whether it plans to present the new European recommendations to the public. The second question was whether or not it plans to issue its own guidelines and, if it plans them, when their publication can be expected. The question of just how ready Croatia genuinely is for more serious crisis situations, what the current state of the shelters is, how many of them are functional and whether there are plans for their renovation was also posed. Information was also requested on the sufficiency of state strategic commodity reserves in the event of a longer-lasting crisis.

there are serious issues with croatia’s shelters

The state of Croatian shelters is called into question by the finding of the State Audit Office from 2024, which warned of numerous omissions in their management and maintenance. The audit established that of the 476 shelters managed by the 14 covered cities, 306 of them were not regularly used, and the cities did not undertake the necessary activities to put them into use. In seven cities only visual inspections of the shelters were carried out, without minutes on their correctness. The auditors also stated that the Directorate of Civil Protection did not have reliable and updated data on the condition and equipment of the shelters, and inspection supervisions did not cover the checking of the public shelters themselves.

City risk assessments did not cover threats such as wars and terrorist attacks. Due to the established deficiencies the State Audit Office issued a total of 158 orders and recommendations, and assessed the management of shelters in seven cities and the Directorate of Civil Protection as partially effective.

there are also massive problems with medicines…

According to the Government report for 2025, state commodity reserves were distributed at a total of 357 locations throughout Croatia. The total value of state commodity reserves at the end of last year amounted to 93 million euros, which is 6.87 percent more than the year earlier. Particularly worrying is the fact that Croatia at the end of 2025 in the strategic commodity reserves did not have recorded medicines, sanitary or consumable medical material, although their holding is provided for by regulations. Namely, the Act on Strategic Commodity Reserves from 2022 expressly includes among strategic products medicines, vaccines, antidotes and medical material, while the state balance determines the concrete products that need to be secured.

In total, it is a matter of 106 types of products for which it is expressly stated in the report itself that they need to be held in state reserves, but they are not in stock. Their procurement has been announced for years, but even at the end of 2025 that part of the strategic reserves was not filled. According to unofficial information from Jutarnji list, the Ministry of Health has for years not amended the regulations necessary for the procurement of medicines into state reserves. The Ministry of Economy confirmed that there are legal obstacles and that the situation has not changed even during 2026.

In the warehouses there were cereals, oil, sugar, cans, tents and other necessities, but certain hygiene products were missing, including soap, incontinence diapers and means for disinfecting water and space. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Economy for 2025, the total filling of the planned balance of strategic commodity reserves amounted to only 51.39 percent. The filling of food reserves amounted to 72.4 percent, and of non-food 81.75 percent. This is the realisation of the state stock plan.

risks already faced by croatia

As we have already written, the European Commission warns of a series of threats, from geopolitical tensions and possible military conflicts to cyber attacks, sabotage of critical infrastructure, natural disasters and disruptions in supply. It is clear that such risks do not bypass Croatia either, especially when it comes to cyber attacks, possible supply disruptions and other disruptions that can spread across national borders. However, there are also dangers that the Croatian institutions themselves warn about. According to official data of the Directorate of Civil Protection, among the significant risks for Croatia are earthquakes, floods, open space fires, landslides, extreme temperatures, strong winds and epidemics. Croatia has in recent years already experienced the consequences of devastating earthquakes in Zagreb and in Banovina, large fires and floods.

Such natural disasters can cause longer-lasting interruptions in the supply of electricity and water, damage transport infrastructure and hinder the work of emergency services.

the great power outage of 2024 – a stark warning

How possible such disruptions are is also shown by the example of the 21st of June 2024, when due to a major failure in the electricity system across a lot of southeastern Europe, a large part of Dalmatia was left without electricity, as were large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Albania. The power outage caused problems in traffic, communications and the everyday functioning of people and almost all infrastructure.

According to the report of the Croatian Energy Regulatory Agency for 2024, the supply interruption in Croatia affected almost 200 thousand network users, and individual users were without electricity for almost four hours. The incident showed how quickly a disruption in interconnected electricity systems can spread across state borders. Therefore the question of preparedness is not related only to possible war and security threats, but also to the dangers that Croatia has already faced. The question remains how ready the civil protection system, shelters and state commodity reserves are today to respond to a new major crisis.

World.title: Dinamo Shock Premier League Sunderland With 2-0 Away Win
World.content:
Dinamo produced one of their best European results in years on Thursday night, beating Sunderland 2-0 in the fourth round of the Europa League league phase.

It was a dream debut for interim coach Jerko Leko, who took over only days earlier after Mario Kovačević was sacked. Luka Stojković opened the scoring in the 23rd minute and set up Dion Drena Beljo for the second in the 39th, before Dinamo held firm through a second half in which the Premier League side had a goal disallowed and hit the woodwork.

The win lifts Dinamo to seven points from four matches, level with Sunderland, and brings in €450,000 in UEFA prize money, the reward for every league-phase win in the Europa League. Combined with the earlier win over Anderlecht and the draw with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, Dinamo’s results in the league phase alone have now earned them more than €1 million, and their total European earnings this season stand at close to €16 million.

Lineups

Sunderland: Roefs; Meunier, Danso, Alderete, Methalie; Xhaka, Ahoka; Rigg, Angulo, Fofana; Isidor

Dinamo: Kotarski; Valinčić, Domínguez, Galešić, Goda; Stojković, Mišić, Kačavenda; Lisica, Beljo, Oršić

Dinamo started well. Josip Mišić pounced on a loose ball in the 2nd minute and shot over from 18 meters, while Wilson Isidor’s falling effort from the edge of the box three minutes later was a simple take for Dominik Kotarski. Oršić blazed a shot well over in the 9th minute.

Sunderland’s best early move came in the 11th minute, when Chris Rigg found space on the right and crossed for Jules Ahoka, whose header was gathered by Kotarski. Isidor then headed over from a Nilson Angulo cross in the 17th minute, and three minutes later a scramble from an Angulo free kick ended with Thomas Meunier’s shot blocked by Mišić.

Dinamo almost took the lead in the 22nd minute. Moris Valinčić crossed from the right, and Beljo controlled the ball in the box, but his close-range shot was blocked at the last moment. From the resulting corner, the breakthrough came. Oršić delivered from the right, Sunderland headed it out only as far as Stojković on the edge of the box, and the midfielder took it on his chest before firing a volley into the net for 1-0.

It should have been 2-0 a minute later. Stojković played in Oršić, who rounded goalkeeper Robin Roefs and shot towards an empty net, only for Meunier to clear off the line. Galešić was booked in the 25th minute, and Xhaka followed a minute later after a painful collision with Mišić in midfield that left both captains needing treatment.

Sunderland nearly equalized in the 30th minute. Meunier sent a curling ball from the right into the Dinamo box, and it evaded everyone in the crowd of bodies before striking the post. Kotarski saved an Isidor effort two minutes later, and Kevin Danso was booked in the 36th minute for stopping Valinčić.

Stojković went close again in the 38th minute, forcing Roefs into a save with a low shot from 18 meters. A minute later, Dinamo doubled their lead. Stojković intercepted a Danso pass and immediately slipped Beljo in behind the defense, and the striker lifted the ball over Roefs from five or six meters for 2-0.

Mišić needed treatment just before half-time after being stepped on, but returned after a minute on the sidelines. Three minutes were added, and Dinamo went in 2-0 up.

Sunderland coach Régis Le Bris made four changes at the break. Leko made one, with Stjepan Radeljić replacing Sergi Domínguez.

Kačavenda was booked within 20 seconds of the restart for a foul on Fofana, and after 70 seconds, Sunderland had the ball in the net. Isidor headed in from close range after a Xhaka free kick, but VAR ruled it out for offside.

Sunderland challenged the Dinamo box in the 55th minute: Mišić blocked a Malick Fofana shot, and Hume’s fierce follow-up struck Kačavenda in the head. Hume was booked a minute later for a heavy challenge on Kačavenda, and Isidor shot wide from a Fofana cross. Sunderland’s biggest chance came in the 58th minute. Kotarski saved from Reinildo from close range after a Xhaka set piece, and Danso’s rebound crashed off the crossbar.

Dinamo finally threatened on the counter in the 59th minute, when Valinčić found Mateo Lisica on the right, and his cut-back fell for Stojković, whose 20-meter shot went wide. A minute later, Kotarski saved a powerful effort from the edge of the box.

Brian Brobbey replaced Isidor in the 63th minute, while Ivanušec came on for the outstanding Stojković. Brobbey had his first chance in the 67th minute, when the ball dropped to him after Radeljić misjudged it, but he failed to connect cleanly and caught Kotarski, who needed treatment. Prevljak replaced Beljo in the 70th minute, and Brobbey headed wide from a Le Fée free kick.

Kotarski saved a long-range Xhaka effort in the 76th minute, Galešić produced an excellent block on Fofana two minutes later, and Brobbey’s penalty appeal after going down under a challenge from Radeljić in the 79th minute was waved away. Leko brought on Perez Vinlof and Hoxha for Goda and Oršić, and Sunderland’s attacks grew increasingly toothless. Four minutes of stoppage time passed without incident, and Dinamo held on for a famous 2-0 win.

World.title: Wanderlust: Croatian Islands Most Desirable Region in Europe
World.content:
November 6, 2026 – The season may be over, but the recognition keeps on coming. Croatian islands win big at the prestigious Wanderlist Reader Travel Awards.

Various studies cannot agree on how many there are exactly – some say 1185, others 1244, or even 1246 – but one thing is for sure – Croatian islands are gorgeous, a fact once more reinforced at the 2026 Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards in London earlier this week.

In the category Most Desirable Region (Europe), Croatian islands came away with the Gold Award, accompanied by this glowing tribute:

The rise of the Croatian Islands isn’t about riding a hot trend; it’s more a story of travellers simply discovering what’s there for themselves. With millions of visitors a year heading to Croatia’s Adriatic coast, those escaping its busier spots are realising how much more there is to see offshore. Beyond well-known Hvar, Brač and Korčula lie quiet, car-free communities such as Silba; incredible nature on Mljet, whose entire north-western end is a national park; pristine night skies on Lastovo, a candidate to become an official Dark Sky Park; and history aplenty in island-bound, UNESCO-listed Trogir. Even getting around invites reflection, with sailing trips from Vis aboard traditional sardine-fishing boats offering a recipe for slowing down.

Certain islands such as Hvar are no stranger to international recognition, having also been voted among the best islands in Europe in the 2026 Conde Nast Readers Traveler Awards, home to the first public theatre in all of Europe, and one where no island has more UNESCO heritage. But this was an award for all Croatia’s islands, 50 of which are inhabited, and which provide much of the country’s tourism draw.

While all the islands may look similar on the surface, there is an incredible diversity once you scratch the surface, which reveal some rather surprising facts, many of which I have summarised in this video below, 25 Things You Would Not Expect to FInd on a Croatian Island. These include the first place in the world to abolish slavery (Korcula), the birth of cricket in mainland Europe (Vis), and the birthplace of organise tourism in Europe (Hvar).

You can see the full list of Wanderlust awards here.

World.title: Eurowings to Keep Split Connected to Five German Cities This Winter
World.content:
November the 6th, 2026 – Eurowings will keep Split connected to give German cities this winter. The airline is otherwise one of the airport’s most important airlines.

Eurowings will keep Split connected with five German cities even during the winter months. As Slobodna Dalmacija reports, Eurowings is one of the most important airlines at Split Airport. According to the announced winter flight schedule for the 2026/2027 season, the German carrier plans a total of 130 rotations on the routes between Split and Germany, with an estimated capacity of more than 45,300 seats, reported the specialised portal Croatia aviation.

This is important news not only for Split Airport, but also for the entire Dalmatian tourism sector, which in recent years has been trying to reduce the pronounced seasonality and extend the period of operations outside the main summer months. Maintaining direct air links with Germany opens additional possibilities for the arrival of guests in the period when Split traditionally sinks into winter sleep, and the city centre becomes almost ghostly empty, with the exception during Advent. One of the main problems of the high seasonality of tourism is the lack of flights in the winter period, so this announcement from Eurowings also opens the possibility of the arrival of a larger number of guests from Germany, which is particularly dear to Croatians, from where a large number of tourists traditionally come to us, but still most often in the heart of the summer season. This is an opportunity to show them that we have something to offer even during winter.

stuttgart as the most important connection

Eurowings will during the winter operate on five routes from Germany, to Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Cologne, Berlin and Hamburg. Nevertheless, the traffic will not be evenly distributed throughout the entire winter period. The largest number of rotations is planned on the Split – Stuttgart route, 60 of them, which makes up 46.2 percent of the total number. Düsseldorf follows with 28 rotations and Cologne with 26. These three routes together make up as much as 88 percent of the total planned traffic.

The routes from Berlin and Hamburg will have a significantly shorter period of operation. From Berlin ten rotations are planned, and from Hamburg six are planned. What’s particularly significant is the fact that the route to Stuttgart will operate continuously throughout the entire winter, while Düsseldorf and Cologne will have certain interruptions. Thereby Split is ensured at least one stable direct connection with the German market even in the period of the lowest tourist demand. How significant the German market is for Split is shown by the data of Split Airport. During 2025, passengers from Germany achieved 796,707 passenger arrivals and departures, that is, they made up 20.5 percent of the total traffic of the airport. Eurowings was in the same year the third largest carrier in Split, with approximately 355 thousand passengers transported, almost 55 thousand more than the year before.

Germany is at the same time one of the most important source markets of Croatian tourism. According to data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics, German tourists during 2025 achieved 21 million overnight stays in Croatia, that is, almost a quarter of all overnight stays of foreign guests.

For Dalmatia as whole, it’s particularly important that the interest of German guests does not have to stop with the end of summer. A city like Split has the potential to attract visitors throughout the whole year thanks to Diocletian’s Palace, cultural and historical contents, gastronomy, excursions, active holidays and the proximity of islands and other Dalmatian destinations.

a prerequisite for extending the season

The announced capacity of more than 45,000 seats doesn’t mean that so many passengers will actually arrive in Split, but it is an important prerequisite for maintaining tourist traffic outside the summer months. Direct flights, namely, reduce the time and costs of travel and facilitate the organisation of shorter holidays and weekend visits, which in the time of a hectic lifestyle is very important. This is also important for Split hoteliers, private renters, restaurants, tourist guides and excursion organisers. Every additional guest in the winter months contributes to the filling of accommodation capacities and the maintenance of business, which without such demand would be concentrated almost exclusively on a few summer months.

How pronounced this problem is is also shown by the Eurostat data according to which Croatia in 2025 was among the most seasonal tourist destinations of the European Union: as many as 54.5 percent of all overnight stays were achieved during July and August. Precisely because of that the development of air connections during winter has a wider meaning than the mere number of flights. Nevertheless, air routes by themselves cannot extend the season. Open hotels, year-round offer of restaurants and cultural contents, quality excursions and coordinated promotion of the destination on source markets are needed.

Eurowings’ winter schedule is therefore a positive signal for Split tourism, but also a reminder of how important it is to develop contents because of which guests will come to Split also in November, January or February, and not only during the months of July and August.

World.title: Croatian Defence Minister: Vučić Was Southeastern Europe’s Biggest Issue
World.content:
November the 6th, 2026 – Croatian Defence Minister Ivan Anušić has told Americans during his visit to the USA that Serbia under Aleksandar Vučić was southeastern Europe’s biggest issue.

Defence Minister Ivan Anušić stated during an official visit to the United States of America that Serbia under the leadership of Aleksandar Vučić was the biggest source of instability in southeastern Europe. Index reports that he added that the new Serbian authorities must very clearly distance themselves from the Greater Serbian policies of the 1990s. Anušić was recently at Harvard University upon the invitation of the former US ambassador to Croatia Nathalie Rayes. At the Belfer Centre for Science and International Affairs which took place there, he participated in a seminar on the security situation across southeastern Europe, where he commented on the recent elections in Serbia in which Vučić’s regime was finally overthrown.

serbia’s new leadership must make a clean break from the greater serbian policies of the 1990s

In his presentation, the defence minister emphasised that the new authorities in Belgrade, which are yet to be formed after the parliamentary elections held on 25 October, must renounce the previous political direction if they want peace and cooperation in the region. “Serbia under the leadership of Aleksandar Vučić was the biggest source of instability in southeastern Europe. In the interest of peace and stability, the new Serbian authorities must very clearly distance themselves from the Greater Serbian policies of Aleksandar Vučić, that is, from those of Slobodan Milošević from the 1990s,” Anušić stated, speaking about the political changes that in addition to Serbia also include the recent change of government in neighbouring Hungary.

security in bosnia and herzegovina is crucial

Speaking about Croatia’s specific role, Anušić pointed out that the country within the European Union and NATO is a guardian of stability that supports the Euro-Atlantic path of neighbouring countries. In doing so he particularly emphasised the importance of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the continuation of the American military presence in Kosovo as part of the KFOR mission.

“For Croatia the stability of southeastern Europe is of national interest, and especially the preservation of stability and peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is of key importance for the security of our entire neighbourhood,” the minister said. Anušić also commented on the ongoing war in Ukraine, emphasising the need for the continuation of military and political assistance to Kyiv and recalling that Ukraine with its defence is already almost in the fifth year keeping the conflict away from the borders of the rest of the continent.

World.title: Gallery: PÖFF presents lifetime awards on opening night
World.content:
The 30th Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) opened at Alexela Concert Hall in Tallinn Friday, with lifetime achievement awards given out to three people.

Animator Priit Pärn, composer Sven Grünberg, both from Estonia, plus Icelandic director Hilmar Oddsson were the recipients.

Oddsson, 69, is one of the film-makers who helped put Icelandic cinema on the world map in the 1980s. His most recent film, "Á Ferð með Mömmu" ("Driving Mum"), which involved Estonian film-makers, won PÖFF's grand prix in 2022. Awarding him is also a nod to the Nordic auteurs the festival began with in 1997 — Oddsson was one of them, and his film "Tár úr steini" ("Tears of Stone"), which brought him to Tallinn 29 years ago, screens again in the anniversary program "PÖFF tähistab" ("PÖFF celebrates").

Grünberg, who turns 70 shortly, was honored for his contribution to Estonian film music. He has scored nearly 130 Estonian and foreign films, seen by tens if not hundreds of millions of people. His credits include "Hukkunud Alpinisti hotell", "Leiutajateküla Lotte", and "Naksitrallid"," and the series "Wikmani poisid".

Pärn, who recently turned 80, was honored for his contribution to Estonian animation and is Estonia's most internationally known film-maker. This is his 13th lifetime achievement award. His 1987 film "Eine murul" remains one of the deepest portraits of the oppressive Soviet everyday, and his own teaching system has produced a generation of animators in Finland, Estonia and beyond.

The 30h annual PÖFF festival got underway on Friday and runs until Sunday, November 22, with 230 feature films and 259 shorts from 87 countries being screened during that time.

World.title: Parties still compiling candidate lists ahead of March Riigikogu elections
World.content:
Parties are still recruiting Riigikogu candidates with some list places unfilled. The coalition Reform Party will not announce its lead candidates until late on this month.

The opposition Center Party has yet to decide which electoral district party chairman and former Tallinn mayor Mihhail Kõlvart will head up.

The Riigikogu elections take place in March and final candidate lists are due by mid-January, meaning parties are deep into the process of deciding who to run where, to optimize results.

Due to the d'Hondt proportional representation system used in Estonia, parties usually place their vote magnet candidates, usually leading politicians, high up on their ordered lists – excess votes these candidates have after clinching a seat can be distributed to candidates lower down on the list, who may not win a seat in their own right.

Kõlvart is one such vote magnet, and Center's Secretary General Anneli Ott told "Aktuaalne kaamera": "The party chairman would be a major vote-winner in any constituency. But which constituency he will head the list in remains undecided."

The party's two MEPs Jana Toom and Jaak Madison, will head electoral lists, Center, whose traditional bedrock areas include Tallinn and Ida-Viru County, confirmed.

Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

The Social Democrats (SDE) have made more apparent progress. The party leader, Lauri Läänemets, will run in Järva and Viljandi, while new member, former foreign ministry secregary general and prime ministerial candidate Jonatan Vseviov, is to run in Harju and Rapla. "The regional branches have not yet made their final decisions on the order of candidates or who will ultimately stand," said SDE Secretary General Piret Hartmann

The Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) has finalized leading candidates in half its constituencies, with chairman Martin Helme running in Tallinn's Mustamäe and Nõmme. Helme said the party faces difficulty winning votes in the bigger cities, meaning great efforts must be focused there. "A third of the Riigikogu is elected from Tallinn. So naturally, we are focusing on Tallinn," Helme said. EKRE's traditional stronghold has been southwestern Estonia.

Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu is to run in Harju and Rapla, just south of Tallinn and including the capital's commuter belt, with MEPs Jüri Ratas, a former prime minister, and Riho Terras also standing. Secretary General Andres Metsoja said regional branch proposals matter most when making decisions.

Looking for its first ever Riigikogu seats is Parempoolsed, whose chairwoman Lavly Perling is prepared to run in Harju and Rapla, though the party has not completed all its leads and has even turned some aspirants away. Deputy chairman Siim Kiisler said ideological conviction matters to the party more than profile.

Eesti 200, who in summer saw two MPs defect, is still compiling its full list.

Several of the parties have been hit by a wave of departures of high profile candidates who are not running this time around. SDE has lost Raimond Kaljulaid, a prominent MP who sits on the Riigikogu's national defense committee but is returning to the private sector, as well as MEP Marina Kaljurand. Former education minister Liina Kersna (Reform) is not seeking re-election and neither is Hanno Pevkur, defense minister until September and once a challenger for Reform's leadership. Parempoolsed has lost defense and security expert Rainer Saks, who cannot run due to taking up a post as presidential adviser.

High profile candidates may run for a party even if they cannot then take up the seat won, usually because they hold another post which bars that. MEPs and local government leaders fall into that category for instance. Their votes won will be transferred to candidates lower down the party's ordered list.

Polling day is March 7, 2027.
