World.title: FACT CHECK: SC didn’t rule Marcos’ budget signing unconstitutional
World.content:
The Court faulted Congress for raising the President's proposed budget, and with the decision not yet final, no formal probe has been opened

Claim: The Supreme Court (SC) ruled that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s signing of the national budget was unconstitutional.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A graphic shared by the Facebook page Makata Ng Bayan on November 1 shows an edited photo of Marcos, former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo, and Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla.

The text on the graphic reads: “Sinabi na ng Supreme Court na Unconstitutional ang Pagpirma ni Marcos sa Budget! Tungkulin ng Ombudsman, DOJ at COA mag Imbestiga, Pero bakit di nila ginawa? Mga Duwag ba sila o Mukhang Pera?”

(The Supreme Court has already said Marcos’s signing of the budget was unconstitutional! It’s the duty of the Ombudsman, Department of Justice (DOJ), and Commission on Audit (COA) to investigate, but why didn’t they? Are they cowards or money-hungry?)

At the time of writing, the post had 4,900 reactions, 1,200 comments, and 2,400 shares.

The facts: The SC did declare national budgets unconstitutional, but because of what Congress added to them, not because of the President’s signature.

In a ruling released on October 20, written by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the Court voted 13-2 to strike down the 2024 and 2025 national budgets, along with two rules in this year’s budget on how standby funds can be released.

The Court said Congress is not allowed to make the budget bigger than what the President proposed. In 2024, lawmakers added P449.5 billion in standby funds to the budget, and P17.99 billion more for the 2025 DPWH Special Road Fund. (READ: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations)

Not yet final: Court spokesperson Camille Ting said the ruling is not yet final, and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) could file a motion for reconsideration within 15 days from notice.

The OSG has since filed a motion for clarification and partial reconsideration, signed by Solicitor General Darlene Berberabe. The motion asks the Court to spell out which projects already funded under the budgets can continue, and to declare that the 2025 Special Road Fund increase was constitutional.

It also asked the Court not to count standby funds under the same spending limit as the rest of the budget, and to treat its new rules on releasing those funds as guidance rather than binding requirements.

No ongoing investigations: As of writing, the Ombudsman, DOJ, and COA have not opened a formal probe. The Ombudsman is also waiting for the SC’s final decision.

In 2025, it temporarily put on hold a graft complaint against House leaders over the 2025 budget until the Court resolved the constitutional question with finality.

The Court said officials behind the budget increases could still face criminal, civil, or administrative cases, unless the proper court or body finds they acted in good faith. On October 26, Remulla announced a “budget watch” and said he would form a team to study the decision and determine who may be held liable.

Vice President Sara Duterte said Marcos and Congress should answer for approving the budgets, while Malacañang said it disagreed with parts of the ruling. Senator Panfilo Lacson and Representative Leila de Lima welcomed the decision as a win for accountability. – Jake Gomez/Rappler.com

World.title: Fresh off shock reelection, Brazil President Lula to join ASEAN Summit in Manila
World.content:
LEADER. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva speaks as he attends a meeting of the National Council for Critical and Strategic Minerals (CIMCE), at the Planalto Palace in Brasilia, Brazil, on November 5, 2026.

Just weeks after a historic election triumph, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will head to the Philippines to join global leaders at the 49th ASEAN Summit

MANILA, Philippines – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will travel to the Philippines to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, just over two weeks after winning an unprecedented fourth term.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed Lula’s attendance on Friday, November 6, noting he was invited as a guest of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“Brazil was invited as Guest of the Chair,” said ASEAN spokesperson Dax Imperial.

Lula will join other global leaders, including US President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres in the main summit from November 15 to 18.

Prior to arriving in the Philippines on November 13, Lula is expected to be in Antalya, Turkey, for the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) from November 11 to 12.

Just a few weeks ago, the 81-year-old Lula pulled off a shock election victory over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, won a historic fourth term in a stunning October 25 result that defied polls and marked another comeback in his career.

Last August, DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro met with Lula to reinforce bilateral ties as the Philippines and Brazil celebrated their 80th diplomatic anniversary.

Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century.

He was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.

Lula’s fourth term, though, could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s. – with a report from Reuters/Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: China Wields Carrot and Stick at Beijing Meet, Regime Seeks Elections in Shan, and More
World.content:
We’ll always hold your hand, Beijing promises Myanmar regime

“China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe on the sidelines of the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday.

The reassurance came as part of a carrot-and-stick package amid alarm in Beijing over recent meetings between U.S. and Myanmar officials that seemed to augur the start of re-engagement.

The U.S. has released an Integrated Country Strategy for its mission in Myanmar, which identifies goals for expanding Washington’s diplomatic, economic and humanitarian influence in the country. Besides singling out scam networks, it also sets goals for boosting American exports to the impoverished war-torn country and gain access to Myanmar’s “bountiful” rare earth resources—besides aiming to “counter China’s influence.”

Myanmar is China’s most important external source of rare earth minerals and a major global source of heavy rare earth elements, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which are essential for electric cars, wind turbines, advanced electronics and military technologies. But mines are concentrated in areas beyond the reach of the regime in Kachin and Shan states.

Online scam operations have become a major point of convergence and competition in the two superpowers’ approach toward Myanmar. During the meeting with Aung Kyaw Hoe, Wang urged his regime to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to the vast scam compounds that flourished there.

China grows impatient over stalled investment projects

But in the same meeting Wang applied plenty of stick, urging Myanmar’s regime to get a move on in realizing long-stalled projects that form part of the planned China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) that would provide Beijing with overland access to the Indian Ocean. Wang told Aung Kyaw Hoe the two sides must “coordinate development and security” so they can “steadily advance” key CMEC projects.

Wang’s message echoed remarks made by his President Xi Jinping during regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Beijing in June, when Xi also called for swift implementation of CMEC projects.

The corridor’s flagship schemes include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and special economic zone in Rakhine State and a planned railway linking Kyaukphyu with Yunnan via Mandalay and Muse. On China side, the railroad is already entering its final phase but on the Myanmar side fighting continues across many parts of the route.

Aung Kyaw Hoe promised the regime is doing all it can but, true to form, also used the occasion to beg for even more Chinese investment.

Border trade gates reopen as armed groups consolidate control

China has significantly eased restrictions on trade through several Myanmar border crossings controlled by Beijing-linked ethnic armed organizations, allowing fuel, medicines, construction materials and other previously banned goods to enter northern Shan and Kachin.

The move suggests China is adjusting its border policy to accommodate new realities on the ground, where it appears the military regime in Naypyitaw has permanently lost control. With Operation 1027, key border trade gates and routes in northern Shan fell into the hands of the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and its erstwhile partner in the Brotherhood Alliance, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

Beijing initially closed the crossings to pressure them into making peace with the generals, but trade has long resumed and is now growing exponentially.

According to Chinese Customs at the Mengding crossing with MNDAA-controlled Chinshwehaw, the total value of trade there and at nearby Mangka eached 4.92 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, up 49.3 percent on-year.

Customs figures also show increased trade through Namhkam crossing controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army, as well as through the Kyin San Kyawt gate controlled jointly by the Brotherhood Alliance in Muse Township, which once accounted for some 70 percent of cross-border trade. The regime still controls a couple of crossings in Muse, where it bans the import of fuel from China.

In a move to prevent those groups from financing their armies through cargo taxation, the cash-strapped regime is now reduced to blocking routes south of Lashio, imposing a crackdown on what it calls “smuggled” goods—which in reality means roadside extortion.

Late last month, Min Aung Hlaing urged his ministers to intensify their crackdown on illegal trade and make sure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through “legal” channels, i.e. those his regime controls. Myanmar’s consul general in Kunming met with the customs department director this week to discuss facilitating flows of “officially traded goods” between the neighbors and improving cooperation on customs procedures.

Naypyitaw seeks to roll out elections into Shan borderlands

Defence Minister Yar Pyae who also chairs the junta’s peace negotiation committee, this week visited areas held by China-linked ethnic armed groups with a view to rolling out the regime’s sham elections across their part of the country as well.

Yar Pyae went to Panghsang, the headquarters of United Wa State Army (UWSA), and Mongla, the fiefdom of the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA) near the Chinese border. The visit comes after Chinese Special Envoy to Myanmar Deng Xijun urged granting “high-level” autonomy to ethnic minorities.

Together with the MNDAA, they are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, with Chinese widely spoken and the yuan used as the major currency in their territories.

All three trace their origins to the 1989 mutiny that fractured the Communist Party of Burma. Most people in NDAA territory are ethnic Chinese with roots in Yunnan, but the Wa are a Mon‑Khmer-speaking people more closely related to the Palaung.

Both the UWSA and NDAA have long upheld ceasefires they signed with the military in 1989 in return for de-factor autonomy in their areas, sustained by cross‑border trade and Chinese investment.

In Mongla, Yar Pyae discussed holding the vote, which was omitted there when the regime orchestrated polls in the parts of Myanmar it controls in the winter of 2025-26 that led to military dictator Min Aung Hlaing declaring himself president. Naypyitaw is aiming for next April, regime media said. But none of the townships under the control of the UWSA or NDAA were included on the junta’s recently announced list of constituencies slated for catch-up and by-elections.

Historically, no national elections have been conducted either in Mongla or Panghsang, although voting has taken place in some townships of the constitutionally defined Wa Self-Administered Division where government administration was present. Formally, the UWSA is stuck at a stage of demanding official statehood, and the NDAA is demanding official autonomous status.

World.title: Arakan Army Faces Second Front at Bangladesh Border
World.content:
Amid intensified fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) closes in on the Arakan (Rakhine State) capital of Sittwe, a second front is heating up along the border with Bangladesh, where regime-aligned Rohingya armed groups are escalating conflict.

These attacks are not isolated border incidents. They reflect a history of cooperation between Myanmar’s military and Muslim armed organizations during the 2024 battles for Buthidaung and Maungdaw. For Bangladesh, they raise difficult questions about its security interests and the prospects of repatriating the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees now within its borders. For the AA, they raise the question whether it can maintain stability across its home state.

A major concern is that armed networks established during the military regime’s territorial retreat are continuing to exert pressure on the AA while the main body of its forces confronts the regime elsewhere.

From cooperation to proxy warfare

During the 2024 Arakan offensive, the military suffered major territorial losses. Facing the AA’s advance, it cast around for additional manpower and local allies, and alighted on armed organizations that, ironically, were associated with a population it had systematically persecuted. One of them was the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).

The International Crisis Group has documented the regime’s ammunition supplies to ARSA, along with recruitment arrangements that transferred Rohingya refugees to military facilities for training.

ARSA and another armed group, the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), received training, weapons and tactical support during the fighting while maintaining contacts with regime personnel after the AA captured Maungdaw in December 2024, according to the Transnational Institute.

Here was the military that was responsible for the 2017 atrocities that drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh, brazenly cooperating with Rohingya armed organizations against the AA.

For the junta, however, the strategic advantages outweighed any qualms it might have had. Armed groups operating along the state’s northern frontier could challenge AA positions even after its own conventional military bases had fallen, and thereby divert precious resources from the AA’s other battlefronts.

As a bonus for a regime that has long sustained itself by divide-and-rule tactics, it risked deepening mistrust between the state’s Arakanese and Muslim communities.

Maungdaw remains a strategic front

Thus when the AA eventually captured Maungdaw, it transformed the military balance along the Bangladesh border but could not fully eliminate the armed groups operating through remote terrain and cross-border networks.

In September last year, ARSA fighters attacked an AA border security position near Inn Chaung village in northern Maungdaw. AA forces subsequently retook the position, while the attackers reportedly fled to Bangladesh.

Further clashes followed, and by late October this year, residents reported that ARSA was renewing recruitment, armed movements and attacks against AA outposts in northern and southern Maungdaw.

“ARSA activities have resurged in both northern and southern Maungdaw Township,” one resident told my news organization, Development Media Group.

With the AA confronting regime forces around Sittwe, repeated ARSA attacks could now force it to divert much-needed troops, intelligence resources and supplies to the border.

This would benefit Myanmar’s military even without direct command of these operations.

There is an important caveat. ARSA, RSO and a third militia active at the border, the Arakan Rohingya Army (ARA) have distinct leadership structures and interests. Their historical cooperation with the military regime does not mean that every recent attack was centrally coordinated.

Bangladesh’s border dilemma

A further complication lies in Bangladeshi involvement in these skirmishes. The AA accuses certain officers of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) of providing the Rohingya armed groups with logistical assistance, ammunition and intelligence, and allowing them to operate near border security positions.

The International Crisis Group, too, has documented the complicated relationships between these groups and elements of Bangladesh’s security establishment.

The allegations require credible investigation, but any such shenanigans must also be distinguished from official Bangladeshi government policy. Publicly, the BGB has denied supporting ARSA or the RSO.

Bangladesh faces legitimate challenges involving border security, with more than 1 million Rohingya refugees and the prospect of their eventual repatriation creating a massive headache for Dhaka.

But it will eventually have to confront the reality that the territory from which the refugees fled is now controlled by the AA, and that fundamentally changes the political realities.

Some Bangladeshi security personnel may still regard these avowedly Muslim armed organizations as potential leverage over the AA. But helping them with their cross-border attacks would now in fact undermine border stability and make peaceful repatriation more difficult.

In other words, Bangladesh’s security interests would be better served by stopping ARSA and co. from exploiting refugee communities, and instead maintaining effective communication with the AA authorities controlling the opposite side of the border.

Beyond armed groups and military control

The motivations behind Rohingya armed mobilization long predate any cooperation with Myanmar’s military.

Decades of discrimination, statelessness, displacement and uncertainty have created grievances that armed organizations can exploit. Refugees facing declining humanitarian assistance and limited opportunities are particularly vulnerable to recruitment and intimidation. But that cannot justify attacks on civilians, abductions or forced recruitment.

Nor should ARSA, RSO and ARA be treated as representative of Muslim communities as a whole. The Arakanese, Muslim and other communities in Maungdaw face threats from armed violence, disrupted livelihoods and insecurity. Abuses by all armed participants, including the AA, require impartial investigation and accountability.

The AA’s territorial gains have brought responsibilities extending beyond military security. Effective governance means it must protect civilians regardless of ethnicity or religion, address grievances and prevent communal tensions from escalating.

The Maungdaw conflict demonstrates that territorial control does not necessarily end a war.

Myanmar’s military has lost most of its positions in Arakan, yet its airpower, remaining military strongholds and historical relationships with armed groups continue to complicate the AA’s security calculations.

Preventing further escalation requires credible investigation of alleged weapons supplies and cross-border assistance, effective border management, protection of refugees from coercive recruitment, and sustained engagement between Bangladesh and the AA.

It also requires meaningful dialogue with Muslim civilian representatives and equal protection for all communities.

Unless the networks and grievances sustaining violence are addressed, no lasting peace can come to Arakan.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Hurry Up With Our Investment Projects, China tells Myanmar Regime
World.content:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has renewed Beijing’s call for the Myanmar regime to “steadily advance” key projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), which is designed to give Beijing direct access to Indian Ocean.

Wang made the remarks during a meeting on Tuesday with Myanmar Investment and Foreign Economic Relations Minister Aung Kyaw Hoe, who is in Beijing for the 11th Lancang–Mekong Cooperation Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

A clearly exasperated Wang stressed the need for the two sides to “coordinate” development and security, as many parts of Myanmar are plagued by civil war, making it hard for the China-backed projects to proceed.

In turn, Wang promised Chinese support for the rebranded regime’s efforts to achieve international recognition. “China will always be a strategic partner that Myanmar can rely on,” he said.

The remarks come as the U.S. shows signs of re-engaging with Naypyitaw in search of business.

Wang also called for stronger efforts to combat scams and online gambling. He urged Myanmar to prevent the “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, referring to online scam operations that flourished along the Thai-Myanmar border.

He urged Naypyitaw to do more to ensure the safety of Chinese nationals, organizations and projects operating in the country.

Aung Kyaw Hoe, for his part, promised that his regime does want to accelerate the CMEC projects and step up cooperation with China and regional countries in combating online scam operations. He duly thanked his hosts for supporting Myanmar in international forums, according to a statement from the Chinese Embassy.

When Myanmar’s putschist leader Min Aung Hlaing last visited Beijing in June after declaring himself president, Chinese President Xi Jinping also urged him to speed up the CMEC projects, a key component of Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

He too urged the regime to provide stronger security guarantees for Chinese personnel and investments in Myanmar, many of which are in areas now controlled by the resistance or ethnic armed organizations over which Beijing holds no sway.

The planned corridor includes several flagship projects, notably the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State and a railway linking Kyaukphyu through Mandalay and Muse with China’s Yunnan Province.

The Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project is particularly important for Beijing because it would provide China with direct access to the Indian Ocean while supporting economic development in Yunnan and other southwestern Chinese provinces.

But other than pay lip-service to the plans and hold out its hand for more investment, the Myanmar regime has done little to advance these projects, instead losing itself in dreams of reviving the long-mothballed Myitsone Dam Project in quite a different part of the country.

In its frustration, China has now reopened border crossings with areas controlled by ethnic armed organizations in northern Shan State to allow lucrative trade to resume, whether the regime likes it or not.

A China analyst told The Irrawaddy that Beijing “knows very well that Min Aung Hlaing’s stubbornness is holding everything up. The fighting is still going on, the peace talks haven’t delivered any results, there’s been no progress in northern Shan State, and the border crossings are still not operating normally.”

For the CMEC projects to move forward, Min Aung Hlaing “has to engage in talks with the ethnic armed groups first,” she added. “In that sense, I think China was quite deliberately sending that message.”

World.title: Kyat Slump Disrupts Thai Border Trade as Import Costs Rise
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of Myanmar’s currency has disrupted border trade with Thailand, prompting some traders and money changers along the border to suspend transactions as they struggle to cope with volatile exchange rates and mounting import costs.

The currency weakened to around 680 baht per 100,000 kyats this week, down from more than 700 baht in recent weeks. The currency also fell against the U.S. dollar, with the market exchange rate rising from just above 4,700 kyats per dollar at the end of October to more than 4,900 on Wednesday. The rate was just around 4,400 kyats in early October.

The latest slump is fueling concerns over another wave of inflation in a country heavily reliant on imports from Thailand. Myanmar imports a wide range of goods from its neighbor, including electrical appliances, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and foodstuffs, making fluctuations in the baht exchange rate significant for consumers.

Market insiders attributed the kyat’s latest decline to the regime’s plan to borrow 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to finance a budget shortfall for fiscal year 2026-27, which ends on March 31. The regime has already sold treasury bonds worth trillions of kyats, leading to speculation that it will simply print banknotes to cover the deficit.

They also pointed to Myanmar’s continued inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist, delays in export licensing and policy inconsistencies between ministries as factors undermining confidence in the market.

The swift depreciation of the kyat has left traders struggling to price goods and manage working capital.

“A gradual rise doesn’t create much difficulty. The problem is when rates surge rapidly,” a trader in Myawaddy told The Irrawaddy.

“If exchange rates rise further, we will need more capital to restock. Some traders have temporarily stopped trading and making payments, and are waiting to see where the market moves.”

The uncertainty has spread beyond traders. Some major money changers in Myawaddy and across the border in Thailand suspended transactions on Wednesday, opting to wait for the next day’s opening rates before resuming business, according to border exchange operators.

The volatility is not confined to the Thai border. Traders in Muse, on Shan State’s border with China, are facing similar difficulties as the kyat continues to weaken against the yuan, market sources said.

Traders warn that prolonged instability in foreign exchange markets could further squeeze trade. Importers say their profits are shrinking, but are reluctant to increase prices for fear that demand may decline further.

A trader in Myawaddy said transport costs remain a major contributor to rising prices, with expenses along trade routes increasing because of checkpoints and demands for unofficial payments.

“Price increases are caused more by transport costs than exchange rates,” he said. “Costs at checkpoints rise sharply whenever authorities announce crackdowns or tighter controls.”

Exporters also say the weaker kyat is raising shipping costs because freight charges, container fees and port services are paid in U.S. dollars. At the same time, they complain that mandatory foreign-exchange conversion rules prevent them from fully benefiting from higher market exchange rates.

Under existing regulations, exporters must convert 35 percent of their export earnings at the Central Bank’s official rate, creating a significant gap between official and market rates. The Central Bank’s official reference rate remains 2,100 kyats per dollar, while its market trading rate is about 3,660 kyats per dollar. The market rate was around 4,900 kyats on Thursday. Before the coup, the kyat traded at roughly 1,300-1,400 per U.S. dollar.

An exporter from Mon State explained that the depreciation of the kyat has sharply increased the capital required to buy export commodities such as corn and onions.

“Previously, we could buy a container of goods for 10 million kyats from local producers. Now it can require more than 15 million kyats,” he said.

Traders say prices of Thai imports, particularly electrical goods, household products, cosmetics, construction materials and food items, are already climbing as a result of the stronger baht and rising transportation costs.

World.title: Thai Foreign Minister to Visit Myanmar Ahead of ASEAN Summit
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thailand’s foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on November 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalize ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow’s trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries’ shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar’s military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.

His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a November 16-18 summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila.

Myanmar’s leaders have not been invited to high-level ASEAN meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.

Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to “hear Myanmar’s latest position” ahead of the summit.

“De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process,” he said.

“If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for ASEAN to consider at the leaders summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar’s participation in ASEAN meetings,” he added.

Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on November 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was “in the works”.

In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several ASEAN member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.

The following month Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations’ military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.

Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several ASEAN nations.

Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.

Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week’s cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar’s military blamed “terrorist insurgents”—the term it commonly uses to refer to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces—for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.

World.title: Myanmar’s NUG Warns US Against Prioritizing Its Interests Over Peace
World.content:
In response to the new U.S. Mission Strategy for war-torn Myanmar, the parallel civilian National Unity Government (NUG) and observers urged Washington to help solve the country’s political crisis first instead of prioritizing its own security and economic interests.

Speaking with The Irrawaddy, NUG Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister David Gum Awng said that if the U.S. had a genuine desire to see sustainable peace and economic development in the country, the root cause of the political crisis must be solved first.

“An approach that sidelines the core principles such as democracy, human rights and establishment of a federal union in favor of prioritizing its [own] security and economic interests is not sufficient and lacks the comprehensive scope needed to solve the Myanmar crisis,” he added.

The U.S. State Department recently published its latest strategy for Myanmar, prioritizing the fight against online scam networks that target Americans, increasing U.S. investment, and access to rare earth minerals. Additional objectives include expanding U.S. regional influence and brokering a peace agreement by 2030.

Recently, U.S. officials held talks with junta leaders in Naypyitaw and Tokyo, increasing Washington’s engagement with the internationally isolated coup regime that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Washington said in its latest statement that facilitating dialogue and supporting multi-stakeholder engagement would help lay the groundwork for lasting peace and national reconciliation.

However, Gum Awng argued that peace cannot be achieved simply by forcing stakeholders to sit together at a negotiating table, noting that the primary challenge is whether the regime is genuinely willing to give up its dictatorship and accept real change.

“Without the definitive end of the military dictatorship, the emergence of an inclusive political process involving all stakeholders (including ethnic groups), and the establishment of robust monitoring mechanisms to guarantee agreements, any hastily brokered peace driven by a specific timeline will only temporarily de-escalate the conflict without solving the underlying root problem.”

Regarding the U.S. goal of building regional influence, the NUG minister said Myanmar cannot be viewed solely as a proxy battleground for U.S.-China influence, adding that the sovereignty and the right to self-determination of the nation’s people remain paramount.

“If the U.S. wishes to build long-term, sustainable influence, engaging with the military council alone is insufficient. The U.S. must respect the democratic will of the Myanmar people, increase its engagement with federal democratic forces, and prove through practical actions that it is a reliable partner,” Gum Awng said.

“U.S. influence cannot be measured solely by its ability to counter China. It depends entirely on earning the trust of the Myanmar people and participating constructively in the building of a future federal democratic nation.”

Regarding U.S. efforts to gain access to rare earth minerals through its peace efforts, the NUG’s deputy foreign minister warned that the country’s resources cannot be treated merely as a component of a peace process or a political compromise, since they are directly tied to the long-term interests of the people, the rights of ethnic groups, and the resource management rights of the future federal union.

Regarding Washington’s move to boost engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative ASEAN Network on Burma, said a strategy based on appeasing the root cause of Myanmar’s notorious transnational crime hubs is doomed to fail. U.S. citizens, along with the people of Myanmar and the region, continue to suffer due to this irresponsible approach, she said.

“It is like engaging serial killers in order to persuade them to kill fewer people instead of acting to stop their crimes,” she said.

“It is both illogical and immoral to bribe [coup president] Min Aung Hlaing’s junta with trade and aid to secure rare earths while looking away from the security, economic and humanitarian crises he is intensifying every day.”

She also warned that the U.S. was in danger of falling into Min Aung Hlaing’s trap, in which he is able to pit Moscow, Beijing and Washington against each other to secure more weapons, more cash and more legitimacy without concrete solutions.

Regarding U.S. peace efforts, Myanmar political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said, “I don’t think it [a U.S.-brokered peace plan] will work. Myanmar’s political situation and its underlying problem cannot be resolved easily or quickly. Its peace plan is likely either a strategic miscalculation or merely a gesture to show the U.S. is interested in it.”

World.title: Kazakhstan, Tajikistan Expand Trade and Economic Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Tajikistan reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening strategic partnership and expanding economic ties during talks between Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon in Astana on Nov. 7, reported Akorda.

Welcoming the Tajik leader, Tokayev described his visit as a sign of the special respect and friendship between the two countries, emphasizing their close historical and cultural ties.

“The Kazakh people hold the Tajik people, an ancient nation with a rich history, distinctive culture and great spiritual heritage, in sincere respect and special affection. Under your wise, forward-looking leadership, Tajikistan is making impressive progress in many areas while steadily implementing large-scale reforms. The results are reflected in sustained economic growth and improved public welfare,” he said.

Tokayev highlighted growing trade ties, with annual bilateral trade consistently exceeding $1 billion. Kazakhstan remains one of Tajikistan’s three largest trading partners.

Tokayev said the two governments were working to implement existing agreements, expand the range of traded goods and increase freight transportation between the countries. He also noted growing business contacts and the implementation of agreements reached at business forums and trade missions.

He added that the two countries had agreed on additional measures to expand mutual trade and adopted a road map to increase trade turnover through 2030.

Rahmon, in turn, noted that cooperation between the two countries was developing dynamically across all key areas.

“Bilateral trade exceeded $1 billion in the first nine months of this year, up nearly 26% compared with the same period in 2025,” he said.

He added that the two countries had agreed to take additional measures to increase annual trade turnover to $2 billion.

“Investment cooperation is also expanding. More than 130 enterprises with Kazakh capital operate in Tajikistan, while Kazakhstan hosts more than 580 companies with Tajik participation, including 500 wholly owned by Tajik investors,” Rahmon said.

The two leaders also discussed cultural and humanitarian cooperation, including exchanges in education, science and youth policy.

Tokayev highlighted reciprocal Days of Culture and the unveiling of monuments honoring prominent historical figures, including a bust of Abai in Dushanbe and a monument to Ibn Sina in Astana.

The opening of the new Tajikistan Embassy complex in Astana was another highlight of Rahmon’s visit.

“This is more than a single building. It is an entire complex. It is impressive and demonstrates that Tajikistan will have a permanent and prominent presence in our country. This is a worthy reflection of our brotherly relations,” Tokayev said.

During the visit, Tokayev presented Rahmon with the newly established Order of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, recognizing his contributions to education, science, culture and international relations.

Tokayev noted that the award carried particular significance as Khoja Ahmed Yasawi’s legacy belongs not only to Kazakhstan but to the broader civilization and the peoples of Central Asia, which share centuries-old spiritual traditions.

“Our region has given the world a whole galaxy of outstanding thinkers, scientists, poets and educators, whose legacy has gone far beyond the borders of individual countries and peoples. One of the most prominent figures of the Islamic Renaissance was Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. His name holds special significance for the Kazakh people and occupies a sacred place in our historical memory,” Tokayev said.

World.title: US, Chevron Extend Initiative Bringing STEAM Education to Kazakh Youth
World.content:
ASTANA – More than 54,000 young people in Kazakhstan have benefited from a U.S.-Chevron initiative offering free access to STEAM education, as the partners extended their Makerspace program for another three years on Nov. 5.

Launched in 2020, the initiative promotes practical learning in science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM) through a network of free laboratories established at American Corners across Kazakhstan. The facilities provide spaces for creativity, experimentation and technology-based learning.

The network currently operates in seven cities, including Astana, Almaty, Aktobe, Uralsk, Oskemen, Pavlodar and Petropavlovsk. Since its launch, it has hosted nearly 2,300 workshops and training courses.

U.S. Ambassador to Kazakhstan Julie M. Stufft and Chevron Eurasia President Derek Magness signed an updated memorandum of understanding, securing the program’s continuation through the next three years.

“In our Makerspaces, Kazakh youth build robots, design 3D models, and explore Super Intelligence,” Stufft said.

“These tremendously talented young people tell us that they gain creativity, teamwork, and confidence through these U.S. programs. By renewing our partnership with Chevron for three more years, the United States is proud to build the next generation of talented Kazakh engineers and scholars,” she added.

Magness highlighted the importance of providing young people with opportunities to explore technology and develop new skills.

“We are pleased to continue this partnership and help create more opportunities for young people across Kazakhstan to explore technology, learn new skills and bring their ideas to life. We look forward to seeing where their curiosity and creativity take them,” he said.

The Makerspaces are open to school and university students, as well as young professionals. Equipped with advanced tools and technology, they offer free courses led by experienced instructors in robotics, artificial intelligence, 3D modeling, programming, rocketry and creative arts.

Through these activities, the initiative helps young people develop critical thinking, teamwork and practical skills that can support their future careers and contribute to Kazakhstan’s innovation-driven economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Autumn Skies Come Alive with Migrating Birds
World.content:
ASTANA – Autumn brings one of nature’s most remarkable seasonal events to Kazakhstan, as migratory birds cross the country on their way to warmer wintering grounds. Its diverse landscapes serve as an important corridor for numerous species, including rare birds listed in Kazakhstan’s Red Book.

Whooper swans fly over Katon-Karagai National Park

In East Kazakhstan, flocks of whooper swans have been spotted flying over Katon-Karagai National Park, adding to the region’s autumn scenery, reported the Forestry and Wildlife Committee of the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources on Nov.3.

Kazakhstan is an important stopover along the migration route of northern whooper swan populations. After raising their young in wetlands across western and eastern Siberia, the birds head toward Central and South Asia as winter approaches.

The committee has also highlighted the swans’ distinctive behavior, which has inspired legends for centuries. The birds form strong pairs that can remain together for many years and often for life, although they may find new mates after losing a partner.

“Whooper swans are indeed monogamous. They form strong pairs that can last for many years and often for life. However, after a period of loss, a swan can eventually find a new mate. This is a natural part of life in the harsh conditions of the wild,” the committee said.

Experts encourage residents and visitors to look up while walking through the region’s mountain valleys. The flocks’ distinctive trumpet-like calls can be heard until the lakes and rivers freeze over.

Young steppe eagle begins its first migration

While the swans follow established seasonal routes, researchers are also tracking the first migration of a young steppe eagle named Tungysh, whose journey offers a closer look at how individual birds navigate the region.

Born in Altyn-Emel National Park, Tungysh was still a nestling earlier this summer. On July 20, park staff and specialists from the Institute of Zoology fitted the young eagle with a solar-powered GPS tracker to monitor its movements.

“Now it has begun its migration. Alone, without its parents, without a map, for the first time in its life,” the national park said.

The eagle’s route has taken it through Altyn-Emel, Konayev, Almaty, Bishkek, Taraz, Shymkent and Samarkand.

According to the latest GPS data, Tungysh is now in Uzbekistan’s Kashkadarya Region, near Karshi. The bird has traveled around 1,400 kilometers since beginning its journey.

Tracking the eagle’s movements also has scientific value. The steppe eagle is listed in Kazakhstan’s Red Book, and GPS monitoring helps specialists study migration routes, identify stopover sites and determine where the birds may face threats.

Young black vulture reaches the Kyrgyz Republic

Tungysh is not the only young bird whose journey is being followed by researchers. A young black vulture named Emel has also begun exploring new territory, recently crossing into the Kyrgyz Republic as part of a satellite-tracking project called Emel’s Diary.

Emel’s story began in July 2026, when staff at Altyn-Emel National Park discovered a black vulture chick. The species typically nests on high cliffs and raises only one chick a year, making each young bird that survives to independent flight important for the population.

To monitor the chick’s development and activity at the nest, specialists installed a camera trap. It recorded the parents bringing food and the chick growing. Researchers later fitted Emel with a satellite tracker, allowing them to follow its movements after it left the nest.

In October, experts reported that Emel had begun flying independently and gradually exploring the surrounding area. Satellite data showed that the bird had traveled around Basshi and Aktobe, the Kapchagai Reservoir area and the Ili River valley.

With each flight, the young vulture is exploring more distant territory. Scientists say it may continue south through Central Asia and could eventually reach India.

Satellite monitoring allows specialists to track Emel’s route and study the species’ migration patterns. The Kyrgyz Republic is the latest stop on the bird’s journey, while its next destination remains uncertain.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s AI Ambitions, Football, Global Trade and Water Challenges
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest explores the country’s ambitions to become a regional artificial intelligence hub, Kairat Almaty’s draw against Italian club Atalanta, expanding freight connections with Mexico, plans to attract investment into data center infrastructure, and the challenges of balancing industrial development with water resources.

Kazakhstan seeks to turn energy resources into AI exports

Kazakhstan could emerge as a major artificial intelligence and computing hub connecting Europe and Asia, but its long-term success will depend on its ability to develop domestic technologies rather than simply host foreign infrastructure, reported Global Banking & Finance Review on Nov. 2.

The article examined the country’s digital development and growing partnerships with international technology companies, following NVIDIA co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan. During a public discussion in Astana, Huang described the country as “a future computing center and artificial intelligence factory for all of Europe.”

The report also examined the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, which is expected to begin commercial operations in the third quarter of 2027.

Kairat Almaty holds Atalanta to draw in European competition

Kazakhstan’s Kairat Almaty secured a 1-1 draw against Italian club Atalanta in Bergamo on Nov. 5, earning a valuable point against the 2024 Europa League winners, reported The Times of Central Asia on Nov. 6.

Spanish forward Marc Gual gave Kairat the lead in the 53rd minute after an attack created by Brazilian teammate Edmilson. Atalanta equalised in the 82nd minute through substitute Nikola Krstović, preventing a home defeat.

The result came during a period of change for the Almaty club. Head coach Rafael Urazbakhtin resigned on Oct. 26 after Kairat finished second in Kazakhstan’s 2026 Premier League, three points behind champions Ordabasy Shymkent. Interim manager Zhora Arutyunyan took charge of the team.

Kazakhstan expands freight connections to Mexico through Caspian route

Kazakhstan’s national railway operator is expanding its international freight network, with its freight forwarding subsidiary KTZ Express organising a container shipment from Almaty to the Mexican port of Veracruz, reported RailFreight.

The route combines rail and maritime transport. Containers are transported from Almaty to Georgia’s port of Poti, crossing the Caspian Sea and passing through Azerbaijan’s Port of Alat. From Poti, Danish shipping company Maersk carries the cargo across the sea to Veracruz.

Kazakhstan attracts investment for second phase of Data Center Valley

Kazakhstan has reached preliminary agreements with international companies to develop up to 620 megawatts of additional computing capacity as part of the second phase of its Data Center Valley project in the Pavlodar Region, reported Trend news agency on Nov. 6.

According to the report, preliminary agreements with Gaw Capital, Boosteroid and Firebird cover 480 megawatts, with the potential to increase capacity to 620 megawatts. The project was discussed at a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, where officials reviewed construction progress and plans to attract further investment.

Kazakhstan’s industrial ambitions raise questions over water resources

Kazakhstan’s plans to expand mineral processing and other water-intensive industries will require careful assessment of their impact on regional water supplies, particularly in areas already facing irrigation constraints, wrote Zamirbek Minbayev in an opinion article for The Times of Central Asia.

The article examined the Shalkiya lead-zinc mine in the Kyzylorda Region, where a planned processing plant could handle four million metric tons of ore annually. The facility would require a substantial water supply, with a pumping station designed to circulate up to 2,400 cubic meters of water per hour. However, the plant would still need additional fresh water, raising questions about its impact on local agriculture.

Minbayev noted that Kazakhstan has been seeking to increase domestic mineral processing to retain more skilled jobs and export earnings. However, he stressed that industrial projects must account for the availability of water before construction begins.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UNODC Discuss Stronger Cooperation Against Transnational Crime
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) have discussed expanding cooperation to combat cybercrime, drug trafficking, corruption and transnational organized crime during a meeting in Astana on Nov. 6.

First Deputy Foreign Minister of Kazakhstan Erzhan Ashikbayev met with UNODC Regional Representative for Afghanistan, Central Asia, Iran and Pakistan Oliver Stolpe to review bilateral cooperation and identify priorities for further engagement.

The sides highlighted the role of the Central Asian Regional Information and Coordination Centre (CARICC) as a specialized regional platform for combating transnational drug crime.

They also discussed the implementation of the UNODC Program for Central Asia for 2022-2027 and supported preparations for a new regional programme for the next cycle. Both sides reaffirmed their interest in strengthening the partnership through joint initiatives and projects in priority areas of cooperation.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Hold Biennial Symposia on Al-Farabi and Yasawi Heritage, Vice President Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will hold an international symposium dedicated to the intellectual heritage of medieval philosopher Abu Nasr Al-Farabi (870-950) and theologian Khoja Ahmed Yasawi (1094-1166) on a rotating basis every two years, Vice President Erlan Karin announced at an international symposium in Almaty on Nov. 6.

The symposium is dedicated to Al-Farabi’s philosophical and scientific legacy and is being held at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed making such gatherings a regular event.

At the opening ceremony, Karin read out a welcoming address from Tokayev, who emphasized the importance of studying and promoting the ideas of great thinkers among younger generations and examining their relevance to contemporary science.

“Al-Farabi promoted enduring universal values and left behind a unique legacy. His teachings on the prudent individual and virtuous society will never lose their relevance,” Tokayev said in his address.

Speaking at the symposium, Karin said the philosopher’s ideas were particularly relevant in an era of globalization and technological progress. He also highlighted the intellectual contributions of Al-Farabi, Khoja Ahmed Yasawi and Abai, saying their legacy remains important for academic research and strengthening society’s moral foundations.

Karin said the symposia would alternate between Turkistan and Almaty, with each city hosting an event every four years.

“This means that the study of our strategic and spiritual heritage is moving to a systematic and institutional level,” he said, adding that Kazakhstan had embarked on a comprehensive effort to study and promote its historical and spiritual legacy.

Participants discussed Al-Farabi’s philosophical teachings in the context of global humanitarian dialogue and the promotion of universal values. More than 150 Kazakh and international scholars, researchers, experts and representatives of leading international organizations attended the event.

Kazakhstan discusses cultural cooperation with ICESCO

On the sidelines of the symposium, Karin met with Salim AlMalik, director-general of the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO), to discuss cooperation on cultural heritage, education and scientific research.

Karin highlighted Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which identifies the development of human capital, education, science and innovation as strategic priorities.

He also conveyed Tokayev’s appreciation for ICESCO’s support in promoting Al-Farabi’s legacy internationally and its decision to designate Turkistan as the Cultural Capital of the Islamic World for 2027.

The two sides discussed preparations for joint cultural events in Turkistan, as well as research and initiatives to promote the heritage of Al-Farabi and Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. They also considered including 10 new Kazakh nominations in the ICESCO Islamic World Heritage List and expanding joint scientific and educational programmes.

Karin outlined Kazakhstan’s priorities for cooperation with ICESCO within the framework of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions. These include promoting Tokayev’s initiative to establish a Global Movement for Peace and implementing documents adopted at the Congress’s 24th Secretariat meeting.

The meeting also covered ICESCO’s participation in preparations for the 25th Secretariat meeting in 2027 and the ninth Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions in 2028.

World.content:
ASTANA – Enjoy the weekend with a mix of ballet, theater, exhibitions and live music. From classical performances to familiar film soundtracks, The Astana Times editorial team has curated a list of events you can attend with friends and family.

Astana

“Carmen Suite and Arcana of Fate” ballet, Nov. 7

Venue: National Museum of Kazakhstan; Tickets are available here.

Popular hits from the 2000s return in new arrangements performed by a symphony orchestra and choir. The programme brings together familiar songs and energetic performances, turning the evening into a musical journey through the biggest pop hits of the decade.
