World.title: Azerbaijani gymnast wins silver medal at World Championships (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 7. The Azerbaijani national team has claimed another medal at the World Trampoline and Tumbling Championships being held in Nanjing, China.

According to the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation, national team member Tofiq Aliyev, who competed in the individual tumbling event, delivered a successful performance in the final, scoring 29.700 points to win the silver medal at the World Championships.

This achievement is particularly significant in Tofiq Aliyev's career, as the Azerbaijani gymnast has won a World Championship silver medal in the individual event for the first time.

In a fiercely contested final, Portugal's Vasco Peso won the gold medal, while the United States' Kaden Brown finished third.

Thus, Azerbaijan's representatives have concluded their participation in the tumbling events at the World Championships.

World.title: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan congratulates President Ilham Aliyev on occasion of Victory Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 7. President of the Republic of Türkiye, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sent a congratulatory letter to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear President, Dear Brother,

On behalf of my nation and on my own behalf, I extend my most sincere congratulations to Your Excellency and all my Azerbaijani brothers and sisters on the sixth anniversary of Victory Day, which marked the liberation of ancient Azerbaijani lands that had been under occupation for thirty years.

Azerbaijan’s just struggle, crowned with the Great Victory, has also become a source of pride for the entire Turkic world. The rapid progress in the reconstruction and revival of the liberated territories fills us all with pride.

Drawing strength from our unwavering bonds of friendship and brotherhood, founded on the principle of “One nation, two states” and elevated to the highest level through the Shusha Declaration, I am fully confident that we will continue to work in close cooperation and solidarity, both in our bilateral relations and in the international arena.

Thanks to our coordinated efforts to establish lasting peace, tranquility and stability in our region, the South Caucasus is no longer seen as a zone of conflict and instability, but rather as a region of cooperation and development.

I pray for God’s mercy upon our heroic martyrs who sacrificed their lives in the struggle for their Motherland’s independence. I honor their cherished memory with deep respect and reverence and express my gratitude to our veterans.

My dear brother, I take this opportunity to extend my warmest wishes for your robust health and happiness, and to wish the brotherly people of Azerbaijan a prosperous and peaceful future," the letter reads.

World.title: Iran now exports military equipment to numerous countries – IRGC spokesman
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 7. Iran is now exporting a wide range of domestically manufactured weapons, ammunition, and military equipment to numerous countries, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said.

According to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), he made the remarks at a press conference in Tehran on Saturday, November 7.

"Various military aerial systems are currently being exported to several countries. These include the Arman missile, the 357 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), and the 3rd Khordad air defense system. This is considered a historic achievement for Iran. The country has traditionally been an importer of military weapons and equipment. However, it is now meeting its domestic needs and has also become an exporter," he said.

The IRGC official noted that over the past one to two weeks, Iran had captured seven US MQM-170 UAVs without damaging them, describing this as evidence of the technical capabilities of the Iranian Armed Forces.

Mohebbi added that the IRGC Aerospace Force would unveil new achievements and surprise the world if Iran came under another attack.

"During the 12-day war last year and the 40-day war this year, the IRGC Aerospace Force shot down more than 260 military aircraft belonging to the opposing side. These included F-35, F-16, F-5, and F-8 fighter jets, as well as MQ-1, RQ-4, Orbiter, Lucas, and numerous other smaller aerial vehicles," he said.

The latest escalation in US-Iran relations began on July 8. On that day, the US Armed Forces launched several waves of strikes on Iranian territory for the first time since the memorandum was signed between Washington and Tehran, citing a response to an attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

That same day, US President Donald Trump announced the termination of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began striking US facilities in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, and Oman.

The conflict has brought maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz to a standstill.

World.title: Iran stresses need to prevent further escalation – Araghchi
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 7. Iran emphasizes the need to prevent further escalation by respecting countries' sovereignty, recognizing the importance of regional countries, avoiding foreign interference, and ending aggression and threats.

Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi made the remarks in a post on his Instagram account.

He added that over the past 48 hours, he had held separate phone conversations with his counterparts from 12 countries in the region, during which they exchanged views on recent regional and international developments and the consequences of actions by the US and Israel.

"During the phone conversations, we stressed Iran's legitimate right to defend its sovereignty and security, as well as the importance of establishing regional security arrangements without interference from powers outside the region," he said.

The latest escalation in US-Iran relations began on July 8. On that day, the US Armed Forces launched several waves of strikes on Iranian territory for the first time since the memorandum was signed between Washington and Tehran, citing a response to an attack on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.

That same day, US President Donald Trump announced the termination of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began striking US facilities in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE, and Oman.

The conflict has brought maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz to a standstill.

World.title: Cross-code star scores hat-trick as Kiwi Ferns make another final
World.content:
New Zealand cross-code superstar Stacey Waaka has led her country to another women's Rugby League World Cup final, scoring three tries in a dominant win over Fetu Samoa.

The Kiwi Ferns had made the final in all six previous editions of the women's world championship, but faced a stern early test from Fetu Samoa in their maiden semifinal.

But three tries to Waaka, and poor execution from the Samoans, ensured New Zealand would make it to a seventh consecutive decider.

Waaka, who won two Olympic gold medals in rugby 7s and two women's Rugby Union World Cups with New Zealand, continued her brilliant tournament where she has already scored six tries.

"A really close first half, but the team who was going to win was the one who played right to the end, then I think we done that," Waaka told the 7 Network post-match

"I love playing games with these young guns. It's fun learning off them too, because they've been in the game a little bit longer, but I'm just enjoying the whole experience.

"I can't wait for this next week and bring on whoever is in the final with us."

New Zealand will face either Australia or Fiji, who play the second semifinal in Sydney on Sunday.

In their maiden semifinal, Fetu Samoa suffered a horrible start with hooker Mary-Jane Taito throwing a forward pass in the first set of the match.

The Kiwi Ferns punished them immediately, with winger Mackenzie Wiki crossing in the right corner to claim an early lead after two minutes.

Fetus Samoa got themselves back into the contest with firm defence, as handling errors cruelled both sides. The Kiwi Ferns had nine errors and Samoa had seven, highlighting the tension of a semifinal.

Samoa's best chance of the first half came midway through the 35 minutes when they had four consecutive sets at the Kiwi Ferns' goal-line. But the first-time semifinalists failed to score, and would not come close again before half-time.

As the wind picked up and dark clouds closed in on Hunter Stadium, New Zealand scored a second try when Stacey Waaka charged onto a kick that was allowed to bounce by the Samoans to ensure her nation had an 8-0 lead.

Otesa Pule of New Zealand is tackled during the 2026 Women's Rugby League World Cup Semi Final match between New Zealand Kiwi Ferns and Samoa at Hunters Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Newcastle, Australia. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

As Fetu Samoa's errors continued, the Kiwi Ferns were able to punish them and take away any confidence the Pacific Island nation had.

Another kick to the in-goal was caught by a flying Waaka in the 44th minute for her second try, extending the lead to 14 points.

The Kiwis continued to press and iced the match with a three-try burst in six minutes to Mele Hufanga (58th minute), Kaiyah Atai (60th minute) and Waaka (64th minute).

Kiwi Ferns captain Raecene McGregor scored three minutes from time to cap off a well-earned win.

World.title: Man arrested and charged for alleged harassment of SA Speaker
World.content:
South Australian Police have arrested a man for alleged online harassment of a member of parliament, understood to be Speaker of the South Australian House of Assembly, Nat Cook.

In a statement, police said they attended a 33-year-old man's home in Reynella East on Friday, where he was arrested and charged with stalking and harassment.

They will allege the man breached a caution issued to him earlier this year by posting "numerous times on social media about the person".

He has been bailed to appear in Christies Beach Magistrates Court on December 7.

The man is understood to be Luke Poulton, a southern suburbs activist, who shared time-stamped CCTV footage of an arrest at his property to Facebook and Instagram pages he operates.

In his Facebook post, Mr Poulton was critical of the police's handling of his arrest and wrote the material prompting his arrest related to "3 facebook posts including a video montage showing people involved in bullying myself and my family".

He also wrote: "Australian Labor Party are really turning it on with the Helen Haines incident," referring to the recent attack on the federal Indi MP in Wangaratta.

Mr Poulton declined to respond to a request for comment, or permit ABC News to share the footage of his arrest.

World.title: Man, 75, dies in Goldfields mine incident
World.content:
A 75-year-old man has died following a workplace incident at a mine site in Western Australia's Goldfields.

The incident happened at Regis Resources' Duketon South operation, about 130 kilometres north of Laverton and more than 700km from Perth.

Emergency services were called to the mining camp at Bandya about 12:30pm on Friday, November 6, where mine site medical staff provided first aid before they arrived.

The man could not be revived.

Regis Resources confirmed the man was a member of its contract team and was carrying out work at the Duketon South operation when the incident occurred.

Regis Resources says operations at Duketon have been stood down while investigations continue.

WorkSafe is investigating the death, with investigators and inspectors making arrangements to attend the scene as soon as practicable.

WA Police will also prepare a report for the Coroner.

WorkSafe Commissioner Sally North has extended her condolences to the man’s family, friends and colleagues.

Regis Resources says it is providing support to those affected by the incident, with employee assistance programs activated.

World.title: PM Luxon says 'National is once again the largest party in parliament'
World.content:
New Zealanders have finished casting their ballots this election. (AP: Alex Robertson)

Voting has closed in New Zealand's election and we will soon see results trickling in.

In an election campaign overshadowed by cost of living pressures and an economy buffeted by international shocks, the National Party has been making its case to stay in government and Labour has tried to prise back votes it needs to regain office.

But experts say both parties ran negative campaigns.

"I'm not sure anyone has much enjoyed it," Richard Shaw, a professor of politics at Massey University, told the ABC.

"The policy contest which marked the opening stanzas has largely fallen away into an acrimonious exchange between the left and the right about how to game the electoral system through strategic voting."

National and Labour focused on criticising not just their rival parties but also the people involved, with Labour trying to seize on the unpopularity of Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and National seeking to exploit similar sentiment about Labour's Chris Hipkins, said Tom Jamieson, a senior lecturer in political science at Victoria University of Wellington.

"For a party leading the incumbent government, National ran less on their record than you might have expected on their record and more about what their opponents were likely to do in power."

On the other hand, smaller parties including New Zealand First, ACT, the Green Party, Te Pāti Māori and the Opportunity party focused their efforts on policy initiatives and their vision for the country, Dr Jamieson said.

"In an electorate with a plurality that has consistently indicated they are on the wrong track, it could be that these parties benefit from dissatisfaction with the direction of the government," he said.

Polls have indicated it could be a tight election.

Results released tonight will indicate the election outcome and are expected to arrive over several hours. The official count begins tomorrow, and the Electoral Commission is aiming to release the official results by November 27.

Professor Shaw expected it would be a long three weeks and said special votes — which take longer to count — may be consequential.

"We may have a clear result tonight, but that seems unlikely," he said.

World.title: Ponga leads Kiwis to final after pre-match stare down lights up World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga has returned to the field 23 days after breaking his arm to lead New Zealand to its first Rugby League World Cup final since 2013.

Ponga, who suffered the broken arm in the tournament's opening match against Australia, had three try assists and a try-saving tackle to inspire the Kiwis to a 34-10 win.

But the highlight of the contest came before the opening whistle, when both sets of players engaged in one of the great moments in rugby league.

After New Zealand performed its Haka, in reply to the Sipi Tau from Tonga, the two sides stared each other down as time stood still.

A packed house at Hunter Stadium in Newcastle got louder as the stare-down lengthened, a precursor to the historic semifinal that was to come.

Kiwi centre Casey McLean, who scored a crucial second-half try for his country, told ABC Sport the pre-match stare-down was a special moment that had him ready to give everything for his teammates on Saturday.

"We have such mana boys in our team that are leaders," he said.

"We've just got to follow them, especially myself.

New Zealand defeat Fetu Samoa New Zealand cross-code superstar Stacey Waaka leads her country to another women's Rugby League World Cup final, scoring three tries in a dominant win over Fetu Samoa.

"I can learn so much off them, not just about being a player, but [also] my culture. They're front runners for Māori boys and Kiwi boys."

Ponga's impact on the match was immediate, setting up back-rower Briton Nikora for the opening try in the third minute.

New Zealand dominated the opening quarter, before Tonga winger Jojo Fifita made a line break from his own goal-line, setting up a break down the left wing by Tolutau Koula, who then threw it back to Fifita for the length-of-the-field try.

The belief in the Tongan camp grew, and they looked destined to score again when forward Demitric Vaimauga was clear and only had the much smaller Ponga to beat.

But Ponga produced a stunning try-saving tackle, one-on-one, to stop the much larger man.

"It just shows how much this Kiwi jersey means to him," McLean said.

"To be able to put on a performance like that, it just shows how much of an amazing person he is."

Just one minute later, Fifita was in for a second to give Tonga the lead off a perfectly executed scrum play.

But a mistake from fullback Lehi Hopoate allowed Kiwi Dane Gagai to score and give the Kiwis a 12-10 half-time lead.

Down by just two points, Tonga had every reason to believe they could advance to the World Cup final for the first time.

But a significant change in weather at half-time meant they played into a howling headwind for the second 40 minutes.

Hopoate was peppered with high kicks he could not reach as the wind made predicting the landing near impossible, while halfback Isaiya Katoa struggled to kick the ball much further than 30 metres at the end of sets.

It meant the Kiwis were able to camp themselves in the Tongan half of the field for the entire second half, wearing them down and scoring four tries to seal a 24-point win.

"No excuses, you've got to take your hats off to the Kiwis," Katoa said.

"The way they played footy tonight is the way you play in these conditions."

New Zealand will face either Australia or Samoa in next Sunday's final at Lang Park in Brisbane.

Relive all the action from Saturday's Rugby League World Cup semifinals in the blog below.

World.title: Supercars, SUVs take to Perth suburb to support teen assault victim
World.content:
Revving their Ferraris and family cars, dozens of Ellenbrook residents have rallied behind a 13-year-old boy who was allegedly bashed and threatened with a knife by a group of teenagers in the north-east Perth area.

More than 100 cars and 25 motorbikes took part in the "community cruise" motorcade, which started with a gathering at Coolamon Park late yesterday, followed by a drive down to a nearby retail outlet.

The rally began at the local park. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

The rally comes as a 14-year-old boy was charged over the group attack, which was filmed and shared on social media.

Police today said another five teenagers - aged between 13 and 17 - were also charged with causing bodily harm, and with aggravated armed robbery in relation to the attack. Investigations are continuing.

Teen charged over alleged attack of boy A 14-year-old boy appears in court charged over an alleged attack on a 13-year-old boy which was filmed and shared on social media.

Cars for community

A graphic video shared on social media shows a group following a teenager asking, "where's the vape?" before the alleged victim is pushed to the ground.

The Perth Children's Court heard the boy was then allegedly dragged along the ground, punched and kicked and forced to say "derogatory things", before his t-shirt and jumper were stolen.

The victim was allegedly punched, kicked and threatened with a knife. (Supplied)

He was able to walk home and later went to Midland Hospital with a concussion, multiple lumps on his head, black eyes and bruising to his upper and lower body.

Local resident Terry Mason organised the motorcade after hearing about the attack.

He said the news hit home after finding out his nephew had allegedly been harassed in the area.

Local Terry Mason (right) organised the rally. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"I've dealt with the same situation when I was the same age, and it's inappropriate. It's disgusting.

"And then to see a young man out there with a knife, too, it's unacceptable," he said.

After organising the car meet in only 12 hours, Mr Mason said he was proud of how quickly the community rallied behind the alleged victim and his family.

The motorcade was held in Ellenbrook to show support for the teenage victim and his family. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"I'm part of the car community here and I know how fast we can put things together and how much family means to us," he said.

Local MP Tania Lawrence said the car meet was the community's quirky way of coming together.

Tania Lawrence says the rally was the community's "bit unique" way of showing support. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"What Ellenbrook has chosen is a little bit unique but absolutely resonates by having a car and bike rally to demonstrate just how many people do care," she said.

"We want to make sure that those people affected understand that we have their back, that we absolutely do support them, we're with them, and we will not allow community to be anything but loving and supportive."

World.title: Demons rally and Kangaroos cruise into AFLW prelims
World.content:
Melbourne has stormed home with the last five goals of the game to beat Geelong by four points in their AFLW qualifying final.

After Demons star Paxy Paxman put them in front with a snapped goal, Chloe Scheer marked and had a shot at goal for Geelong with 20 seconds left.

But the Geelong forward missed and the Demons won 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52) on Saturday at Princes Park.

In the later game, North Melbourne booked its prelim ticket with a commanding 7.7 (49) to 1.7 (13) win over Carlton.

Melbourne kicked the only three goals of the last quarter after looking well out of the game in the third term.

Geelong onballer Georgia Prespakis was easily best afield in the first half, but Melbourne midfielder Liv Purcell helped spark the comeback and they had 34 possessions apiece.

It was the first time Geelong's Mick Stinear has gone up against his old club since the 2022 premiership coach left Melbourne at the end of last season.

Melbourne now has the week off, while Geelong's semi-final opponent will be the winner of Sunday's Sydney-Western Bulldogs elimination final.

The threat of lightning delayed the start of the game on Saturday by 10 minutes, but Melbourne's changeable spring weather meant much of the game was played in sunshine.

The Cats kicked clear in the second term, with four goals to one and led by 22 points at the main break. They twice led by 28 in the third quarter, before the Demons hit back.

With Purcell and 100-gamer Tyla Hanks leading the way, the Demons kicked four goals to three and cut the margin to 12 points at the last change.

Alyssa Bannan's accurate snap in the first 30 seconds of the final quarter brought the Demons to within a goal. Prespakis kicked a behind, then Bannan kicked her second.

Paxman put Melbourne in front for the first time since the first quarter with her goal at 17 minutes.

Injury concern in big Roos win

Two-time North Melbourne premiership player Alice O'Loughlin is a significant casualty out of the Kangaroos' comprehensive AFLW qualifying final win.

O'Loughlin was emotional on the bench after she hurt her knee in the last quarter of Saturday's 36-point win over Carlton at Ikon Park.

She was in agony and needed two trainers to help her off the field after Gab Pound caught her in a tackle.

It was the one negative for the two-time defending premiers, who withstood a game challenge from the Blues in the first quarter.

The usual suspects starred for the Kangaroos — Jasmine Garner racked up 31 possessions, and fellow midfielder Ash Riddell had a game-high 33.

Key defender Harriet Cordner was mighty for Carlton, especially early, but eventually there was little she could do when the dam wall broke.

Carlton will next host the winner of Sunday's elimination final between Gold Coast and Hawthorn.

World.title: Tasmanian nurses rally following 'disappointing' government pay offer
World.content:
Nurses and midwives have stepped up a pay dispute with the Tasmanian government, walking off the job at two southern hospitals today.

The Royal Hobart Hospital and the Repatriation Centre in Hobart were affected by the stop work action, as members from the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (ANMF) and the Health and Community Services Union rallied to protest against a state government pay offer.

The offer, which is the first the government has made, consists of a 3 per cent pay rise for the first year of the new agreement, followed by 2.75 per cent and 2.5 per cent in the subsequent years.

Addressing rising violence and aggression has been a major issue for staff during the bargaining period.

Will Lincoln spoke about escalating violence against nurses. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Nurse Will Lincoln, who works in Mental Health Services, told the crowd of hundreds that health care workers had reported being "punched, kicked, spat on, verbally abused, threatened and intimidated".

"Every nurse and midwife should be able to come to work knowing they will be safe — yet for far too many of us, that basic expectation is not being met," Mr Lincoln said.

"We are not simply asking for acknowledgement that violence and aggression exist, we are asking for meaningful measures that provide protection, support and recovery."

Nurses were offered an 8.25 per cent pay rise over three years. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The current bargaining agreement for nurses and midwives expired in June.

A spokesperson told the ABC the government was "committed to delivering" a pay rise and improved conditions.

⁠"An offer has been made and we are working constructively with unions on the next steps," they said.

The current enterprise bargaining agreement expired in June. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Union 'disappointed' by lack of action on priorities

When announcing the offer last week, Premier Jeremy Rockliff said:

"We have worked collaboratively to address a number of issues raised through the unions' logs of claims."

ANMF state secretary Emily Shepherd welcomed "positives" in the offer, which included new pay allowances for some staff.

Emily Shepherd says nurses were disappointed by the government's offer. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

However, Ms Shepherd said members had been left "disappointed", saying several "priority matters" were either not included or needed improvement.

She said members were shocked that extra "personal impact" leave days were only applicable to those in mental health, the emergency department and intensive care unit.

"No matter where nurses and midwives work, they are subjected to distressing and traumatic situations," Ms Shepherd said.

"Midwives face supporting mothers as they deliver stillborn babies in the maternity setting, medical oncology members support those receiving treatment for cancers — treatment which can at times make patients incredibly sick," she said.

"And nurses in schools are engaging with students, receiving disclosures of abuse while also facing aggression and violence."

Nurses want more "personal impact" leave days to deal with the trauma they regularly face. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

'Community pays the price' for understaffing

Speakers at the rally told the crowd the government's offer was under inflation, and would not be enough to tackle understaffing.

James Lloyd, an after-hours nurse manager at the Royal Hobart Hospital and branch president of the ANMF Tasmania, said workers were suffering from "fatigue, stress and burnout".

" On some of those early shifts it's not uncommon for me to see 20 plus gaps across the whole hospital with only three or four casual staff available to fill them. "

James Lloyd says the community pays the price for hospital understaffing. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

He also claimed it was also contributing to bed block, saying, "ultimately the Tasmanian community pays the price".

Nurse Audrey McAllister received a loud response from the crowd when she asked who had experienced the ordeal of a double shift, which can mean workers clock in for 16 to 20 hours.

Audrey McAllister says double shifts due to understaffing mean nurses are working while exhausted. (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

Ms McAllister spoke about research which has found being awake for upwards of 17 hours can cause the same level of impairment as a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05 per cent.

"We're not allowed to drive home with this state of impairment, but somehow we're allowed to give someone a blood transfusion. We're allowed to give someone chemotherapy," she said.

Ms McAllister has previously spoken publicly of being chased by a group of men at night, when walking to her car after a shift at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

World.title: Why doubling a recipe isn’t always a simple matter of maths
World.content:
Tips & adviceKnow how Why doubling a recipe isn’t always a simple matter of maths Scaling a recipe up or down is often more complicated than just increasing or decreasing the ingredients and cook time. Eden Faithfull November 8, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It seems simple enough: if the head count at your next dinner party doubles, the ingredients for your dinner do the same. Conversely, if you’re looking to scale down the size of your favourite cake for a late-night treat, you should be able to simply halve the recipe. Unfortunately, it’s not quite that simple. You’ll probably end up with bland curry and sunken cakes if you don’t account for a few things first. It’s easy to look at a recipe as a set of ratios you can multiply or divide at will. But recipe developers have to account for the physical and chemical processes that ingredients go through when you combine and cook them, and many of those processes don’t scale in lockstep with your shopping list. Sometimes, making two batches of a recipe and serving them together is the safest way to ensure that you’re not walking into the pitfalls that inadequately scaling your recipe can present. But if you must scale a dish, whether up or down, here are five scenarios where you might run into trouble. Adam Liaw’s Lancashire hot pot. Steve Brown; STYLING Emma Knowles



Braising The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up If you want to double the quantity of your favourite dinner party stew, you’ll end up with twice the volume of ingredients (great!) and the same pot you started with (not so great). Evaporation is a function of surface area, not volume, and your surface area hasn’t budged — so in the hour the recipe allots, you’ll drive off the same amount of liquid you would have before. Against twice the volume, that’s only half the reduction you need. Halving your ingredients presents the same issue but in reverse. The surface area remains the same, but there’s only half as much liquid to lose. The same hour’s evaporation leads to scorched meat and a dry pot. Related Recipe collection 10 classic one-pots every cook should have in their repertoire The safest fix is to adjust your cooking vessel. If you can’t do that, here’s a good rule of thumb: Instead of directly doubling the entire recipe, use about 1½ times the liquid ingredients, and double the rest. If you’re halving the recipe, use about 60 per cent of the liquid and half of the rest of the ingredients.



This all matters most for braises you finish uncovered, or ones that you reduce at the end of cooking. If your pot stays lidded in the oven, evaporation is admittedly a much smaller factor. But you’re not out of the woods yet. Even when evaporation isn’t a factor, you still have to adjust the clock when scaling a recipe. A much larger volume of food is going to take considerably longer to finish cooking, and vice versa with a smaller volume. Katrina Meynink’s grain salad with corn, chickpeas and avocado with chipotle lime dressing. KatrinaÂ Meynink Grains and (some) beans While cooking, rice absorbs a fixed amount of water — but the amount of water called for in a recipe doesn’t just account for what the grain absorbs. Part of it is to account for what escapes as steam, which depends on the surface area available and the time it takes to cook, so it doesn’t change when you double the rice. Double both quantities, and you’ve doubled the water allowance for steam that should have stayed put. Related Recipe collection 25 interesting and filling grain- and rice-based salad recipes



So, when scaling a recipe for grains (or beans that cook using the absorption method), adjust the absorption and leave the allowance alone. A safe bet is to figure about 1¼ cups of water per 1 cup of rice, then add about ¼ cup for what steams off, no matter how much rice is in the pot. For example, if a recipe calls for 1 cup of rice cooked in 1½ cups of water, your gut instinct might tell you that to double it, you should use 3 cups of water; not so. Instead, you would use 2 cups of rice cooked in 2¾ cups of water. Photo: iStock Baking When baking a cake, the oven’s heat works its way in from the outside. With double the batter for the heat to penetrate, the centre stays liquid much longer. The leaveners in the batter are working faster than it takes for the other ingredients to set and bake, due to that larger quantity needing more time to reach the right temperature. This creates air bubbles that usually help to inflate our baked goods (creating a beautifully domed cake), but without the structure of a set crumb the cake will crumble and crater, as the air pockets created by the leaveners merge and escape through the batter that hasn’t fully set.



When scaling a baking recipe, your safest option is to simply make two batches. If you must scale your ingredients, be sure to swap your pan out (if doubling, for a larger pan; if halving, for a smaller one), so the batter sits at roughly its original depth. That way, the oven’s heat can uniformly bake your sweet treat without allowing your cakes to collapse. A few more quick tips when scaling a baking recipe up or down: Weigh your ingredients. The volume of a cup of flour can vary significantly depending on how it’s packed, and doubling a recipe can compound those errors.

Need to halve an egg? Crack it into a small bowl, whisk to combine the white and yolk, and measure out half of that mixture.

Go off visual and flavour cues. If you can see that your cookies have reached that perfect golden brown, or that your dish is already salty enough before reaching the “double” mark, trust your gut. Photo: iStock Fat in the pan



Finally, the fat in your skillet (the tablespoon or so of oil you sauté your garlic and onion in) doesn’t need to be doubled along with the ingredients that you’re cooking in it. Its job is to cover the pan and conduct heat into whatever you’re cooking, so it scales with the pan, not with the food. If you need to double a stir-fry, you don’t need to double the oil that’s in the pan all at once, but you do need to make two batches. By simply dumping double the ingredients into a single wok, you’re going to steam the food rather than allowing it to develop a flavourful browning. This is only the case for browning, though. If you want to sweat some onions for a soup or a braised recipe, crowding isn’t an issue, so you’re welcome to add double the onions and just enough fat to coat the larger volume of ingredients. World.title: Lindsay Park and Rawiller mastermind Five Diamonds day heist
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Lindsay Park and Rawiller mastermind Five Diamonds day heist Craig Kerry November 7, 2026 — 9:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Lindsay Park and Nash Rawiller stole the show on Five Diamonds day at Rosehill as Evaporate claimed the $2 million feature to set up a potential West Australian campaign and Act Up took out the $1 million Golden Gift at Rosehill to book his place in the Golden Slipper. Rawiller claimed the rich double with contrasting rides, putting Evaporate from a start in gate four to sit on the fence behind the leaders in the 1800m Five Diamonds before driving the $10 chance to a half-length victory over Zambardo. Hayes-trained Plymouth was third. Evaporate wins the Five Diamonds. Getty Images The champion rider earlier took Act Up through the field from second last on the bend, after a start in gate 11, before lifting him the $8 chance to a half-length victory over Silent Intent. Rawiller and the training team of Will, Ben and JD Hayes have now combined for nine wins and five placings from just 22 runners together.



“He’s a high talent, he’s very good and we got exactly the ride that we needed from him there, so that was just super,” Will Hayes said after the Five Diamonds. Evaporate was ninth and 10th in group 1s before finishing seventh in the Five Diamonds Prelude. He could not race on to WA, where he is nominated for the Railway and Northerly Stakes. “We thought he had his excuses in the group 1s,” Hayes said. “The Sir Rupert Clarke from the wide barrier, and in the Toorak getting slightly held up, so today we had our confidence in the horse and he did well, thriving between runs. “It didn’t go well in the prelude with that tricky run in transit and then he got produced again here today and we got the right barrier and the right ride.”



Colt Act Up earlier belied his name under a gun ride from Rawiller to win the Golden Gift. Act Up, one and a half lengths fourth in the 1000m Debutant Stakes at Caulfield, settled well and was second last approaching the bend after jumping from gate 11 in the $1 million race. Rawiller then navigated a path through the field on the $240,000 Castelvecchio colt and lifted him past Tony and Calvin McEvoy-trained Silent Intent in the final strides for a half-length victory. Hawkes Racing’s Torshavn was third on debut. Nash Rawiller wins the Golden Gift on Act Up. Getty Images The $580,000 and $190,000 prizemoney effectively puts the Victorian-trained quinella into the $5 million Golden Slipper in March. The Hayes brothers earlier won the $200,000 Inglis Banner at Flemington with Debutant Stakes victory Soldi.



“We were really keen to see him over 1100m, and we needed every metreage today,” Will said. “It was a terrific ride by Nash to go back and through. We were beaten for early speed and we were just hoping for an over correction, which is what we got. Full credit to the horse, he handled the occasion. Our two-year-olds are on fire.” Rawiller then made life hard for Tommy Berry and Chris Waller-trained favourite Lazzura in the $500,000 group 2 Hot Danish Stakes (1400m) aboard Chris and Corey Munce-prepared Gerringong. The pair battled down the straight as $1.35 favourite Lazzura raced outside leader Gerringong ($6.50) before edging past in the final 100m for a half neck victory. Stablemate Surf’s Up was third. Waller representative Darren Beadman believed Lazzura would likely be spelled after back-to-back “gut-busting” victories in the $2 million Invitation and on Saturday.



More Midway goals ahead for Ible Kembla Grange trainer Joe Ible was looking to the Midway Handicap at home on The Gong program in two weeks with Common Goal after the five-year-old led and kicked strongly for a first win in the Saturday races. Apprentice Coriah Keatings, using her three-kilogram claim, controlled the 1300m Midway for a one and a quarter-length victory from Hellova Nature, after a fourth first-up in the grade last start. The win continued an enjoyable spring for Ible, who trains a team of 20. His stable star won two Midways and was second in the $750,000 Sydney Gold Cup before going for a spell. “There’s a 1400m Midway on Gong day at home, so that was the progression, 1200, 1300, 1400 and have a runner at Kembla on Gong day,” Ible said of Common Goal’s next target.



He said Cabbucio, which was second in the Midway on Tuesday at Randwick, would race in the 1600m Midway at Newcastle next Saturday and potentially rise to the 2000m race two weeks later at Rosehill. Wyong trainer Nacim Dilmi was also looking to the Gong program with Probability Theory after the four-year-old mare won the 1400m benchmark 78 by three-quarters of a length at Rosehill, taking her record to five wins in nine starts. The Domeland head trainer said the benchmark 88 1600m race at Kembla was a likely next target. Brave effort puts championships in frame Scone trainer Luke Pepper will weigh up a Country Championships campaign for Brave Xena after apprentice Mollie Fitzgerald bounced back from a fall two days earlier to take the four-year-old mare to victory in the 1200m class 3 Highway Handicap. Fitzgerald fell pre-race at Gosford on Thursday and was stood down for the day, but was cleared of any fractures. In her first ride back, Fitzgerald made the most of a draw in three to take Brave Xena to a half-length win.



Fitzgerald said she had “just general soreness in my back, shoulder and ribs” and did everything she could to be right for Saturday. Pepper said he had hoped to get Brave Xena into last month’s $2 million Kosciuszko, but after the consolation win on Saturday, he would discuss the possibility of stretching her out to 1400m with breeder-owner Glenn Burrows for the Country Championships after a short break. Burrows, who owns Willow Park Stud in Scone, kept the Saxon Warrior-Warrior Woman filly after believing she was too small for the sales. Fitzgerald went to the lead in the Sydney apprentices’ title on six, one ahead of Braith Nock and defending champion Siena Grima, who had also had a win on Saturday when She Moves Too scored a three-length victory in the 1800m benchmark 78 for boss Chris Waller. Grima was later fined $500 for not riding Waller-trained Medatsu fully to the line in the third when nosed out for fourth place. Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott-trained four-year-old Savvy Spy stamped himself a stayer of the future with an easy win in the 2400m benchmark 78 handicap, before wanting to go further post-race.



The $80,000 son of Savabeel made it three wins in a row, jumping from a 2000m benchmark 64 at Hawkesbury to a Warwick Farm midweek benchmark 78 over 2400m before Saturday’s length and a quarter win under Tim Clark. Savvy Spy then dislodged Clark on the way back to the winners’ stall and took off down the home straight in the opposite direction before the clerks of the course reeled him in. Rider and horse were unharmed. Meanwhile, Kiwi apprentice Amber Riddell came away with a two-meeting suspension for careless riding after a frightening and chaotic trip on Bjorn Baker-trained Swordplay in race nine. In her first Saturday Sydney ride, the champion New Zealand apprentice was penalised for allowing Swordplay to shift out in the straight and check Regimental Colours approaching the 200m mark. Riddell was lucky to stay on the four-year-old mare when it raced fiercely forward to lead and shifted in abruptly from a wide gate to hit the rail.



When questioned about the early troubles, Riddell said she hit the inside rail aboard Swordplay in trackwork this week and almost went through it. Stewards banned Swordplay, which finished last, from racing again until she trialled to their satisfaction.

World.title: Domestic violence is everyone’s business
World.content:
Under the diesel fuel credit scheme 18 major mining companies receive on average $22 for every dollar they pay to compensate for their insurance-and-food-cost-increasing emissions. Meanwhile, a third of Australian households feel food insecurity, and services to help people facing homelessness are overwhelmed (“ Broke? Don’t blame yourself ”, November 1) There’s money there for the corporations but not the struggling families. Our government’s priorities need fixing. Lesley Walker, Northcote (Vic)

The more things change, the more things stay the same, or so says the old adage (“ ‘I thanked God for the axe’: Historic case shines light on women who kill ”, November 1). It is hard to believe that literally in my lifetime many things have changed, but much has stayed the same. Many women still are not safe in relationships, nor are their children. The Mrs K 1955 axe killing of her abusive husband is a prime example of how far some women are forced to go to protect themselves and their children. The indicators are usually there in a potentially abusive relationship. We all need to be better at not just identifying those behaviours, but at doing something about them. We are more aware nowadays, but perhaps still hampered by the “it’s none of my business” approach. It’s everyone’s business. Geoff Nilon, Mascot

I usually enjoy Jacqueline Maley’s columns, but her suggestion that the Marrickville Golf Club controversy might define Anthony Albanese’s prime ministership left me shaking my head (“Golf club gaffe might be mistake to remember on Albanese’s record”, November 1). Who really cares about the plumbing arrangements at Marrickville Golf Club? Yes, public money should be properly accounted for, but must every political misstep become a national drama. Political reporting increasingly reminds me of why I fell out of love with My Kitchen Rules. Somewhere along the way, it became less about the cooking and more about confected personal dramas, petty squabbles and manufactured outrage. I sometimes wonder whether the Canberra press gallery has gone the same way. The personalities, the scandals, the political point-scoring and the daily dramas dominate, while the actual business of governing becomes almost incidental. Meanwhile, policies affecting Medicare, wages, education and the cost of living struggle to compete for attention. The banal gets a loudspeaker. The substantial barely gets a whisper. Denise McHugh, Tamworth

Mother of all train delays

In 1928, at the centenary of Manly Area, a booklet was put out with early photos (“Facilities the key to increase in housing”, November 1). In it was a full-page add for the newly opened Warringah Shire (northern beaches), encouraging the purchase of land and saying that, within 10 years, there would be a railway to the area. That decade was mighty long, and getting longer. Michael Payne, West Pymble

One Nation brains bust

One Nation may be the “new” Liberal party on the block, albeit an extreme right version, but one has to question if its new-found support and record polling is a result of the Liberals committing harakiri, angry voters lashing out in protest or some social media bots giving the appearance of support (“One Nation facing new challenges”, November 1). I suspect the answer is all of the above. Parnell Palme McGuinness points out what is both a strength and the greatest weakness of One Nation; its so-called brains trust. Politicians like Hanson and Joyce may enjoy a cult-like following, but throw in foreign-born Queensland senator Malcolm Roberts and you hardly have a brains trust. There lies the problem with One Nation. Few, if any of its radical policies have been costed and those that have been are way off the mark. Hanson in particular can hardly string together a coherent sentence unless she is vilifying someone or a group of people. Before the next federal election hopefully oil will be flowing again, which will ease the cost of living and reduce some of the pressure and scrutiny that the prime minister is currently experiencing. If the Liberals can elect a more inspiring leader than its current lame duck Angus Taylor, support for One Nation will drop to a point where they will just be an annoying background noise. We have two state elections to be held before the next federal one and this may give us a more accurate picture where One Nation stands. Peter Miniutti, Ashbury

World.title: Conservative bloc takes slim lead in NZ election that’s still too close to call
World.content:
Updated WorldOceaniaWorld elections Conservative bloc takes slim lead in NZ election that’s still too close to call Ben McKay Updated November 7, 2026 — 8:37pm ,first published 6:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

With more than 80 per cent of the votes counted, New Zealand’s election produced no definitive victory for the right or the left on Saturday, but the incumbent conservative government hovered on the brink of a wafer-thin majority that could allow it to eke out a precarious return to power. Christopher Luxon’s National Party and its minor party coalition partners, libertarian ACT and populist NZ First, were getting close to the slimmest possible return – by just one seat. It suggested that securing a second term could take lengthy negotiations and would rely on votes counted after election day, which have historically skewed left. Left to right: NZ PM Chris Luxon, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong and the Labour Party’s Chris Hipkins. Fairfax Media The left-wing bloc, led by the Labour Party and Chris Hipkins, appeared to have fallen short of a majority. As New Zealand’s Electoral Commission unveiled the counts, it became clear the night would likely end without certainty about who would form the next government. Arriving at Labour headquarters in Upper Hutt, outside of Wellington, a smiling Hipkins didn’t concede defeat.



“Tonight, New Zealand has spoken,” Hipkins told supporters. “It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said.” Still, the unclear outcome was punishing for both National and Labour, the major political parties that have long dominated New Zealand politics. Deputy leader of the National Party Nicola Willis (left) at the party’s election night event in Auckland. Getty Images The two were neck and neck, both recording under 30 per cent of the vote – underscoring opinion polls before election day that showed little public enthusiasm for either party. A newcomer to politics is poised to enter parliament



Voters instead bolstered power for minor parties on the ideological flanks, and propelled to office a centrist political newcomer, Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity Party, who has pledged a non-partisan and pragmatic agenda that draws from socially liberal, technocratic and pro-environment ideals. Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong, a former KPMG consultant, says she is open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government. AP It was too soon to know whether the support of 38-year-old Wong, whose party appeared set to enter parliament for the first time, would be required for any leader seeking to form a government. New Zealanders don’t elect prime ministers. Instead, they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and one to select a local representative. Parties must either win a constituency seat, or win 5 per cent of the preferred party vote, to enter parliament. New-entrant parties are rare and Opportunity, on current results, would be the first in more than a decade.



The magnitude of Wong’s success was still undecided, with the count Saturday showing Opportunity had just crossed the 5 per cent threshold, giving the party seven seats. Related Article Analysis

China relations New Zealand’s biggest pivot since the 1980s Wong has said that if she held the tiebreaker power, she was open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government and would deal first with whichever major party won the most votes. The right-wing bloc might not need her, and Luxon has ruled out governing with Opportunity. Analysts say, however, that both major party leaders would likely answer the phone if Wong held the only path to power on election night. Early results show conservatives with a wafer-thin majority



To govern, a coalition of parties must hold more than half of parliament’s seats. The total number of seats is determined by official calculations on election night based on quirks of the country’s vote. Saturday figures showed there could be a 129-seat parliament, with 65 seats needed for a majority. However, parties negotiating shared governing arrangements would prefer a more comfortable margin. Results suggested a coalition of National, ACT and NZ First would hold 66 seats, a number that fluctuated as the night continued. Loading The 66 included 41 for National, 13 for ACT and 12 for NZ First – a drop for National and a gain for the two minor parties. The result will likely cause headaches for Luxon, whose detractors criticised his political inexperience during his tenure in a power-sharing deal with two veteran and canny politicians, David Seymour of ACT and Winston Peters of NZ First. Both will want greater influence in any coalition on Saturday’s results, and Luxon’s woes won’t end there.



Lawmakers from the conservative parties who spoke to news outlets Saturday night avoided declaring victory. So-called special votes cast by New Zealanders who live abroad or are travelling on election day are counted later, and historically favour the left. In the past four elections, National lost one or two seats when the special votes were counted, while left-wing parties won between one and three additional seats. Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaks to supporters on election night. Getty Images Saturday’s emerging results also suggested a shocking exit from parliament for a few of National’s most senior figures, including the incumbent government’s Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Speaker of the House Gerry Brownlee, and Defence and Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. The left-wing bloc has fallen short so far



Meanwhile, the left bloc, led by Hipkins and Labour, held a combined 56 seats, though numbers there also fluctuated. The environmentally focused Greens were celebrating a best-ever result of an apparent 16 seats in parliament, with Labour sitting on 35 and Te Pāti Māori, an Indigenous rights group, securing five. Related Article World elections It’s a New Zealand election with a twist. What’s at stake? Hipkins was seeking a second chance at power after a resounding defeat three years ago, but he hadn’t benefited much from Luxon’s slumping popularity in pre-election opinion polling. The results showed minor parties on both the left and right winning more seats than at the 2023 election, which propelled Luxon to power. Analysts had suggested that economic woes, including inflation, living costs and unemployment – and apathy about the prime ministerships of either Luxon or Hipkins – would see minor parties grow in popularity, granting them greater bargaining power in forming a governing coalition and forcing the major parties to enact more of their agendas.



Voting began on October 26 and ended on Saturday, with nearly 3.8 million people eligible to participate. New Zealand is a South Pacific nation that’s home to 5.6 million people. Results from 95 per cent of ballots cast are expected by the end of Saturday night. A final, verified tally is due on November 27, including the special votes. After the final count, coalition negotiations between presumptive governing parties often take weeks, even when their majority is clear. AAP

Close Share A A A

With 18 seconds left on the clock at Ikon Park, Geelong star Chloe Scheer took a deep breath and lined up for a set shot, directly in front and about 20 metres from goal. After a dominant first half of Saturday’s qualifying final, the Cats coughed up a 28-point margin to a surging Melbourne to find themselves five points down in the dying minutes of the final quarter. Sheer joy: The Demons snatched the win. Getty Images An always-reliable Scheer took her shot as Melbourne defenders watched on helplessly – but it sailed wide for a point. Cue pandemonium from the euphoric Demons, who won the nail-biting game by four points, and devastation for the Cats in what will go down as one of the greatest AFLW finals in history.



It was a fourth-quarter masterclass from the Demons to snatch the lead and win 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52), booking a preliminary final berth. Saturday’s highly anticipated match-up saw Cats coach Mick Stinear face his old Demons – a team he coached for 10 seasons. A gracious Stinear conceded Melbourne were the better team and said the Cats would rally around a disappointed Scheer. “The outcome of the game is not on her; that’s on us as a coaching team and a playing group to be more consistent,” he said post-match. “We shouldn’t have put ourselves in that position.”



Stinear praised Geelong’s pressure in the first half, but said the team lost their way in the third quarter and Melbourne “made us pay on turnover”. “I thought our pressure and effort and intent was really good for the whole game, but our method and ability to execute fundamentally lacked at critical times, and to their credit, they came over the top of us, and we nearly escaped with a win. “But I didn’t feel like we’d earned it with the second half we had.” Georgie Prespakis was sensational for the Cats on Saturday via Getty Images At half-time the Cats seemed to have the game locked away, boasting a 22-point margin. But the Demons found their groove, and a star turn from Alyssa Bannan helped them home.



Geelong should have been playing in front of a home crowd at GMHBA Stadium but had to settle for Ikon Park after a venue-booking clash with the AUSX Supercross Championship – a dirt-bike racing series. Editor's pick AFLW A Cat brought this Irish move to the AFLW. It’s made the AFL consider a rule change Due to the AFLW season structure and length, the Cats and Demons hadn’t faced each other in more than a year, with the Demons winning their round 12 clash back in 2025. Since then, both teams have experienced significant change, with Stinear departing for the Cats and Melbourne welcoming new coach Tom Wilson. There were nerves in the opening term, with both sides missing opportunities to convert. But Rebecca Webster’s long-range effort from 50 with a fortunate bounce gave the Cats the opening goal and steadied the ship.



A blistering second quarter from Georgie Prespakis, Scheer and Jacqueline Parry pushed the Cats further up the scoreboard and almost left the Demons goalless for the first half, but they were saved by a last-minute snap from Eliza McNamara. Momentum shifted in the third, with a goal from a 100-game Melbourne veteran Tyla Hanks followed by a brilliant running goal from Kate Hore. Suddenly, there were holes in the Cats’ defence and the Demons pounced. Melbourne came roaring back into the contest and a second goal from Bannan cut the margin to just one point with less than eight minutes left. A thrilling few minutes followed and an extraordinary Paxy Paxman kicked truly to put the Demons in front. View post on X



Post-match, Wilson praised veteran Paxman and star Tayla Harris, who laid some sensational tackles in critical moments. Their teammate Tahlia Gillard joked her heart rate was still through the roof, well after the final siren. “There’s [so] much excitement, [that was] just such a team performance, and for some of those girls to get their first finals win, that’s pretty good one to experience,” she said. View post on X Both teams made it through with minimal injuries, with Cats star Nina Morrison briefly coming to the bench after a hard hit from Harris, but later returning to play. Demon Saraid Taylor – who has been nursing a calf injury for most of the season – also left the field after getting her leg trapped and twisted under her opponent, but also returned to play.



In typical Melbourne weather, Ikon Park was hit by flashes of torrential rain followed by a 15-minute lightning delay and then patches of sunshine. There’s a short break before the second qualifying final starts at 4.05pm at Ikon Park, with reigning premiers North Melbourne facing the Carlton. The Kangaroo juggernaut is eying a historic three-peat this year and have cruised through the season, but they aren’t invincible. Hawthorn defeated the Roos back in round six and Carlton came close earlier in the year. Reigning premiers cruise to victory



The rampant Kangaroos flexed their muscles to record a dominant six-goal win over the Blues, who spent the majority of their qualifying final on Saturday goalless. After a slow first quarter, the Roos seized the momentum, swarming Carlton defenders and cruising to victory with repeated strings of unanswered goals to win 7.7 (49) to 1.7 (13) in front of 5028 fans. Soccer star Mackenzie Arnold become affectionately known as “a brick wall” for her goal-saving efforts for the Matildas. But, in the goalless first quarter of this game, that label belonged Blues defender Harriet Cordner, who was recently named in the All-Australian squad and had some crucial interceptions and limited North’s scoring ability. Another win for the impressive North Melbourne AFL Photos But by the second term, North had it all figured out, booting four consecutive goals and taking full control of the game. The Blues were overwhelmed but also inaccurate, missing crucial converting opportunities.



At one point in the third quarter, AFLW statisticians reported a staggering number – the Kangaroos had recorded 109-59 uncontested possessions to that point, a number that would only continue to grow. The heavens opened up in the fourth quarter, further dampening the spirits of Blues fans who were forced to sprint up into the Ikon Park stands to take shelter. The Blues will be anxiously awaiting scans for Ciara Fitzgerald, who left the field clutching her knee, while North will also be sweating on results for Alice O’Loughlin, who screamed out in agony after her leg got trapped under her opponent. View post on X The star Kangaroo was helped off-field by trainers and gestured towards her right knee when sitting on the bench.



North continued to pile on the scoreboard pressure, and with three minutes remaining it looked like Carlton would be goalless. Blues star Sophie McKay booted the team’s only goal in the closing stages. Carlton Coach Mathew Buck passionately defended his team in his post-match press conference, denying the Blues’ morale levels would be low after their near goalless defeat. “We know we were outplayed today, and by a team that played really well, so we weren’t at the level,” he said. “But we’ve taken lessons from this, and been fortunate enough and played well enough throughout the year to earn a top-four spot. So, you dust yourself off, and we’ll get ready for next week.” Buck maintained the group had “finished top four for a reason” and said they would be ready for their semi-final next week.



Meanwhile, star Kangaroo and reigning league best-and-fairest winner Ash Riddell said it was important for North Melbourne to “not get ahead of ourselves” as they eye a historic three-peat. Riddell said the group had more fire in the belly after their loss to Hawthorn in round six – a defeat that ended their record-breaking 32-game winning streak. “It’s probably one where it’s just a reminder that you hate losing more than anything,” she said. “I think the group really hates it ... so just keep striving towards that winning feeling and being process-driven along the way.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Not our fault’: The students having second thoughts about Destination Australia
World.content:
NationalUniversity ‘Not our fault’: The students having second thoughts about Destination Australia Sally Rawsthorne November 7, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Magdiel Silva Da Luz has a job, a partner and an almost-complete master’s of strategic communications. But would he choose Australia again? Magdiel Silva Da Luz feels “like we live in a parallel life besides local people” . Simon Schluter “I would definitely think twice,” the Brazilian international student said. Silva Da Luz is not alone. Australia’s $54 billion international education industry is under siege as the world’s highest visa application fees, eye-watering degree costs for international students, the extraordinary cost of living, changes to work rights and a so-called “genuine student test” come together to undermine the appeal of an Australian education.



But it’s the rising tide of populism that has most alarmed students. Related Article Immigration With their families barred, international students say they face an agonising choice “When I arrived [in 2022], the situation was a bit more open for international students,” Silva Da Luz said. “Now it seems like it’s a bit more unstable, it feels a bit more insecure.” “When I came here in 2022, in Brazil we had [former Brazilian president Jair] Bolsonaro, and he was very conservative and very homophobic. So I left Brazil and went to Australia because I think here is not the right place for me. And now I’m here and it’s happening again.” The Herald spoke to numerous international students for this story, all of whom made allegations of “microaggressions” ranging from rude comments to being spat at. All of the students said the increasingly tense and public migration debate had led to them feeling less welcome or unwelcome in Australia. None of those students wanted to be identified for fear of reprisal from the government or cancellation of their visas.



“I don’t feel like it’s our fault, most of the problems that the country has,” Silva Da Luz said. “So it’s very hard to have [people say] ‘Oh international students are the problem, so let’s just boot them.’ ” Universities and the international students who prop them up face a friendless future, with all future governments planning to rein in numbers. The Albanese government has announced sweeping reforms that it hopes will curb the numbers through barring family members of international students and ending visa hopping. Hardline plans to slash the numbers have also been announced by both the Coalition and One Nation. An “excellent study experience for students who then return home” is the government’s hope for the future of the system, according to a presentation by the Department of Education’s Dr Damien Oliver last week. (This is not borne out in reality, with about 170,000 former students currently on a temporary bridging visa after graduation.) The government wants to focus on the “composition, quality and integrity” of the sector rather than chasing greater enrolment numbers, Oliver said.



Visa data shows these planned reductions are coming off a low base – 31,000 higher education visas were granted between July and September this year, a 40 per cent decline since the peak in 2024 and down 16 per cent on pre-pandemic numbers from 2019. All of this spells big trouble for the nation’s universities, which rely heavily on funding from international students. “For years, governments have asked universities to do more while public funding has failed to keep pace with the cost of teaching, research and infrastructure. International education has helped fill that gap,” Universities Australia CEO Luke Sheehy said. This year, the Herald revealed that the University of NSW and the University of Sydney took $1.7 billion each from international students. “It’s pretty serious,” higher education expert Andrew Norton said. “We’ve already seen a couple of unis announcing job cuts due to this – Adelaide University, Murdoch University, Charles Sturt University. This will be, in my view, extremely common over the next few years.”



International student fees are used to subsidise domestic ones, particularly at struggling smaller and regional universities. Then there’s research. “There is absolutely no doubt that they are critical for the scale – just over half of research funding is dedicated sources, the rest is coming from other income sources,” Norton said. “There are … profits of commercial operations and endowments. But there’s simply no way those sums could add up without significant international student profits.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy.
