World.title: Is there a future for malls without their department store anchors?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesDavid Jones collapse Is there a future for malls without their department store anchors? Elias Visontay November 7, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For almost a century, they were the one-stop shop providing a sense of opulence and occasion that drew reliable foot traffic into shopping centres across Australia. But the slow, then sudden, demise of David Jones has thrown into question the symbiotic relationship that underpinned decades of prosperity for both department stores and malls. Westfield Bondi Junction, Sydney. Oscar Colman Now, operators of suburban shopping centres are facing their own identity crisis, as they try to figure out how to re-engineer their offerings and layouts to thrive in an era without the anchor tenants that built them. Thursday’s decision from David Jones’ chief executive and board of directors to hand over control of the company to voluntary administrators and receivers, and the looming closure of potentially most of its stores and thousands of associated job cuts, contained echoes of a trend seen across the world in recent years as the department store concept loses relevance.



World’s oldest department store Founded in Sydney in 1838, David Jones holds the title of the world’s oldest department store still operating under its original name. However, its glamorous history and current strife form the hallmarks of a global narrative arc – complete with retail legend and obituary – that have already been written overseas. Two women take advantage of a fur coat sale at David Jones during a heatwave in February 1939. Gordon Short They all begin in a similar way. Opening an initial shop on a high street in the 18th or 19th century and subsequently booming as a centre of high-end fashion and consumer goods through the first half of the 20th century.



“Department stores were the high street under one roof,” said Gary Mortimer, a professor of retail and consumer behaviour at the Queensland University of Technology. Related Article Fashion retail David Jones hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Dior – but nostalgia won’t save it Big name brands sold exclusively through different department stores. Shop windows were erected to celebrate holidays and woo customers and children ahead of Christmas. Bathrooms and other services meant people, especially women, dwelled longer. “It was iconic, you’d walk into the Elizabeth Street David Jones [in Sydney] and there’s a pianist playing, you’d go downstairs for the champagne and oyster bar, you’d wander around, try on. It was a sense of occasion,” he said. In the United Kingdom, the obvious parallel is with Debenhams, which began as a high street shop in 1778 and expanded to more than 100 locations across the country and became a household name. In the United States, it was the likes of Macy’s, Nordstrom and Saks Fifth Avenue, which grew to consume rival Neiman Marcus.



In the 1960s, David Jones was the epicentre of Australian high society. “It was the place to see and be seen,” 90-year-old Laudie Sneddon, who worked as a graduate pharmacist at the flagship Elizabeth Street store in Sydney in its heyday, recalled to this masthead. Melbourne Central shopping centre Louis Trerise Push into the suburbs Then came the expansion into suburban shopping centres. These stores were often less flashy outlets to capitalise on the explosion of malls and car travel in the years after World War II. “In the past, having a Myer, Grace Brothers or David Jones was vital for a shopping centre, but it’s become less vital.” Gary Mortimer, professor of retail and consumer behaviour at the Queensland University of Technology.



However, this was ultimately the first of several waves of change that would spell upheaval for Australia’s department stores, Mortimer said. The next wave was brands opening their own stores instead of selling through the likes of DJs, Myer and Grace Bros, followed by the more brutal waves of e-commerce and cheap fast fashion, he said. “You didn’t need to go to the department store any more,” Mortimer said. Sales began slowing, and attempts to compete with cheap new retail players with much lighter, cheaper retail and staffing costs proved difficult. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift away from bricks and mortar. In 2021, Debenhams entered administration, with all physical shopfronts subsequently liquidated. It exists solely as an online retailer today. The recently renovated Chatswood Chase shopping centre in Sydney. Steven Woodburn



Meanwhile, in the US, Macy’s store count has shrunk dramatically, while Nordstrom is closing its legacy high-end stores to open more of its Rack discount offshoots. And in January this year, Saks Global filed for bankruptcy, with just a fraction of its stores emerging from the process. Similarly, while David Jones managed to push its online sales to 20 per cent of its overall revenue, this wasn’t enough to help meet its bricks-and-mortar rent payments. From here, many observers say a slimmed-down version of David Jones could emerge from administration, perhaps limited to its flagship CBD locations plus certain others at boutique, profitable shopping centres. Focussing on its legacy of prestige and grandeur will be key, Mortimer believes. London’s Harrods and Selfridges, and Paris’ Galeries Lafayette and Le Bon Marché have been flagged as models of success for historic department stores thriving in the modern day.



Malls move on Related Article David Jones collapse Last time David Jones collapsed there was a rescuer. Who will save it this time? Just as their fortunes were intertwined in the good years, the global decline of department stores had coincided with a downturn for shopping centres. “In the past, having a Myer, Grace Brothers or David Jones was vital for a shopping centre, but it’s become less vital,” Mortimer said. Data from Scentre Group, which operates Westfield centres, show David Jones was charged less than half the rent rate per square metre compared to other customers renting its retail spaces. Without the pull from the likes of David Jones, many suburban centres will have to do much more to justify their premiums.



While the death and the rebirth of the mall has been well documented over the past decade, experts say there are green shoots in the future for shopping centres – providing they innovate. After years of issues, a new report released by Urbis and the Shopping Centre Council of Australia notes retail sales grew three per cent over the year to June 2026, with customer foot traffic at shopping centres up by 2 per cent nationally. Younger shoppers are driving the trend. PwC research found shopping centre foot traffic among consumers aged 14 to 29 rose by 57 per cent year-on-year. Elissa Stewart, director at Urbis, said most centres have actually seen an increase in foot traffic in the post-department store era, with curation of new tenants key. She gives the example of replacing three levels of a David Jones-type department store with three “mini-major” tenants such as a supermarket, a JB Hi-Fi, Rebel Sport or a Mecca. “You’ve got to ensure balance, but the combined power of those three tenants can be more than a department store to draw people in,” Stewart said.



Discount retailers are also a promising trend. Mortimer said that as cheap fast fashion was a factor in the demise of department stores, outlets such as Kmart, Big W, TK Maxx and Harris Scarfe “have suddenly become the ideal tenant”. A third space Related Article Opinion

Inflation Cutting government spending may slow prices, but it could bring on something worse Millie Muroi Economics Writer Services that draw people in are another trend for centres, notes Vanessa Rader, head of research at Ray White. Entertainment businesses, fine dining, activities, and gyms are sought after as they bring customers in during typically quiet late nights and early mornings. Installing EV chargers in a car park also draws in potential shoppers with time to kill while they wait. Healthcare and libraries are another growth opportunity, Mortimer predicts, for centres that successfully innovate.



“Despite interest rate increases, people are still spending on small luxuries, on what they eat or a fun activity to do,” Rader said. “Wellness is a big area too. We still spend on gyms and float tank facilities.” Ultimately, the goal for centres now is to get customers to spend more time dwelling in between activities. “It’s about removing some of the sterile elements that we think of with shopping centres,” Urbis’ Stewart said. Seizing an opportunity to be a go-to “third space” – a term for environments outside of home or work where people can spend time comfortably while spending little or no money – is an important way to stand out, Stewart said. “Enhancing that sense of place, bringing the outdoors and nature inside, water features, lighting, better food options, lounging and creating that space where people actually want to be.” Malls have previously held this role, especially for teens after school and retirees whiling away a day. However, with the cost of everything going up, and investment in centres capitally constrained, “it’s not an easy fix,” she said. With Courtney Thompson The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Why doubling a recipe isn’t always a simple matter of maths
World.content:
Tips & adviceKnow how Why doubling a recipe isn’t always a simple matter of maths Scaling a recipe up or down is often more complicated than just increasing or decreasing the ingredients and cook time. Eden Faithfull November 8, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It seems simple enough: if the head count at your next dinner party doubles, the ingredients for your dinner do the same. Conversely, if you’re looking to scale down the size of your favourite cake for a late-night treat, you should be able to simply halve the recipe. Unfortunately, it’s not quite that simple. You’ll probably end up with bland curry and sunken cakes if you don’t account for a few things first. It’s easy to look at a recipe as a set of ratios you can multiply or divide at will. But recipe developers have to account for the physical and chemical processes that ingredients go through when you combine and cook them, and many of those processes don’t scale in lockstep with your shopping list. Sometimes, making two batches of a recipe and serving them together is the safest way to ensure that you’re not walking into the pitfalls that inadequately scaling your recipe can present. But if you must scale a dish, whether up or down, here are five scenarios where you might run into trouble. Adam Liaw’s Lancashire hot pot. Steve Brown; STYLING Emma Knowles



Braising The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up If you want to double the quantity of your favourite dinner party stew, you’ll end up with twice the volume of ingredients (great!) and the same pot you started with (not so great). Evaporation is a function of surface area, not volume, and your surface area hasn’t budged — so in the hour the recipe allots, you’ll drive off the same amount of liquid you would have before. Against twice the volume, that’s only half the reduction you need. Halving your ingredients presents the same issue but in reverse. The surface area remains the same, but there’s only half as much liquid to lose. The same hour’s evaporation leads to scorched meat and a dry pot. Related Recipe collection 10 classic one-pots every cook should have in their repertoire The safest fix is to adjust your cooking vessel. If you can’t do that, here’s a good rule of thumb: Instead of directly doubling the entire recipe, use about 1½ times the liquid ingredients, and double the rest. If you’re halving the recipe, use about 60 per cent of the liquid and half of the rest of the ingredients.



This all matters most for braises you finish uncovered, or ones that you reduce at the end of cooking. If your pot stays lidded in the oven, evaporation is admittedly a much smaller factor. But you’re not out of the woods yet. Even when evaporation isn’t a factor, you still have to adjust the clock when scaling a recipe. A much larger volume of food is going to take considerably longer to finish cooking, and vice versa with a smaller volume. Katrina Meynink’s grain salad with corn, chickpeas and avocado with chipotle lime dressing. KatrinaÂ Meynink Grains and (some) beans While cooking, rice absorbs a fixed amount of water — but the amount of water called for in a recipe doesn’t just account for what the grain absorbs. Part of it is to account for what escapes as steam, which depends on the surface area available and the time it takes to cook, so it doesn’t change when you double the rice. Double both quantities, and you’ve doubled the water allowance for steam that should have stayed put. Related Recipe collection 25 interesting and filling grain- and rice-based salad recipes



So, when scaling a recipe for grains (or beans that cook using the absorption method), adjust the absorption and leave the allowance alone. A safe bet is to figure about 1¼ cups of water per 1 cup of rice, then add about ¼ cup for what steams off, no matter how much rice is in the pot. For example, if a recipe calls for 1 cup of rice cooked in 1½ cups of water, your gut instinct might tell you that to double it, you should use 3 cups of water; not so. Instead, you would use 2 cups of rice cooked in 2¾ cups of water. Photo: iStock Baking When baking a cake, the oven’s heat works its way in from the outside. With double the batter for the heat to penetrate, the centre stays liquid much longer. The leaveners in the batter are working faster than it takes for the other ingredients to set and bake, due to that larger quantity needing more time to reach the right temperature. This creates air bubbles that usually help to inflate our baked goods (creating a beautifully domed cake), but without the structure of a set crumb the cake will crumble and crater, as the air pockets created by the leaveners merge and escape through the batter that hasn’t fully set.



When scaling a baking recipe, your safest option is to simply make two batches. If you must scale your ingredients, be sure to swap your pan out (if doubling, for a larger pan; if halving, for a smaller one), so the batter sits at roughly its original depth. That way, the oven’s heat can uniformly bake your sweet treat without allowing your cakes to collapse. A few more quick tips when scaling a baking recipe up or down: Weigh your ingredients. The volume of a cup of flour can vary significantly depending on how it’s packed, and doubling a recipe can compound those errors.

Need to halve an egg? Crack it into a small bowl, whisk to combine the white and yolk, and measure out half of that mixture.

Go off visual and flavour cues. If you can see that your cookies have reached that perfect golden brown, or that your dish is already salty enough before reaching the “double” mark, trust your gut. Photo: iStock Fat in the pan



Finally, the fat in your skillet (the tablespoon or so of oil you sauté your garlic and onion in) doesn’t need to be doubled along with the ingredients that you’re cooking in it. Its job is to cover the pan and conduct heat into whatever you’re cooking, so it scales with the pan, not with the food. If you need to double a stir-fry, you don’t need to double the oil that’s in the pan all at once, but you do need to make two batches. By simply dumping double the ingredients into a single wok, you’re going to steam the food rather than allowing it to develop a flavourful browning. This is only the case for browning, though. If you want to sweat some onions for a soup or a braised recipe, crowding isn’t an issue, so you’re welcome to add double the onions and just enough fat to coat the larger volume of ingredients. Washington Post Related Article How to read a recipe and avoid common cooking pitfalls

World.title: Lindsay Park and Rawiller mastermind Five Diamonds day heist
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Lindsay Park and Rawiller mastermind Five Diamonds day heist Craig Kerry November 7, 2026 — 9:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Lindsay Park and Nash Rawiller stole the show on Five Diamonds day at Rosehill as Evaporate claimed the $2 million feature to set up a potential West Australian campaign and Act Up took out the $1 million Golden Gift at Rosehill to book his place in the Golden Slipper. Rawiller claimed the rich double with contrasting rides, putting Evaporate from a start in gate four to sit on the fence behind the leaders in the 1800m Five Diamonds before driving the $10 chance to a half-length victory over Zambardo. Hayes-trained Plymouth was third. Evaporate wins the Five Diamonds. Getty Images The champion rider earlier took Act Up through the field from second last on the bend, after a start in gate 11, before lifting him the $8 chance to a half-length victory over Silent Intent. Rawiller and the training team of Will, Ben and JD Hayes have now combined for nine wins and five placings from just 22 runners together.



“He’s a high talent, he’s very good and we got exactly the ride that we needed from him there, so that was just super,” Will Hayes said after the Five Diamonds. Evaporate was ninth and 10th in group 1s before finishing seventh in the Five Diamonds Prelude. He could not race on to WA, where he is nominated for the Railway and Northerly Stakes. “We thought he had his excuses in the group 1s,” Hayes said. “The Sir Rupert Clarke from the wide barrier, and in the Toorak getting slightly held up, so today we had our confidence in the horse and he did well, thriving between runs. “It didn’t go well in the prelude with that tricky run in transit and then he got produced again here today and we got the right barrier and the right ride.”



Colt Act Up earlier belied his name under a gun ride from Rawiller to win the Golden Gift. Act Up, one and a half lengths fourth in the 1000m Debutant Stakes at Caulfield, settled well and was second last approaching the bend after jumping from gate 11 in the $1 million race. Rawiller then navigated a path through the field on the $240,000 Castelvecchio colt and lifted him past Tony and Calvin McEvoy-trained Silent Intent in the final strides for a half-length victory. Hawkes Racing’s Torshavn was third on debut. Nash Rawiller wins the Golden Gift on Act Up. Getty Images The $580,000 and $190,000 prizemoney effectively puts the Victorian-trained quinella into the $5 million Golden Slipper in March. The Hayes brothers earlier won the $200,000 Inglis Banner at Flemington with Debutant Stakes victory Soldi.



“We were really keen to see him over 1100m, and we needed every metreage today,” Will said. “It was a terrific ride by Nash to go back and through. We were beaten for early speed and we were just hoping for an over correction, which is what we got. Full credit to the horse, he handled the occasion. Our two-year-olds are on fire.” Rawiller then made life hard for Tommy Berry and Chris Waller-trained favourite Lazzura in the $500,000 group 2 Hot Danish Stakes (1400m) aboard Chris and Corey Munce-prepared Gerringong. The pair battled down the straight as $1.35 favourite Lazzura raced outside leader Gerringong ($6.50) before edging past in the final 100m for a half neck victory. Stablemate Surf’s Up was third. Waller representative Darren Beadman believed Lazzura would likely be spelled after back-to-back “gut-busting” victories in the $2 million Invitation and on Saturday.



More Midway goals ahead for Ible Kembla Grange trainer Joe Ible was looking to the Midway Handicap at home on The Gong program in two weeks with Common Goal after the five-year-old led and kicked strongly for a first win in the Saturday races. Apprentice Coriah Keatings, using her three-kilogram claim, controlled the 1300m Midway for a one and a quarter-length victory from Hellova Nature, after a fourth first-up in the grade last start. The win continued an enjoyable spring for Ible, who trains a team of 20. His stable star won two Midways and was second in the $750,000 Sydney Gold Cup before going for a spell. “There’s a 1400m Midway on Gong day at home, so that was the progression, 1200, 1300, 1400 and have a runner at Kembla on Gong day,” Ible said of Common Goal’s next target.



He said Cabbucio, which was second in the Midway on Tuesday at Randwick, would race in the 1600m Midway at Newcastle next Saturday and potentially rise to the 2000m race two weeks later at Rosehill. Wyong trainer Nacim Dilmi was also looking to the Gong program with Probability Theory after the four-year-old mare won the 1400m benchmark 78 by three-quarters of a length at Rosehill, taking her record to five wins in nine starts. The Domeland head trainer said the benchmark 88 1600m race at Kembla was a likely next target. Brave effort puts championships in frame Scone trainer Luke Pepper will weigh up a Country Championships campaign for Brave Xena after apprentice Mollie Fitzgerald bounced back from a fall two days earlier to take the four-year-old mare to victory in the 1200m class 3 Highway Handicap. Fitzgerald fell pre-race at Gosford on Thursday and was stood down for the day, but was cleared of any fractures. In her first ride back, Fitzgerald made the most of a draw in three to take Brave Xena to a half-length win.



Fitzgerald said she had “just general soreness in my back, shoulder and ribs” and did everything she could to be right for Saturday. Pepper said he had hoped to get Brave Xena into last month’s $2 million Kosciuszko, but after the consolation win on Saturday, he would discuss the possibility of stretching her out to 1400m with breeder-owner Glenn Burrows for the Country Championships after a short break. Burrows, who owns Willow Park Stud in Scone, kept the Saxon Warrior-Warrior Woman filly after believing she was too small for the sales. Fitzgerald went to the lead in the Sydney apprentices’ title on six, one ahead of Braith Nock and defending champion Siena Grima, who had also had a win on Saturday when She Moves Too scored a three-length victory in the 1800m benchmark 78 for boss Chris Waller. Grima was later fined $500 for not riding Waller-trained Medatsu fully to the line in the third when nosed out for fourth place. Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott-trained four-year-old Savvy Spy stamped himself a stayer of the future with an easy win in the 2400m benchmark 78 handicap, before wanting to go further post-race.



The $80,000 son of Savabeel made it three wins in a row, jumping from a 2000m benchmark 64 at Hawkesbury to a Warwick Farm midweek benchmark 78 over 2400m before Saturday’s length and a quarter win under Tim Clark. Savvy Spy then dislodged Clark on the way back to the winners’ stall and took off down the home straight in the opposite direction before the clerks of the course reeled him in. Rider and horse were unharmed. Meanwhile, Kiwi apprentice Amber Riddell came away with a two-meeting suspension for careless riding after a frightening and chaotic trip on Bjorn Baker-trained Swordplay in race nine. In her first Saturday Sydney ride, the champion New Zealand apprentice was penalised for allowing Swordplay to shift out in the straight and check Regimental Colours approaching the 200m mark. Riddell was lucky to stay on the four-year-old mare when it raced fiercely forward to lead and shifted in abruptly from a wide gate to hit the rail.



When questioned about the early troubles, Riddell said she hit the inside rail aboard Swordplay in trackwork this week and almost went through it. Stewards banned Swordplay, which finished last, from racing again until she trialled to their satisfaction.

World.title: Conservative bloc takes slim lead in NZ election that’s still too close to call
World.content:
Updated WorldOceaniaWorld elections Conservative bloc takes slim lead in NZ election that’s still too close to call Ben McKay Updated November 7, 2026 — 8:37pm ,first published 6:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. With more than 80 per cent of the votes counted, New Zealand’s election produced no definitive victory for the right or the left on Saturday, but the incumbent conservative government hovered on the brink of a wafer-thin majority that could allow it to eke out a precarious return to power. Christopher Luxon’s National Party and its minor party coalition partners, libertarian ACT and populist NZ First, were getting close to the slimmest possible return – by just one seat. It suggested that securing a second term could take lengthy negotiations and would rely on votes counted after election day, which have historically skewed left. Left to right: NZ PM Chris Luxon, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong and the Labour Party’s Chris Hipkins. Fairfax Media The left-wing bloc, led by the Labour Party and Chris Hipkins, appeared to have fallen short of a majority. As New Zealand’s Electoral Commission unveiled the counts, it became clear the night would likely end without certainty about who would form the next government. Arriving at Labour headquarters in Upper Hutt, outside of Wellington, a smiling Hipkins didn’t concede defeat.



“Tonight, New Zealand has spoken,” Hipkins told supporters. “It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said.” Still, the unclear outcome was punishing for both National and Labour, the major political parties that have long dominated New Zealand politics. Deputy leader of the National Party Nicola Willis (left) at the party’s election night event in Auckland. Getty Images The two were neck and neck, both recording under 30 per cent of the vote – underscoring opinion polls before election day that showed little public enthusiasm for either party. A newcomer to politics is poised to enter parliament



Voters instead bolstered power for minor parties on the ideological flanks, and propelled to office a centrist political newcomer, Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity Party, who has pledged a non-partisan and pragmatic agenda that draws from socially liberal, technocratic and pro-environment ideals. Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong, a former KPMG consultant, says she is open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government. AP It was too soon to know whether the support of 38-year-old Wong, whose party appeared set to enter parliament for the first time, would be required for any leader seeking to form a government. New Zealanders don’t elect prime ministers. Instead, they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and one to select a local representative. Parties must either win a constituency seat, or win 5 per cent of the preferred party vote, to enter parliament. New-entrant parties are rare and Opportunity, on current results, would be the first in more than a decade.



The magnitude of Wong’s success was still undecided, with the count Saturday showing Opportunity had just crossed the 5 per cent threshold, giving the party seven seats. Related Article Analysis

China relations New Zealand’s biggest pivot since the 1980s Wong has said that if she held the tiebreaker power, she was open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government and would deal first with whichever major party won the most votes. The right-wing bloc might not need her, and Luxon has ruled out governing with Opportunity. Analysts say, however, that both major party leaders would likely answer the phone if Wong held the only path to power on election night. Early results show conservatives with a wafer-thin majority



To govern, a coalition of parties must hold more than half of parliament’s seats. The total number of seats is determined by official calculations on election night based on quirks of the country’s vote. Saturday figures showed there could be a 129-seat parliament, with 65 seats needed for a majority. However, parties negotiating shared governing arrangements would prefer a more comfortable margin. Results suggested a coalition of National, ACT and NZ First would hold 66 seats, a number that fluctuated as the night continued. Loading The 66 included 41 for National, 13 for ACT and 12 for NZ First – a drop for National and a gain for the two minor parties. The result will likely cause headaches for Luxon, whose detractors criticised his political inexperience during his tenure in a power-sharing deal with two veteran and canny politicians, David Seymour of ACT and Winston Peters of NZ First. Both will want greater influence in any coalition on Saturday’s results, and Luxon’s woes won’t end there.



Lawmakers from the conservative parties who spoke to news outlets Saturday night avoided declaring victory. So-called special votes cast by New Zealanders who live abroad or are travelling on election day are counted later, and historically favour the left. In the past four elections, National lost one or two seats when the special votes were counted, while left-wing parties won between one and three additional seats. Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaks to supporters on election night. Getty Images Saturday’s emerging results also suggested a shocking exit from parliament for a few of National’s most senior figures, including the incumbent government’s Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Speaker of the House Gerry Brownlee, and Defence and Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. The left-wing bloc has fallen short so far



Meanwhile, the left bloc, led by Hipkins and Labour, held a combined 56 seats, though numbers there also fluctuated. The environmentally focused Greens were celebrating a best-ever result of an apparent 16 seats in parliament, with Labour sitting on 35 and Te Pāti Māori, an Indigenous rights group, securing five. Related Article World elections It’s a New Zealand election with a twist. What’s at stake? Hipkins was seeking a second chance at power after a resounding defeat three years ago, but he hadn’t benefited much from Luxon’s slumping popularity in pre-election opinion polling. The results showed minor parties on both the left and right winning more seats than at the 2023 election, which propelled Luxon to power. Analysts had suggested that economic woes, including inflation, living costs and unemployment – and apathy about the prime ministerships of either Luxon or Hipkins – would see minor parties grow in popularity, granting them greater bargaining power in forming a governing coalition and forcing the major parties to enact more of their agendas.



Voting began on October 26 and ended on Saturday, with nearly 3.8 million people eligible to participate. New Zealand is a South Pacific nation that’s home to 5.6 million people. Results from 95 per cent of ballots cast are expected by the end of Saturday night. A final, verified tally is due on November 27, including the special votes. After the final count, coalition negotiations between presumptive governing parties often take weeks, even when their majority is clear. AAP

World.title: Dee-lighted: Melbourne storm back from the brink to leave Cats heartbroken; Roos smash Blues
World.content:
AFLW finals SportAFLAFLW Dee-lighted: Melbourne storm back from the brink to leave Cats heartbroken; Roos smash Blues Hannah Kennelly Updated November 7, 2026 — 8:02pm ,first published 3:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. With 18 seconds left on the clock at Ikon Park, Geelong star Chloe Scheer took a deep breath and lined up for a set shot, directly in front and about 20 metres from goal. After a dominant first half of Saturday’s qualifying final, the Cats coughed up a 28-point margin to a surging Melbourne to find themselves five points down in the dying minutes of the final quarter. Sheer joy: The Demons snatched the win. Getty Images An always-reliable Scheer took her shot as Melbourne defenders watched on helplessly – but it sailed wide for a point. Cue pandemonium from the euphoric Demons, who won the nail-biting game by four points, and devastation for the Cats in what will go down as one of the greatest AFLW finals in history.



It was a fourth-quarter masterclass from the Demons to snatch the lead and win 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52), booking a preliminary final berth. Saturday’s highly anticipated match-up saw Cats coach Mick Stinear face his old Demons – a team he coached for 10 seasons. A gracious Stinear conceded Melbourne were the better team and said the Cats would rally around a disappointed Scheer. “The outcome of the game is not on her; that’s on us as a coaching team and a playing group to be more consistent,” he said post-match. “We shouldn’t have put ourselves in that position.”



Stinear praised Geelong’s pressure in the first half, but said the team lost their way in the third quarter and Melbourne “made us pay on turnover”. “I thought our pressure and effort and intent was really good for the whole game, but our method and ability to execute fundamentally lacked at critical times, and to their credit, they came over the top of us, and we nearly escaped with a win. “But I didn’t feel like we’d earned it with the second half we had.” Georgie Prespakis was sensational for the Cats on Saturday via Getty Images At half-time the Cats seemed to have the game locked away, boasting a 22-point margin. But the Demons found their groove, and a star turn from Alyssa Bannan helped them home.



Geelong should have been playing in front of a home crowd at GMHBA Stadium but had to settle for Ikon Park after a venue-booking clash with the AUSX Supercross Championship – a dirt-bike racing series. Editor's pick AFLW A Cat brought this Irish move to the AFLW. It’s made the AFL consider a rule change Due to the AFLW season structure and length, the Cats and Demons hadn’t faced each other in more than a year, with the Demons winning their round 12 clash back in 2025. Since then, both teams have experienced significant change, with Stinear departing for the Cats and Melbourne welcoming new coach Tom Wilson. There were nerves in the opening term, with both sides missing opportunities to convert. But Rebecca Webster’s long-range effort from 50 with a fortunate bounce gave the Cats the opening goal and steadied the ship.



A blistering second quarter from Georgie Prespakis, Scheer and Jacqueline Parry pushed the Cats further up the scoreboard and almost left the Demons goalless for the first half, but they were saved by a last-minute snap from Eliza McNamara. Momentum shifted in the third, with a goal from a 100-game Melbourne veteran Tyla Hanks followed by a brilliant running goal from Kate Hore. Suddenly, there were holes in the Cats’ defence and the Demons pounced. Melbourne came roaring back into the contest and a second goal from Bannan cut the margin to just one point with less than eight minutes left. A thrilling few minutes followed and an extraordinary Paxy Paxman kicked truly to put the Demons in front. View post on X



Post-match, Wilson praised veteran Paxman and star Tayla Harris, who laid some sensational tackles in critical moments. Their teammate Tahlia Gillard joked her heart rate was still through the roof, well after the final siren. “There’s [so] much excitement, [that was] just such a team performance, and for some of those girls to get their first finals win, that’s pretty good one to experience,” she said. View post on X Both teams made it through with minimal injuries, with Cats star Nina Morrison briefly coming to the bench after a hard hit from Harris, but later returning to play. Demon Saraid Taylor – who has been nursing a calf injury for most of the season – also left the field after getting her leg trapped and twisted under her opponent, but also returned to play.



In typical Melbourne weather, Ikon Park was hit by flashes of torrential rain followed by a 15-minute lightning delay and then patches of sunshine. There’s a short break before the second qualifying final starts at 4.05pm at Ikon Park, with reigning premiers North Melbourne facing the Carlton. The Kangaroo juggernaut is eying a historic three-peat this year and have cruised through the season, but they aren’t invincible. Hawthorn defeated the Roos back in round six and Carlton came close earlier in the year. Reigning premiers cruise to victory



The rampant Kangaroos flexed their muscles to record a dominant six-goal win over the Blues, who spent the majority of their qualifying final on Saturday goalless. After a slow first quarter, the Roos seized the momentum, swarming Carlton defenders and cruising to victory with repeated strings of unanswered goals to win 7.7 (49) to 1.7 (13) in front of 5028 fans. Soccer star Mackenzie Arnold become affectionately known as “a brick wall” for her goal-saving efforts for the Matildas. But, in the goalless first quarter of this game, that label belonged Blues defender Harriet Cordner, who was recently named in the All-Australian squad and had some crucial interceptions and limited North’s scoring ability. Another win for the impressive North Melbourne AFL Photos But by the second term, North had it all figured out, booting four consecutive goals and taking full control of the game. The Blues were overwhelmed but also inaccurate, missing crucial converting opportunities.



At one point in the third quarter, AFLW statisticians reported a staggering number – the Kangaroos had recorded 109-59 uncontested possessions to that point, a number that would only continue to grow. The heavens opened up in the fourth quarter, further dampening the spirits of Blues fans who were forced to sprint up into the Ikon Park stands to take shelter. The Blues will be anxiously awaiting scans for Ciara Fitzgerald, who left the field clutching her knee, while North will also be sweating on results for Alice O’Loughlin, who screamed out in agony after her leg got trapped under her opponent. View post on X The star Kangaroo was helped off-field by trainers and gestured towards her right knee when sitting on the bench.



North continued to pile on the scoreboard pressure, and with three minutes remaining it looked like Carlton would be goalless. Blues star Sophie McKay booted the team’s only goal in the closing stages. Carlton Coach Mathew Buck passionately defended his team in his post-match press conference, denying the Blues’ morale levels would be low after their near goalless defeat. “We know we were outplayed today, and by a team that played really well, so we weren’t at the level,” he said. “But we’ve taken lessons from this, and been fortunate enough and played well enough throughout the year to earn a top-four spot. So, you dust yourself off, and we’ll get ready for next week.” Buck maintained the group had “finished top four for a reason” and said they would be ready for their semi-final next week.



Meanwhile, star Kangaroo and reigning league best-and-fairest winner Ash Riddell said it was important for North Melbourne to “not get ahead of ourselves” as they eye a historic three-peat. Riddell said the group had more fire in the belly after their loss to Hawthorn in round six – a defeat that ended their record-breaking 32-game winning streak. “It’s probably one where it’s just a reminder that you hate losing more than anything,” she said. “I think the group really hates it ... so just keep striving towards that winning feeling and being process-driven along the way.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Lessons for Australia from US election result
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Lessons for Australia from US election result November 7, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Lessons for Australia

As the dust settles on the US midterm elections, which resulted in the Democrats winning control of both houses in the US Congress, there are lessons for us in the Australian context. Those of us who prefer their politics in the sensible middle hope the repudiation of Donald Trump is replicated in the Victorian elections this month and the next federal election with the repudiation of Pauline Hanson’s extreme right-wing populism and One Nation. Can the Democrat wave reach our shores?

Nick Toovey, Auckland, NZ Hubris without bounds

Your correspondent (Letters, 6/11) accurately describes Donald Trump, the vainglorious US president who will be adjudged the worst president in the history of the US.

His hubris knows no bounds and he cannot and will not accept responsibility for the harm his ill-thought-out actions cause. It is very doubtful that any post-Trump government will honour his presidency with triumphal arches or naming important government buildings after him.

He has therefore taken it upon himself, with the aid of his handpicked lackeys, to raise monuments to himself and to try to add his name to monuments commemorating past revered presidents.

Harry Kowalski, Ivanhoe Vulnerable targets

Your correspondent (Letters, 6/11) asks if the RBA has given enough time to judge the impact of previous interest rate rises. The RBA should also explain why a prolonged period of an underlying inflation rate of 3.6 per cent is more damaging than a prolonged period of unemployment above the full employment rate. Yes, over the long run high inflation reduces the wealth of everyone. But an extended period of unemployment can have lifelong impacts on people.

″⁣The economy″⁣ is but the sum total of the individuals and businesses within it. Our system seems to be designed to sacrifice some individuals so the remainder can be better off. The RBA’s inflation target range is 2 per cent – 3 per cent. An underlying rate of 3.6 per cent, even if stubborn, doesn’t intuitively seem high, or at least not high enough to inflict mortgage stress and unemployment on those least likely to benefit from a rate within the target.

Brendan Harrison, Soldiers Hill



Change the system

The Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock has stated that an unemployment rate of 4.5 to 5 per cent is required to cool stubborn inflation and ease wage pressures. This means our current monetary policy framework relies on a deliberate percentage of the population being out of work for the broader financial good of the country.

If a certain level of joblessness is deemed structurally necessary to keep the Australian economy stable, unemployed people deserve fairer compensation.

When human wellbeing is treated shoddily in the race to reach economic targets and protect corporate profit margins, we do not just curb inflation – we actively deepen social inequality.

If our economic system requires a segment of our society to be unemployed to stay functional, the very least we can do is ensure our social safety net prevents them from falling into poverty.

Jennie Epstein, Little River New order needed

I read that a ″⁣bold new economic agenda to drive productivity and investment″⁣ is required (Niki Savva, 5/11). Time after time, workers are told that productivity needs to be increased, and time after time, business takes the bulk of that increased productivity, with a tiny proportion going to those who produce the increase. A bold new economic agenda would ensure that those who produce the increase are the beneficiaries.

Vaughan Greenberg, Chewton Mean-spirited PM

Anthony Albanese looks mean-spirited in not offering Senator Fatima Payman the same number of staff as other independents. The least he could do is to set up an independent body so that it removes his power of getting concessions from independents for their voting powers.

Alan Inchley, Frankston Ray of sunshine

On this grey morning, Megan Herbert’s cartoon (6/11) was a ray of sunshine. It made me laugh, and I expect shall be having a quiet giggle all day. Thank you Meagan.

Veronica Paskins, Somers Jess, heed Jeff

Jess Wilson needs to take note of Jeff Kennett’s advice that victory is not in the bag and too much arrogance can be her downfall. Answering questions and releasing her costings is expected by the voter. Walking away from questions does not instil confidence in an inexperienced politician.

Wilma Buccella, Hawthorn



Never assume anything

I recently received an unsolicited email from the Liberal Party signed by Jess Wilson and my electorate’s endorsed Liberal candidate entitled ″⁣Important Electoral Information″⁣.

Included in it they assert: ″⁣We know you’re angry, you should be.″⁣ Whether I am and should be or not is entirely irrelevant. What is relevant is the explicit presumption on their part that I am, without any evidence to justify it. They do not know me nor do they know what I think on any subject, let alone matters to do with Victorian politics and the upcoming election. If any politician thinks such correspondence will make me more likely to vote for them, they are sadly mistaken.

Kevin Bailey, Croydon Impunity and defence

When people such as your correspondent (Letters, 6/11) say they hope Israel’s impunity ends, they really mean Israel’s right to defend itself against terrorists the same way any other country would do in the same circumstances.

The claim is simply untrue. To give just some examples, the UN and some of its agencies pass more motions about Israel than every other country combined.

The UN Human Rights Council also has a permanent agenda item devoted solely to Israel and a unique standing commission of inquiry, made up of veteran anti-Israel activists, which pumps out skewed reports all but ignoring the terrorist groups Israel defends against. The UN has a massive bureaucracy devoted to advancing the Palestinian cause. Countless NGOs do the same. Meanwhile, genuine human rights-abusing countries slip under the radar. If that’s impunity, I can’t imagine what scrutiny would look like.

Danny Samuels, Malvern Insane spending

Governments of both colours can instantly find billions for a nuclear submarine we may never receive, to counter a threat that may never eventuate. But we are too cash-strapped to provide psychiatric beds for the most seriously unwell. That is surely an insane choice.

Kairen Harris, Brunswick Picked up a pencil, wrote

My late parents were primary school teachers. I can’t remember being taught how to use a pencil or pen (Letters, 5/11). I just picked up the pencil and wrote.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East The German word for it

Regarding Donald Trump’s woes, Inow have a better understanding of the German word “schadenfreude″⁣.

Kevin Brown, Moonlight Flat



Weighty decision

Your correspondent’s choice to avoid voting for major parties is an important right, but the consequences are important, too (Letters, 6/11). These parties made Australia great and deserting them in difficult times should not be taken lightly.

David Wright, Launceston, Tas Wishful thinking

Surely those actually making money out of the interest rate rise will begin sharing with those at the bottom of the pyramid.

Bruce Dudon, Woodend

World.title: ‘Not our fault’: The students having second thoughts about Destination Australia
World.content:
NationalUniversity ‘Not our fault’: The students having second thoughts about Destination Australia Sally Rawsthorne November 7, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Magdiel Silva Da Luz has a job, a partner and an almost-complete master’s of strategic communications. But would he choose Australia again? Magdiel Silva Da Luz feels “like we live in a parallel life besides local people” . Simon Schluter “I would definitely think twice,” the Brazilian international student said. Silva Da Luz is not alone. Australia’s $54 billion international education industry is under siege as the world’s highest visa application fees, eye-watering degree costs for international students, the extraordinary cost of living, changes to work rights and a so-called “genuine student test” come together to undermine the appeal of an Australian education.



But it’s the rising tide of populism that has most alarmed students. Related Article Immigration With their families barred, international students say they face an agonising choice “When I arrived [in 2022], the situation was a bit more open for international students,” Silva Da Luz said. “Now it seems like it’s a bit more unstable, it feels a bit more insecure.” “When I came here in 2022, in Brazil we had [former Brazilian president Jair] Bolsonaro, and he was very conservative and very homophobic. So I left Brazil and went to Australia because I think here is not the right place for me. And now I’m here and it’s happening again.” The Herald spoke to numerous international students for this story, all of whom made allegations of “microaggressions” ranging from rude comments to being spat at. All of the students said the increasingly tense and public migration debate had led to them feeling less welcome or unwelcome in Australia. None of those students wanted to be identified for fear of reprisal from the government or cancellation of their visas.



“I don’t feel like it’s our fault, most of the problems that the country has,” Silva Da Luz said. “So it’s very hard to have [people say] ‘Oh international students are the problem, so let’s just boot them.’ ” Universities and the international students who prop them up face a friendless future, with all future governments planning to rein in numbers. The Albanese government has announced sweeping reforms that it hopes will curb the numbers through barring family members of international students and ending visa hopping. Hardline plans to slash the numbers have also been announced by both the Coalition and One Nation. An “excellent study experience for students who then return home” is the government’s hope for the future of the system, according to a presentation by the Department of Education’s Dr Damien Oliver last week. (This is not borne out in reality, with about 170,000 former students currently on a temporary bridging visa after graduation.) The government wants to focus on the “composition, quality and integrity” of the sector rather than chasing greater enrolment numbers, Oliver said.



Visa data shows these planned reductions are coming off a low base – 31,000 higher education visas were granted between July and September this year, a 40 per cent decline since the peak in 2024 and down 16 per cent on pre-pandemic numbers from 2019. All of this spells big trouble for the nation’s universities, which rely heavily on funding from international students. “For years, governments have asked universities to do more while public funding has failed to keep pace with the cost of teaching, research and infrastructure. International education has helped fill that gap,” Universities Australia CEO Luke Sheehy said. This year, the Herald revealed that the University of NSW and the University of Sydney took $1.7 billion each from international students. “It’s pretty serious,” higher education expert Andrew Norton said. “We’ve already seen a couple of unis announcing job cuts due to this – Adelaide University, Murdoch University, Charles Sturt University. This will be, in my view, extremely common over the next few years.”



International student fees are used to subsidise domestic ones, particularly at struggling smaller and regional universities. Then there’s research. “There is absolutely no doubt that they are critical for the scale – just over half of research funding is dedicated sources, the rest is coming from other income sources,” Norton said. “There are … profits of commercial operations and endowments. But there’s simply no way those sums could add up without significant international student profits.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Is there a future for malls without their department store anchors?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesDavid Jones collapse Is there a future for malls without their department store anchors? Elias Visontay November 7, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For almost a century, they were the one-stop shop providing a sense of opulence and occasion that drew reliable foot traffic into shopping centres across Australia. But the slow, then sudden, demise of David Jones has thrown into question the symbiotic relationship that underpinned decades of prosperity for both department stores and malls. Westfield Bondi Junction, Sydney. Oscar Colman Now, operators of suburban shopping centres are facing their own identity crisis, as they try to figure out how to re-engineer their offerings and layouts to thrive in an era without the anchor tenants that built them. Thursday’s decision from David Jones’ chief executive and board of directors to hand over control of the company to voluntary administrators and receivers, and the looming closure of potentially most of its stores and thousands of associated job cuts, contained echoes of a trend seen across the world in recent years as the department store concept loses relevance.



World’s oldest department store Founded in Sydney in 1838, David Jones holds the title of the world’s oldest department store still operating under its original name. However, its glamorous history and current strife form the hallmarks of a global narrative arc – complete with retail legend and obituary – that have already been written overseas. Two women take advantage of a fur coat sale at David Jones during a heatwave in February 1939. Gordon Short They all begin in a similar way. Opening an initial shop on a high street in the 18th or 19th century and subsequently booming as a centre of high-end fashion and consumer goods through the first half of the 20th century.



“Department stores were the high street under one roof,” said Gary Mortimer, a professor of retail and consumer behaviour at the Queensland University of Technology. Related Article Fashion retail David Jones hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Dior – but nostalgia won’t save it Big name brands sold exclusively through different department stores. Shop windows were erected to celebrate holidays and woo customers and children ahead of Christmas. Bathrooms and other services meant people, especially women, dwelled longer. “It was iconic, you’d walk into the Elizabeth Street David Jones [in Sydney] and there’s a pianist playing, you’d go downstairs for the champagne and oyster bar, you’d wander around, try on. It was a sense of occasion,” he said. In the United Kingdom, the obvious parallel is with Debenhams, which began as a high street shop in 1778 and expanded to more than 100 locations across the country and became a household name. In the United States, it was the likes of Macy’s, Nordstrom and Saks Fifth Avenue, which grew to consume rival Neiman Marcus.



In the 1960s, David Jones was the epicentre of Australian high society. “It was the place to see and be seen,” 90-year-old Laudie Sneddon, who worked as a graduate pharmacist at the flagship Elizabeth Street store in Sydney in its heyday, recalled to this masthead. Melbourne Central shopping centre Louis Trerise Push into the suburbs Then came the expansion into suburban shopping centres. These stores were often less flashy outlets to capitalise on the explosion of malls and car travel in the years after World War II. “In the past, having a Myer, Grace Brothers or David Jones was vital for a shopping centre, but it’s become less vital.” Gary Mortimer, professor of retail and consumer behaviour at the Queensland University of Technology.



However, this was ultimately the first of several waves of change that would spell upheaval for Australia’s department stores, Mortimer said. The next wave was brands opening their own stores instead of selling through the likes of DJs, Myer and Grace Bros, followed by the more brutal waves of e-commerce and cheap fast fashion, he said. “You didn’t need to go to the department store any more,” Mortimer said. Sales began slowing, and attempts to compete with cheap new retail players with much lighter, cheaper retail and staffing costs proved difficult. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift away from bricks and mortar. In 2021, Debenhams entered administration, with all physical shopfronts subsequently liquidated. It exists solely as an online retailer today. The recently renovated Chatswood Chase shopping centre in Sydney. Steven Woodburn



Meanwhile, in the US, Macy’s store count has shrunk dramatically, while Nordstrom is closing its legacy high-end stores to open more of its Rack discount offshoots. And in January this year, Saks Global filed for bankruptcy, with just a fraction of its stores emerging from the process. Similarly, while David Jones managed to push its online sales to 20 per cent of its overall revenue, this wasn’t enough to help meet its bricks-and-mortar rent payments. From here, many observers say a slimmed-down version of David Jones could emerge from administration, perhaps limited to its flagship CBD locations plus certain others at boutique, profitable shopping centres. Focussing on its legacy of prestige and grandeur will be key, Mortimer believes. London’s Harrods and Selfridges, and Paris’ Galeries Lafayette and Le Bon Marché have been flagged as models of success for historic department stores thriving in the modern day.



Malls move on Related Article David Jones collapse Last time David Jones collapsed there was a rescuer. Who will save it this time? Just as their fortunes were intertwined in the good years, the global decline of department stores had coincided with a downturn for shopping centres. “In the past, having a Myer, Grace Brothers or David Jones was vital for a shopping centre, but it’s become less vital,” Mortimer said. Data from Scentre Group, which operates Westfield centres, show David Jones was charged less than half the rent rate per square metre compared to other customers renting its retail spaces. Without the pull from the likes of David Jones, many suburban centres will have to do much more to justify their premiums.



While the death and the rebirth of the mall has been well documented over the past decade, experts say there are green shoots in the future for shopping centres – providing they innovate. After years of issues, a new report released by Urbis and the Shopping Centre Council of Australia notes retail sales grew three per cent over the year to June 2026, with customer foot traffic at shopping centres up by 2 per cent nationally. Younger shoppers are driving the trend. PwC research found shopping centre foot traffic among consumers aged 14 to 29 rose by 57 per cent year-on-year. Elissa Stewart, director at Urbis, said most centres have actually seen an increase in foot traffic in the post-department store era, with curation of new tenants key. She gives the example of replacing three levels of a David Jones-type department store with three “mini-major” tenants such as a supermarket, a JB Hi-Fi, Rebel Sport or a Mecca. “You’ve got to ensure balance, but the combined power of those three tenants can be more than a department store to draw people in,” Stewart said.



Discount retailers are also a promising trend. Mortimer said that as cheap fast fashion was a factor in the demise of department stores, outlets such as Kmart, Big W, TK Maxx and Harris Scarfe “have suddenly become the ideal tenant”. A third space Related Article Opinion

Inflation Cutting government spending may slow prices, but it could bring on something worse Millie Muroi Economics Writer Services that draw people in are another trend for centres, notes Vanessa Rader, head of research at Ray White. Entertainment businesses, fine dining, activities, and gyms are sought after as they bring customers in during typically quiet late nights and early mornings. Installing EV chargers in a car park also draws in potential shoppers with time to kill while they wait. Healthcare and libraries are another growth opportunity, Mortimer predicts, for centres that successfully innovate.



“Despite interest rate increases, people are still spending on small luxuries, on what they eat or a fun activity to do,” Rader said. “Wellness is a big area too. We still spend on gyms and float tank facilities.” Ultimately, the goal for centres now is to get customers to spend more time dwelling in between activities. “It’s about removing some of the sterile elements that we think of with shopping centres,” Urbis’ Stewart said. Seizing an opportunity to be a go-to “third space” – a term for environments outside of home or work where people can spend time comfortably while spending little or no money – is an important way to stand out, Stewart said. “Enhancing that sense of place, bringing the outdoors and nature inside, water features, lighting, better food options, lounging and creating that space where people actually want to be.” Malls have previously held this role, especially for teens after school and retirees whiling away a day. However, with the cost of everything going up, and investment in centres capitally constrained, “it’s not an easy fix,” she said. World.title: Mahesh Muralidhar makes history as National takes back Tāmaki
World.content:
Mahesh Muralidhar is set to become the National Party's first Indian MP to win an electorate seat, taking back one of the party's traditionally safest constituencies in an election night upset for ACT.

The party's two previous Indian-origin MPs, Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi and Parmjeet Parmar, both entered Parliament through the party list.

Muralidhar led ACT's James Christmas by more than 5300 votes in Tāmaki after 97 percent of the votes had been counted on Saturday night.

He had secured 15,303 votes, compared with 9961 for Labour's Max Harris and 7659 for Christmas, who is expected to enter Parliament through ACT's party list.

The result marks a return of the electorate to National after former ACT deputy leader Brooke van Velden defeated National's Simon O'Connor in 2023, ending his four-term hold on the seat.

The closely contested election has Labour narrowly ahead of National in the party vote, with the two parties separated by less than one percentage point as counting nears completion.

Preliminary projections suggest National, ACT and New Zealand First could secure a narrow majority in Parliament, although special votes are yet to be counted, with that total to be revealed on 27 November.

Muralidhar said getting out into the community from the beginning of the campaign had been crucial to his success.

"The day after I was chosen as the candidate for Tāmaki, the next day I went out door-knocking, and that's the most important thing," he said.

He said he had knocked on about 16,000 doors during the campaign, crediting his visibility, party support and volunteers for helping secure the result.

"Tāmaki appreciates someone with a commercial background, and my campaign was launched by the prime minister," he said.

"I raised $15,000 for a community patrol in Glen Innes, and this is the result."

National's Mahesh Muralidhar speaks to volunteers at Colin Maid Rugby Club during election night. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Muralidhar is chief executive of Phase One Ventures, a venture capital firm investing in New Zealand start-ups. He also worked at online graphic design platform Canva between 2015 and 2017.

Tāmaki is one of the country's three wealthiest electorates, alongside Epsom and the newly created Wellington North.

Established in 1946, the electorate has voted Labour only twice.

Former Prime Minister Robert Muldoon secured the seat for National in 1960 and represented it until he left Parliament in 1991.

National's Clem Simich and Allan Peachey followed, before Simon O'Connor held the electorate from 2011 to 2023.

Even during Labour's landslide victory in 2020, when the party won the Tāmaki party vote with 39 percent against National's 37 percent, O'Connor secured more than 50 percent of the electorate vote.

That changed in 2023 when van Velden campaigned successfully to unseat O'Connor, winning by a majority of 4158 votes in what was considered a major upset for National.

Earlier on election night, Muralidhar told RNZ the mood at his campaign gathering was upbeat.

At Colin Maiden Rugby Club in Stonefields, he appeared confident as the results began coming in.

"The mood is really great, and I'm looking forward to seeing a centre-right government coming in and the National Party doing well," he said.

The result is Muralidhar's second attempt to enter Parliament.

In 2023, he contested Auckland Central but lost to Green Party MP Chlöe Swarbrick.

Muralidhar, who describes himself as a proud Kiwi-Indian, said he wanted to make sure the Indian community's concerns were heard.

"I'll be there for the community in regards to making sure that the community is understood and heard," he said.

He thanked Tāmaki voters for choosing him to represent them, saying he intended to live up to a promise his father had made during the campaign.

World.title: 'Too close to call': Wait begins for special votes after cliffhanger Election night
World.content:
National appears on track to lead the next Government, but Labour hasn't conceded, and the final result remains too close to call without counting the special votes.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke around midnight to National party faithful gathered in Auckland, telling them it was "heartening" that his party was still the largest.

"We have a pathway to forming the next Government, but it is too close to call," Luxon said, acknowledging that "about 300,000 special votes" would have to be counted to determine the final result.

However it goes, Parliament appears set to have a new look with Opportunity arriving, and the exit of some senior National MPs, including Finance Minister Nicola Willis.

The result on the night, with 98.5% counted, gave National 29.3% of the party vote, down from 38.1% in 2023, but it did remain the biggest party by claiming 42 of the 64 electorate seats nationwide.

Winning so many electorates relative to their party vote result meant National had contributed to a 10-seat overhang in Parliament, along with Te Pāti Māori with 5 seats.

Samuel Rillston

Labour claimed 29.3% of the party vote for 35 seats, the Greens got 13.3% for 16 seats, and Opportunity crossed the 5% threshold with 6% for 7 seats.

"Tonight, New Zealand has spoken," Labour leader Chris Hipkins said as he carefully commented on how close the election race remained, and how the election night numbers could still move.

"It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said. Every vote matters, and every vote must now be counted," he said.

Coalition Government partners ACT and NZ First both recorded increases to their party vote from the 2023 election, returning 10.9% and 9.8% respectively for 13 and 12 seats.

While these numbers could still change slightly once the special votes were counted, there was no path back to Parliament for list-only Willis, nor senior National MPs Paul Goldsmith (Epsom) and Chris Bishop (Hutt South) who both lost their electorate races.

"Politics is a rough business, and we've given it our best shot, but ultimately it's the people who get to choose," Goldsmith said at the National election event in Auckland.

Willis was forward-looking, saying, "the National Party is an extremely strong team and institution". She called it a "process of renewal", and was "confident there will be a great team there".

She also reflected on how, "it's been a very difficult time to be in government, for governments around the world".

"You know, we've had petrol up at $3.60. We've had global tariffs. We've had extraordinary cost of living challenges for New Zealanders, and they have felt that deeply," Willis said.

Bishop, in conceding the Hutt South electorate race said the point of it all was the bigger picture, "it's not about me, it's not about Nicola and it's not about Paul".

"What actually matters is the type of government and the policies," Bishop said.

When Luxon spoke at the National party event in Auckland, and acknowledged his departing MPs, he omitted Bishop by name, despite naming lower-ranked candidates.

Speaker Gerry Brownlee would also exit Parliament, and he said he had "no regrets" about only standing on the list.

Fellow senior minister Mark Mitchell said National had "campaigned as hard as we could" on party vote, but said losing these colleagues was "a blow to our party".

"They've all been outstanding ministers, we don't want to lose any of our people," Mitchell told RNZ as he celebrated his own success winning the Whangaparāoa seat.

"I'm really happy with the result we're getting," Mitchell said, reflecting on how democratic elections had been challenging for sitting governments everywhere.

"If you look around the world, incumbent governments are finding it very hard," he said, explaining the shift to a "power order" had unsettled voters in other democracies.

National MP Paul Goldsmith Edward Gay

Willis, Goldsmith and Bishop between them held 19 ministerial portfolios, out of about 50 substantive ones, leaving a big hole to fill should National lead the next Government. Among them were major portfolios, including finance, justice, transport and housing.

The personnel changes and worse party vote result for National would likely impact coalition negotiations with the apparent right bloc voter shift to NZ First and ACT.

This meant a change to the balance of a coalition, and the two minor parties may lay claim to greater roles in Government with stronger positions based on total vote share.

Nicola Willis Fiona Goodall

The final result would not be known until the special votes were counted, with that total to be revealed in three weeks' time, on 27 November.

"What's clear is nothing's clear tonight," ACT leader David Seymour said at a party event in Auckland.

NZ First leader Winston Peters Mark Papalii

NZ First leader Winston Peters described the campaign as "difficult" in his brief election night speech acknowledging his party would be returned to Parliament.

Neither leader commented on the situation ahead, only taking a short opportunity to thank their supporters for campaigns that returned them a greater share of the vote.

While the Opportunity party was set to enter Parliament for the first time, with an election night count of 6%, they may not get to play the hyped role of kingmaker.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong was joyful at making it to Parliament, but spoke to party faithful before final count permutations could be calculated effectively.

"You have voted for unity over division," Wong said.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong Phil Walter/Getty Images

"To some of you watching, it might seem like we just arrived, but to many in this room this result has been a long time coming," she said, reflecting on the party's 10-year history.

Wong said the election had been "a really tight race" and reiterated the party would speak first to the party with the greatest number of votes.

That was a close run thing on election night with Labour on 29.3% and National on 29.3%.

Hipkins said he would "get straight to work" if Labour had the opportunity to form a government.

The election was still undecided, with special votes potentially able to sway the final outcome. The Electoral Commission had forecast about 700,000 special votes.

World.title: Election results: Christopher Luxon says outcome 'too close to call'
World.content:
National leader Christopher Luxon addressed supporters late on Saturday night after one of the most uncertain elections in New Zealand's MMP history.

"I have to tell you right now it is too close to call," he told a crowd at Auckland's Viaduct Events Centre.

"Tonight New Zealand has voted and it looks like certainly an MMP special," he said, but expressed optimism that the coalition could return to power.

"It is heartening to see that on the numbers so far, National is once again the largest party in Parliament and we have a pathway to forming the next government."

Both National and Labour have struggled to break 30 percent of the party vote tonight, with only a few thousand votes separating the two.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408061251112

Luxon, who didn't speak until midnight Saturday, was greeted with chants of "three more years!" by supporters.

Luxon said the outcome would depend on the counting around 300,000 special votes, which will take several weeks and be announced on 27 November.

"That will then determine the final shape of our next Parliament," he said.

Luxon said that caretaker conventions will apply in the meantime and the government's business will continue as usual.

"With those final results there can there be meaningful negotiations and in due course, a new government and the 55th Parliament will come together," he said.

Negotiation and compromise are going to be required, he added.

Luxon also congratulated Labour leader Chris Hipkins on a well-fought race, and singled out the Opportunity party and its leader Quilae Wong, who look set to make it into Parliament with nearly 6 percent of the vote.

He paid tribute to many National MPs who appear to have lost their seats tonight and many other races that have yet to be called.

"Hang in there, whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and every one of you."

"Some of the hardest phone calls tonight have been colleagues and friends who look unlikely to be able to return to Parliament."

He praised Finance Minister and deputy party leader Nicola Willis.

"I want to thank you, Nicola, for your dedication, for your determination and for your years of service to this party and this great country of ours."

Luxon also thanked Paul Goldsmith, Gerry Brownlee, Melissa Lee, Nancy Lu and Vanessa Weenink, who appear to have lost their seats.

"To all our MPs from all parties who are not returning, can I say thank you as well. You have all served your communities with real decency and this country is certainly better for your work."

World.title: Rugby League World Cup: Kiwis kick Tonga out on way to final
World.content:
New Zealand ended Tonga's dream run at the Rugby League World Cup in Newcastle, beating the islanders 28-10 in their semifinal clash.

The win means the Kiwis make their first final since 2013.

While New Zealand struggled in the first half to contain their fiery opponents, the second half saw a dominant by James Fisher-Harris' men, where they completely shut Tonga out.

In the end the Kiwis scored six tries, one each by Briton Nikora, Dane Gagai, Casey McLean, Jahrome Hughes, Xavier Wilson and Charnse Nicoll-Kickstad.

Top goal-kicker Jamayne Isaako converted five of the tries.

New Zealand led 12-10 at halftime and scored four unanswered tries in the second 40 to claim victory and secure their final spot.

Man of the match Kalyn Ponga, who fought off an injured arm suffered in the opening clash against Australia, said it was a different game and praised his teammates.

"Tonight was different," he said post-match.

"It was a big game obviously and it was a good feeling representing your people, your country, especially in front of the red sea and I was looking forward to it.

"The first half was obviously tough and obviously the wind helped us in the second half."

Tongan playmaker Isaiya Katoa thanked the fans, and apologized they had not done the job, while also praising the Kiwis for the win.

"No excuses, you gotta take your hats off to the Kiwi boys," he said.

"The way they played that footy is the way you play in this tough conditions.

"The way they really around us doesn't matter the result, we can't thank you enough," he told fans.

The pre-game challenges set the stage for the on-the-field battle.

Former Kiwi captain Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, led the Tongan sipitau, having changed allegiance for the world meet.

The Kiwis response of their haka led by captain Fisher-Harris.

Tonga did not move an inch as they stared down the Kiwis at halfway following the haka.

The Kiwis started with a bang, Nikora going over in the fourth minute, after livewire fullback Kalyn Ponga stood the defence up and put Nikora

through the gap.

But Tonga returned the favour, twice in a row through winger Jojo Fifita, who scored a double, the first in the 21st minute, who ran through the Kiwis defence from close to his own tryline.

However, New Zealand got five more tries after that and left Tonga regretting their lost opportunities.
